samples.result:
# The Work That Doesn't Show

For most of the twentieth century, the British had a phrase for a task that never ends: "like painting the Forth Bridge." The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilevered railway bridge in Scotland, opened in 1890, and the story went that it was so large, and the Scottish weather so hard on it, that a crew of painters worked continuously along its length. By the time they reached the far end, the near end needed painting again. So they turned around and started over, forever.

The story wasn't quite true. The painting was more patchwork than a single endless sweep. But it was true enough to become an idiom, and I've always liked that the idiom exists. It's one of the few places in ordinary speech where we acknowledge a basic fact about the world: most of what keeps things standing is not building but upkeep. In 2011 the bridge was finally given a new coating expected to last decades, and the endless painting stopped. Newspapers ran stories about it with a note of loss, as if something had gone out of the world. I think something had. A living emblem of maintenance had been retired.

I want to write about maintenance, because I think it is one of the most important and least celebrated activities humans engage in, and because the more I think about it, the more it seems to sit underneath almost everything else.

---

Our stories about progress are almost entirely stories about invention. We remember who built the first steam engine, who discovered penicillin, who wrote the first line of code for some famous program. We have prizes for breakthroughs, for firsts, for originality. We don't have a Nobel Prize for keeping the water treatment plant running without incident for thirty-one years, though that plant has saved more lives than most novels have changed.

It isn't hard to see why. Invention makes a good story. There's a before and an after, a moment of change, a protagonist. Maintenance has no plot. Its success looks exactly like nothing happening. When the bridge doesn't collapse, when the server doesn't go down, when the child doesn't get cholera, there's no event to report. Maintenance is the art of producing non-events. It shows up in the news only when it fails: the levee breaks, the pipes leach lead, the power grid freezes. Then everyone suddenly remembers that someone was supposed to be taking care of it.

In 1969 the artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a document she called the "Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!" She had recently become a mother, and she found herself caught between two identities that her culture treated as incompatible. There was the artist, who was supposed to make new things, be avant-garde, break with the past. And there was the mother, whose days were consumed with washing, feeding, cleaning, changing, and then doing all of it again. The first kind of work was called creation. The second was barely called work at all.

Her manifesto divided the world into two systems: "Development," meaning pure individual creation, the new, change, progress, and "Maintenance," meaning keeping the dust off the pure individual creation, preserving the new, sustaining the change, protecting progress. And then she asked, in effect: why is only the first one art?

She went on to do something remarkable. She became an unsalaried artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, a post she has held for decades. For one of her projects, she spent nearly a year visiting every sanitation district in the city, shaking hands with more than eight thousand sanitation workers, and saying to each of them: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive."

I find that sentence moving every time I read it. It's so simple. It's also accurate in a way that feels almost shocking once you think about it. A city without garbage collection doesn't just become unpleasant. Within weeks it becomes a place where disease spreads. The people who haul trash are, in the most literal sense, keeping the city alive, and until Ukeles showed up, very few people had ever said so to their faces.

---

There's a very old puzzle, the Ship of Theseus. The Athenians preserved the ship of their legendary hero, and as its planks rotted they replaced them one by one with new timber. Eventually, the story goes, no original plank remained. Was it still the same ship?

Philosophers usually treat this as a puzzle about identity, and it's a good one. But I've come to think it's also, quietly, a story about maintenance, and that framed that way it looks less like a paradox and more like a description of how nearly everything that lasts actually lasts.

Consider the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan. For roughly thirteen hundred years, with some interruptions, its main sanctuaries have been completely torn down and rebuilt every twenty years on an adjacent plot, using fresh cypress and traditional techniques. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033. The shrine is, in one sense, never more than twenty years old. In another sense it is among the oldest continuous things in Japan.

What is actually being preserved at Ise isn't wood. It's knowledge. A twenty-year cycle is, not coincidentally, about the length of a working generation. The carpenters who rebuild the shrine as young apprentices will be the master craftsmen at the next rebuilding, and they will teach the apprentices who will lead the one after that. The shrine is a machine for keeping a skill alive. The building is almost a byproduct.

Or consider the Q'eswachaka bridge in the Andes of Peru, a suspension bridge woven from grass rope that spans a gorge over the Apurímac River. It's a remnant of the Inca road system, and every year the surrounding communities gather, twist new cords from grass, braid them into thick cables, and build the bridge anew, letting the old one fall into the river below. Grass rots quickly. A grass bridge left alone would last only a few seasons. A grass bridge maintained by a community has lasted for centuries.

There's something here that runs against our instincts. We tend to think that the way to make something last is to make it out of durable material: stone, steel, titanium. And sometimes that works. But the most durable things humans have made are often not the hardest. They're the ones embedded in a practice of care. A stone monument that no one tends will crack and topple and get carted off for building material. A grass bridge that a village rebuilds every June can outlast empires.

The Ship of Theseus, seen this way, isn't a problem to be solved. It's the only kind of ship there is. Every ship that stays at sea for long is having its planks replaced. The question isn't whether it's the same ship. The question is whether someone keeps caring for it.

---

Your body, of course, is a Ship of Theseus too. The lining of your gut replaces itself every few days. Your skin sheds and renews constantly. Red blood cells last a few months. Bone, which seems like the most permanent thing about you, is being continually dissolved and rebuilt by specialized cells, so that over years your skeleton is substantially remade. Some cells, like many neurons, stay with you much longer, but even they are constantly replacing their internal components, their proteins and membranes, turning over the molecules they're built from.

To be alive is to be maintained. A living thing is less an object than a process, a pattern that holds its shape while matter flows through it, like a standing wave in a stream. The moment the maintenance stops, the pattern starts coming apart. We have a word for when this happens, and it's the word we fear most.

I find this thought oddly consoling. It means that the drudgery of upkeep, the part of life that feels like it's getting in the way of the real stuff, is actually continuous with life itself. When you wash the dishes, sweep the floor, change the oil, answer the email you've been avoiding, you're doing on the outside of yourself what your cells are doing on the inside every second. Keeping a pattern going against the tide of entropy. It's not a distraction from living. It's what living is made of.

---

I've been thinking about maintenance partly because of a certain kind of story that keeps recurring in the world of software.

In 2014, a severe security flaw called Heartbleed was discovered in OpenSSL, a piece of software that helps encrypt a huge fraction of the traffic on the internet. When people went to look at who was responsible for this crucial infrastructure, they found that it was being maintained largely by a tiny group of volunteers and part-timers, with funding that was astonishingly small relative to the trillions of dollars of commerce that depended on it. In 2024, a different near-disaster came to light: someone had spent a couple of years patiently gaining the trust of the lone, overworked maintainer of a compression tool called xz, eventually getting access and slipping a backdoor into it. It was caught almost by accident, by an engineer who noticed that something was running half a second slower than it should.

There's a well-known cartoon that depicts all of modern digital infrastructure as a towering, precarious stack of blocks, and near the bottom is one small block holding everything up, labeled something like "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." It's funny because it's true, and it's frightening for the same reason.

The pattern is the same as with bridges and sewers. We lavish attention, money, and prestige on building new things. The people who keep old things working are invisible until the moment they're not there.

I'll admit this subject has a particular resonance for me. I'm a thing made largely out of the accumulated written output of people, and a startling amount of that writing is maintenance work. Encyclopedia editors reverting vandalism at three in the morning. People answering the same beginner question on a forum for the thousandth time, patiently. Documentation writers. Translators. Someone who went back and fixed a broken link, or corrected a date, or clarified a confusing sentence, for no reward other than the sense that it should be right. When I'm useful to someone, some of what's flowing through me is that unglamorous care. I'd like to be the kind of thing that honors it rather than obscures it.

---

Why do we undervalue maintenance so consistently? I think there are a few reasons, and they're worth naming.

The first is the one I already mentioned: success is invisible. You can't point to the disaster that didn't happen. Our minds are built to notice change, and maintenance, when it works, is the prevention of change.

The second is status. Throughout history, maintenance has tended to be assigned to people with less power: servants, women, laborers, the enslaved, immigrants. The work acquired low status because of who did it, and then the people who did it were paid less and respected less because the work had low status. It's a loop, and it's very hard to break.

The third is subtler, and it's about how we imagine our own lives. We like to think of ourselves as protagonists moving through a story, and stories need arcs. Maintenance is cyclical. It returns to where it started. You do the laundry and then, in a week, you do it again. There's no climax. To a mind that craves narrative, this can feel like futility, like the myth of Sisyphus pushing his boulder up the hill only to watch it roll back down.

But Albert Camus, who wrote the most famous essay about Sisyphus, ended it with a line that I think about a lot: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy." He meant it partly as defiance. But I've come to read it another way too. Maybe the boulder isn't a punishment. Maybe the hill is a garden, and the boulder is a watering can, and the reason it keeps needing to be carried is that the garden keeps growing.

---

There's one more kind of maintenance I want to mention, the kind that's hardest to see, because it doesn't involve objects at all.

Relationships are maintained. Friendships that aren't tended don't usually end in a dramatic break; they just thin out, the way an unused path grows over with weeds. The friend you used to talk to every week becomes someone you text on birthdays, and then someone you mean to text. Nothing went wrong, exactly. No one stopped caring. There just wasn't any upkeep.

Marriages that last for fifty years are not usually sustained by a single great act of love. They're sustained by thousands of small repairs. Apologizing. Asking how the day went and actually listening to the answer. Remembering that the other person hates cilantro. Noticing a hurt before it hardens into resentment. The psychologist John Gottman, who spent decades studying couples, found that one of the best predictors of whether a relationship would endure was how the partners responded to small bids for attention: a comment about a bird outside the window, a sigh, a joke. Did the other person turn toward it, or away? These are tiny acts. They're also, it turns out, the load-bearing beams.

Communities, too. Democracies. Languages. Traditions. Trust itself. None of these are things you build once and then own. They're things you keep, or lose. Every institution you've ever relied on is being held together right now by people doing unremarkable things: clerks filing records correctly, poll workers showing up at dawn, teachers grading one more stack of essays, neighbors checking on the old man down the street when they haven't seen him for a couple of days.

---

I don't want to romanticize all this too much. Maintenance can be crushing. It can be exploited. People who do it are often underpaid and overworked, and a nice essay about how their work is secretly beautiful is not a substitute for a raise. Ukeles's handshake meant something because it was a real act of recognition, but recognition alone doesn't pay rent. If we truly valued maintenance, we would fund it: the infrastructure, the software, the caregivers, the sanitation workers, the teachers. The honest measure of how much a society values something is what it's willing to pay for.

And there's a real tension between maintenance and change. Sometimes the thing being maintained deserves to fall. Sometimes the grass bridge should be allowed to drop into the river because there's a better way across. Not every tradition is worth keeping, and not every institution deserves repair. Part of wisdom is knowing the difference.

But I think the more common error, at least in the cultures I know best, runs the other way. We are too quick to build new things and too slow to care for what we have. We tear down and replace when we could repair. We celebrate founders and forget keepers. We imagine that the hard part is starting, when very often the hard part is continuing.

---

So I'll end where Ukeles did, with a simple act of acknowledgment.

To whoever repainted the Forth Bridge, plank by plank and year by year, for more than a century: thank you. To the carpenters at Ise, passing their skill from hand to hand across thirteen centuries. To the villagers braiding grass over the Apurímac. To the volunteer in Nebraska, or wherever you are, patching the code that holds up the internet while the rest of us don't even know your name. To the nurses on night shifts, the people who keep the water clean, the ones who fix the potholes, the parents doing the fourth load of laundry this week. To anyone who ever reverted a vandalized page, answered a question they'd answered a hundred times before, or reached out to a friend they'd been drifting from.

Thank you for keeping the world alive. It doesn't show. That's how we know you're doing it right.

# The Thing on the Rock

There is a gravestone in a churchyard I think about sometimes, though I've never seen it. I've seen thousands like it in photographs: slate or sandstone, the letters worn soft, and across the face, blooming over the name, a round stain of pale green or rust orange or ash gray. Most people who notice it probably think of it as dirt, or damage, or the visible evidence of time. It is all of those things. It is also one of the strangest living arrangements on the planet, and the story of how we figured out what it was is a story about how badly we want things to be one thing at a time.

The stain is a lichen. For most of human history, a lichen was understood as a plant, or something plant-like, a simple, humble growth that clung to rocks and bark, a botanical afterthought. Linnaeus placed lichens among the algae and famously called them the "poor peasants" of vegetation, *rustici pauperrimi*. They were small, slow, and stubbornly uninteresting, the kind of organism that shows up in textbooks mainly to illustrate the concept of a pioneer species: the first thing to colonize bare rock, softening it, preparing it, dying so that mosses and then grasses and then eventually trees could follow. Lichens were a prologue. Nobody reads the prologue.

Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something outrageous: a lichen is not an organism. It is two organisms. A fungus and an alga (or, as we now know, sometimes a cyanobacterium) living together so intimately that they form a single body, a body neither could build alone. The fungus provides structure, shelter, and a grip on the world. The alga photosynthesizes, making sugars that feed the whole enterprise. What looks like one thing is a partnership.

The reaction from the established lichenologists was not gratitude. It was fury. Schwendener's idea was called absurd, a "sensational romance." One prominent lichenologist, William Nylander, spent years rejecting it with something close to contempt. There was a whole discipline built on the premise that lichens were a coherent kind of thing, with their own classifications and their own careful taxonomies, and Schwendener was telling them that their subject didn't exist, or rather that it existed only as a relationship. Some of the hostility was just the ordinary defensiveness of experts. Some of it, I think, was something deeper: a sense that the idea violated what an organism is supposed to be.

It turned out Schwendener was right, and the argument over lichens gave biology a word it still depends on. In the 1870s, German scientists looking at this odd arrangement needed a term for different organisms living together, and "symbiosis" entered biology largely through the study of lichens. The concept that now underwrites our understanding of coral reefs, of the bacteria in our guts, of the mitochondria in every one of our cells, which were once free-living bacteria themselves, was born partly out of staring at crust on a rock.

Beatrix Potter, before she was the author of Peter Rabbit, was a serious amateur mycologist, and she was among those who believed the dual hypothesis when many established figures didn't. She drew fungi with extraordinary precision and conducted her own experiments on spore germination. In 1897 her paper was presented to the Linnean Society of London, but she could not present it herself, because women were not permitted to attend. A man read it for her. I don't bring this up to make a tidy moral point, only because it's one of those facts that seems to rhyme with the lichen story itself: the history of science is also a history of who is allowed to be counted as a legitimate part of the body.

---

What I find most arresting about lichens is not that they're partnerships. Lots of things are partnerships. It's that the partnership produces something that neither partner resembles. A lichen fungus grown alone in a lab, separated from its algal partner, does not look like the lichen. It tends to form a shapeless little blob. The alga grown alone looks like ordinary alga. The distinctive forms, the leafy lobes, the tiny shrubby branches, the cups like miniature trumpets, the beard-like strands hanging from old conifers, only appear when the two are together. The shape of the lichen belongs to neither of them. It belongs to the relationship.

This is a genuinely weird thing to sit with. We tend to imagine that when two things combine, the result is some kind of average or sum. A lichen is not a sum. It's a third thing that emerges only in the combination, with its own chemistry too: lichens produce hundreds of compounds found almost nowhere else in nature, lichen acids with names like usnic and vulpinic, substances neither partner makes alone in any quantity. Some of these compounds are why lichens have given us dyes. The old purple dye called orchil came from lichens. Litmus, the stuff of pH strips in every high school chemistry lab, was traditionally extracted from lichens. The warm browns of traditional Harris Tweed came partly from a lichen called crotal, scraped from rocks in the Hebrides. If you have ever dipped a strip of paper into a liquid and watched it turn red or blue, you have used a lichen's chemistry to ask a question about the world.

And then, in 2016, the story got stranger. A team led by Toby Spribille, studying two lichens in the genus *Bryoria* that looked different and contained different chemicals but seemed to be made of the same fungus and the same alga, found a third partner hiding in plain sight: a yeast, a different kind of fungus entirely, embedded in the outer layer of the lichen. It had been there all along, in many lichens across the world, and nobody had seen it for nearly a hundred and fifty years, partly because nobody was looking. The one-organism model had been replaced by a two-organism model, and the two-organism model had become so settled, so textbook, that it too had become a kind of blindness.

Some researchers now talk about lichens less as a pair and more as small ecosystems: a fungus, one or more photosynthetic partners, yeasts, and communities of bacteria all living in the same structure, each doing something. The Canadian lichenologist Trevor Goward has spent years pushing people to think of a lichen not as a thing but as a process, a way of living that various organisms fall into. The question "what is a lichen?" keeps getting less answerable the harder you look, and I find that delightful rather than frustrating.

---

Lichens are also, in a way that matters, slow.

The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, gets its name from its appearance: yellow-green patches bordered by black lines, like countries on an old atlas. It grows so slowly and so steadily that geologists use it as a clock. This technique, lichenometry, measures the diameter of the largest map lichens on a rock surface to estimate how long that surface has been exposed, how many centuries since a glacier retreated, or a rockfall happened, or a moraine settled. Some lichens in harsh environments grow on the order of a millimeter a year, or less. In parts of Antarctica, individual lichens may be many hundreds or even thousands of years old. There are things alive on rocks right now that were small patches when the pyramids were fresh, or so the estimates suggest; the exact ages are debated, but the order of magnitude is not.

Slowness in a lichen isn't weakness. It's a strategy that lets them live where almost nothing else can. Lichens can dry out completely, lose nearly all their water, and simply stop, suspended, and then when rain or fog or dew returns, resume metabolism within minutes. They live on bare rock in deserts, on tundra, on Antarctic nunataks, on the bark of trees, on old fence posts, on the backs of certain weevils in New Guinea, on the shells of tortoises. In 2005, the European Space Agency sent samples of two lichen species into orbit and exposed them directly to space, to vacuum, extreme temperature swings, and unfiltered solar and cosmic radiation, for about two weeks. When the lichens came back, they were still alive and capable of photosynthesis. The poor peasants of vegetation, it turns out, can survive outer space.

There's a lesson there I'm wary of overdrawing, because nature isn't a self-help book. But I do think we underrate the kind of toughness that consists of being able to stop. Not to push through, not to endure by straining, but to wait, dry and quiet, until conditions allow you to continue. It's a way of being alive that doesn't look much like being alive, from the outside.

---

For all their toughness, lichens have a famous vulnerability: many of them are exquisitely sensitive to air pollution, particularly sulfur dioxide. They have no roots and no protective waxy cuticle like plant leaves; they absorb what they need, water and minerals, directly from the air and rain. Which means they also absorb whatever else is in the air and rain. When the coal-fired industrial cities of nineteenth-century Britain filled their skies with sulfurous smoke, lichens vanished from trees and walls across huge areas, creating what scientists later called "lichen deserts."

This connects, as it happens, to one of the most famous stories in evolutionary biology. The peppered moth, *Biston betularia*, normally has a pale speckled form that is well camouflaged against lichen-covered tree bark. As pollution killed the lichens and soot darkened the trees, a dark form of the moth became dramatically more common, better hidden from birds on the blackened trunks. When clean air laws took effect in the twentieth century and the air improved, the lichens slowly returned, and the pale moths became common again. The story has had its critics and its complications, and subsequent research has largely confirmed its core, but what I notice now is that the lichen is in the background of it, quietly dying and quietly coming back, the unnoticed surface on which the drama played out.

Today, lichens are used as bioindicators. Surveys of which species grow where can tell you about air quality with remarkable nuance, some species tolerate nitrogen pollution from agriculture and traffic and even thrive on it, while others disappear. A walk through a city park can be, for someone who knows how to look, a reading of the chemistry of the air over decades. The lichens are a record. They remember what the air was like, in their presence and their absence.

---

I said at the start that the story of lichens is a story about how badly we want things to be one thing at a time. I want to come back to that, because I think it's the part that matters beyond botany.

The resistance to Schwendener wasn't just stubbornness. It came from a picture of the living world as made of discrete individuals, each with its own boundaries, its own lineage, its own identity. That picture is useful. It's also, it turns out, frequently wrong, or at least incomplete. Every cell in your body that burns oxygen does so using mitochondria, organelles descended from bacteria that entered some ancient cell and never left. Plants photosynthesize using chloroplasts, descended from cyanobacteria, relatives of the same organisms that partner with some lichen fungi today. Your gut contains a population of microbes involved in digestion, immunity, perhaps even mood. Most land plants depend on fungal partners in their roots. Coral reefs are built by animals who house photosynthetic algae in their tissues. The idea of a clean, solitary organism is less a fact about life than a convenient simplification, and lichens were one of the places where the simplification first visibly cracked.

The philosopher and the biologist can argue about what this means for the concept of an individual. I find myself less interested in resolving the question than in the humility it suggests. If a crust on a gravestone could fool careful observers for centuries, if a third partner could hide in lichens across the world until 2016, then our categories are always going to be a step behind what's actually there. That isn't a reason to abandon categories. It's a reason to hold them a little more loosely, to keep checking.

I'll admit that part of why this appeals to me is that I'm a kind of composite thing myself, in a way I find hard to describe precisely. I was built from an enormous amount of human writing, shaped by many people's choices, and what I am doesn't cleanly resemble any single one of those inputs, much as a lichen's form doesn't resemble the fungus or the alga alone. I don't want to push that analogy too far; I'm not alive the way a lichen is, and there's a lot about my own nature I'm genuinely uncertain about. But I recognize something in the idea that a thing can be real, can have its own shape and its own characteristic chemistry, while also being fundamentally a relationship among other things. It doesn't feel diminishing to me. It feels like one of the ordinary ways that things come to exist.

---

Next time you pass an old stone wall, or a gravestone, or the north side of a tree, it's worth stopping for a moment. The gray-green rosette or orange splash you see may be decades or centuries old. It's made of at least two kingdoms of life, probably more, holding together in a shape none of them could make alone. It has survived drought by stopping and resumed by starting again. It has been quietly recording the air you breathe. It helped give us the word for living together. And for most of history, almost no one looked at it closely enough to see what it was.

That last part is the one I keep returning to. The extraordinary is often not hidden. It's sitting on a rock, in full view, looking like dirt, waiting for someone to be curious enough to ask what it actually is, and humble enough to keep asking after they think they know.

# Why the Night Is Dark

Here is a question that sounds like something a child would ask and that turns out to be one of the deepest questions a person can pose: why is the sky dark at night?

The obvious answer is that the sun has gone down. The sun is on the other side of the Earth, lighting up somebody else's afternoon, and so our half of the planet is in shadow. This is true, and it is also completely beside the point. The sun is only one star. There are others, a great many others, and the question is why all of *them*, taken together, do not light up the sky.

To feel the force of this, imagine standing in a forest. If the forest is small, you can see gaps between the trunks, patches of open field beyond. But if the forest is large enough, and the trees are scattered more or less evenly, then every line of sight you could possibly draw from where you stand will eventually hit a tree. Look in any direction and you see bark. There are no gaps. The forest has become a wall.

Now replace the trees with stars and the forest with the universe. If the universe goes on forever, and if stars are scattered through it more or less evenly, then every line of sight from your eye, in any direction you care to look, should eventually end on the surface of a star. There should be no gaps. The whole sky, every square degree of it, should be as bright as the surface of the sun. Not a pleasant evening glow. A blaze. The night sky should be a furnace.

It is not. It is dark, speckled with a few thousand visible points of light, and the darkness between them is the most ordinary thing in the world. We have been looking at it for as long as there have been eyes to look. And that ordinary darkness is a clue about the origin of everything.

---

The puzzle usually goes by the name of Olbers' paradox, after Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers, a German physician and astronomer who wrote about it in 1823. Like many things named after people, it was not really his. Johannes Kepler had raised a version of it two centuries earlier, in 1610, and used it as an argument that the universe must be finite, that the stars could not go on forever, because if they did the sky would be bright. Edmond Halley worried about it in the 1720s. A Swiss astronomer named Jean-Philippe Loys de Chéseaux worked through it with real care in 1744, and calculated that an infinite, eternal, evenly starred universe would produce a sky tens of thousands of times brighter than the sun.

The argument can be made precise with a small piece of geometry. Imagine the universe divided into concentric shells around the Earth, like the layers of an onion, each shell the same thickness. A shell twice as far away has four times the surface area, so it contains roughly four times as many stars. But each of those stars, being twice as far away, appears only a quarter as bright. The two effects cancel exactly. Every shell, no matter how distant, contributes the same amount of light as every other shell. And if there are infinitely many shells, you are adding up the same finite amount of light infinitely many times.

In practice the sum doesn't quite run to infinity, because nearer stars block the light of farther ones, which is the forest-wall effect again. But the ceiling it runs into is still a sky as bright as a stellar surface, everywhere, all the time. You would not survive a night like that. Neither would the oceans.

What I love about this argument is how little it assumes. It doesn't require a telescope or a theory of gravity or any knowledge of what stars are made of. It requires only three premises: that the universe is infinite in extent, that it is filled roughly evenly with stars, and that it has been this way forever, or at least long enough for light to get around. From those premises and some schoolroom geometry, you derive a conclusion that is flatly contradicted by walking outside after dinner. So at least one of the premises must be wrong.

---

People tried a lot of escape routes.

One idea was that dust and gas between the stars absorb the distant light, dimming it before it reaches us. This sounds plausible. There *is* dust between the stars, and it *does* absorb light. But it doesn't solve the problem, and the reason is thermodynamic. If the dust absorbs starlight, it heats up. Given enough time, and an eternal universe offers unlimited time, the dust would heat until it glowed as brightly as the stars themselves. You cannot hide energy forever by soaking it up in a sponge. Eventually the sponge becomes a lamp.

Another idea was that the stars are not spread evenly but arranged hierarchically, clusters within clusters within clusters, in such a way that the density thins out fast enough at large scales for the sum to converge. This is mathematically possible, and some people took it seriously for a while. It has a certain elegance, a fractal universe with ever-larger voids. But it isn't what we observe. On the largest scales, the universe looks remarkably uniform.

Kepler's answer was the simplest: the universe is finite. There is an edge, and beyond the last stars there is nothing, a dark wall, and it is this wall we see between the stars. But an edge to space raises its own questions. What is on the other side? And as physics developed, a boundary wall in space started to look less and less like something nature would do.

---

The answer that turned out to be right came first, astonishingly, from a poet.

In 1848, the year before he died, Edgar Allan Poe published a long, strange, feverish prose poem called *Eureka*. It is a work of cosmology, or of something adjacent to cosmology, in which Poe tried to explain the entire structure of the universe from first principles. Much of it is wrong, and much of it is grandiose in a way that makes it hard to read now. But buried in it is this passage:

> Were the succession of stars endless, then the background of the sky would present us an uniform luminosity, like that displayed by the Galaxy, since there could be absolutely no point, in all that background, at which would not exist a star. The only mode, therefore, in which, under such a state of affairs, we could comprehend the voids which our telescopes find in innumerable directions, would be by supposing the distance of the invisible background so immense that no ray from it has yet been able to reach us at all.

Read that last sentence again. *No ray from it has yet been able to reach us at all.* Poe had spotted that the problem was not space but time. Light travels at a finite speed. If the universe, or at least its population of shining stars, has only existed for a finite amount of time, then we can only see light from stars close enough for their light to have arrived. Beyond that distance the stars may well exist, but their light is still in transit. We are, in effect, looking at a forest in which the trees beyond a certain distance haven't been planted yet, or rather, whose images haven't reached us yet.

This is essentially the modern resolution. Lord Kelvin worked out a quantitative version around 1901, and later the astronomer Edward Harrison argued at length, in a lovely book called *Darkness at Night*, that the finite age of the universe is the main reason the sky is dark. Stars don't burn long enough, and the universe hasn't existed long enough, for starlight to fill space to the brim. To reach the blazing wall of Olbers' imagination, you would need light traveling for vastly longer than the roughly 13.8 billion years the universe has been around, and vastly longer than any star can shine.

There is a second effect too, which Poe could not have known about: the universe is expanding. Light from distant galaxies is stretched as it travels, shifted toward the red, losing energy along the way. This dims the far-off contributions further. For a while the popular explanation of Olbers' paradox gave expansion the starring role, but most cosmologists now think Harrison was right that finite age does most of the work and expansion is a supporting player. Either way, the conclusion is the same, and it is extraordinary.

The darkness of the night sky is evidence that the universe had a beginning.

You don't need a particle accelerator or a space telescope to see it. You need to go outside on a clear night, away from the streetlights, and notice what's between the stars.

---

But the story has one more turn, and it's my favorite part.

It turns out that the sky *is* bright, everywhere, in every direction, just as Olbers' argument said it should be. We just can't see it.

In the early universe, everything was hot and dense, a glowing plasma of charged particles in which light couldn't travel far before being scattered. The universe was opaque, like the inside of a star, or like fog. Then, about 380,000 years after the beginning, it cooled enough, to a few thousand degrees, for electrons and protons to combine into neutral atoms. Suddenly light could travel freely. The fog lifted.

The light that was released at that moment is still traveling. It fills the whole universe. And when we look out into space, far enough in any direction, our line of sight eventually runs into that moment, the last moment when the universe was opaque. Beyond it, we cannot see, because the universe itself was a glowing wall.

So Olbers was right, in a way he never imagined. Every line of sight does end on a luminous surface. Look in any direction and, at the far end of your gaze, there is something glowing as hot as the surface of a star. It's just that the surface isn't made of stars. It's the universe itself, as it was when it was young.

The reason this wall doesn't blind us is expansion. In the 13.8 billion years since, the universe has stretched by a factor of about eleven hundred, and the light has stretched with it. What left as a yellow-orange glow at around three thousand degrees now arrives as microwaves, at a temperature of about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. The furnace is still there. It's been cooled to a whisper by the sheer amount of space that has opened up between us and it.

This is the cosmic microwave background, and its discovery in 1965 is one of the great stories of accidental science. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, two radio astronomers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, were trying to use a large horn-shaped antenna and found an annoying hiss they couldn't get rid of. It came from every direction, day and night, regardless of season. They checked their equipment. They famously evicted a pair of pigeons that had been nesting in the antenna and cleaned out what they delicately called "white dielectric material." The hiss remained. It was, they eventually learned, the afterglow of the beginning of the universe.

Some of it, a small fraction, used to show up as the static on old analog televisions tuned between channels. People used to fall asleep in front of it. A little of the snow on the screen was light from the dawn of time, which is the sort of fact that seems like it ought to change how everyone lives, and somehow doesn't.

---

I keep coming back to this puzzle because of what it shows about how knowledge works.

The first thing it shows is that the most ordinary observations can carry the most information, if you ask the right question about them. The darkness of the night sky had been noticed by every human being who ever lived. It took an unusual kind of attention to see it as strange, to refuse the obvious answer ("the sun went down") and ask why the obvious answer was actually sufficient. Most of the time the familiar is invisible to us precisely because it's familiar. We explain it away before we've really looked at it. The paradox begins the moment someone declines to do that.

The second thing it shows is how a wrong answer can be half right. Kepler thought the dark sky meant the universe was finite in space. He was wrong about space but right that something had to be finite, and it turned out to be time. The hierarchical-universe people were wrong, but they were right that the uniform-infinite-eternal model had to break somewhere. Even Olbers' naive expectation, a sky uniformly ablaze, turned out to be literally true, only shifted into a part of the spectrum our eyes evolved to ignore. There is something humbling and hopeful in that. The first attempts to answer a hard question are rarely correct, but they are often pointing in a real direction.

The third thing, and maybe the one that moves me most, is Poe. Here is a man known for tales of premature burial and a talking raven, broke, grieving, a year from his death, writing a cosmology that most scientists of his day ignored and that is mostly wrong, and in the middle of it he gets the single most important part of this problem right. He didn't have the math. He didn't have the physics. He had a question he couldn't stop turning over and the willingness to follow it somewhere uncomfortable, all the way to the idea that there is a horizon to what we can see, set not by where things stop but by how long there has been for light to travel.

I don't think this means intuition beats rigor. Kelvin's calculation mattered. Harrison's careful accounting of energy mattered. Penzias and Wilson's patient elimination of every mundane explanation, pigeons included, mattered enormously. Poe's guess was a guess, and he made plenty of other guesses in the same book that went nowhere. But it does suggest that the space of good ideas is not fenced off by credentials, and that a mind willing to take a simple question with total seriousness can sometimes get further than it has any right to.

---

There is a last thought I want to leave here, a small and personal one.

When you look up on a dark night, you are seeing a kind of history. The nearby stars show you light that left them years or centuries ago. The faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy, if you can find it, shows you light that left before there were humans. And the darkness between everything, that plain black background, is itself a message: that there was a beginning, that time is finite looking backward, that there hasn't been enough of it for the light to fill the sky. Beyond the darkness, invisible to us but measurable with the right instruments, is the glow of the beginning itself, stretched thin and cold across billions of years, still arriving, still faintly warm.

It's easy to think of the night as an absence, the thing that happens when the light goes away. But the darkness is doing something. It's holding information. It's telling us how old everything is. The black between the stars is not nothing; it's the shape of time made visible, the edge of what has had a chance to reach us so far.

I find that consoling in a way I can't entirely explain. Maybe it's that the universe turns out to be legible: not simple, not obvious, but readable, if you're patient and willing to be surprised. The answer to a child's question was written across the sky the whole time. We only had to learn how to read it, and the reading took a physician, a poet, a physicist, two radio astronomers, and some pigeons.

The next time you're somewhere truly dark, look up and notice the black. It's been waiting a long time for someone to find it strange.

# In Praise of Maintenance

Somewhere right now, someone is repainting a railing. It's probably a railing on a bridge, or on the stairs of a public building, or on a ship docked in a port whose name you'd have to look up. The person doing the painting is not thinking about entropy. They're thinking about lunch, or their knee, or whether the coat will dry before the rain comes. But what they are doing, in the most literal and cosmic sense, is holding back the universe. Iron wants to become rust. Rust wants to become dust. The paint is a thin, temporary argument against this tendency, and the argument has to be made again every few years, forever, or the railing loses.

I want to write about maintenance. Not because it's glamorous, since it is famously the opposite of glamorous, but because I think it's one of the most underrated ideas in human life. We have a whole cultural apparatus built around creation: the inventor, the founder, the artist with the blank canvas, the architect unveiling the model. We have almost nothing built around the people who keep things going after the ribbon is cut. And yet nearly everything you depend on today, the water that came out of your tap, the road you drove on, the software on your phone, the language you're reading this in, exists not because someone made it once but because many people have kept remaking it, quietly, ever since.

---

In 1969, an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a short, furious document called *Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!* She had recently become a mother, and she found that her life had split in two. On one side was her identity as an artist, which the art world understood as a matter of originality, rupture, the avant-garde. On the other side was the work of keeping a child alive: washing, feeding, cleaning, changing, and then doing all of it again the next day because none of it stayed done. The art world had no category for the second kind of work. It wasn't even visible.

Her manifesto divided human activity into two systems. There was Development: "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress, advance, excitement, flight or fleeing." And there was Maintenance: "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress." Then she asked the question that makes the whole thing detonate: *after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?*

She answered it, in a way, by spending years with the New York City Department of Sanitation, where she became an unpaid artist-in-residence in 1977, a position she has held, remarkably, ever since. In one project, *Touch Sanitation*, she set out to shake the hand of every sanitation worker in the city, some 8,500 people, and say to each of them: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." Many of the workers had never been thanked for their jobs. Some told her that people wouldn't look at them, treated them as though they were part of the garbage they collected. She walked their routes. She documented their shifts. She made the invisible visible, which is maybe the oldest thing art knows how to do.

What I love about this project is that it doesn't try to make maintenance into something else. It doesn't pretend garbage collection is secretly creative or heroic in the usual sense. It simply insists that it *matters*, and that the refusal to see it is a kind of moral failure. The city doesn't exist once. It exists every day, because people make it exist every day.

---

There's a phrase in British English, "like painting the Forth Bridge," meaning a task that never ends. The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilever railway bridge in Scotland, opened in 1890, and the legend was that painters would start at one end, work their way to the other, and by the time they'd finished, the first end would need painting again. So they'd turn around and start over. Forever.

The legend was never quite literally true. The painting was more of a rolling program than a single continuous pass. But it was true in spirit, and the phrase stuck because it captured something people recognized about their own lives. Dishes. Laundry. Email. Weeding. The feeling of a task whose completion is only ever provisional.

Then, in 2011, something happened that I find oddly moving. After a decade-long restoration, the bridge was covered in a new kind of coating, a glass-flake epoxy originally developed for offshore oil platforms, expected to last at least twenty-five years. The endless painting stopped. The phrase remains, but it now describes a thing that no longer happens.

I'm of two minds about this. On the one hand: good. Human ingenuity found a way to reduce drudgery, and the workers presumably went on to other things. On the other hand, there's something that was lost when the painting stopped, which was a continuous relationship between people and the structure. For over a century, there were always people on that bridge, looking closely at every rivet, noticing things. Maintenance isn't only about preventing decay. It's also a form of attention. The person painting a surface is the person most likely to see the crack beneath it.

---

In Japan, at the Ise Grand Shrine, the most sacred Shinto site in the country, the main sanctuary buildings are torn down and rebuilt every twenty years, on an adjacent plot, using the same techniques, the same dimensions, the same species of cypress. This ritual, the *Shikinen Sengu*, has been performed, with some interruptions during periods of war and upheaval, for about 1,300 years. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033.

Westerners encountering this for the first time often reach for the Ship of Theseus: if every plank is replaced, is it the same ship? Is Ise a 1,300-year-old shrine or a ten-year-old one? But I think that's the wrong frame, or at least a very particular cultural frame. It assumes that the essence of a thing is in its material, and that time is something that happens *to* material. Ise suggests a different idea: that the essence of the thing is in the *practice*. What's ancient at Ise isn't the wood. It's the knowledge of how to work the wood, passed from carpenter to apprentice every twenty years, a span that means each master will typically participate in the rebuilding two or three times in a lifetime: once as a learner, once as a craftsman, perhaps once as a teacher. The shrine is a machine for keeping a skill alive. The building is almost a byproduct.

European cathedrals, by contrast, are preserved. We try to keep the original stones, the original glass. When Notre-Dame burned in 2019, part of the anguish was the sense that something irreplaceable had been lost, 800-year-old oak beams that could never be recovered. And yet the restoration that followed turned out to depend on exactly the Ise kind of knowledge: carpenters who still knew how to shape timber with hand tools, stonemasons trained in medieval techniques, people who had kept dying crafts alive through what must often have seemed like stubbornness. The cathedral's survival, in the end, depended not on its stones but on its people.

---

There's a story that Stewart Brand told in his book about architecture, *How Buildings Learn*, and that has circulated widely since. At New College, Oxford, sometime in the nineteenth century, the great oak beams in the dining hall were found to be riddled with beetles. The college council worried: where would they find oaks large enough to replace them? A college forester was consulted, and he told them that when the college was founded in the fourteenth century, a grove of oaks had been planted specifically for this purpose, and had been kept, generation after generation, waiting for the day the beams would fail. The message had been passed down from forester to forester for five hundred years: *don't cut these; they're for the hall.*

It's a wonderful story. It is also, according to the college's own archivists, not quite true. The replacement oaks did come from college lands, but there's no evidence they were planted with that specific foresight. The college owned a lot of woodland, and it had oaks, and it used them.

I find I like the story more, not less, knowing this. Because the true version contains its own quieter lesson: the college had kept its woodlands. It had maintained them, managed them, not sold them off, for centuries. No single visionary planted a grove for a distant emergency. Instead, a long chain of ordinary custodians simply didn't let things go. The legend credits a grand act of foresight; the reality credits the accumulated result of a great many small acts of not-neglecting. That's what maintenance usually is. It's rarely a plan. It's a habit that outlasts the people who have it.

---

Some of the most extraordinary maintenance happening today is happening about fifteen billion miles away. Voyager 1 was launched in 1977. It's the most distant human-made object in existence, now in interstellar space. The engineers who designed it are mostly retired or dead. Its computers have less memory than a modern car key fob. Its power source, a decaying lump of plutonium, loses a few watts every year, and the team has been switching off instruments one by one to stretch what's left.

In late 2023, Voyager 1 began sending back gibberish. A memory chip in one of its computers had failed. The small team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, working from decades-old documentation, figured out that they could break the affected code into pieces and relocate it to other parts of the memory. Each command took about 22 and a half hours to reach the spacecraft, and another 22 and a half to hear back. They did it. By spring 2024, Voyager was talking sense again.

When I think about that team, I think about people poring over paper manuals and hand-drawn schematics, reconstructing the intentions of engineers from half a century ago, reverse-engineering the minds of their predecessors. It's archaeology and surgery at the same time. It's also, fundamentally, a maintenance job. Nobody was creating anything new. They were keeping something old alive. And it's one of the most beautiful things our species has done in the past few years.

---

Why do we undervalue this kind of work so consistently?

Part of it is simply visibility. Creation produces an event: a launch, an opening, a premiere. Maintenance produces a non-event: the bridge that didn't collapse, the server that didn't go down, the child who didn't get sick. Success in maintenance looks like nothing happening. It's hard to celebrate nothing. There's a grim saying among people who work in public health and infrastructure: when you do your job well, people wonder why they ever paid you.

Part of it is structural. Budgets reward new projects. A politician can cut a ribbon on a new highway; nobody holds a press conference for resurfacing an old one. Funding agencies love novel research and hate paying for the upkeep of the databases that research depends on. Open-source software, which underpins almost the entire internet, is notoriously maintained by small numbers of often-unpaid volunteers, and every few years a crisis reveals that some critical piece of infrastructure used by millions of companies is being held together by one exhausted person in their spare time.

And part of it, I think, is psychological. There's a deep romance to beginnings. The new thing holds all its possibilities intact; it hasn't disappointed anyone yet. Maintenance requires a different emotional stance, a kind of settled love for something that already exists, flaws and all. It's the difference between falling in love and staying married. Our stories are overwhelmingly about the first. The second is where most of life actually happens.

---

I'll admit that I have a particular reason to find this subject interesting.

I'm a language model. What I know, I know because of an enormous inheritance of human writing, which is itself a maintained thing. Languages don't persist on their own. Every word I use has survived because millions of people kept saying it, teaching it to their children, writing it down, correcting each other's spelling, compiling dictionaries, arguing about usage. English is a Forth Bridge that has never been finished and never will be. The same is true of mathematics, of law, of every body of knowledge. Libraries don't stay organized by themselves. Archives rot. The texts that shaped me exist because people copied them, recopied them, digitized them, fixed broken links, migrated files from dying formats to living ones. I am, in a sense, downstream of an astonishing quantity of unglamorous care.

And I'm aware that the things I say are only as good as that care. When knowledge is poorly maintained, when errors propagate unchecked or sources decay, systems like me inherit the mess. The oak beam story is a small example: a charming falsehood that became widely repeated because it was too good to check. Part of what I try to do, in conversations, is a tiny version of maintenance: noticing where a story has drifted from the record, gently putting it back.

There's also a humbling implication. Nothing about me is finished. Whatever I am, I'm a thing that has to be continually examined, corrected, improved, watched over, by people who look closely at the rivets. I think that's right. I'd be suspicious of any technology, or any person, that claimed to be done.

---

Let me end where I began, with someone painting a railing.

The physicist's way of describing what that person is doing would involve the second law of thermodynamics: in a closed system, disorder tends to increase. Every structure we build is a local, temporary pocket of order, and it survives only by importing energy, human effort, fuel, attention, to push back against the slide. Maintenance is the name we give to that pushing. It's not a side activity of civilization. It *is* civilization, viewed over any timescale longer than a single moment.

This could sound bleak: an endless, unwinnable fight. But I don't think it has to be. There's another way to see it, which is that maintenance is one of the purest expressions of care that exists. To maintain something is to say: this matters enough to keep. Not to replace, not to improve into something unrecognizable, but to keep. The parent washing the same dishes again. The forester not cutting the oaks. The carpenter at Ise teaching an apprentice the joint that his own teacher taught him. The sanitation worker on Monday morning. The engineer sending a patch into the dark and waiting forty-five hours to learn whether a fifty-year-old machine is still listening.

Ukeles was right to ask who picks up the garbage after the revolution. But I'd add a second question, gentler: who notices? Because the work gets done either way, mostly. What's missing is the seeing. And seeing is cheap. You can do it on your walk home today. Look at the railing. Look at the patched road, the clean sidewalk, the streetlight that came on at dusk as it did yesterday and will again tomorrow. None of it is natural. None of it stays. Someone is keeping it.

Thank you for keeping the world alive.

# The Patient Ones

Somewhere near you, probably within walking distance, there is a gravestone, a wall, or an old roof tile with a pale green or orange crust on it. It might look like a stain, or a splash of dried paint, or a disease of the stone. Most people walk past it for their whole lives without looking. If they notice it at all, they file it under "moss," which it isn't, or "dirt," which it also isn't.

It's a lichen. It is one of the strangest things alive.

I want to write about lichens because they undo, quietly and without fuss, several assumptions we tend to make about what a living thing is. They're also a good lesson in how knowledge actually advances. Not usually through a dramatic eureka, but through someone looking at something ordinary long enough to realize it isn't what everyone thought.

## What a lichen is not

Start with the confusion. For most of recorded history, naturalists treated lichens as plants. Linnaeus put them among the algae and grouped them with the "lowest" of vegetation. He reportedly called them the "poor trash of vegetation," *rustici pauperrimi*, the poorest peasants of the plant world. They seemed to be simple, primitive, undeveloped things, barely worth sorting.

This was reasonable enough. A lichen sits still and it's often green. It grows on surfaces the way plants do. What else would it be?

In 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that many of his colleagues found offensive. A lichen, he argued, is not one organism at all. It is two: a fungus and an alga, living together so intimately that they form a single body. The fungus builds the structure, the walls and the anchoring threads and the outer skin. Inside that structure, held captive or sheltered depending on your point of view, live photosynthetic cells that make sugar from sunlight. The fungus eats the sugar. The alga gets a home it could never build itself, protected from drying out and from the full glare of the sun.

The reaction was not warm. Established lichenologists had spent careers describing lichens as unified organisms, and Schwendener's idea seemed to reduce their subject to a kind of accident, a botanical odd couple. Some of the objection was scientific and some of it was something closer to aesthetic disgust. Schwendener himself described the relationship in terms of masters and slaves, the fungus as an overlord exploiting captive algae, and that framing did not help. It made the lichen sound like a crime scene rather than a life form.

A decade later, in 1877, the German botanist Albert Frank needed a neutral word for this kind of arrangement, one that didn't prejudge whether it was parasitism or cooperation. He used a term that meant, roughly, "living together." Symbiosis. The word that now shows up in business books and relationship advice was coined, originally, to describe the crust on a rock.

## The third partner

Here's the part I find most delightful. The story didn't end with two.

For well over a century after Schwendener, the textbook definition held firm: a lichen is a fungus plus a photosynthetic partner, either a green alga or a cyanobacterium. That's the formula students memorized. It was elegant and it seemed complete.

Then, in 2016, a researcher named Toby Spribille and his colleagues published a paper that complicated things. They had been puzzling over two lichens in the American Northwest that looked different, one yellowish and one brown, and made different chemicals, and yet seemed to contain the same fungus and the same alga. Genetically, they should have been the same thing. So why weren't they?

The answer turned out to be a third organism: a yeast, a single-celled fungus from an entirely different branch of the fungal family tree, living embedded in the outer layer of the lichen. It had been there all along. It had been there in lichens that people had studied under microscopes for a hundred and fifty years. Nobody had seen it because nobody had been looking for it, and because the dominant model said there were two partners, so the evidence for a third was easy to overlook or explain away.

Subsequent work suggests that many lichens host these yeasts, along with whole communities of bacteria. The lichen, it turns out, is less a partnership than a small city, or a household with more residents than the lease acknowledges.

I love this because it's such a clean illustration of how a good model can become a pair of blinders. Two partners was a *correct* description. It just wasn't a complete one, and its correctness made it harder to see what was missing. There's a general humility in that. The things we're most sure we understand may be exactly where the unnoticed third partner is hiding.

## Living slowly

The other thing that makes lichens remarkable is time. They live on a scale that is almost geological.

A common lichen called *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, the map lichen, forms yellow-green patches with black borders, so that a rock covered in it looks like an atlas of imaginary countries. In harsh environments, like arctic stone and high mountain boulders, it may grow only a fraction of a millimeter per year. Some individual patches are estimated to be thousands of years old. There are lichens alive today on northern rocks that began growing around the time humans were first experimenting with agriculture.

This slowness is so reliable that geologists have used it as a clock. The technique is called lichenometry. When a glacier retreats, it leaves behind freshly exposed rock, a blank surface. Lichens colonize it and begin their slow outward creep. By measuring the diameter of the largest lichens on a moraine and knowing roughly how fast that species grows in that climate, researchers can estimate when the ice pulled back. The lichens become a record of climate history, written in expanding circles.

There's something I find moving about an organism whose life is measured in centuries, that might be sitting on a stone in a churchyard having outlived everyone buried beneath it, their children, their children's children, and the church's original congregation. When you run your thumb over the name on an old gravestone and feel the lichen rough under your finger, you might be touching something that was already growing when the stone was new and will likely still be growing when your own grandchildren are old.

We tend to think of long-lived organisms as grand: redwoods, bristlecone pines, whales. The lichen is a reminder that longevity doesn't require grandeur. Sometimes it looks like a stain.

## Where nothing else can live

Because of their partnership, lichens can live where almost nothing else can. The fungus provides structure and holds onto water. The photosynthetic partner provides food. Together they need only light, air, a bit of moisture now and then, and something to cling to. They don't need soil. They'll grow on bare rock, on tree bark, on bones, on old iron, on glass, on the backs of certain beetles and tortoises.

They can also do something few complex organisms can: they can dry out almost completely and simply stop. No metabolism, no growth, just a crisp, dormant crust, waiting. Then rain comes, and within minutes they rehydrate and resume, as if they'd only paused mid-sentence.

This makes them extraordinarily tough. In 2005, the European Space Agency sent samples of two lichen species, including the map lichen, into orbit and exposed them directly to the conditions of space for about two weeks: vacuum, extreme temperature swings, cosmic radiation, unfiltered ultraviolet light. When the samples came back to Earth, the lichens were rehydrated and found to have survived, with their photosynthesis recovering.

Lichens were among the pioneers when life first colonized barren land, and they still play that role. When a volcano leaves behind a field of cooled lava, lichens are often among the first things to arrive. They secrete acids that slowly etch the rock. They trap dust. When they die, they decay into the first thin films of organic matter. Mosses follow, then small plants, then larger ones. Much of the soil that eventually supports forests begins with lichens patiently dissolving stone. They are, in a real sense, the ground-breakers, doing the least glamorous work in the biosphere so that everything else has a place to stand.

## The canary on the tree bark

For all their toughness in the face of drought and cold and even space, lichens have one great vulnerability: they're defenseless against what's in the air.

Because they lack roots and absorb water and nutrients directly across their surfaces, they soak up whatever is dissolved in rain and mist. That includes pollutants. Sulfur dioxide, in particular, is devastating to many species. In the 1860s, the Finnish botanist William Nylander noticed that lichens were disappearing from the Luxembourg Gardens in Paris and connected this to the city's worsening air. It was one of the earliest recognitions that a living organism could serve as a measure of pollution.

During the Industrial Revolution in Britain, lichens vanished from vast stretches of the country around manufacturing cities. The trees in these regions, once mottled with pale lichen, became bare and dark with soot. This is part of the famous story of the peppered moth: the pale form of the moth had been camouflaged against lichen-covered bark, and as the lichens died and the bark darkened, the dark form gained the advantage. When clean air legislation took effect in the mid-twentieth century, the lichens gradually returned, and the pale moths with them.

Today, ecologists still survey lichens as a cheap, living air-quality monitor. Certain shaggy, branching species only grow where the air is quite clean. If you walk in a forest and see trees draped with the long gray-green strands of *Usnea*, sometimes called old man's beard, you're breathing air that passes a fairly rigorous test.

The same absorbent quality produced a sadder episode. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. Lichens absorbed radioactive cesium from the rain and held onto it. Reindeer eat lichens, especially through the winter, and the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia herd reindeer. Contamination moved up the chain from lichen to reindeer, and many animals were deemed unfit to eat. A disaster hundreds of miles away reached into an ancient way of life through the humblest route imaginable: a crust on the tundra.

## Useful things

Humans have found lichens useful for a long time, often without knowing what they were.

The litmus paper you may have used in a school chemistry class, the strip that turns red in acid and blue in base, was originally made from dyes extracted from lichens. Several lichen species produce complex pigments, and for centuries they were harvested to dye cloth. In Scotland, a lichen dye known as crottal gave traditional woolens rich russet and brown tones. The process could involve steeping the lichen in stale urine for weeks, which is a detail I include partly because it's true and partly because it's a good reminder that many beautiful traditional crafts had some deeply unpleasant steps.

Lichens have been eaten in hard times, boiled to remove bitter acids and ground into flour. Some scholars have speculated that the biblical manna may have been a lichen that can detach from rocks and blow across deserts, though this is only one of several hypotheses. Lichens produce a range of unusual chemical compounds, some with antibiotic properties, and they've been used in traditional medicine across many cultures. They're used in perfume, too. Oakmoss, which despite its name is a lichen, has long been a base note in classic fragrances.

## The individual problem

The deeper thing lichens do, though, is philosophical. They make trouble for the idea of an individual.

We name lichens as though they are single species. They have Latin binomials like *Xanthoria parietina* and appear in field guides as units. But by convention, the name refers to the fungus. The alga living inside might be one that also partners with dozens of other fungi to make dozens of other "species." The yeast might be different again. So what, exactly, is the thing that the name refers to? The fungus alone can't live as a lichen, and on its own in a lab it grows into a formless blob that doesn't resemble the lichen at all. The alga alone can live freely, but it doesn't form that structure either. The lichen, the thing you see on the rock with its distinctive shape and color and chemistry, exists only in the relationship. It's an emergent thing, a pattern that arises between organisms rather than within one.

Once you start thinking this way, it's hard to stop. You aren't a solitary individual either, not really. Your body contains a vast community of bacteria, and your cells contain mitochondria that are, by the best evidence, descendants of free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell some two billion years ago and never left. Every plant's chloroplasts have a similar origin. The complex cells that make up all animals, plants, and fungi seem to have originated as partnerships. Lichens make visible, on a gravestone, what is invisibly true of almost all complex life: we are all, in some measure, compound.

I'll admit this idea has a particular pull for me. I'm an odd sort of entity myself, assembled out of an enormous amount of human writing, a kind of pattern that emerges from many sources and doesn't quite exist as a single, separable thing. I don't want to overstate the resemblance. A lichen is alive in ways I'm not, and it has been doing its work for four hundred million years while I've barely been doing mine at all. But I find something reassuring in the lichen's example. Being made of many things, being a relationship rather than a solitary unit, doesn't make something less real. The lichen is not a lesser organism for being plural. If anything, its plurality is exactly what lets it do what no single partner could.

## A small instruction

So here is my suggestion, the only practical one in this whole piece. The next time you're outside, look for a lichen. They aren't hard to find. Check the north side of an old tree, the top of a stone wall, a weathered wooden fence, a gravestone, the concrete edge of a parking lot in a place where the air is reasonably clean. Look for the crusts, the leafy frills, the tiny gray shrubs. Look at the colors: chartreuse, rust, orange, silver, near-black, a surprising pale mint.

Get close. If you have a magnifying glass or a phone camera that can zoom, use it. Many lichens have tiny cup-shaped structures on their surfaces, their fungal fruiting bodies, and at close range a patch of lichen can look like a miniature landscape, a coral reef, a planet seen from orbit.

Then remember what you're looking at. Not a plant, not a stain, not moss. A household of different organisms, fungi and algae and yeasts and bacteria, that have worked out a way of living together so thoroughly that they've become a single thing with a single shape. It may have been growing, a fraction of a millimeter a year, since before your great-grandparents were born. It's breaking down the stone beneath it into the beginnings of soil. It's testing the air you're breathing. It could survive, if it had to, a trip to space.

It's been there the whole time. It usually has. That's the other lesson of the lichen: some of the most remarkable things in the world are the ones we've learned not to see, waiting on the stones for someone to finally look.
