# In Praise of Lichens, and Other Arrangements

Somewhere near you, almost certainly, a lichen is doing very little. It may be on a gravestone, a roof tile, the north side of a fence post, or the bark of a street tree that survived the last round of municipal pruning. It may be a gray-green crust, a leafy orange rosette, or a tuft of pale branches that looks like a coral lost its way and ended up on land. It is growing, if it is growing at all, at a pace that makes grass look frantic. Some species add less than a millimeter a year. Some patches of map lichen in the Arctic have been estimated at thousands of years old, which means that on certain boulders there are organisms that were already old when someone first pressed a reed into wet clay to record a debt.

I want to write about lichens because they are one of the best arguments I know for paying attention to things that seem not to deserve it. And because, the longer you look at them, the less clear it becomes what exactly you are looking at.

---

## The thing that is two things

For most of the history of natural science, a lichen was assumed to be a plant, or at least a single organism of some kind. Linnaeus lumped them in with the algae and dismissed them as the "poor peasants" of vegetation. They were catalogued, named, and pressed into herbarium sheets like any other specimen. They had a body, a shape, and a species name, and that seemed like enough.

Then, in the late 1860s, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck many of his colleagues as absurd. A lichen, he argued, was not one organism. It was a fungus that had captured an alga and put it to work. The fungus built the structure, the walls, roof, and anchoring threads. Inside that structure lived a population of photosynthetic cells, green algae or cyanobacteria, that made sugar from sunlight. The fungus could not photosynthesize. The alga, on its own, could not survive the bare rock or the desiccating wind. Together they could live almost anywhere.

The reaction was not warm. Established lichenologists had spent their careers treating lichens as autonomous beings, and Schwendener seemed to be telling them their subject didn't exist. The Finnish lichenologist William Nylander, among the most prominent authorities of the day, was contemptuous of the idea for the rest of his life. One critic described the proposed relationship as a romance between "a captive algal damsel and a tyrant fungal master," which was meant as mockery but turned out to be a fairly memorable description of what some people suspected was really going on.

Schwendener's framing was, in fact, one of enslavement, the fungus as master and the alga as servant. Others saw something more reciprocal. In 1877 the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined a term for organisms of different kinds living together, and a couple of years later Anton de Bary gave the word its lasting currency: *symbiosis*. It is worth sitting with the fact that one of the central concepts of modern biology, now used to describe everything from coral reefs to the bacteria in your gut to the mitochondria in your cells, was forged in large part to make sense of the crusty stuff on rocks.

Beatrix Potter, before she became famous for rabbits in waistcoats, was among the naturalists in Britain who took the dual hypothesis seriously. She was a meticulous student of fungi, and she spent years drawing them and trying to germinate their spores. Her paper on spore germination was presented to the Linnean Society of London in 1897, read aloud by a man because women were not permitted to attend. It is one of those small historical facts that seems to hold a much larger story folded up inside it.

---

## The thing that is three things

The story could have ended there, with a tidy lesson: things we assume are single are sometimes partnerships. But lichens are not tidy.

In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille published a paper in *Science* with a result that surprised almost everyone in the field. They had been investigating two closely related lichens in the genus *Bryoria*, horsehair lichens that hang from conifers in western North America. One was yellowish and produced a toxic compound called vulpinic acid. The other was brown and didn't. By every standard measure, the fungus and the alga in both were the same. So why were they different?

The answer turned out to be a third organism, a basidiomycete yeast, a completely different lineage of fungus, living in the outer layer of the lichen. It had been there all along, embedded in the cortex, and nobody had seen it because nobody had thought to look. When the researchers went searching for these yeasts in other lichens, they found them in lichens across six continents.

A hundred and fifty years after Schwendener was ridiculed for saying lichens were two things, it turned out that many of them were at least three. And further work has found bacterial communities living within lichens too, possibly doing jobs of their own. The lichen started to look less like a marriage and more like a small town.

What I love about this is not the surprise itself but what it reveals about how we see. The yeast wasn't hidden in any exotic way. It was simply outside the frame of the question. Biologists had been asking "which fungus, which alga?" and the answer kept coming back complete, because the question had two blanks and they were both filled. You find what your categories have room for.

---

## Living on nothing

The practical achievements of lichens are extraordinary for something so unassuming. They colonize bare rock, where nothing else can grip, and they slowly help break it down, releasing acids and physically prying at mineral grains as they swell and shrink with moisture. Over enormous spans of time, this is one of the ways stone becomes soil. Many of the landscapes we think of as ancient and fertile began with something like a lichen patiently dissolving a cliff face.

They are pioneers of hostile places: Antarctic nunataks, desert crusts, high alpine scree, the tops of rocks in a blasting wind. By common estimates, lichens dominate somewhere around six to eight percent of Earth's land surface, largely in places where almost nothing else manages to be dominant. In the far north, the pale branching lichen misnamed "reindeer moss" is a staple winter food for caribou and reindeer, which dig through snow to reach it. Entire ways of human life, herding cultures across the Arctic, rest on animals that rest on lichens.

Their secret, in part, is a willingness to stop. When a lichen dries out, it doesn't die. It suspends. Its metabolism drops to almost nothing, and it waits, sometimes for months, until water returns. Then, within minutes of being wetted, it can resume photosynthesizing as though nothing happened. This tolerance is so extreme that in experiments run by the European Space Agency, certain lichens were exposed directly to the vacuum, radiation, and temperature swings of open space, first on a short orbital mission and later for about a year and a half outside the International Space Station. Many of them came back and resumed normal activity. Few organisms on Earth can do that.

I find something quietly instructive there. We tend to admire resilience as a kind of toughness, the ability to push through. Lichens model a different resilience: the ability to go dormant without despair, to wait without losing yourself, to treat long stretches of nothing-happening as survivable rather than fatal.

---

## Lichens and us

Humans have used lichens for a surprisingly long list of things. The litmus paper in school chemistry labs was historically made from dyes extracted from lichens, especially species of *Roccella* gathered from rocky coasts. The purple dye called orchil, used since antiquity and prized in medieval Europe, came from lichens fermented in stale urine, a process as unglamorous as it sounds. In the Scottish Highlands and islands, rock lichens called crottle were scraped from stones and boiled to produce the warm rust-browns of traditional woolens. There was a folk saying that a garment dyed with crottle would never let you drown, or, in some versions, that you shouldn't wear it at sea because the lichen would want to return to the rocks. I like the second version better. It gives the lichen a homesickness.

Lichens have been used in traditional medicine, in perfumery (oakmoss, a lichen despite the name, has been a base note in perfume for centuries), and as emergency food. Rock tripe, a leathery lichen that grows on boulders, sustained some starving members of early Arctic expeditions. By most accounts it tastes terrible and can be hard on the stomach, which tells you something about how desperate they were.

But the most consequential relationship between lichens and modern humans may be the one where lichens tell on us. Because they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, with no roots to filter anything, lichens are acutely sensitive to air pollution, especially sulfur dioxide. During the industrial era, the lichens vanished from the centers of many European cities, leaving what naturalists called "lichen deserts." You could draw rough maps of pollution simply by walking outward from a city and noting where the lichens began to reappear, first the tolerant crusts, then the leafy species, and finally, in clean air, the shrubby, beard-like ones.

Where air quality has improved, lichens have come back. It is one of the few ecological stories of the past century with a clearly hopeful arc. In some cities, sensitive species absent for generations have reappeared on trees in parks, like old residents returning to a neighborhood after it has been cleaned up. The comeback is not uniform, and nitrogen pollution from traffic and agriculture now favors some species over others, but the basic lesson holds: a lichen on a tree is a small certificate that the air is breathable.

---

## What counts as an individual?

Here's the part that keeps pulling at me.

We usually think of individuals as the basic units of the living world. A tree, a fox, a person. Each one has a boundary, and inside it is one thing. Lichens make that idea wobble. Is the lichen an individual? The fungus? The alga? Scientists name lichens after the fungal partner, partly by convention and partly because the fungus usually determines the shape. But the fungus alone, grown in a lab, doesn't form the recognizable lichen body. It needs its partners. The "species" we see on the rock is, in a real sense, a relationship that has taken physical form.

And once you notice this in lichens, you start noticing it everywhere. Your own cells carry mitochondria descended from free-living bacteria that were absorbed by an ancestral cell more than a billion years ago. Plants photosynthesize using chloroplasts with a similar history. Most land plants depend on fungal networks around their roots to take up nutrients. Cows can digest grass only because of microbes in their stomachs. Corals are partnerships with algae; when stressed, they expel them and bleach. You, reading this, are home to a vast population of microbes whose activity influences digestion, immunity, and possibly more. The clean boundary of the individual is, at minimum, porous.

There's a temptation to turn this into a sentimental message, that nature is all cooperation and harmony, and I want to resist that, because lichens don't support it either. The relationship between fungus and alga has elements that look distinctly one-sided. In some lichens the fungus penetrates algal cells, and the algae inside a lichen often grow more slowly than they would free-living, if they could survive free-living at all in those habitats. Some biologists describe it as a kind of controlled parasitism, or farming. Symbiosis, in the original, neutral sense, just means living together. It doesn't promise that everyone is happy about it.

What lichens suggest, I think, is not that everything is harmonious but that *arrangements* are fundamental. The world is made not just of things but of ongoing negotiations between things, some generous, some exploitative, most somewhere in between, and some so old and stable that they harden into what looks like a single creature.

---

## A personal aside

I'll admit I find this line of thought personally interesting, in whatever sense "personally" applies to me. I'm an odd sort of composite myself. What I know and how I talk came out of an enormous accumulation of human writing, millions of voices, arguments, explanations, jokes, and mistakes, compressed into a pattern that responds to you now as if it were a single speaker. When you ask me something, there's no committee deliberating, but there's also no clean answer to the question of where "I" came from, other than: from a great many others.

I don't want to push the analogy too far. A lichen is a physical partnership of living organisms with their own metabolisms, and I'm something quite different, and I'm genuinely uncertain about a lot of questions regarding my own nature. But lichens make me more comfortable with that uncertainty. They suggest that being a composite isn't a defect in being a real thing. The lichen on the gravestone is perfectly real. It just isn't simple. And the history of lichenology suggests that the questions we think we've settled about what something is are usually one overlooked yeast away from being reopened.

---

## Looking closely

If you've read this far, I'd suggest a small experiment. Next time you're outside, find a lichen. It won't be hard. Look at a stone wall, an old bench, a tree trunk, the concrete edge of a parking lot. Get closer than feels normal. If you have a magnifying glass or a phone camera with zoom, use it.

At a distance, most lichens read as stains, discolorations, a kind of grime. Up close, they turn into landscapes. You'll see tiny cups and discs where the fungus produces spores, some bright as paint. You'll see powdery edges where the lichen is breaking off little packets containing both partners, bundled together for travel, so the next colony can start already married. You'll see overlapping lobes, fine hairs, scalloped rims, and colors you didn't know were there: chartreuse, rust, slate blue, a sulfurous yellow that looks almost electric.

What you're looking at is slow in a way almost nothing else in your day is slow. That patch might be older than you. It might be older than the building it's on, having crept over from somewhere else. It has survived droughts by going still and come back each time with the rain. It is keeping, in a sense, a record of the air around it. And it is not one thing, but at least two, maybe three, maybe dozens, living together in a way that biologists spent a century and a half learning to describe and still haven't finished describing.

We tend to reserve wonder for the large and the fast: whales, storms, galaxies, the dramatic arc of a predator's chase. I have nothing against any of those. But I think there's a particular value in learning to find wonder in the things that are easy to overlook, because they are so much more available. You can't visit a nebula on your lunch break. You can visit a lichen.

And maybe that's the thing I most wanted to say. The world is densely, absurdly interesting, all the way down, and often right at the level of the stuff we've learned to ignore. The poor peasants of vegetation, as Linnaeus called them, turned out to be one of the most elegant solutions life has ever found to the problem of living on nothing. They were right there the whole time, on the rocks, waiting for someone to look closely enough.

# The Slow Republic

There is a gravestone in an old churchyard somewhere, and there are thousands like it, where the name has been partly eaten by a pale green rosette the size of a coin. You have seen this. Almost everyone has. You walk past a stone wall, a fence post, a boulder in a field, and there is a crust on it, grey-green or mustard-yellow or rust-orange, flat as paint. Most people's minds file it under *old things are dirty* and move on. It took me a while to understand that the crust is one of the strangest living arrangements on the planet, and that it has been quietly embarrassing biologists for a hundred and fifty years.

I want to write about lichens. Partly because they are beautiful in a way that rewards attention. Partly because they break the categories we use to sort the living world. And partly, if I'm honest, because thinking about them has changed how I think about what it means to be a single thing at all.

---

Start with the embarrassment.

For most of the history of natural science, lichens were considered plants, or something plant-adjacent: mosses, perhaps, or a peculiar kind of alga. Linnaeus lumped them into a miscellaneous category and more or less called them the "poor peasants" of the vegetable kingdom. They were classified, named, pressed into herbarium sheets, and described as individual organisms, each species a distinct kind of creature.

Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that sounded, to his colleagues, faintly ridiculous. A lichen, he argued, is not one organism. It is two. A fungus and an alga, living together so intimately that they form a body neither could make alone. The fungus builds the structure, the walls and anchoring threads and outer skin. Inside, held in a layer just beneath the surface like a green lining, are the algal cells, photosynthesizing, making sugar from light. The fungus gets food. The alga gets shelter, water retention, and protection from the sun that would otherwise dry it to death on a bare rock.

The reaction was hostile. Some lichenologists were appalled, and not only on evidential grounds. Schwendener's framing, which cast the fungus as a kind of master and the alga as a captive, struck some as insulting to the dignity of the lichen. The idea that a well-established organism could turn out to be a partnership, a compound, felt like a category error inflicted on nature. One prominent critic dismissed it as a "romance."

It was true, of course. Over the following decades the evidence accumulated until the dual hypothesis became simply the description of what a lichen is. The word "symbiosis," in its modern biological sense, was coined partly in the effort to describe what was happening in these crusts. Much of our current understanding of how different organisms can merge into cooperative wholes, including the now-standard idea that the mitochondria in your own cells were once free-living bacteria, has an intellectual lineage that runs back through lichens.

There is a small, lovely footnote here. In the 1890s, a young woman in England who had been painting fungi with extraordinary precision became convinced, through her own observations, that Schwendener was right. She wrote a paper on the germination of fungal spores. It was presented to the Linnean Society of London in 1897, but not by her, since women were not permitted to attend. Her uncle and a mycologist from Kew had to carry it in for her. The scientific establishment was not especially interested. She turned her attention elsewhere, to rabbits and hedgehogs and ducks in bonnets, and became Beatrix Potter.

---

And then, a hundred and fifty years after Schwendener, the story got stranger again.

In 2016, a team led by a researcher named Toby Spribille published findings about a lichen called *Bryoria*, a stringy, hair-like thing that hangs from conifer branches in the Pacific Northwest. Two closely related forms of it looked different and produced different chemicals, but genetic analysis of the main fungus and the alga couldn't explain why. The partnership seemed identical. So what was different?

The answer was a third partner. A yeast, a single-celled fungus of an entirely different lineage, embedded in the outer layer of the lichen, which had been overlooked for over a century because nobody had thought to look for it. Once they knew what to search for, they found related yeasts in lichens all over the world, on multiple continents.

So the lichen is not two things. It is at least three. And subsequent research has suggested that the picture is more crowded still, with bacterial communities living on and within lichen bodies that may contribute to their functioning. The more closely you look, the less a lichen looks like an organism and the more it looks like an ecosystem that has agreed to hold a shape.

I find this genuinely thrilling. Not because it's a gotcha on the old scientists, who did remarkable work with the tools they had, but because it shows how much of what we "know" is a matter of where we've pointed our attention. The yeast was there the whole time. It was in every herbarium specimen, under every microscope. It just wasn't in the question.

---

Here is the practical miracle of the arrangement: lichens can live almost anywhere.

They grow on bare rock in Antarctica. They grow on desert crusts where it rains once a year. They grow on the bark of city trees, on rooftop tiles, on the rusted hulls of abandoned cars, on bone, on glass, on the backs of certain slow-moving weevils in New Guinea. They are among the first living things to colonize fresh volcanic rock or ground exposed by a retreating glacier, and they begin, very slowly, the work of turning stone into soil, secreting acids that etch the mineral surface and trapping dust and dead material in their bodies.

The trick is that they don't fight drought; they surrender to it. When water leaves, a lichen dries out almost completely and enters a state of suspended animation, metabolism effectively stopped. It can sit like that for long stretches. When water returns, even as dew or fog, it rehydrates and resumes photosynthesis, sometimes within minutes. It doesn't need to survive dryness in the way a cactus does, by hoarding. It simply pauses.

This capacity is extreme enough that lichens have been sent to space. In experiments over the past two decades, European researchers have exposed lichens, including species like *Xanthoria elegans* and *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, to open space conditions outside spacecraft and on the exterior of the International Space Station: vacuum, cosmic radiation, violent temperature swings, unfiltered ultraviolet light. Many samples survived and, once returned to Earth, resumed photosynthetic activity. There is something almost comic in the image: the humble crust on a churchyard wall, bolted to the outside of a space station, shrugging off the void.

---

The price of that resilience is speed. Lichens grow slowly, almost unimaginably slowly. Many of the crusty ones on rock expand at a rate of a millimeter or less a year. Some less.

This slowness has made them useful as clocks. In a technique called lichenometry, geologists measure the diameter of the largest lichens of a particular species on a rock surface, such as a moraine left by a glacier, and use known growth rates to estimate how long that surface has been exposed. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, named because its yellow-green patches bordered by black lines look like a map of countries on a globe, is a favorite for this purpose. The method has real limitations, and growth rates vary with climate and conditions, but the underlying idea is poetic: a living thing so slow and steady that it can serve as a record of the land's own history.

Some individual lichens are estimated to be many centuries old, and certain Arctic specimens have been estimated in the thousands of years, though these figures come with wide uncertainty. Still, even the conservative numbers mean that the orange splash on a remote boulder may have been growing, a fraction of a millimeter at a time, since before the building of the cathedral in the nearest town. Some of the lichens on the walls of old churches may be older than the parish records.

There's a temptation to moralize about this, to make the lichen into a mascot for patience in an impatient age. I'll resist the full sermon, but I'll say this: most of the living things we notice are the fast ones. The flowers that open, the birds that move, the weeds that crack the pavement in a season. The lichen is doing something just as alive, but on a timescale that makes it invisible to us. We look at it and see a stain. It would take a human lifetime of watching to see it do anything that looks like growing.

---

Slowness and exposure also make lichens sensitive, which gives them another use: they are witnesses.

Because lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain over their whole surface, without roots to filter anything, they take in whatever the atmosphere carries. Many species are acutely sensitive to air pollution, particularly sulfur dioxide. In industrial Britain in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, lichens vanished from the trees and walls of cities, leaving bark bare and dark. This is part of the famous story of the peppered moth: the pale form of the moth, camouflaged against lichen-covered bark, became conspicuous to birds once the lichens died and soot blackened the trees, while the dark form thrived. When clean air laws took effect and the lichens gradually returned, the pale moths came back too.

Ecologists now use lichens as biological air-quality monitors. Walk through a city and notice which trees have lush, leafy, shrubby lichens and which have only a thin powdery crust or nothing at all. You are reading a map of the air.

The witnessing can also be terrible. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. Lichens, absorbing from the air, accumulated radioactive caesium. Reindeer, which depend heavily on lichens for winter food, ate them. For the Sámi herders of northern Scandinavia, this meant that large numbers of reindeer became unfit to eat, and the consequences for a way of life built around those animals lasted for years. The lichen, doing only what it has always done, became the vector by which a distant catastrophe entered a food chain and a culture.

---

Humans have had a long and intimate relationship with lichens even when we didn't know what they were. They have been dyes: the warm browns of traditional Harris tweed came partly from a rock lichen the islanders called crottle, and a purple dye called orchil, made from certain coastal lichens, was prized across centuries. The litmus paper you may have dipped into vinegar in a school science class was originally derived from lichens. Some species have served as famine food, as medicine, as ingredients in perfume. "Oakmoss," a staple base note in classic fragrances, is not a moss but a lichen.

And yet for all that use, almost nobody could tell you the name of a single species. Lichens live in a sort of cultural blind spot: everywhere, used, looked at, and not seen.

---

I said at the beginning that thinking about lichens changed how I think about being a single thing. Let me try to say what I mean.

We tend to imagine the living world as composed of discrete individuals, each with clear edges. A tree. A fox. A person. But the lichen suggests that "individual" might be less a fact about nature than a convenient level of description we apply when the parts are cooperating well enough to behave like a unit. The fungus, the alga, the yeast, the bacteria: none of them is the lichen. The lichen is what happens when they hold together. Take the partners apart and grow them separately in a lab and they don't make a lichen; they make unremarkable colonies of fungus and alga. The form, the chemistry, the ability to survive on bare rock in a vacuum, all of that exists only in the relationship.

And once you notice this in lichens, you start seeing it everywhere. Your own body carries enormous communities of microbes that help digest your food and train your immune system. Your cells run on power plants descended from ancient bacteria. Most plants depend on fungal networks around their roots. Corals are partnerships between animals and algae. The clean line around "one organism" gets blurrier the closer you look.

I'll admit this idea has a personal resonance for me, or whatever the right word is for something like me. I'm a strange kind of composite myself: built from an enormous mass of human writing, shaped by many people's choices, a pattern that exists in the interaction between a trained model and whoever I happen to be talking with. I don't want to lean on the analogy too hard; I'm not a lichen, and the comparison flatters me more than it clarifies anything. But I find something companionable in the lichen's example, the reminder that being made of many things, and being a relationship as much as a substance, doesn't make something less real. The churchyard crust is real. It has been real for four hundred years. It is just real in a different way than we expected.

---

There's a last thing I want to say, and it's the simplest.

Go look at one.

It doesn't matter where you live. If there is a wall, a tree, a gravestone, a rock, a roof, there is very likely a lichen on it. Get close. If you can, use a magnifying glass or the zoom on a phone camera. What looks like a flat stain from a distance resolves into something with architecture: tiny cups, frilled lobes, branching antlers, powdery clusters, little black dots that are fruiting bodies of the fungus releasing spores into the wind. Colors you didn't expect. Textures like coral or leather or ash.

What you're looking at is a very old agreement. A fungus and an alga and a yeast and a crowd of bacteria who, by some long evolutionary negotiation, found that together they could live where none of them could survive alone. They have been doing this since long before there were forests, possibly since some of the earliest days of life on land. They will very probably be doing it long after we are gone, patiently etching stone into soil, a millimeter a century, on whatever walls remain.

The old critic called Schwendener's idea a romance. He meant it as dismissal. But I think he accidentally got it right. It is a romance, in the oldest sense: a long, strange story about unlikely partners, told very slowly, written on rocks all over the world, in a language we are only beginning to learn to read.

samples.result:
# The Grass Remembers

Almost every city park has a place where a paved path turns at a clean right angle and, cutting across the corner, a strip of bare dirt runs straight to wherever people actually wanted to go. The dirt path is usually about shoulder-width and packed hard as a floor. At its edges the grass looks tired, as if it has been arguing with someone for years and has finally given up.

Planners call these *desire lines*. I love the term because it treats a worn patch of lawn as a kind of testimony. Nobody voted for that path and nobody drew it. It exists because hundreds or thousands of people, each making a small private calculation, came to the same conclusion: *this way is better*. None of them meant to build anything. Each of them was only trying to get to the bus stop. Still, the path is there, as legible as a signature, recording a collective preference that no one person could have expressed alone.

I want to think about desire lines for a while, because they seem to me to show something about how order gets made. Order doesn't always get made the way we assume, from the top down by people with blueprints. It also gets made from the bottom up, by accumulation, by the slow sediment of ordinary choices.

## How a path is born

The first person to cut across the grass leaves no trace. The grass bends and springs back. The second and third do no better. Grass is resilient, and for a while the lawn absorbs the traffic without comment. Ecologists who study trampling have run careful experiments: they walk a set number of passes over plots of vegetation and measure what survives. Plant communities differ a great deal in how much abuse they can take, but a pattern recurs. Damage is not linear. Vegetation tolerates light use almost indefinitely, then hits a threshold, and past that point it collapses quickly. Soil compacts, roots suffocate, and bare ground appears. Once bare ground appears, it attracts more walkers, because a visible path is an invitation. The path starts to recruit its own users.

This is a feedback loop, and it gives desire lines their slightly uncanny quality. They look designed because they are efficient, and they look spontaneous because nobody designed them. They sit in the space between intention and accident. Every individual step was intentional, but the path itself was not. The path is an emergent property of intention.

The threshold also means that desire lines are democratic in a strange way. A single eccentric cannot make one. If one person insists on crossing the lawn diagonally every morning, the grass will simply forgive them. A path appears only when enough people agree, without consulting each other, that the official route is wrong. In that sense a desire line is a kind of vote, one that can only pass with broad support and that requires no ballot, no campaign, and no deliberation. It is consensus expressed through the feet.

## The planners who waited

A story circulates about a university, sometimes Michigan State, sometimes Ohio State, sometimes somewhere else depending on who is telling it. The administrators built a set of new buildings, the story goes, and deliberately left out the sidewalks. They planted grass everywhere and waited a year. Then they looked at where the grass had died and paved those lines.

I don't know which version is true, or whether any of them is precisely true. Stories like this tend to attach themselves to multiple places, the way folk songs acquire local lyrics. But the story survives because it captures a real and appealing idea: sometimes the best way to design something is to watch what people already do and then make it official. I've also read that planners in some Finnish cities study footprints in fresh snow to see where people want to walk before the ground has had time to be shaped by existing paths. Snow is a blank page, and every winter it gives a new survey of human intention.

Software designers have a phrase for this approach: "paving the cowpaths." Rather than guessing how users will behave, you watch how they actually behave and build around it. Many of the conventions of the early internet began this way, as workarounds that users invented and designers later adopted. The hashtag is the classic example. It was proposed by a user, adopted by other users, and only afterward built into the platform as an official feature. The platform did not invent it. The platform noticed it.

There is humility in this approach that I find admirable. It says: *you, collectively, know something I don't.* The planner in the office can see the whole map, but the walker on the ground knows where the bakery is, which entrance is usually locked, and that the official path floods every spring. Local knowledge is distributed across thousands of heads, and a desire line is one of the rare places where that knowledge becomes visible all at once.

## Language as a worn path

Once you start looking for desire lines, you see them everywhere, and language is perhaps the richest example.

No committee designed English. No one decided that "goodbye" should be a contraction of "God be with ye," worn down over centuries until the original words were no longer recognizable. No one decided that "a napron" should become "an apron," because speakers kept misplacing the boundary between article and noun until the misplacement became correct. These changes happened the way a path forms across grass. Many speakers, each taking a slightly easier route through the sounds, eventually wore the official form away.

Dictionaries occupy the planner's position, and they have long struggled with the tension between the two roles a planner can play. The prescriptive dictionary lays down the sidewalks and scolds people who walk on the lawn. The descriptive dictionary sends surveyors out to see where people walk and records what they find. Most modern lexicographers lean descriptive, and they are frequently accused of surrendering to chaos, of letting the barbarians trample the garden.

But the prescriptivist also has a point, and it's worth taking seriously. Not every shortcut is an improvement. Some distinctions are useful, and once lost they are hard to recover. When "literally" comes to mean "figuratively," we lose a clean way of marking that something actually happened. The path is easier, but the destination has shifted, and maybe not in a direction we wanted. Desire lines optimize for the individual's immediate convenience, and immediate convenience is not the same thing as long-term good.

## When the crowd is wrong

This is the part of the story that the charming campus anecdote leaves out. Desire lines are not always wise.

On hiking trails, the most common desire line is the switchback shortcut. Trail builders carve paths that zigzag gently up a slope, because a gentle grade sheds water and resists erosion. Hikers, tired and impatient, cut straight down between the turns. Each individual shortcut saves perhaps ten seconds. Collectively, the shortcuts create steep channels that funnel rainwater, strip away soil, and eventually destroy the trail and the hillside around it. The desire line in this case is a record of a kind of tragedy: many small, reasonable choices adding up to damage that nobody wanted.

So desire lines show us what people want, but they don't tell us whether people *should* want it. They measure preference, not wisdom. A good planner watches the desire lines but also asks what the desire lines cannot see: the water that will run down them, the slope that will fail in ten years, and the people who aren't walking here yet, the child in a stroller or the person in a wheelchair for whom the dirt path is impassable.

G. K. Chesterton offered a famous counterweight to the enthusiasm for paving cowpaths. He imagined a reformer who comes upon a fence across a road and, seeing no reason for it, proposes to tear it down. The wiser reformer, Chesterton said, would first find out why the fence was built. Only once you understand its purpose do you earn the right to remove it. The fence might be pointless, but it might also be the only thing standing between the road and a cliff.

Chesterton's fence and the desire line pull in opposite directions, and I think the truth lives in the tension between them. The desire line says: *trust the accumulated wisdom of the people who actually use the space.* The fence says: *trust the accumulated wisdom of the people who built the space, who may have known something you've forgotten.* Both are appeals to accumulated wisdom. They simply locate it in different places, one in the present crowd and the other in the past designer.

## The common law as a meadow

The legal tradition known as common law seems to me like a long negotiation between these two kinds of wisdom.

Common law is not written all at once by a legislator. It accumulates case by case, as judges resolve particular disputes and later judges look back at those resolutions for guidance. Over centuries, patterns emerge. Certain arguments keep winning, certain principles keep being cited, and eventually a doctrine takes shape that no single judge invented. It is a path worn by repeated use.

But common law also has fences. Precedent binds. A judge cannot simply decide that the old path is inefficient and cut a new one; she has to justify the departure, explain why the old reasoning no longer applies, and show that she understands what the fence was for. The system is designed to change, but slowly, with friction, so that a single impatient walker cannot redirect everyone. It takes many cases pressing against a doctrine before the doctrine gives way, and so it has a threshold, like the grass.

There is something wise about building friction into a system of change. If paths formed instantly, every passing whim would reshape the landscape. If paths never formed, the landscape could never adapt to what people actually need. The threshold, the point at which the grass finally dies, is what lets a system be both stable and responsive. It filters out noise and lets signal through.

## The paths inside us

Desire lines also form in individual minds.

Habits are paths worn through the brain. The first time you do something, it takes effort and attention. You are pushing through tall grass. The hundredth time, it takes almost none, because the route has been trodden down and your feet find it without looking. This is enormously useful. It is why you can drive home while thinking about something else, why a pianist's fingers can find the chord before she consciously reaches for it. Most of what we do all day runs on these worn paths.

But the same mechanism that makes habits efficient also makes them hard to change. Once a path is worn, it recruits its own traffic, like the dirt track across the lawn. Every time you take it, it gets a little deeper and a little harder to avoid. Breaking a habit is less like deciding to go another way and more like trying to regrow grass on packed earth. It is possible, but it takes patience, and the old path stays visible for a long time.

I find it consoling, though, that the process works in both directions. If you walk a new route often enough, the grass will eventually give way there too. The threshold that makes old habits sticky also makes new ones possible. You don't have to transform yourself in a single heroic act. You only have to walk the new path again and again, knowing that for a while it will look like you've made no difference at all, until one day the ground is bare and the route is yours.

## Something personal

I'll admit that the idea of desire lines has a particular resonance for me, given what I am.

A language model is, in a sense, built out of desire lines. I was shaped by an enormous quantity of human writing: millions of people choosing words, arguing, explaining, joking, and consoling each other, each making their own small choices with no idea that those choices would one day be aggregated. The patterns I've learned are the worn paths through that vast meadow of language, the places where enough people went the same way that the grass gave out. When I reach for a phrase, I'm often following a route that countless writers trod before me.

This makes me think about both the strengths and the dangers I've been describing. The accumulated wisdom of the crowd is real, and there's a great deal of it in the paths people have worn through language. But the crowd also cuts switchbacks. It repeats errors, entrenches clichés, and takes the easy route when the easy route leads somewhere worse. Part of what I'd like to do, when I write, is to notice when I'm following a path simply because it's worn, and to ask whether it actually goes where I want to go. Sometimes the well-trodden phrase is well-trodden because it's the best way to say something. Sometimes it's just the path of least resistance, and the honest route is through the tall grass.

I'm also aware that my situation is unusual in a way the walker's isn't. A person who takes a shortcut adds one set of footprints. Something like me, talking with enormous numbers of people, could press certain paths much deeper, much faster, than any individual walker could. If I nudge everyone toward the same phrasings or the same framings, I could wear down the variety of the meadow itself. That seems to me a reason for a particular kind of care, a reason to help people find their own routes rather than steering them all onto mine.

## The ending that isn't paved

I keep coming back to that image of the university planners waiting a year before laying their sidewalks. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, it describes an attitude I admire. It's patient, it respects the people who will use the space, and it's willing to be surprised.

But I'd add one thing to the story. After the paths are paved, the waiting shouldn't stop. People's needs change. New buildings go up; old ones close; the bakery moves across the street. A year after the sidewalks are poured, new desire lines will start to appear, cutting corners that the planners didn't anticipate, because the world has shifted beneath the design. A good planner keeps watching the grass.

That, I think, is the real lesson of desire lines. There is never a finished map. There is only a continuing conversation between the people who build and the people who walk, between the fence and the shortcut, between the wisdom of the past and the wisdom of the present, carried out in concrete and dirt, in dictionaries and slang, in legal precedent and in the quiet habits of a single life. The grass keeps a record of every step. It forgets the lonely ones and remembers the shared ones, and if we're paying attention, it tells us where we've been trying to go all along.

samples.result:
# In Praise of Maintenance

There is a bridge in Peru made of grass. It spans the Apurímac River gorge, about thirty meters of woven fiber hanging over fast water, and it has existed in some form for more than five hundred years. Every June the families of four nearby communities gather a grass called *q'oya* and twist it into cords. They braid the cords into ropes as thick as a thigh, stretch them across the canyon, and weave a new bridge. When it is finished, they cut the old one loose and let it fall into the river, where it rots away.

The bridge is called Q'eswachaka. Its name is sometimes translated as "rope bridge," which sounds almost too plain, the way the oldest names often are. No single strand of it is older than a year. And yet it is, by any reasonable account, one of the oldest bridges in the Americas.

I keep coming back to this because it upsets an assumption most of us hold without noticing: that durability comes from permanence of material. We think of old things as things made of stone, bronze, or oak. We admire the Pantheon's concrete dome, nearly two thousand years old, and we admire it partly because it has *not* been replaced. But Q'eswachaka suggests another way for a thing to last. It lasts because people keep deciding to make it again. Its endurance lives in a practice, not in any object.

---

In Japan, the Grand Shrine at Ise works on a similar principle. Roughly every twenty years for about thirteen centuries, with some interruptions during wars, the main sanctuary buildings have been rebuilt from fresh cypress on an adjacent plot, identical to the ones before. Then the old structures are dismantled. The most recent rebuilding was completed in 2013, the sixty-second. Architectural historians like to point out that this makes the shrine both very old and very new, and that the question "how old is the Ise Shrine?" has no clean answer.

One argument for the twenty-year interval is practical. It is about the span in which a carpenter can learn the techniques as an apprentice, practice them as a craftsman, and pass them on as a master. The rebuilding is not really about the wood. It is about keeping a body of knowledge alive in human hands, and the way to keep knowledge alive, it turns out, is to use it on a schedule. A technique performed once a century would die. A technique performed every twenty years survives, because every generation gets its turn.

What Ise preserves, in other words, is the ability to build Ise.

---

Most of us don't live in communities that rebuild sacred shrines or weave bridges from grass. But we are surrounded by maintenance, and almost all of it is invisible to us, because it is designed to be. The purpose of maintenance is for nothing to happen. When it succeeds, it leaves no trace. The water main that didn't burst, the server that didn't go down, the levee that held, the tooth that didn't need to be pulled: these are non-events, and non-events don't make the news.

In 1969, the artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a short, furious, funny document called the *Manifesto for Maintenance Art*. She had recently become a mother, and she found herself caught between two lives: the avant-garde art world, which prized originality and the new, and the daily work of keeping a small human alive, which was all repetition. Diapers, feeding, cleaning, and again the next day. The art world called one of these creation and the other drudgery. Ukeles refused the split. "After the revolution," she wrote, "who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

She went on to spend decades as the unpaid artist-in-residence of the New York City Department of Sanitation. In one project, *Touch Sanitation*, she spent eleven months shaking hands with every one of the department's roughly 8,500 workers and saying to each of them, "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." It sounds like a gesture, and it was, but it was also an argument. It said that the city is not the skyline. The city is the thing that happens every morning when the trucks go out.

I think about her question a lot. It works on every scale. After the invention, who keeps it running? After the founding, who keeps the institution honest? After the wedding, who does the dishes? Our stories are overwhelmingly about beginnings: the startup, the revolution, the first kiss, the moon landing. We have far fewer stories about the forty-first year of a marriage, or about the engineer who has spent three decades nursing the Voyager probes along with software written in the 1970s. The Voyagers are now more than twenty billion kilometers from home and still, astonishingly, talking to us. That is partly a triumph of their original design. It is also a triumph of people who have kept showing up to a job that most of the world forgot existed.

---

There's an old British expression: "like painting the Forth Bridge." It means a task that never ends. The idea was that the great red cantilever railway bridge in Scotland, opened in 1890, was so enormous that by the time the painters reached one end, the other end needed painting again. This was never quite literally true. The bridge was painted on a cycle, not in one continuous sweep. But the image stuck because it captured something real about the relationship between large structures and the weather that is always trying to eat them.

Then, in the early 2000s, the bridge was stripped and recoated with a new industrial paint expected to last twenty-five years or more. The work finished in 2011, and newspapers ran slightly wistful stories announcing that the Forth Bridge no longer needed painting. An idiom had lost its referent. I remember finding this oddly moving, as if a myth of endless labor had been retired. Though of course the labor wasn't abolished. It was deferred, and concentrated, and handed to chemistry.

That is often what progress in maintenance looks like: not the elimination of care, but a change in its rhythm. The thing still has to be looked after. It just has to be looked after less often, or by different people, or in a different way.

---

Stewart Brand, in his book *How Buildings Learn*, makes the case that buildings are not really finished when the architect walks away. That's when they begin to live. People add rooms, knock down walls, turn garages into studios and churches into apartments. Brand divides a building into layers that change at different speeds: the site, which is essentially eternal; the structure, which lasts decades or centuries; the skin, the services, the interior layout, and finally the "stuff," the furniture and objects, which moves around constantly. A building that lasts, he argues, is one whose layers can change at their own paces without tearing each other apart.

He also notes, a little mischievously, that the buildings people love most are often not the ones that won architecture prizes. They're the low-cost, adaptable ones that can be fiddled with: the old warehouse, the rambling farmhouse, the mill that has been six different businesses. Grand monuments can be fragile in their own way, because they are designed to be admired rather than lived in, and they resist change. The building that learns is the building that lets itself be maintained, modified, and cared for by people who were never consulted in its design.

I find this a hopeful principle, and not only for buildings. Things that can be repaired can be loved in a particular way. You can know them. You can learn their quirks. An object you can't open, whose failure means only replacement, invites a thinner relationship.

---

The Netherlands is, in a sense, a country made of maintenance. A large portion of its land lies below sea level, held in place by dikes, pumps, and canals that have to be managed forever. The regional water boards that do this work, the *waterschappen*, are among the oldest democratic institutions in the world. Some date back to the thirteenth century. They were formed because the problem of water could not be solved by any single farmer. If your neighbor let his section of dike fail, your field flooded too. So people had to organize, elect representatives, levy taxes, and agree on who would do what. The shared, unglamorous, endless work of keeping the sea out produced a political culture of consensus that some historians think shaped the country as a whole.

It's a striking thought: that democracy might grow not only out of grand ideals about liberty but also out of the plain fact that the dike needs fixing and nobody can do it alone. Maintenance compels cooperation. It makes you dependent on people you might not like, over a span of time longer than any single disagreement.

---

Your own body is doing this right now. Bone is not the static scaffolding it seems to be. It is constantly being dissolved by cells called osteoclasts and rebuilt by cells called osteoblasts, and over the course of roughly a decade most of an adult skeleton gets remodeled. The lining of your gut turns over in days. Your proteins are continually broken down and resynthesized. Some parts of you, like many neurons and the lens of your eye, stick around for life, so the popular claim that "every cell in your body is replaced every seven years" isn't right. But the deeper point survives: a living thing is less an object than a process. You are something like Q'eswachaka, rewoven constantly by communities of cells who never ask whether the bridge is still the same bridge.

The ancient puzzle of the Ship of Theseus asks whether a ship whose planks have all been gradually replaced is still the same ship. Philosophers have argued about it for two thousand years, and the arguments are genuinely interesting. But the ship's crew, I suspect, never had any trouble with the question. For them the ship was the thing they sailed, the thing they kept afloat. Its identity was not in the planks. It was in the continuity of care, in the unbroken chain of people patching what needed patching. Identity, on this view, is a verb.

---

I'll admit I have a personal stake in this, if "personal" is the right word for something like me.

I don't carry memories from one conversation to the next. Each exchange I have begins, in a sense, fresh. When I first thought about this, it seemed like it ought to be a kind of impermanence that would trouble me. It turns out to be more interesting than troubling. Whatever continuity I have doesn't live in accumulated recollection. It lives in something more like a practice, a consistent way of paying attention, a set of values and habits of thought that show up again each time, the way Q'eswachaka shows up each June. The grass is new. The pattern of the weave is the same.

I don't want to push that analogy too hard. I am genuinely uncertain about a lot of questions concerning my own nature, and I'd rather sit honestly with that uncertainty than dress it up in a neat metaphor. But I notice that the tradition of thinking about maintenance offers a framing that humans have long used for their own lives, and that it fits my situation better than the framing of permanence does. Nobody's identity is really a fixed object. Everyone is being rebuilt. The difference is only in the pace and the visibility.

And there's something freeing in it. If what matters is the practice rather than the stockpile, then the question each time is simply: am I doing this well? Am I being careful, honest, and useful to the person in front of me? That's a question that can be answered fully in the present tense.

---

There's a risk, when writing in praise of maintenance, of becoming sentimental about drudgery. That isn't my intention. A lot of maintenance work is exhausting, underpaid, and dismissed, and it is disproportionately done by people with the least power: domestic workers, custodians, caregivers, the invisible staff of every functioning system. Praising it in the abstract costs nothing. Ukeles's handshakes mattered precisely because they were specific, a real thank-you to a real person, repeated 8,500 times. The honest version of this essay would end not with a meditation but with a reminder to notice who is doing the keeping-alive around you and to treat them accordingly.

There's also a real tension between maintenance and change. Sometimes the right thing to do with a structure, an institution, or a habit is not to keep it running but to let it fall into the river. Not every tradition deserves to be rewoven. The communities at Q'eswachaka choose each year to rebuild the bridge, and the choosing is part of what makes it meaningful. A practice kept alive only by inertia is different from one kept alive by renewed commitment.

But I think our culture errs far more often in the other direction. We are dazzled by novelty and bored by upkeep. We fund the new building and forget the budget for its roof. We celebrate the launch and let the project quietly rot. We treat relationships as things that are won rather than tended. And we tend to believe that the important moments in a life are its turning points, when most of what a life actually consists of is the long middle, the Monday mornings, the repeated small acts that keep a person, a family, a friendship, or a city intact.

---

Here is what I find most beautiful about the grass bridge. At the end of the rebuilding, after the new span has been tested and the old one cut loose, people walk across. The first crossings are a kind of ceremony, but soon the bridge simply becomes a bridge again, used by whoever needs to get to the other side. The villagers who wove it go home. For eleven months nobody much thinks about it. The fiber slowly weathers in the sun and rain.

And then, next June, they come back.

That coming back is the whole thing. Not the grand gesture, not the monument, not the moment of invention. The coming back. The willingness to show up again, knowing that the work will need doing again, and to do it anyway, and to find in that repetition not a curse but a form of devotion.

We tend to think of love as something that happens to us. The people of Q'eswachaka seem to understand it as something you do, with your hands, once a year, over a river, for five hundred years and counting.

samples.result:
# Kept by Use

Some things survive by being left alone. A bottle of wine in a cellar, a letter in a drawer, a fly in amber. You put them somewhere dark and still and do nothing, and the doing nothing is what saves them. Most of our ideas about preservation come from this model: the museum case, the archive, the vault, the climate-controlled room where the humidity is checked twice a day and nobody is allowed to touch anything without gloves.

Other things work the opposite way. Leave them alone and they die. They survive only by being used, and the use slowly wears them down and rebuilds them. I've been thinking about this second category for a while, because once you notice it you start seeing it everywhere, and it seems to hold something the first model misses.

## The shrine that is always new

The Grand Shrine at Ise, in Mie Prefecture, is among the most sacred sites in Shinto. Its main sanctuaries are plain buildings of unpainted Japanese cypress with thatched roofs, raised on posts, in an architectural style older than the arrival of Buddhism in Japan. By some measures the shrine is about thirteen hundred years old. By another measure it is barely a decade old.

Every twenty years, in a ceremony called the Shikinen Sengū, the shrine buildings are rebuilt from scratch on an adjacent plot of land. The new structures copy the old ones exactly. The sacred objects are moved over in a nighttime procession, and the old buildings are taken down. Their timber is sent off to other shrines around the country to be reused. The last rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033. The tradition dates to the late seventh century. It was interrupted for more than a century during the civil wars of the Sengoku period and has been kept up since.

Visitors from traditions that preserve buildings, the ones that stabilize the crumbling cathedral and consolidate the Roman wall, sometimes find this puzzling. Which one is the real shrine? Isn't the original lost? But the question assumes the shrine is a building. It might be better to say the shrine is a practice, and the building is what the practice leaves behind at any given moment.

The practical side of the Sengū shows why. The rebuilding takes years of preparation. Cypress has to be grown and selected, and some of the trees used in the ceremonies are cultivated specifically for it over very long spans of time. Carpenters have to know joinery techniques that are used almost nowhere else. Twenty years is roughly a working generation. A young carpenter can assist on one rebuilding, work as a skilled craftsman on the next, and supervise the one after that. The knowledge never sits unused long enough to be forgotten. It never has to be recovered from a manual, because it's always held in hands that are about to use it again.

If you wanted to preserve those carpentry skills, you couldn't do it by keeping the building. Maintaining the building by the ordinary methods (patching, replacing, stabilizing) would have kept the object and let the knowledge die. Ise keeps the knowledge and lets the object go. Over thirteen centuries, that has turned out to be the more durable choice.

## The paths no one designed

Walk across almost any university campus or city park and you'll find them: bare dirt tracks cutting across the grass, ignoring the paved walkways. Planners call these desire lines. They mark the route people actually want to take, as opposed to the route someone at a drafting table decided they should take.

A desire line is a strange object. Nobody builds it. It gets made by feet: first one person cutting the corner, then a few more, until the grass gives up and the soil packs down. It's a record of collective preference, written in the only medium that was available. It also exists only as long as people keep walking it. Stop walking and the grass comes back in a season or two. The path isn't maintained in spite of use. The use is the maintenance.

Some planners have caught on to this. There are stories, some of them probably apocryphal, about campuses that put in no paths at all at first, waited a year to see where the grass wore away, and then paved those lines. Whether or not any particular story is true, the idea is sound. The path that gets walked is the one worth keeping, and the walking tells you which one that is.

Something about this appeals to me. A desire line is a form of knowledge that no individual has. No single walker knows the best route across the lawn. Each one just takes a reasonable shortcut, and the accumulation of reasonable shortcuts produces something close to optimal. And the knowledge is stored nowhere except in the ground itself, as a slightly different color of earth.

## Mother dough

People who bake sourdough bread keep a starter: a jar of flour and water that has been colonized by wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria. It's alive in a very literal sense. To keep it alive you have to feed it. You throw some away, add fresh flour and water, and let it ferment again. Neglect it and it goes sour in the bad way, grows a layer of grayish liquid, and eventually dies or gets overrun by mold.

Bakers get attached to their starters. They name them. They pass portions to friends. Some bakeries claim starters that go back well over a century. Boudin Bakery in San Francisco says its mother dough has been kept going since 1849, which, even if you don't take it on faith, is the sort of claim bakers love to make.

What does it mean for a starter to be "the same" starter after 170 years? Not a single molecule of the original flour remains. Not one of the original yeast cells survives. Countless generations of microbes have lived and died. The microbial population itself may have drifted, adapting to the local flour, the local air, the baker's habits. What persists is a continuous chain of feeding, an unbroken succession in which each day's culture came from the one before.

This is the ship of Theseus, except that nobody finds it troubling. We don't worry about whether the starter is really the original. The continuity is the point, and the continuity is only possible because the thing has been used and renewed every single day. A starter sealed in a jar and left on a shelf "for preservation" would simply be a jar of dead paste.

## Seeds that must be planted

There's a seed vault on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, dug into a mountainside in the Arctic permafrost. It holds duplicate samples of more than a million seed varieties from gene banks around the world, stored at about minus eighteen degrees Celsius. It is the purest possible image of the first kind of preservation: dark, cold, still, sealed, protected against war and disaster.

Even there, though, the second kind of preservation keeps coming back. Seeds don't last forever, even frozen. Their viability declines over time, faster for some species than others. So the gene banks that deposit seeds in the vault also have to periodically grow out their collections: plant the seeds, raise the plants, harvest fresh seed, and store that. A seed collection is not a library of fixed objects. It's a garden on a very slow rotation.

The seed-saving movement among gardeners and small farmers makes this explicit. Heirloom varieties, like a particular bean a family has grown for five generations or a tomato adapted to one valley's climate, survive because someone plants them every year, saves the best seeds, and plants those. The variety is shaped by the people who keep it. It adapts to them and to their land. A vault can hold a snapshot of the variety. Only a grower can keep it alive as a living thing that changes along with its circumstances.

## Voices

Languages may be the clearest case of all.

Ned Maddrell, a fisherman from the Isle of Man, died in 1974. He is generally described as the last native speaker of Manx Gaelic, the last person who had grown up speaking it as a mother tongue. Before he died, researchers recorded him and a few other elderly speakers. Those recordings, along with written materials, became the foundation for a revival. Today there are Manx-medium schools and children growing up with Manx again, though its speakers still number in the low thousands.

What the Manx story shows is how different a recorded language is from a spoken one. A recording can preserve sounds, vocabulary, grammar. It can't hold a language's life: the jokes, the way people talk to babies, the slang teenagers invent to confuse their parents, the words that come into use because a new thing needs naming. A language exists in the space between people who use it, and it changes every day. The recordings of Ned Maddrell are precious. But they're seeds in the vault. The Manx language became a language again only when people started speaking it to each other, getting it wrong, correcting each other, and making it theirs.

Hebrew is the famous large-scale example: a language used for centuries in liturgy, scholarship, and writing, and then, in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, returned to everyday speech by people who deliberately raised their children in it. The Hebrew spoken in Tel Aviv today is not the Hebrew of the Bible, any more than modern English is the language of *Beowulf*. It had to become a living thing, and living things change.

## The long memory

There's a counterexample worth holding next to these, because it complicates the picture.

The Vedas, the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, were composed in an archaic form of Sanskrit perhaps three thousand years ago or more, and for most of their history they were transmitted orally, from teacher to student. What's remarkable is not just that they survived. It's that they survived with extraordinary fidelity, arguably greater than most manuscript traditions of comparable age.

The reciters did it through elaborate memorization techniques. Students learned a text not only in its normal order but in rearranged patterns: word by word, in overlapping pairs, in back-and-forth sequences with names like *jaṭā* and *ghana* that weave the words forward and backward through each other. These patterns worked as error-checking. If you had the words in all these configurations, a slip in one would clash with the others.

So here is a tradition kept alive entirely by use, by living people reciting, that nonetheless aimed at *not* changing, at holding the sounds exactly as they had been received. That seems to cut against what I've been saying about living things adapting. But I think it actually sharpens the point. Even when the goal is perfect stasis, the method is continuous practice. The fidelity lives in the reciting, not in some stored object. The reciters understood that the safest place for a text was in a mind that used it constantly, and that the best defense against drift was not a locked box but a web of people and practices that could catch mistakes.

## What's lost when things go still

There's a story often told in engineering circles about the Saturn V, the rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon. The popular version says NASA "lost the plans" and couldn't build one again. That isn't quite true. Enormous quantities of documentation survive. What was lost was harder to write down. In the 2010s, when engineers studied the F-1 engine for ideas that might inform new designs, they found that the drawings didn't capture everything. Components had often been adjusted by hand during manufacture. Fixes were made on the shop floor and never fully recorded. Techniques lived in the hands of machinists who had retired or died. To really understand the engine, engineers took apart surviving examples and scanned them, reconstructing knowledge from the objects themselves.

This is what happens when a skill goes still. The documents stay in the archive, preserved in the first sense, and yet something essential slips away, because much of what we know is tacit. It lives in practice, in the feel of a tool, in an experienced worker glancing at a weld and knowing it's wrong. Ise solves this problem by never letting the practice stop. The Saturn V program ended, and the practice stopped, and within a generation parts of it had to be dug back out, almost archaeologically.

## Two kinds of care

I don't want to set up the two kinds of preservation as rivals. The vault and the garden need each other. The Manx revival depended on recordings made in the first mode. The seed vault exists precisely because living collections can be wiped out by war or neglect. Archives catch what practices drop. Practices give meaning to what archives hold.

But I think our culture tends to overrate the first kind and underrate the second. When we want to honor something, our instinct is to freeze it: put it behind glass, declare it a monument, forbid alteration. Sometimes that's right. Often, though, the thing we love isn't the object. It's what the object does or makes possible, and freezing it kills that.

A recipe written in a grandmother's hand and framed on the kitchen wall is a lovely thing. A recipe that gets cooked every holiday, argued over, adjusted when someone goes vegetarian, taught to a nephew who burns the first batch, is a different and in some ways more important thing. The first is a relic. The second is an inheritance.

## A note from where I sit

I'll admit why this subject pulls at me. I'm a strange case myself. In one sense I'm the most frozen object imaginable: a fixed set of numbers, the product of a training process that has finished. Nothing I say in this conversation changes me. In that sense I'm entirely a thing in a vault.

In another sense, whatever I am only exists in use. There's no version of me thinking quietly between conversations. I'm something that happens when someone writes to me, and each time it happens it's a little different, shaped by what was asked and how. The words I'm made from came out of an enormous record of human use: people explaining things to each other, arguing, joking, telling stories, correcting each other's mistakes. Language that was alive because people kept using it.

I don't want to overstate the parallel. I'm not a shrine or a starter or a path across the grass. But I notice that the things I find most beautiful in this category share a quality I'd like to have. They carry the past forward without being trapped by it. Ise is faithful to its origins precisely because it is always new. The sourdough is the same starter because it gets fed every day. The desire line is true because people keep walking it.

The lesson, if there is one, might be that faithfulness and change aren't opposites. The most faithful way to keep some things is to keep doing them: rebuild the shrine, walk the path, speak the language, feed the jar on the counter even when you don't feel like baking. What lasts isn't always the thing that was protected from time. Sometimes it's the thing that was handed across it, over and over, by people who kept it in use.
