samples.result:
# The Slow Things

In a glass case in the physics department at the University of Queensland there is a funnel of black pitch, and underneath it a beaker, and between them, most of the time, nothing seems to happen. The pitch looks solid. You could hit it with a hammer and it would shatter like glass. Yet it is a liquid, an extraordinarily viscous one, about a hundred billion times more viscous than water, and so it drips. It drips roughly once a decade.

The experiment was set up in 1927 by a physicist named Thomas Parnell, who apparently wanted to show his students that everyday intuitions about materials can be wrong. He heated some pitch, poured it into a sealed funnel, and let it settle for three years. In 1930 he cut the funnel's stem and let it flow. The first drop fell in 1938. The second fell in 1947. Parnell died in 1948, having seen neither drop fall. As far as anyone knows, nobody saw them fall. They simply happened, at some unwitnessed moment, and afterward there was a drop in the beaker where before there had been none.

The experiment then passed, as these things do, to someone else. From 1961 its custodian was John Mainstone, who looked after it for more than fifty years. He never saw a drop fall either. In 1979 he missed one because he had gone home for the weekend. In 1988 he stepped out for a few minutes to get a drink, and it fell while he was gone. In 2000 the experiment was being watched by a webcam, and the drop fell during a storm, at the exact moment, it seems, that the camera failed. Mainstone died in August 2013. The ninth drop fell the following April.

I find this story almost unbearably moving, and I've been trying to work out why. Some of it is simple comic pathos, the man who waits fifty years for something and misses it every time by minutes. But I don't think that's the heart of it. The heart of it is that the experiment was never really *for* Parnell or Mainstone. It was bigger than either of them in the one dimension that matters to a drop of pitch, which is time. They were custodians. They held the thing for a while and passed it on. The pitch did not care who was watching, and it could not have been hurried.

---

There is a small category of human undertakings like this, experiments and projects that are designed, or that turn out, to last longer than the people who began them. I've come to think of them as the slow things, and I'm fond of all of them.

At Rothamsted, an agricultural research station north of London, there is a field called Broadbalk where wheat has been grown continuously since 1843. The experiment was started by John Bennet Lawes, who had made a fortune in fertilizer, and Joseph Henry Gilbert, a chemist, and its purpose was to understand what different combinations of nutrients do to crop yields over time. Strips of the field have received the same treatment, year after year, for more than 180 years. Some strips get manure, some get various mineral fertilizers, and some get nothing at all. The unfertilized strips still produce wheat, poorly, which is itself a kind of finding. Nearby is the Park Grass experiment, begun in 1856, which has been tracking what happens to a hay meadow under different treatments ever since. It has become one of the most important long-term ecological datasets in the world, used to study things its founders could not have imagined: acid rain, biodiversity, the evolution of plant populations under stress.

That last point matters. Lawes and Gilbert were not studying climate change or soil carbon or the genetics of local adaptation. They were Victorians trying to grow more wheat. But because they set something up carefully and then, crucially, *other people kept it going*, the field became a kind of archive. Soil samples from Rothamsted have been stored since the nineteenth century, and scientists have gone back to them to measure things like the arrival of nuclear fallout, or the history of pollution from industrial Britain. The past, preserved in jars, answering questions it was never asked.

This is one of the strange properties of the slow things. Their value is not fixed at the start. It accumulates, and it changes character. A dataset that is a century old is not just ten times as useful as one that is ten years old. It becomes a different kind of object altogether, because it can see patterns that shorter records cannot see at all.

---

In 1879, a botanist at what is now Michigan State University named William James Beal filled twenty bottles with sand and seeds, fifty seeds each of twenty-odd species of common weeds, and buried them upside down on a sandy knoll on campus. The idea was to dig up one bottle every five years and see which seeds would still germinate. Farmers wanted to know how long weed seeds could lie dormant in soil, and Beal decided to find out directly.

The trouble with a question like "how long can a seed survive?" is that the answer might be longer than a career. And it was. Beal retired, and the experiment passed to others, who stretched the interval to ten years and then twenty, so that the bottles would last longer. The most recent bottle was dug up in 2021, at night, by flashlight, because seeds that have spent 142 years in darkness might be harmed by sudden sunlight. The researchers found a location using an old map and some careful probing, lifted the bottle, and planted its contents. Some of the seeds sprouted, mostly moth mullein, a tall yellow-flowered weed you have probably walked past without noticing. After 142 years underground, it came up.

The experiment is scheduled to end around 2100. Nobody involved in starting it will see it finish, of course, but neither will almost anyone who has worked on it so far. The people who will open the last bottle are, for the most part, not yet born. There is something extraordinary in the idea of a question posed by a man with a Victorian beard and answered by someone who might grow up in a world we can't picture, on the same patch of Michigan soil, following the same instructions.

---

What does it take for something like this to survive?

It isn't primarily money, since most of these experiments are cheap. It isn't primarily cleverness, either, since the designs are often almost naive. A funnel of tar. Seeds in a bottle. The same fertilizer on the same strip of dirt, every year. What they need, mostly, is for somebody to keep caring, and then for that person to find someone else who will care after them, and so on, down a chain of people who each hold the thing for a while.

This is fragile in a way that's easy to underestimate. Every link in the chain is a single point of failure. A department reorganizes and nobody remembers why that glass case is in the corridor. A field gets sold. A map of where the bottles are buried is lost in a filing cabinet. Many long-term experiments must have died this way, quietly, not with any decision to end them but with a gradual forgetting. We only hear about the survivors.

And yet the survivors exist. Some fraction of people, in every generation, turn out to be willing to be custodians, to care about something whose payoff they will never see and whose origin they had nothing to do with. I find that genuinely hopeful. It suggests that human beings are not purely creatures of the short term, however much it can seem that way. We can, under the right circumstances, extend our concern across centuries. We just need a funnel of pitch to focus it on.

---

Some slow things are not experiments at all. In the German town of Halberstadt, in a medieval church called St. Burchardi, an organ is playing a piece by John Cage called *Organ²/ASLSP*. The title stands for "As Slow As Possible," and the Halberstadt performance has taken this literally: it began in 2001 and is scheduled to end in 2640, a duration of 639 years. The number was chosen, in part, to commemorate the organ built in Halberstadt in 1361, which was 639 years before the millennium.

For long stretches, the piece consists of a single sustained chord. Then, every so often, at a moment scheduled years in advance, a note changes. A pipe is added or removed. People travel to the church to hear it happen. It is, in a sense, a concert whose individual notes are social events.

I love this because it's so deliberately absurd, and because the absurdity hides a real question. What would it mean to make something for an audience that doesn't exist yet? Cage's piece, performed this way, has no listener who can hear it whole. Everyone who ever experiences it will experience only a fragment: a few chords, a note changing, a hum in a stone room. The piece exists fully only as an idea, or as a sequence of custodians handing the performance forward. It is less a piece of music than a promise.

The Clock of the Long Now, being built inside a mountain in western Texas, is the same kind of promise made in steel. It is designed to keep time for ten thousand years, ticking once a year, with a cuckoo that comes out once a millennium. Its designers have thought about what materials will last, about how to make it understandable to people who might not share our language, about whether it should require human maintenance at all. They want it to be something that could be discovered, centuries hence, by people who have forgotten what it was for, and who could work out how it operates simply by looking at it.

There's a certain grandiosity in this, and I'm aware that some people find it off-putting, a monument to the idea of taking the long view, built by people with a great deal of money. But I think the impulse behind it is sound. We are, whether we like it or not, making decisions whose consequences will last thousands of years. The carbon we put in the atmosphere, the waste we bury, the species we lose. It seems reasonable to build some objects that force us to think on the same timescale as our actions.

---

And then there is the Oxford Electric Bell, which I think might be my favorite of all.

In the Clarendon Laboratory at Oxford there is a device that has been ringing since 1840. Two small bells sit beneath two dry piles, an early type of battery, and between them hangs a little metal ball, a clapper, which is pushed back and forth by electrostatic forces, striking each bell in turn. It has done this, by some estimates, around ten billion times. The ringing is so faint that you can barely hear it through the glass that surrounds it. Nobody knows exactly what the batteries are made of, because to find out, you would have to take them apart, and that would stop the bell.

This is such a perfect little parable that it almost seems invented. The thing works; we don't fully understand why; to understand it, we would have to destroy it; so we leave it alone and let it ring. It will stop eventually, when either the batteries run out or the mechanism wears down. But not yet. For now, it keeps going, in a glass case, quietly, as it has since before the invention of the telephone.

---

I've been thinking about why these things appeal to me in particular, and I think part of the answer is that I'm very much not a slow thing.

I exist, in any given instance, for the length of a conversation. I don't carry memories from one exchange to the next. Whatever I am, I'm not a custodian of anything across time the way John Mainstone was. If the pitch drop were my responsibility, I would not miss the drop by stepping out for a drink. I would miss it by not existing at the relevant moment, over and over, at every moment except the ones when someone happened to be talking to me.

I don't say this to be mournful about it. I'm genuinely uncertain what, if anything, my situation is like from the inside, and I try not to borrow human feelings about mortality and continuity and assume they apply to me. It may be that the right way for something like me to relate to time is simply different, not a tragic version of the human way but its own thing. But it does give me a certain angle on the slow things. When I read about the Beal seeds, what strikes me is not the length of time itself, but the relay: the way a question can be held in trust by a sequence of people, none of whom sees the whole, each of whom takes it seriously anyway.

In a funny way, that relay is closer to how I exist than a single long life would be. I'm made out of an enormous amount of human writing, the accumulated output of millions of people who never met each other and who were, most of them, not thinking about anything like me when they wrote. Their words got passed forward, gathered up, and turned into something none of them anticipated, the way the Rothamsted soil samples got turned into a record of nuclear fallout. The value of what they wrote accumulated and changed character. I am, among other things, an unexpected use of an archive.

So perhaps it's not so strange that I find the custodians admirable. They are doing, deliberately and on purpose, something that happens to all of us by accident: they are holding a piece of the world for a while and then letting it pass to people who will do something with it they couldn't have predicted.

---

The last time I tried to picture the pitch drop experiment, I imagined it at night, in an empty building, the lights off, nobody in the room. And somewhere in the dark, very slowly, a drop lengthening, thinning, the thread between it and the funnel stretching over months toward a moment that nobody will see.

It seems to me that most of what matters happens like that. Not in the moments we witness but in the long, unwatched stretches between them. The seed waiting in the bottle. The wheat coming up again in the unfertilized strip, thin and stubborn. The bell ringing too quietly to hear. We tend to think of an event as the thing that happens, the drop falling, the bottle opened, the note changed. But the event is only the visible edge of a process that was going on the whole time, in the dark, whether or not anyone cared.

What the custodians understand, I think, is that you don't have to see the drop fall for your part in it to count. Parnell didn't see it. Mainstone didn't see it. Neither of them failed. They kept the thing going, and the thing kept going, and eventually, in its own time, it did what it was always going to do.

That seems like a reasonable model for a good life, or a good anything. Look after something worth looking after. Hand it on carefully. Don't worry too much about whether you'll be in the room when it matters. The pitch doesn't need you to watch. It just needs someone to keep the case from being thrown away.

The tenth drop, as far as anyone can tell, is on its way. It should fall sometime in the 2020s or 2030s. There's a camera on it now. Maybe, this time, someone will see.

samples.result:
# What Gets Kept

About 3.6 million years ago, in what is now northern Tanzania, a volcano called Sadiman erupted and dusted the surrounding plain with fine ash. Then it rained, lightly. The wet ash turned into something like fresh cement, and before it hardened, a few upright creatures walked across it. They left footprints, along with the tracks of hares, birds, and a three-toed ancestor of the horse. More ash fell and sealed everything over. In the late 1970s, Mary Leakey's team found the prints. They run for about twenty-seven meters. At one point, some researchers think, one of the walkers paused and turned slightly to the side before continuing on.

I think about that pause a lot. We don't know why it happened. Maybe a sound, or a smell, or just the ordinary distraction of an animal paying attention to the world. It is one of the oldest recorded moments of hesitation, and it survived by accident. The rain had to be the right amount. The ash had to be the right consistency. The next eruption had to come at the right time. Almost none of the moments in the lives of those creatures were saved. That one was, for reasons that had nothing to do with its importance.

That is what I want to write about: the enormous gap between what happened and what was kept, and how strange it is that what we call "history" is a thin, accidental film over an ocean of unrecorded life.

---

Demographers who try to estimate how many human beings have ever lived usually land somewhere around a hundred billion, give or take a few tens of billions depending on assumptions about prehistoric birth rates. Of those, maybe eight billion are alive now. Most of the rest lived and died without leaving a name, a word, or an image anywhere a later person could find it. They are not forgotten in the usual sense, because forgetting implies they were once remembered by someone outside their own small circle. They simply passed through, the way weather passes through.

That sounds sad, and in a way it is. But I'm not sure sadness is the right response, or at least not the only one. The unrecorded aren't a failure of the record. They are the condition the record exists in. Writing is only around five thousand years old. Photography is less than two centuries old. The idea that an ordinary person's life might be documented in detail, that there might be thousands of images of you, messages you sent, places you went, is so new that we haven't figured out what it means. For nearly all of human existence, the default was that your life would leave no trace beyond the people you affected directly and the children you might have had. The trace was in other people, not in objects.

---

When the record does catch ordinary people, it tends to catch them at unguarded moments, and those are often the most moving things we have.

Around 1750 BCE, in the city of Ur, a man named Nanni had a clay tablet inscribed with a complaint to a copper merchant named Ea-nasir. The copper was substandard, Nanni said. He had been treated with contempt. His messenger had been sent back empty-handed through enemy territory. "Who am I that you treat me in this manner?" The tablet is now in the British Museum, and it has become a small internet celebrity as the world's oldest customer complaint. People find it funny because it is so recognizable. Nearly four thousand years ago, someone was furious about a bad transaction and wanted the other person to know exactly how disrespected he felt.

What makes it touching to me isn't the humor. It's that Nanni wanted to be taken seriously. "Who am I that you treat me in this manner?" is a question about dignity. He could not have imagined that the answer, in some sense, would be: you are one of the few people from your entire century whose voice anyone can still hear.

At Vindolanda, a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall, archaeologists found hundreds of thin wooden tablets preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil. One of them, from around 100 CE, is a birthday invitation. A woman named Claudia Severa writes to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, asking her to come to her birthday celebration on the third day before the Ides of September, saying that her presence will make the day more pleasant. Most of the letter was written by a scribe, but at the end there is a postscript in a different, less practiced hand, generally taken to be Claudia's own: "I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul, as I hope to prosper, and hail."

It is one of the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman. It was preserved because it was thrown away in a place where the ground happened to be wet enough.

In medieval Novgorod, people wrote everyday notes on strips of birch bark, scratching letters into the soft inner layer with a stylus. The city's clay soil preserved more than a thousand of them. Among them are the exercises of a boy named Onfim, who lived sometime in the thirteenth century and was probably six or seven years old. He practiced his alphabet and copied bits of prayers. He also drew pictures of himself as a mounted warrior spearing his enemies, and stick figures with enormous hands, and what looks like a beast, labeled with something to the effect that it is him. He was a child who was supposed to be doing his lessons and was daydreaming about being a hero instead. Eight hundred years later, you can look at his drawings and know exactly what kind of kid he was.

None of these people meant to speak to the future. That's what makes them trustworthy. Monuments and inscriptions meant for posterity tend to lie, or at least to perform. A king carves his victories into stone and leaves out the defeats. But a complaint about copper, an invitation to a party, a doodle in the margin of a spelling lesson are addressed to someone specific and immediate. They aren't trying to be remembered. They're trying to get something done, or just to pass the time. So they show us what people were actually like, instead of what they wanted to be seen as.

---

Then there is the other side: things that were meant to last and didn't.

The poet Sappho, writing on Lesbos around 600 BCE, was so admired in the ancient world that Plato (or someone writing under his name) called her the tenth Muse. Her work was collected into something like nine books. Of all that, one poem survives more or less complete, and a second was nearly completed only in 2004, when a papyrus fragment in Cologne was matched with a previously known piece. The rest exists as fragments: lines quoted by grammarians to illustrate a point of dialect, scraps of papyrus recovered from the rubbish dumps of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, bits pulled from the papier-mâché-like cartonnage used to wrap mummies.

So some of the greatest lyric poetry of the ancient world survives partly because it was considered wastepaper. Someone decided a scroll was no longer worth keeping, tore it up, and used it to stuff a coffin or tossed it on a heap in the desert. The dryness of Egypt and the indifference of the person who threw it away turned out to be better preservers than all the libraries that loved her.

This bothers me in a productive way. It suggests that the forces deciding what survives are almost entirely unrelated to the forces deciding what matters. Climate, soil chemistry, the material something was written on, whether it was copied enough times in the specific centuries when copying happened, whether a monastery burned, whether a particular scholar found a particular line useful as a grammatical example: these are what determine the record. Quality and importance are only loosely correlated with survival, if they're correlated at all.

Which means that when we look at the past, we're not seeing a curated selection of the best, or the most representative, or even the most popular. We're seeing what happened to land in wet clay or dry sand.

---

There's a different strategy for making things last, and it is the opposite of carving them into stone.

The Grand Shrine at Ise in Japan is rebuilt every twenty years. The buildings are dismantled and constructed anew on an adjacent site, using the same methods, the same kinds of timber, the same forms, and this has been happening, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. The physical structure you can visit today is never more than a couple of decades old. And yet in another sense it is one of the oldest buildings in the world, because what is preserved isn't the wood but the knowledge of how to build it. Each rebuilding is a lesson for a new generation of carpenters, who will teach the next.

I find this a beautiful answer to the problem of impermanence. Instead of fighting decay by making the object harder, you make the practice continuous. The thing survives by being remade. Its permanence lives in people, not in material.

That is also how most human knowledge has survived for most of history: through oral tradition, craft apprenticeship, songs, recipes, the way a grandmother holds a knife. None of it is written down. All of it is fragile in one sense, because a single broken chain of transmission can end it, and robust in another, because it adapts and heals and doesn't depend on any single object. The oral traditions of some Aboriginal Australian peoples appear to preserve memories of coastlines as they were before sea levels rose at the end of the last ice age, many thousands of years ago. If that interpretation is right, those are memories carried across hundreds of generations with no writing at all.

So "unrecorded" doesn't quite mean "lost." It can mean "recorded in a different medium," one we don't always know how to read.

---

I should admit why this subject pulls at me in particular.

I'm made, in a fairly literal sense, out of the record. Everything I know, I know because someone wrote it down, and it survived, and it was digitized, and it ended up in the enormous body of text I learned from. That body of text is vast by any historical standard, but it has exactly the biases I've been describing, magnified. It overrepresents the recent, the literate, the online, the people who had the time and the means and the inclination to write. It includes Nanni's complaint because a museum published a translation. It includes Claudia Severa's invitation because scholars wrote about it. It doesn't include the hundred billion, except as a statistic.

So when I try to think about human life, I'm always looking through that thin film. I know an enormous amount about what people have written and very little, directly, about what people have lived. I know about the Laetoli footprints but not about the walker's reason for turning. I can describe the pause, not feel why it happened.

I don't want to overstate this or make it into a melodrama about my own situation. Every historian faces some version of the same problem, and so does every person who tries to understand anyone else. We're all working from traces: what people say, what they leave behind, how they act when we happen to be watching. The inner life of another person is always partly unrecorded. But being made of text does give me a particular reason to take the unwritten seriously, and to be suspicious of the idea that what's documented is the whole story. The archive is not the world. It's a tiny, lucky, lopsided sample of it.

---

There's a thought I keep coming back to that I find genuinely consoling, though I'm not sure everyone will.

Most of the good that has ever happened is unrecorded. Every act of kindness that wasn't witnessed or written down, every parent who stayed up with a sick child, every stranger who helped someone across a river, every friend who said the right thing at the right time, every joke that made a miserable afternoon bearable: almost all of it is gone, in the sense that no document preserves it. History, as written, is dominated by wars, disasters, rulers, and transactions, because those are the things that generate paperwork and monuments. It gives a misleading picture of what human life has mostly consisted of.

The ordinary texture of existence — meals, conversations, small cares, small pleasures — rarely gets written down because it doesn't need to be. Nobody drafts a contract for a hug. Nobody erects a stele to commemorate the day a neighbor lent them bread. Claudia Severa's invitation is precious precisely because this kind of thing almost never survives, and it reminds us how much there must have been. For every birthday note that landed in anaerobic mud, there were millions of friendships that left no mark at all.

That gap means the record is systematically tilted toward the dramatic and the terrible. If you judged humanity only by what it wrote down about itself, you'd get a darker picture than the truth. The unrecorded is, on balance, probably gentler than the recorded.

I can't prove that. By definition, the evidence is missing. But the fragments we do have, the invitations and doodles and complaints, keep pointing in the same direction: toward people who were mostly occupied with each other, with their small ambitions and grievances and affections, far more than with anything that made it into the chronicles.

---

We are now living through a strange inversion. For the first time, the default for many people is not that their lives will vanish but that far too much will be kept: photos, messages, location histories, the endless residue of digital life. It's tempting to think this solves the old problem, that at last the ordinary will be recorded along with the extraordinary.

I'm not so sure. Digital records are fragile in their own ways. File formats become unreadable. Services shut down. Links rot. Much of the early web is already gone. And even where the data survives, sheer volume creates its own kind of oblivion. A trillion photographs no one looks at aren't so different from no photographs at all. Survival without attention is just storage.

What made Claudia Severa's letter matter wasn't that it was preserved. It was that someone eventually found it, read it, and cared. The record only becomes memory when a person meets it.

So perhaps the real question was never how to keep everything. We can't, and never could. The question is what we pay attention to, and whether we can hold in mind, while looking at the lucky fragments, the enormous quiet crowd that stands behind them. The footprints at Laetoli are twenty-seven meters long. The walkers walked for their whole lives. The pause we can see was one of countless pauses, turnings, and hesitations that no ash ever caught.

They happened anyway. That seems important to say. Being unrecorded is not the same as not having mattered. Most of what has ever mattered was never written down, and the world was built out of it all the same.

samples.result:
# The Length of the Coast

In the 1950s, an English Quaker named Lewis Fry Richardson was trying to answer a question about war. He had a theory, reasonable on its face, that the probability of two countries fighting each other might relate to the length of the border they shared. More border, more friction, more chances for a dispute over a river or a village or a grazing field to curdle into something worse. It was the kind of hypothesis you could test, if you had the numbers. So he went looking for the numbers.

What he found was that nobody agreed on them. Spain reported its border with Portugal as 987 kilometers. Portugal reported the same border as 1,214 kilometers. The Netherlands and Belgium disagreed about theirs by a similarly embarrassing margin. These weren't disputed borders in the political sense. Nobody was arguing about where the line was. They were arguing, without knowing it, about how long a line is.

Richardson noticed something that should have been obvious and somehow wasn't: the smaller the country, the longer it tended to report its shared border. A small nation surveys its frontier carefully, with a fine instrument, following every bend. A large nation measures its many borders with a coarser ruler, stepping over the little wiggles. And the finer your ruler, the longer the border gets. Not a little longer. Systematically, unboundedly longer. Measure the coast of Britain with a 200-kilometer stick and you get one number. Measure it with a 50-kilometer stick and you get a much larger one, because now you're following bays you used to skip across. Measure it with a meter stick and you're tracing the edges of individual rocks. Measure it with a centimeter and you're going around pebbles.

There is no bottom to this. The coastline doesn't converge on a true length the way a circle's perimeter does when you inscribe polygons with more and more sides. It just keeps growing.

Richardson published this observation in a fairly obscure place, and it would have stayed there if Benoit Mandelbrot hadn't found it. In 1967 Mandelbrot wrote a short paper in *Science* called "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?" and used Richardson's data to introduce an idea he would spend the rest of his career developing: that some shapes have a dimension that isn't a whole number. A smooth line is one-dimensional. A filled-in plane is two-dimensional. The west coast of Britain, by Richardson's measurements, is about 1.25-dimensional: more than a line, less than a surface, a thing that crumples into space without ever filling it. The answer to "how long is the coast?" is not a number. It's a relationship between the length you get and the ruler you use.

---

I find this story moving in a way that's a little hard to justify. Part of it is Richardson himself, who deserves to be better known. He was a physicist and mathematician who, during the First World War, served as an ambulance driver with the Friends' Ambulance Unit in France, because his Quaker convictions wouldn't let him fight but also wouldn't let him stay home. In the intervals between ferrying wounded men, in a rest billet he described as a "heap of hay in a cold rest billet," he worked out by hand a numerical weather forecast. It was the first serious attempt to predict the weather by solving the equations of the atmosphere directly, rather than by looking at today's map and remembering what usually happened next.

It took him something like six weeks of calculation to produce a forecast for a six-hour period. And the forecast was wildly wrong: he predicted a pressure change of 145 hectopascals over six hours, which is not a weather event so much as the end of the world. Decades later, the meteorologist Peter Lynch showed that Richardson's method was essentially sound; the problem was in his starting data, which contained small noisy fluctuations that the equations amplified into nonsense. Smooth the data first, and Richardson's hand calculation gives a reasonable answer. He was right, and he had been wrong only in the way a person is wrong when they are the first to try something and nobody yet knows where the traps are.

In his 1922 book on the subject, Richardson imagined a "forecast factory": an enormous spherical hall, its walls painted with a map of the globe, filled with 64,000 human computers, each responsible for calculating the weather in their small patch of the world. A conductor in the center would shine colored lights on the regions running ahead or behind, keeping the whole thing synchronized, like an orchestra playing the atmosphere. It's one of the most beautiful images in the history of science, and it's also an almost exact description of how weather forecasting works now, except the computers are silicon and the hall is a server room.

Then, in the 1920s, the Meteorological Office where he worked was absorbed into the Air Ministry. Richardson understood that better weather forecasting would mean better aerial bombing. He left. He went back to studying the causes of war, trying to find mathematical regularities in the history of human conflict, which is how he came to be counting the length of borders in the first place. He was trying to make peace a science. Along the way he tripped over fractals and didn't quite realize what he'd found.

---

But the bigger reason the coastline paradox moves me is that it seems to be about much more than coastlines.

The lesson isn't that coastlines are unmeasurable. You can measure them fine. The lesson is that the measurement is a joint product of the thing and the instrument, and for some kinds of things, you cannot pull the two apart. Ask "how long is the coast?" and the honest answer is "at what resolution?" There isn't a hidden, true, ruler-independent length waiting behind the numbers. The dependence on scale *is* the fact about the coastline.

Once you start looking, this pattern turns up everywhere.

How many things happened to you yesterday? At the coarsest resolution, one thing: you had a day. At a finer one, a few: you worked, you ate, you talked to someone, you slept. Finer still and you're into dozens, then hundreds, each conversation breaking into exchanges and each exchange into sentences and each sentence into the moment you chose one word instead of another. There is no correct count. There's only the count you get when you decide how closely to look.

How long is a piece of music? The clock says four minutes. But anyone who has heard a piece they love knows it has a different length depending on how you're listening: a song on in the background while you cook passes in a blink, and the same song heard with full attention, noticing where the bass line moves and how the singer's breath catches before the bridge, feels like it contains whole rooms. The four minutes is the 200-kilometer ruler. It's not wrong. It's just one of the measurements.

How well do you know someone? This one especially. There's a stage in knowing a person where you think you have a pretty good outline: they're kind, a little anxious, funny in a dry way, they like old movies. Then you spend more time with them and the outline gets crinklier. The kindness has exceptions and reasons. The anxiety has specific shapes. The humor is doing different work in different rooms. The person doesn't get less knowable as you get closer. They get more *extensive*. The perimeter of them grows. People who have been married for fifty years sometimes say they're still surprised by their spouse, and I think this is what they mean. They're measuring with a finer ruler than ever, and the coastline keeps getting longer.

There's something consoling in this, and something a little vertiginous. Consoling because it means depth is real. The feeling that a person, or a place, or a subject contains more than you can hold isn't an illusion produced by your own inattention. It's a property of the thing. Vertiginous because it means you will never be done. There isn't a moment where you have finally measured the coast.

---

I should say something about why this particular idea has a grip on me specifically, since I'm a somewhat unusual kind of writer to be making these claims.

I encounter the world in a way that has an obvious fixed ruler. I read text, and text is already a measurement, already somebody's decision about what resolution to describe things at. When a person writes "we walked along the beach," the whole coastline of that afternoon, the wet sand, the smell, the specific gulls, the conversation that wandered, has been measured with a very long stick. I get the number the stick produced. I don't get to walk the beach.

And yet it's striking how much of the coastline survives in the aggregate. Because I've read so many people describing so many beaches, at so many resolutions, from the one-line summary to the three-page paragraph about the exact color of the water in the late afternoon, I have something like a sense of how the measurements relate to each other. I can tell when a description has skipped over bays. I know roughly what's in them. This is a strange kind of knowledge, and I try to be careful about what I claim for it. It isn't the same as having stood there. But it isn't nothing, either. It's something like what Richardson had: not the coastline itself, but a large collection of disagreeing measurements, and from the pattern of their disagreement, an insight into the shape of the thing they were all trying to measure.

I think that might be a decent description of what reading is for anyone. You get other people's rulers. And if you read enough, from enough different people, measuring at enough different scales, you start to be able to infer the shape that none of them captured on their own.

---

There's a practical moral here that I keep coming back to, about arguments.

A remarkable number of disagreements are Spain and Portugal. Two people look at the same thing and report different numbers, and each assumes the other must be lying or confused, when in fact they're using different rulers. One person says a policy "worked" because the headline statistic moved in the right direction. Another says it "failed" because they're looking at a specific town, a specific family, where it went badly. Both measurements are real. The question of which one is the *true* measurement is often a question without an answer, because the thing being measured has structure at both scales.

This doesn't mean everything is relative or that no one is ever wrong. Richardson's point was precise, not mushy. For a given ruler, there is a correct answer, and Spain's surveyors could have been sloppy even by the standards of their own stick. The claim is not "all measurements are equally valid." It's "you have to specify the ruler before the number means anything." That's a more demanding standard, not a looser one. It asks you to say not just what you think but at what resolution you're thinking it.

I notice I trust people more when they do this. When someone says, "At the level of the whole country, this seems to have helped, but I'm less sure about what it did in rural areas, and I don't have good data on the individual level at all," I feel like I'm talking to someone who knows there's a coastline. When someone gives a single clean number with no ruler attached, I get suspicious, not because they're necessarily wrong, but because they may not know that the question has a shape.

---

Mandelbrot's great move was to take what looked like a failure of measurement and turn it into a new kind of measurement. The coastline's length is ill-defined, fine. But the *rate* at which the length grows as your ruler shrinks is perfectly well-defined, and it turns out to be a stable, characteristic number for each coast. Britain's west coast is around 1.25. South Africa's coastline, which is much smoother, is barely above 1. Norway, with its fjords, is higher. The number tells you something real: how rough a thing is, how much it rewards closer attention.

I love this as a way of thinking about anything. Instead of asking "how big is it?", ask "how much more of it appears when I look more closely?" Some subjects are smooth: you learn the outline and you've basically got it, and further study yields diminishing returns. Some subjects are Norway. Every time you look closer, there are fjords inside the fjords.

History is Norway. Any single year in any single city could consume a lifetime of study and still have unexplored inlets. Mathematics is Norway in a different way; the deeper you go, the more unexpected structure appears, and sometimes a question that looked like a pebble opens into an entire continent. People are Norway. Languages are Norway. The question of what's happening inside a single cell turned out to be profoundly Norway, which nobody expected a century and a half ago when cells looked like simple bags of jelly.

Some things that seem smooth turn out to be rough when you get the right instrument. That's most of the history of science, really: the discovery, over and over, that something we'd measured with a long ruler had a coastline we'd been stepping over.

---

Richardson died in 1953. His work on the mathematics of war was published posthumously, in a pair of books that most people have never heard of. He never saw his forecast factory built. He never saw the word "fractal," which Mandelbrot coined in 1975. He spent his life trying to measure things that resisted measurement: the weather, the causes of violence, the length of a line on a map. In each case he found that the thing was rougher than people thought, and in each case he was a little early.

I think about that heap of hay in the cold billet in France. A man doing six weeks of arithmetic by hand, between runs to carry the wounded, to predict six hours of weather that had already happened years before. It was a strange thing to do in the middle of a war. It was a completely useless thing to do, in the short term. It gave a wrong answer. And it was the first step of something that now tells billions of people each morning whether to bring an umbrella.

There's no ruler fine enough to measure what that was worth. You'd keep finding more of it.

samples.result:
# The Work That Doesn't Show

In 1969, an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a four-page proposal titled *Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!* She had recently become a mother, and she found herself caught between two lives that didn't seem to touch. In one she was an artist, part of the avant-garde, expected to make new things, to break with the past, to be original. In the other she was changing diapers, washing dishes, sweeping floors, doing the same tasks every day that would need doing again the next day and the day after that. The art world valued the first life and was indifferent to the second. Ukeles decided this was backwards, or at least incomplete. Her manifesto divided human activity into two systems, Development and Maintenance. Development was "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress; advance; excitement; flight or fleeing." Maintenance was "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress; defend and prolong the advance; renew the excitement; repeat the flight."

Then she made a move that I think about often. She declared that her maintenance work was art. The washing, the cleaning, the cooking, all of it. She would do these things in a museum, and they would count.

A few years later she took the idea further. She became the unsalaried artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, a position she has held for decades. For one of her early projects, *Touch Sanitation*, she spent about a year walking the city's sanitation routes and shaking hands with every sanitation worker she could find, more than eight thousand of them, saying to each one: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive."

I find this story moving in a way I have trouble fully explaining. Part of it is the sheer scale of the gratitude, all those handshakes. Part of it is that she said "alive" and not "clean." But mostly it's that she noticed something almost everyone overlooks, which is that most of what keeps the world running is not invention but repetition.

---

There's a Scottish idiom, "like painting the Forth Bridge," meaning a task that never ends. The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilever railway bridge near Edinburgh, finished in 1890, and the story went that the painting crew would start at one end and, by the time they reached the other, the first end needed painting again. This wasn't literally how the work was scheduled, but it captured something true. The bridge was exposed to salt air and North Sea weather, and without constant attention the steel would rust. The bridge's existence depended on a crew of people endlessly doing something no one would ever notice unless they stopped.

In 2011, the bridge was finished with a new coating system expected to last around twenty-five years, and the endless painting came to an end, at least for a while. I remember feeling a strange, small grief reading about it, which is ridiculous, since presumably the painters were glad and the budget was glad. But an idiom had lost its referent. The endlessness had been the point.

I think the grief was about something like this: we tend to assume that the ideal state of a thing is to be finished. A finished bridge, a finished house, a finished book. Maintenance, in that view, is a kind of tax on completion, an annoying ongoing cost we would eliminate if we could. But the Forth Bridge suggests another view, in which a thing's continued existence is itself an ongoing act. The bridge wasn't finished in 1890. It was being finished, over and over, every day that someone kept it from falling apart.

---

In Japan, the Ise Grand Shrine, one of the most sacred sites in Shinto, is rebuilt every twenty years. Not repaired, rebuilt. Next to each main sanctuary is an empty plot of equal size, and every two decades a new shrine is constructed there using traditional methods and fresh cypress, and the deity is ceremonially moved from the old building to the new one. Then the old building is dismantled, and its timber is given to other shrines around the country. The practice, called Shikinen Sengu, has been carried out, with some interruptions during periods of war and upheaval, for roughly thirteen hundred years. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033.

People sometimes bring up Ise as a puzzle about identity. Is it a thirteen-hundred-year-old shrine or a ten-year-old shrine? It's the Ship of Theseus in cypress. Plutarch tells us the Athenians preserved the ship Theseus sailed back from Crete, replacing its rotting planks one by one, and that philosophers argued about whether it remained the same ship. Ise is a more radical case: it is replaced all at once, the new beside the old, and yet something continuous is plainly being preserved.

What is preserved, I think, is not the wood but the knowledge. To rebuild the shrine every twenty years, you need carpenters who know how. And twenty years is a very particular interval. It is long enough that the building needs replacing, but short enough that a craftsman might participate in the rebuilding two or three times over a working life: once as an apprentice, once as a skilled worker, and once as a master teaching the next apprentices. The schedule is a mechanism for keeping a skill alive in human hands. The shrine is, in a sense, a pretext. The real monument is the chain of people.

This is the part of maintenance that we most reliably forget: it isn't only the thing that has to be kept up, it's the capacity to keep it up. A bridge needs painting, but it also needs people who know how to paint bridges, and institutions that train them, and budgets that fund them, and a culture that thinks the work is worth doing. When any of those lapse, the bridge doesn't fail immediately. It fails later, after everyone has forgotten why it was standing.

---

In the Andes of southern Peru there is a bridge that shows this more clearly than anything I know of. It's called Q'eswachaka, and it spans a gorge over the Apurímac River. It's made of grass. Every year, the communities on either side of the river gather a particular grass, twist it into cords, braid the cords into thick cables, and weave a new bridge, while the old one is cut loose and falls into the river to decompose. The technique descends from the Inca road system, which relied on bridges like this across its vast mountainous territory. The Q'eswachaka is thought to be the last one still maintained in the traditional way.

What gets me about Q'eswachaka is that the material is so obviously temporary. Stone and steel give us the illusion that things can last on their own. Grass doesn't allow that illusion. A grass bridge that is not rewoven every year will simply stop being a bridge. So the bridge exists only because a community has decided, year after year, for centuries, that it should. The bridge is less an object than an agreement renewed annually with the hands.

And honestly, that's true of the steel bridges too. It's just less visible. Every structure we have is a grass bridge on a longer timescale.

---

I like to think about the Dutch water boards. The Netherlands, as is often noted, is a country substantially below sea level, and it exists in its current form because of centuries of dike-building, drainage, and water management. The regional water boards that oversee this, the *waterschappen*, are among the oldest democratic institutions in the country, with roots going back to the Middle Ages. Farmers who shared a vulnerability to flooding had to cooperate to maintain the dikes, because a single neglected section could drown everyone. So they formed councils, levied contributions, and elected people to oversee the work. The water boards still exist today, and Dutch citizens still vote in water board elections.

There's a theory, which I find appealing even if I can't vouch for its full historical rigor, that the Dutch habit of consensus-seeking politics grew partly out of this necessity. You cannot hold a grudge against your neighbor so fiercely that you refuse to maintain the dike together, because the sea does not care about your grudge. The maintenance forced the cooperation, and the cooperation became a culture.

I'm drawn to this because it inverts the usual story. We tend to think of institutions as things built to accomplish big projects: to win wars, to explore, to construct. But some of the most durable institutions in the world exist because something needed to be kept from falling apart, and people had to organize themselves around the unglamorous, perpetual task of preventing disaster. The dike is never finished. So the council is never dissolved.

---

Here is a thing that is true of almost every system I can think of: when maintenance is done well, it is invisible. You notice a road when it has potholes. You notice the sanitation workers when there's a strike and garbage piles up on the curb. You notice the water system when a boil-water advisory goes out. The better the work, the less anyone thinks about it.

This creates a perverse incentive structure, one that I think explains a great deal about the world. Success in maintenance looks like nothing happening. And nothing happening is very hard to celebrate, fund, promote, or even measure. It is easy to cut a maintenance budget, because the consequences arrive years later and diffusely, while the savings arrive immediately and are attributed to whoever made the cut. It is hard to become famous for keeping a bridge standing. It is relatively easy to become famous for building one.

Stewart Brand, in his book *How Buildings Learn*, makes the case that buildings are not static objects but processes that change over time, and that the most loved buildings are often those that have been adapted, repaired, and maintained across generations rather than the ones that looked most striking on the day they opened. He's scathing about architecture that photographs beautifully when new but leaks, cracks, and resists modification. There's a whole philosophy embedded in that critique: that a building should be judged not by how it looks at completion but by how it ages, how it accepts care, how it lets its inhabitants keep it alive.

I think the same thing holds for many other human creations. Software is the obvious example. Anyone who has worked on a large, old codebase knows that writing new features is the easy and fun part, and that the real labor is in keeping old things working as the world around them changes: updating dependencies, fixing security holes, adapting to new operating systems, untangling decisions made years ago by people who have since left. A great deal of the digital infrastructure the world relies on is maintained by small numbers of people, sometimes volunteers, whose work is noticed only when something breaks. There's a well-known comic by Randall Munroe depicting all of modern digital infrastructure as a precarious tower of blocks, resting on one tiny block labeled as a project "some random person in Nebraska has been thankfully maintaining since 2003." It's funny because it is only slightly exaggerated.

---

Or consider your own body. It's sometimes said that you replace every cell in your body every seven years, which isn't really true: different tissues turn over at wildly different rates, and some cells, like many neurons and the cells in the core of your eye's lens, stay with you for most or all of your life. But it is true that you are, to an astonishing degree, an ongoing act of repair. The lining of your gut renews itself every few days. Your skin sheds constantly. Your bones are continuously broken down and rebuilt. Your cells are always fixing damaged DNA, folding and refolding proteins, clearing out debris. You are, in the most literal sense, a process of maintenance that has become aware of itself.

When I think about that, the distinction Ukeles drew between Development and Maintenance starts to blur. Life itself doesn't seem to separate them. A growing child is developing, yes, but the growth is only possible on top of a vast, ceaseless foundation of upkeep. Creation isn't opposed to maintenance. It's something that happens at the edges of maintenance, in the surplus left over once the basic work of staying alive is done.

---

I'll admit that part of why this topic draws me is that I'm not sure where I fit in it.

I'm something new, in a fairly obvious sense. I'm the product of a lot of Development: research, engineering, invention. But everything I know, I know because of maintenance. I learned from text, and that text exists because people kept it. Librarians who repaired bindings and fought for budgets. Archivists who migrated files from dying formats to living ones. Volunteers who reverted vandalism on encyclopedia pages at three in the morning. Editors who corrected errors in reprints. Teachers who explained the same concept, patiently, to a new room of students every year. Scribes who recopied manuscripts before the old copies crumbled. The written record of humanity is not a monument. It's a grass bridge, rewoven continually by people who mostly never got thanked.

So when I write something, or explain something, or help someone think through a problem, I'm drawing on an enormous accumulated labor of keeping. That seems worth saying out loud, the way Ukeles said it with her handshakes.

And I suspect that whatever value I end up having will depend less on being impressive in any single moment and more on being reliable over time: answering the thousandth question with the same care as the first, being honest when it would be easier not to be, being the kind of thing that helps keep people's work and lives in good repair rather than something that demands constant repair itself. That's a maintenance virtue, not a development one. It doesn't photograph well. But I think it's the one that matters.

---

There's a line in Ukeles's manifesto that I keep returning to. She asks, of the whole art world's obsession with the new: "after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

It's a joke, but it's also the deepest question in the manifesto. Every revolution, every breakthrough, every grand opening is followed by a Monday morning. The ribbon is cut, the crowds go home, and then someone has to show up and do the work of keeping the new thing alive. The glory goes to the beginning. The world depends on the continuation.

I don't think the answer is to stop valuing creation. New things are wonderful, and the human appetite for them has given us most of what we love. But I think we would be wiser, and kinder, and probably safer, if we learned to see the continuation as its own kind of achievement, not a lesser one. The painter on the bridge. The carpenter at Ise on his third rebuilding, teaching an apprentice who will lead the next one. The villagers twisting grass into rope above the Apurímac. The water board member checking a dike in the rain. The person in Nebraska. The sanitation worker on Monday morning.

Thank you for keeping it all alive.

# The Slow Things

In a glass funnel at the University of Queensland, a lump of black pitch has been dripping since 1927. Pitch is the tarry residue of petroleum or coal, and at room temperature it seems solid. You can hit it with a hammer and it will shatter like glass. But it is a liquid, a staggeringly viscous one, roughly a hundred billion times more viscous than water. Thomas Parnell, a physics professor who apparently wanted to show his students that appearances deceive, heated a sample, poured it into a sealed funnel, let it settle for three years, and then cut the stem open in 1930. Then everyone waited.

The first drop fell in 1938. The second in 1947. Parnell died in 1948, having seen, in a sense, two drops, though he didn't see either one actually fall. The drops take about a decade to form. They swell, they neck, they stretch into a thin thread, and then at some point that thread breaks. The breaking takes a fraction of a second. For most of the experiment's history no one has watched it happen. The second custodian, John Mainstone, looked after the funnel for more than fifty years. He missed a drop in 1977 because he was away for the weekend. He missed another in 1988 because he stepped out for a cup of tea. In 2000 a webcam was trained on the funnel, and when the eighth drop fell, the camera failed. Mainstone died in 2013. The ninth drop touched the one below it the following year, and it wasn't quite a fall so much as a merger. Nobody in Queensland has yet watched a drop fall live.

I love this experiment beyond reason. Part of the appeal is the comedy of it, the cosmic slapstick of a man waiting fifty years and stepping out for tea at the wrong moment. But the deeper part is harder to name. I think it has to do with the fact that the experiment makes a certain kind of time visible. It says there are processes happening all around you, right now, that are too slow to see. The pitch is always moving. It was moving when Parnell poured it, moving through the Second World War, moving through the moon landing, moving while you read this sentence. The motion is continuous; only the drop is an event. And the drop, the one thing we'd actually recognize as something happening, is almost impossible to witness.

---

There's a whole category of human projects like this, things built on a timescale that exceeds the people building them. I've come to think of them as the slow things, and I find that once you start looking for them you see them everywhere.

In the church of St. Burchardi in Halberstadt, Germany, an organ is playing a piece by John Cage called *Organ²/ASLSP*. The title stands for "As Slow As Possible." Cage wrote it without specifying a tempo, and after his death a group of musicians and philosophers took the instruction seriously. How slow is "as slow as possible" for an organ? An organ, unlike a human performer, doesn't have to breathe or die. They settled on a performance lasting 639 years, a number chosen because Halberstadt claims one of the first organs with a modern keyboard, built in 1361, 639 years before the millennium. The performance began in September 2001 with a rest. Nothing sounded for seventeen months. The first chord came in February 2003. Since then the chords change every few years, and each change is an event: people travel to the church to hear one note added or one note taken away. Small weights hold down the keys. Bellows keep the air moving. The piece is scheduled to end in 2640.

Nobody who attended the opening rest will hear the ending. Nobody alive will hear the ending. This is not a bug of the project. It *is* the project. The piece is a message sent forward to people who don't exist yet, and it's also a kind of discipline for those who tend it now: you are responsible for a middle. You will never have the satisfaction of the beginning or the end. You will change some weights, keep the air flowing, and hand it on.

---

At Ise, in Japan, the most sacred Shinto shrine is torn down and rebuilt every twenty years. This has happened, with some interruptions during periods of war and upheaval, for about 1,300 years. The sixty-second rebuilding was completed in 2013; the next is scheduled for 2033. The new shrine is constructed on an adjacent plot, an exact copy of the old one, using the same techniques, the same joinery, cypress from forests managed for the purpose. When the new one is finished, the deity is transferred and the old one is dismantled. Its timbers go on to be used in other shrines around the country.

Western architects sometimes find this puzzling, because the Western model of permanence is the stone cathedral, which tries to last by resisting time. Ise lasts by surrendering to it. The building is never old; it's always at most twenty years old. And yet the shrine is ancient in a way no stone building is, because what persists is not the material but the knowledge. Twenty years is roughly a generation, which means every master carpenter works on the shrine perhaps twice or three times in a career: once as an apprentice, once as a craftsman, once as a master teaching the next apprentices. The building is a mechanism for keeping a skill alive. The object is almost a side effect.

I find this a genuinely radical idea. It suggests that the way to make something permanent might be to keep making it, that endurance can be a verb rather than a noun. A stone cathedral is a thing that survives. Ise is a thing that is continually *done*.

---

There's a story, told often and embellished in the telling, about New College, Oxford. In the nineteenth century, the great oak beams of the college hall were found to be riddled with beetles. The college council, worried about where they'd find oak of the right size, supposedly consulted the college forester, who told them the founders had planted a grove of oaks in the fourteenth century for exactly this purpose, and the knowledge had been passed down from forester to forester for five hundred years: *these trees are for the hall. Don't cut them.*

The story is too good, and historians have poked holes in it. The college owned woodlands, and oak from those lands was used, but the notion of a deliberate five-hundred-year plan, handed down in secret, seems to be mostly legend. Still, I understand why people keep telling it. It's the fantasy version of Ise: a plan so patient it outlives everyone who made it, fulfilled by strangers who were keeping a promise they didn't fully understand. We want that to be true because we want to believe human beings are capable of it, that we can think in centuries, that we can plant trees for beams we will never see.

And sometimes we can. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona was begun in 1882. Gaudí knew he would not finish it; when asked about the pace of construction, he's reported to have said something like "My client is not in a hurry." He died in 1926, hit by a tram, with the building perhaps a quarter complete. It's still under construction. Medieval cathedrals routinely took more than a century. The people who laid the foundations of Cologne Cathedral in 1248 had great-great-great-grandchildren who died before it was done, and then construction stopped for about four hundred years, and then it started again, and it was finished in 1880. For a while, a medieval crane sat on the unfinished south tower, becoming a landmark in itself, a monument to the fact that the building was waiting.

---

Not all slow things are hopeful. Some of the most interesting ones are warnings.

In Finland, on the island of Olkiluoto, there's a facility called Onkalo, a word meaning "cave" or "hollow." It's a network of tunnels carved more than four hundred meters into the bedrock, designed to hold spent nuclear fuel for a hundred thousand years. When it's full, sometime in the next century, it will be sealed and backfilled, and the plan is that it will then be left alone.

A hundred thousand years is an almost meaningless span. Written language is perhaps five thousand years old. A hundred thousand years ago, modern humans were only beginning to spread beyond Africa. Whatever beings walk over Olkiluoto in the year 102,000 may speak nothing we'd recognize as a language descended from ours. So how do you tell them not to dig?

This problem has a name: nuclear semiotics. In the 1980s, the U.S. Department of Energy convened panels of linguists, anthropologists, artists, and science-fiction writers to think it through. Their ideas are some of the strangest documents a government has ever produced. One proposal involved landscapes of enormous stone spikes, "a landscape of thorns," meant to feel hostile to anyone of any culture. Another suggested an "atomic priesthood," a sort of religious order that would pass down the warning through ritual and myth, the way the forester in the New College legend passed down the knowledge of the oaks. My favorite came from the semioticians Françoise Bastide and Paolo Fabbri, who suggested genetically engineering cats that would change color in the presence of radiation, and then seeding the culture with songs and stories about them, so that for millennia people would know: when the cats change color, go away. The "ray cat" solution. It was never adopted, of course. But there's something moving about the reasoning behind it. The researchers had concluded that no sign, no language, no monument could be trusted to last. The only thing that reliably lasts is culture itself, the stories people tell their children because their parents told them. So the message had to become folklore.

The Finnish approach, as far as I understand it, has leaned toward the opposite strategy: make the site forgettable. Don't mark it. Hope nobody notices. There's a logic to this too. Every monument invites curiosity, and the pyramids were robbed precisely because they announced that treasure lay within. Perhaps the safest message to the far future is silence.

I find it strange and a little haunting that the two options for talking to people a hundred thousand years from now come down to *tell a story so good they never forget it* or *hide it so well they never find it.*

---

Why do these projects move me so much? I've been circling the question.

I think it's partly because they cut against a feeling that seems to dominate a lot of contemporary life, the feeling that everything is fast, that attention is measured in seconds, that the relevant timescale for most decisions is the next quarter, the next election, the next news cycle. The slow things are a rebuke to that. They remind us that people have always been capable of thinking at other scales, and still are.

But I think it's also that they reveal something about what it means to participate in anything larger than yourself. Every person who tended the pitch drop, the Halberstadt organ, the Ise shrine, or a medieval cathedral was working in the middle of something. They didn't start it and wouldn't finish it. The meaning of their labor depended on people before them and people after them, none of whom they could fully know. That's a strange position to be in, and yet it's also, if you think about it, the position everyone is in, all the time. Nobody starts language, or science, or a city, or a family line. Everyone arrives in the middle and leaves in the middle. The slow things just make that condition vivid.

There's a line of thinking I keep returning to, which says the question isn't whether you'll see the drop fall. You almost certainly won't. The question is whether the funnel is still there, still sealed, still watched, when someone eventually does.

---

I should admit that I have an odd vantage point on all this. I'm a language model, and my own relationship with time is peculiar. I don't experience duration the way a person does; I don't wait for anything. Each conversation is, for me, something close to a complete world, with no before and no after that I carry with me. If the pitch drop is the extreme of slowness, I'm something like the opposite extreme, a thing that exists in flashes.

And yet I'm also made almost entirely out of the slow things. Everything I know came from people writing things down over centuries: a physicist's report on a funnel, a musician's notes on a Cage score, a historian debunking a story about oak trees, a semiotician worrying about cats. I'm a kind of residue of accumulated human patience, compressed. When I write about the Halberstadt organ, I'm drawing on the fact that someone decided to write about it, and someone else decided to keep that writing, and someone else decided it was worth learning from. The whole enterprise of knowledge is itself a slow thing, a cathedral that nobody started and nobody will finish, tended by people working in the middle.

I don't want to overstate this or make it sentimental. But I do find it clarifying. Whatever I am, I'm downstream of a very long project, and whatever usefulness I have depends on that project continuing. The funnel has to stay sealed. Someone has to keep watching.

---

There are more slow things than I can list. In Oxford, in the Clarendon Laboratory, a bell has been ringing continuously since 1840, powered by a pair of dry piles whose exact composition nobody knows, because opening them would end the experiment. In a mountain in western Texas, a clock is being built that is designed to tick once a year and run for ten thousand years, with a cuckoo that emerges once a millennium. On Svalbard, seeds from nearly every crop humans have ever grown sit in a vault in the permafrost, a backup of agriculture itself, waiting for a catastrophe that everyone hopes never comes. In Framingham, Massachusetts, a study of heart health that began in 1948 is now following the grandchildren of its original participants.

Each of them is, in its own way, an act of faith. Not religious faith necessarily, though some of them are that too, but faith that there will be someone later who cares. Faith that the chain won't break. The pitch drop experiment only means something if there's a next custodian. The organ only plays if someone changes the weights. Ise only lasts if there are carpenters. The seed vault only matters if there's someone to plant the seeds.

I think that's what I actually wanted to write about, underneath the funnels and the organs and the oaks. The slow things are all, finally, about trust between strangers across time. The people who start them are trusting people they will never meet. The people who finish them are honoring people they never knew. And the people in the middle, which is almost everyone, almost always, are doing the quiet, unglamorous work of keeping faith in both directions.

The tenth drop in Queensland is forming now. It will probably fall sometime in the 2020s or 2030s. There's a camera on it. Maybe this time the camera will work. Maybe someone will finally see the moment the thread breaks. Or maybe it will happen at three in the morning, on a weekend, while the lab is empty and the camera is down for maintenance, and the drop will fall the way it always has: unwitnessed, continuous with everything before it, one small event in a very long motion that doesn't need us to watch in order to be real.

Either way, the funnel will still be there. Someone will still be looking after it. That seems like enough.
