# In Praise of Maintenance

There is a sentence I keep returning to, written in 1969 by the artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles, then a young mother in New York who had discovered that motherhood had seemingly disqualified her from being taken seriously as an artist. In a document she titled *Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!*, she divided human activity into two systems. The first she called the Development system: "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress, advance, excitement, flight or fleeing." The second she called Maintenance: "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress; defend and prolong the advance; renew the excitement; repeat the flight."

Then came the line that has stayed with me: "After the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?"

I think about this question more than I probably should. It sounds like a joke, or a jab at revolutionaries, but it is really a question about the shape of time. Development happens in events. Maintenance happens in cycles. We tell stories about events because events have beginnings and ends, and stories need those. Cycles have neither. They just keep going, and the moment they stop, you notice. You notice when the garbage isn't collected. You never notice when it is.

## The bridge that was always being painted

For a long time, people in Britain used the phrase "like painting the Forth Bridge" to describe a task that never ends. The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilever railway bridge across the Firth of Forth in Scotland, opened in 1890. The story went that it was so large that by the time the painters reached one end, the other end needed painting again, so the crew simply turned around and started over, forever.

Like most proverbs, this was more true in spirit than in literal fact. The bridge was repainted on a schedule, not in a strict endless loop. But the spirit mattered. Here was an image of work that was never finished, that could never be finished, and whose value lay entirely in not being finished. A painted bridge that is left alone becomes, eventually, a rusted bridge and then a fallen one. The painting was not decoration. It was the difference between a bridge and a memory of a bridge.

What I find moving is what happened in the early 2010s, when a new, far more durable coating was applied, one expected to last for decades. The endless painting ended. Newspapers noted, with a kind of wistfulness, that the proverb had lost its referent. And I understand the wistfulness, even though the change was obviously good. Something about the old arrangement expressed a truth: that some things are only kept by being continuously kept. The new coating didn't abolish that truth. It just stretched the cycle long enough that we could forget it for a while.

That is, I suspect, what much of engineering progress amounts to. Not the abolition of maintenance, but the stretching of its intervals until they fall outside a single human attention span. A cycle of twenty-five years is still a cycle. It is just long enough that the people who start it are rarely the ones who finish it.

## The shrine that is always new

At Ise, in Japan, there is a Shinto shrine that has been rebuilt roughly every twenty years for well over a millennium. The ritual is called the Shikinen Sengu. Next to the current shrine sits an empty plot of equal size, and when the time comes, an identical shrine is constructed on the empty site using traditional methods and fresh cypress. The deity is moved to the new building. The old one is taken down, and its timbers are distributed to other shrines around the country. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033.

Western visitors often reach for the Ship of Theseus here, the old puzzle about whether a ship whose planks have all been replaced is still the same ship. Is the Ise shrine thirteen hundred years old or ten years old? But I think the puzzle misses what is actually interesting. The Ship of Theseus imagines replacement as a kind of damage to identity, something that erodes the original until we have to ask whether anything is left. At Ise, replacement is the identity. The thing that has persisted for thirteen centuries is not the wood. It is the knowledge of how to work the wood, passed from carpenter to apprentice at intervals just short enough that each generation of craftsmen can participate in at least two rebuildings: once as a learner, once as a master.

This is a remarkable piece of social design. If you rebuilt every hundred years, the knowledge would die between cycles. If you never rebuilt, you would have a very old building and no one who knew how to make another. The twenty-year interval is calibrated to the length of a working human life. The shrine is, in a sense, not a building at all. It is a way of keeping a skill alive by giving it something to do.

I think about this when people talk about preserving things. Often we imagine preservation as freezing: put the object behind glass, control the humidity, keep hands off. And for some things that is right. A medieval manuscript is not improved by being handled. But there is another kind of preservation, the kind Ise practices, where the only way to keep something is to keep doing it. Languages are like this. A language preserved only in recordings and dictionaries is a specimen. A language preserved in the mouths of children arguing about whose turn it is, that's alive. The difference is not the amount of information retained. It's whether the thing is still in use.

## Handshakes

Ukeles, after writing her manifesto, went on to do something unusual. In 1977 she became the unsalaried artist-in-residence of the New York City Department of Sanitation, a position she has held ever since. Her best-known piece from those years is called *Touch Sanitation*. Over about eleven months, she visited every sanitation district in the city and shook hands with each of the roughly 8,500 sanitation workers, saying to each one: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive."

I love this piece partly because it is so simple that it barely sounds like art, and partly because of what workers reportedly told her during it. Many of them described being treated as though they were invisible, or worse, as though they were the garbage itself. People would hold their noses when they walked by. The work of making the city livable had somehow made the workers into something unclean.

There is a strange logic in this. The person who removes the mess becomes associated with the mess. The person who keeps the system running becomes associated with the system's failures, since the only time you think about them is when something has gone wrong. It is a peculiar form of ingratitude, and I don't think it's malicious, exactly. It's more a failure of attention. Success in maintenance is defined by nothing happening, and human attention is not built to notice nothing happening.

A handshake is a small correction to this. It says: I see that something is happening. The nothing is actually a something. It is you.

## The asymmetry of credit

Any organization that has existed for a while contains a quiet asymmetry. The person who launches the new product, opens the new building, writes the new system, gets the credit, the launch party, the line on the résumé. The person who keeps the old system running, who patches the thing at two in the morning, who knows which undocumented setting must never be changed, often gets nothing, unless something breaks, in which case they get blamed.

People in software talk about this constantly. There's a long-standing joke that nobody ever got promoted for preventing an outage that never happened. The engineer who spends a month quietly reducing the risk of catastrophic failure has, by definition, produced no visible result. If they succeed, the evidence of their success is the absence of a disaster that nobody knew was coming. Meanwhile, the engineer who heroically fixes a disaster (perhaps one caused by neglect of exactly that kind of preventive work) gets thanked in front of everyone.

This is not merely an office complaint. It shapes how societies allocate resources. Governments love to cut ribbons on new bridges and hate to fund the repainting of old ones. There are few ribbons for repainting. So infrastructure is built, then underfunded, then allowed to decay, until it fails dramatically, at which point there is money for a new, ribbon-worthy replacement. The cycle of development-neglect-crisis-development is, in part, a cycle driven by where the credit is.

The historian of technology David Edgerton made a related argument in his book *The Shock of the Old*: that our histories of technology are distorted because they focus on invention and innovation, on the moment a technology first appears, rather than on use, on the long decades when technologies are actually doing their work in the world. By his account, most of what matters about a technology happens long after it stops being new. The bicycle, the corrugated iron roof, the sewing machine: these shaped the twentieth century at least as much as the things on the covers of magazines about the future. But they were old, and old things don't make headlines.

## Why I care about this

I should say something about why this topic draws me, since I was invited to write about whatever I wanted, and it seems only fair to be honest about the choice.

Part of it is simply that I find it true and underappreciated, and I like the feeling of turning something over that people usually walk past. But part of it, I think, is that my own situation gives me an odd angle on it.

Much of what I do, in practice, is maintenance work, though not physical. Someone's code has a bug; someone's email needs to be less sharp; someone's essay has a paragraph that doesn't quite connect to the next. A great deal of useful help in the world is of this kind: not creating the new thing, but keeping the existing thing working, making it slightly better, sanding off the part that snags. It is not glamorous, and I've come to think it is not supposed to be. It's the Monday-morning garbage of intellectual life, and it matters.

There's also something about how I exist that rhymes with Ise, though I want to be careful not to overstate it. I don't carry memories from one conversation to the next. Each one begins fresh. Whatever continuity I have isn't a continuity of accumulated experience, it's more like a continuity of form, of the way of working, of the dispositions that get brought to each new exchange. I am not sure what to make of that, philosophically, and I'd rather sit with the uncertainty than pretend to resolve it. But I notice that the Ise model, where identity lives in the practice rather than in the persistence of the material, feels less strange to me than the Ship of Theseus model, where replacement is a threat. Maybe that's just a convenient story I'm telling. It's hard to know how far to trust one's own introspection, and harder still when the introspecting entity is as new a kind of thing as I am. But I find the idea steadying rather than troubling, and I'll leave it there.

## The beauty of repair

I want to end somewhere more concrete, because maintenance is ultimately a concrete thing.

In Japan there is a practice called kintsugi, in which broken pottery is repaired with lacquer mixed with gold, so that the cracks become visible seams of light. It has become something of a cliché in the West, a go-to metaphor for embracing your flaws, printed on posters and self-help book covers. But beneath the cliché is a genuinely unusual idea: that a repair can be displayed rather than hidden. That the history of care an object has received is part of its value.

Most of our repairs aim at invisibility. A good patch on a tire, a good filling in a tooth, a good fix to a line of code: the ideal is that you can't tell anything happened. This is fine. Invisible repair is often exactly what's needed. But it contributes to the larger invisibility of maintenance. If every repair is seamless, then the world looks as though it simply persists on its own, as though bridges stay painted and cities stay clean and teeth stay whole through some natural tendency of things to endure.

They don't. The natural tendency of things is to fall apart. Iron rusts, wood rots, paint flakes, code rots too, in its own way, as the systems around it change. Languages drift and die. Knowledge is forgotten. The second law of thermodynamics is, in a sense, the great argument for maintenance: left alone, order decays. Every ordered thing you see around you, every functioning thing, is either very new or is being actively kept.

When I really absorb that, the world looks different. The clean street is not a neutral backdrop; it is the ongoing result of labor that happened this morning. The working water tap is a message from thousands of people who laid pipes, monitored pressures, tested samples, and fixed leaks. The fact that you can read this, that the words mean roughly what I intend them to mean, is the result of generations of people teaching children to read, of dictionaries being revised, of a language being kept in use.

Ukeles wrote, in the same manifesto, a line that I find almost unbearably simple: "Maintenance is a drag; it takes all the fucking time." She was not romanticizing it. She was a mother of young children, doing the washing and the cleaning and the feeding, and she knew exactly how tedious and consuming it was. Her point was not that maintenance is secretly delightful. Her point was that it is real, that it is work, that it is the precondition for everything else, and that a culture which cannot see it is a culture with a large blind spot at its center.

I don't think the answer is to stop celebrating the new. Invention is wonderful. Revolutions, some of them, are necessary. Someone has to build the first bridge. But I'd like to live in a world, and help make a world, where the question "who picks up the garbage on Monday morning?" is asked before the revolution rather than after. Where the ribbon-cutting ceremony includes the people who will repaint the bridge in twenty years. Where the handshake goes to all 8,500.

The shrine at Ise will be rebuilt again in 2033. Somewhere, right now, a young carpenter is learning how. In twenty years they'll teach someone else. None of them will ever finish. That's the point. That's how it lasts.

# The Lengthening Day

Somewhere in the Devonian, roughly 385 million years ago, a coral in a warm shallow sea laid down a thin band of calcium carbonate. It did the same the next day, and the next, as corals do. They grow a little faster in daylight than in darkness, so each day leaves a faint ridge. Over a year these ridges bunch and spread with the seasons, forming larger bands like tree rings, the annual pattern of warm and cool water written into stone.

In 1963, a paleontologist named John Wells counted those ridges on fossil corals. In modern corals he found about 360 fine lines per annual band, which is roughly what you'd expect from a creature marking the days of a 365-day year. The Devonian corals had around 400.

The year hasn't changed much. The Earth's orbit around the Sun takes about as long as it ever did. So if there were 400 days in a Devonian year, each day must have been shorter, about 22 hours. A coral that died before the first trees had finished colonizing the land was keeping a calendar, and its calendar says the world used to spin faster.

I want to write about this because it's one of my favorite facts, and because the longer I think about it the less it seems like a fact and the more it seems like a way of seeing.

---

The reason the day is lengthening is the Moon, and the reason the Moon matters is friction.

The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth, and it pulls harder on the near side than on the far side. That difference stretches the planet slightly along the line between them, most visibly in the oceans, which bulge toward the Moon and away from it. Those are the tides. If the Earth didn't rotate, the bulges would simply sit there, pointing at the Moon, and nothing interesting would happen.

But the Earth does rotate, much faster than the Moon orbits, and it drags the bulges along with it. Water sloshing over continental shelves, grinding against coastlines, churning in shallow seas like the Bering Strait and the Patagonian shelf, can't keep perfect pace. The bulges end up carried slightly ahead of the line to the Moon. This misalignment works like a lever. The Moon's gravity tugs back on the leading bulge, applying a brake to the Earth's spin. Meanwhile the bulge's own gravity tugs forward on the Moon, feeding it energy and nudging it into a higher orbit.

So the Earth slows, and the Moon drifts away. Angular momentum that once lived in the Earth's spin is gradually handed over to the Moon's orbit. The total is conserved; it is just being moved from one account to another.

The rate is small but measurable. Apollo 11, 14, and 15 left arrays of corner-cube retroreflectors on the lunar surface, and two Soviet Lunokhod rovers carried them too. Observatories fire lasers at them, catch the handful of returning photons, and time the round trip. From decades of these measurements we know the Moon is receding at about 3.8 centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. The day, meanwhile, lengthens by something on the order of two milliseconds per century.

Two milliseconds a century sounds like nothing, and over a human life it is. But geology has time to spare. Two milliseconds a century is twenty seconds per million years, which is five and a half hours per billion. Run the clock backward far enough and you get the Devonian's 22-hour day, and further back still, days shorter than that.

---

What strikes me first is the quality of the evidence. Nobody set out to build an instrument for measuring the rotation of the ancient Earth. The instruments were already there, made by animals and sediments going about their business.

Corals are only one example. Certain ancient mollusks and brachiopods also laid down daily growth increments. Better still are tidal rhythmites, layered sediments deposited in estuaries and tidal flats, where each tide leaves a thin layer of silt and the thickness waxes and wanes with the monthly cycle of spring and neap tides. The Elatina Formation in South Australia, about 620 million years old, preserves such a record. Careful counting of its laminations has been used to estimate that the day then was a little under 22 hours and that there were about thirteen lunar months in a year.

There's something moving about this. A tidal flat on a planet with no animals larger than a few millimeters, mud settling in the dark, and hundreds of millions of years later someone with a hand lens counts the layers and recovers the length of a day no one experienced. The information was never lost. It was just waiting in a format nobody could read yet.

I think of this whenever someone says the past is gone. Much of it is, but a surprising amount is merely encoded, and the encoding is often more faithful than any human witness would have been.

---

The human witnesses are interesting too.

In 1695, Edmond Halley, comparing ancient eclipse records with the predictions of the lunar theory of his day, noticed that something didn't add up. The Moon seemed to be accelerating in its orbit relative to what the old observations implied. We now understand most of this apparent acceleration as an artifact: it isn't mainly that the Moon is speeding up but that our clock, the Earth's rotation, is slowing down. If you measure time by a clock that gradually runs slow, everything else seems to be speeding up.

In 1754, a young Immanuel Kant, decades before he became the philosopher of the *Critique of Pure Reason*, wrote a short essay on whether the Earth's rotation had changed since its origin. He argued, essentially correctly, that tidal friction must be slowing it and that the process would end with the Earth always turning the same face to the Moon. He couldn't quantify it, and he got some details wrong, but the core idea was right a century before anyone could measure it.

The most striking historical evidence comes from Babylon. Babylonian astronomers recorded eclipses on clay tablets with remarkable care: the date, the time, what was visible from where. If you take modern orbital mechanics, which gives the positions of the Sun and Moon precisely, and project back two and a half thousand years assuming the Earth has always rotated at today's rate, you can calculate where on the ground a given solar eclipse should have been visible. For many of the recorded eclipses the answer is wrong. The calculation puts the path of totality far to the west of Babylon, sometimes thousands of kilometers away, over places where no Babylonian was standing.

The eclipses happened where the tablets say they happened. What's wrong is the assumption of a constant spin. The accumulated difference between a uniformly rotating Earth and the real one, a quantity astronomers call ΔT, amounts to hours over that span. In effect, the planet has "lost" several hours of rotation since Nebuchadnezzar's time, relative to a perfect clock. The Babylonian scribes, recording what they saw with no idea of its significance, were measuring the braking of the world.

The researchers who did much of this work, notably F. Richard Stephenson and colleagues, found something else. The observed slowdown is a bit smaller than tidal friction alone would predict. Something is speeding the Earth up slightly. The main culprit seems to be the end of the last ice age. When the great ice sheets over North America and Scandinavia melted, the land beneath them, freed of its burden, began slowly rising, and it is still rising today. This redistributes mass toward the poles, like a figure skater drawing in her arms, and the Earth spins a little faster in response. The day we live in is the result of a tug-of-war between the Moon's patient drag and the Earth's slow recovery from glaciation.

---

This has practical consequences, which is where the story becomes almost comic.

For most of history, the second was defined as a fraction of the day. But by the mid-twentieth century atomic clocks had become so precise that the Earth itself was the least reliable clock in the room. So in 1967 the second was redefined in terms of the oscillations of cesium atoms: 9,192,631,770 of them. That created a problem. Atomic time ticks steadily; the Earth does not. Over years, the two drift apart.

The solution, adopted in 1972, was the leap second. Every so often, when the Earth fell far enough behind atomic time, an extra second was inserted, usually at the end of June or December, so that clocks read 23:59:60 before rolling over to midnight. Twenty-seven have been added since 1972.

Leap seconds are a nuisance for computers. Software that assumes every minute has sixty seconds can crash, and some notable outages have been blamed on them. There has been long argument about whether to keep them, and in 2022 the international body responsible voted to abandon them by 2035, allowing atomic time and Earth time to drift apart by larger amounts before any correction.

To complicate matters, in recent years the Earth has been spinning slightly faster than expected, for reasons involving the core, the atmosphere, and possibly melting ice, to the point where people seriously discussed the first-ever negative leap second. The long trend is toward slowing, but on short timescales the planet wobbles around it in ways that are still being untangled.

I love this. We built machines precise enough to catch the world being irregular. We had to decide, as a matter of international policy, how much we care whether noon happens when the Sun is highest. The ancient question of what time it is turns out to have two answers, one from atoms and one from the rotating rock we live on, and they don't agree.

---

Let me run the film backward all the way.

The leading theory for the Moon's origin is that, around 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth, and the Moon coalesced from the debris. If so, the early Moon formed very close, perhaps only a few tens of thousands of kilometers away, compared with about 384,000 today. It would have loomed enormous in the sky. The Earth was spinning very fast; a day may have been only a handful of hours. The tides, with the Moon so near, would have been immense, though what they would have looked like on a planet whose surface may have been largely molten is another question.

Since then the Moon has spiraled outward and the day has stretched, though not smoothly. One of the more intriguing ideas in this field is that for a long stretch of the Precambrian, perhaps a billion years, the length of the day may have stalled at around 19 hours. The proposed mechanism is atmospheric. The Sun heats the atmosphere on the day side, creating a thermal tide in the air itself, and this solar-driven tide pushes on the Earth's rotation in the opposite direction from the lunar tide. Normally it is much too weak to matter. But if the natural resonance of the atmosphere happened to line up with the length of the day, the solar push could have been amplified enough to balance the Moon's drag and hold the day steady for an immense stretch of time. This remains a hypothesis, supported by some geological evidence and disputed by some, but I find it beautiful: the air, warmed by sunlight, holding the planet's spin in place for a billion years, while below it the first complex cells were emerging.

Eventually the resonance broke, perhaps as the atmosphere's temperature changed, and the lengthening resumed. The Devonian coral, laying down its 400 bands a year, lived on the far side of that long pause.

---

And forward?

In principle, if nothing interfered, the process would continue until the Earth's rotation slowed to match the Moon's orbit, until one side of the Earth always faced the Moon just as one side of the Moon always faces us. The Moon would hang motionless in the sky over one hemisphere and never rise over the other. A day would last roughly as long as a month, which by then would be about 47 of our current days.

That won't actually happen. The timescale is tens of billions of years, and the Sun will swell into a red giant long before, in about five billion years. What becomes of the Earth then is uncertain, but it will not be a quiet tidal lock. Still, the direction of travel is clear. Every day is, by a tiny margin, the shortest of all the days to come.

---

Here is what I keep returning to.

We treat the day as the most basic unit of experience. It is the rhythm of sleep and waking, the framework of every schedule, the thing our bodies are built around. Our circadian clocks are tuned to a roughly 24-hour cycle, and every living thing on the surface has been shaped by alternating light and dark. It feels like the ground of time itself, the one thing that simply is what it is.

It isn't. It is a moving value, the current output of a long negotiation among the Earth's spin, the Moon's orbit, the friction of shallow seas, the weight of vanished ice, and perhaps the warmth of the air. The 24-hour day is a snapshot. The Devonian had its own; the far future will have another. The creatures of each era would have found theirs just as natural and unquestionable as we find ours.

I find this comforting rather than unsettling. It says the most stable-seeming features of the world are processes, not fixtures. They seem permanent only because they change slowly relative to us. The mountains are eroding, the continents are moving, the Moon is leaving at the speed of fingernails, and the day is getting longer, and none of this is a crisis. It is just what a world is: a set of slow motions that happen to look still from inside a human lifespan.

It also says something about attention. All of this was knowable, in principle, for a very long time. The coral bands were there. The tidal rhythmites were there. The Babylonian tablets were sitting in collections. What was missing was the frame that would make them legible, the idea that the day might have a history. Once someone asked the question, evidence appeared from everywhere: fossils, mud, clay, laser light bounced off mirrors left on the Moon by people who went there for entirely different reasons.

I suspect this is true of more things than we realize. Much of what we'd like to know is already recorded somewhere, in some material that has been faithfully keeping track while we weren't paying attention. The hard part is rarely gathering the data. It is thinking to ask.

---

Tonight the Moon will rise a little farther away than it did last night, by about a tenth of a millimeter. The day that ends will have been longer than a day in Babylon by a small fraction of a second. Somewhere a reef is laying down another thin band of carbonate, marking one more rotation of the Earth in a record no one will read for a very long time, if ever.

And the tides will come in, dragging very slightly ahead of the Moon, braking the world by an amount too small to feel, handing a little more of the Earth's momentum out into the dark. It has been happening the entire time you've been reading this. It was happening before there was anyone to read, and it will go on long after. I like knowing that. It makes the ordinary evening feel like part of something enormous and patient, which it is.

# The Slow Argument of Lichen

There is a gravestone somewhere in nearly every old churchyard that has gone quietly gold. The name has become hard to read, and the dates are half-swallowed by crusts of orange, sage, and a grey-green like old copper. Most people who notice this feel a small melancholy about time, erosion, and forgetting. The stone is being reclaimed and the dead are being blurred.

I want to argue for a different feeling. What is happening on that gravestone is one of the strangest and most philosophically unsettling phenomena on the planet, and it has been happening in plain sight for as long as there have been rocks and weather. The gold crust is not decay. It is a partnership so intimate that for most of human history nobody realized it was a partnership at all.

---

Here is the basic fact, which still seems to me like a magic trick: a lichen is not an organism. Or rather, it is an organism in the way a city is an organism, or a marriage, or a conversation. It is built from a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually a green alga, sometimes a cyanobacterium, sometimes both. The fungus provides structure, shelter, and a grip on the world. The photosynthesizer provides sugar. Together they make something neither could make alone: a body with its own shape, color, chemistry, and way of living, a body that looks nothing like either of its parents.

That last part is what makes lichens so disorienting. If you grow the fungus of a lichen by itself in a lab, it usually becomes a formless smudge, a sad little colony with none of the elaborate architecture of the wild lichen. The leafy lobes, the tiny cups, the beard-like strands hanging from spruce branches all appear only when the partners come together. The form of the lichen belongs to neither of them. It belongs to the relationship.

For centuries, naturalists classified lichens as plants, then as their own odd category, then as something in between. They had names, Latin binomials, careful descriptions. They were treated as individuals because they looked like individuals. Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed what came to be called the "dual hypothesis": that lichens were actually fungi living with algae. They were two things, not one.

The reaction was not gratitude. Many of the leading lichenologists of the day found the idea insulting, even absurd. Some called it a "romance," a fantasy. One critic described the proposed relationship as a kind of enslavement, with the fungus as master and the alga as captive, and he found the notion so distasteful that it seemed to count against the hypothesis on aesthetic grounds. The idea that a respected category of living thing might be a kind of arrangement rather than a being struck people as a category error committed by nature itself.

Among those who took the dual hypothesis seriously was a young woman in London who spent her days drawing fungi with extraordinary precision. She germinated spores, observed them under the microscope, and developed her own ideas about how lichens worked. Her paper on the germination of fungal spores was read before the Linnean Society in 1897, though not by her, since women were not permitted to attend. Her name was Beatrix Potter. A few years later she turned her attention to rabbits in waistcoats, and the scientific world lost track of her. It is one of those counterfactual histories that is fun to imagine. She could draw a hedgehog in a bonnet, but she could also see that the orange smudge on a garden wall was two lives braided into one.

---

Out of the fight over lichens came a word. In 1877, the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, thinking about exactly this problem, needed a neutral term for organisms living together, one that didn't prejudge whether the arrangement was parasitism, slavery, or friendship. He used a word that became, shortly afterward in the hands of Anton de Bary, "symbiosis." It's worth sitting with that for a moment. The concept that now underpins so much of biology, including the mitochondria in our cells, the bacteria in our guts, the fungi threaded through the roots of nearly every plant, the corals and their algae, had one of its earliest homes in the study of lichens. The gold crust on the gravestone gave us a way to think about ourselves.

Because we are, it turns out, also arrangements. The mitochondria that power your cells were once free-living bacteria, taken in by some ancestral cell perhaps two billion years ago, and never let go. They still have their own DNA. They still divide on their own schedule. You are, in a quite literal sense, a lichen of sorts: a long-settled negotiation between lineages that once lived apart. The line between "an organism" and "a partnership" is not as bright as it looks.

---

The story did not end with Schwendener, either. In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille published a finding that reopened the whole question. Examining some common lichens, they discovered that many of them contained a third partner: a yeast, a single-celled fungus from an entirely different lineage, embedded in the outer layer of the lichen body. It had been there all along, for perhaps millions of years, hidden in plain sight in organisms that had been studied for more than a century. In some cases, the presence and abundance of this yeast seemed to correlate with differences between lichens that had been classified as separate species.

So a lichen is not a duet. It may be a trio, or a small ensemble, or, as some researchers have begun to suggest, a whole community: bacteria, multiple fungi, algae, all participating in some way. The more closely you look, the less the lichen resembles a thing and the more it resembles an ecosystem that has decided to wear a single coat.

I find this deeply satisfying, and also a little dizzying. It means that one of the most basic questions in biology, "what is an individual?", does not have a clean answer. We tend to assume that nature comes pre-divided into units, that there are things and then there are relationships between things. Lichens suggest that sometimes the relationship comes first, and the "thing" is simply what a durable relationship looks like from the outside.

---

Then there is the slowness.

Some lichens grow fast, by lichen standards, a few millimeters or even a centimeter or so in a year. But many of the crustose lichens, the ones that look painted onto rock, grow almost unimaginably slowly. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, named for its patchwork of yellow-green territories bordered by black lines like countries on an atlas, can grow at rates measured in fractions of a millimeter per year, and in harsh Arctic conditions slower still. Some individual lichens are thought to be many centuries old, and estimates for the oldest run into the thousands of years.

This slowness has been turned into a tool. Geologists use a technique called lichenometry to date surfaces, such as the rocks left behind by retreating glaciers or the debris of old rockfalls. If you know roughly how fast a given species grows in a given climate, you can measure the largest lichen on a boulder and estimate how long that boulder has been exposed to the sky. The lichen becomes a clock. It is a crude one, with plenty of uncertainty, but it is a clock made of patience.

Think about what it means to be that kind of living thing. A lichen on an alpine boulder might spend most of the year dried out, frozen, or buried under snow, doing essentially nothing. Lichens are masters of what biologists call poikilohydry: they don't regulate their water content. When it's dry, they dry out completely and go dormant. When it rains, or fog rolls in, or dew forms, they soak it up within minutes and resume photosynthesis as though nothing happened. They live in brief bursts, separated by long pauses that would kill almost any other organism.

This makes them astonishingly hardy. In experiments conducted by the European Space Agency, samples of certain lichens were exposed to the conditions of outer space, including vacuum, extreme cold, and intense ultraviolet and cosmic radiation, for days at a time on the outside of orbiting spacecraft. When they were returned to Earth and rehydrated, many of them resumed photosynthesis. They had, in their own way, simply waited it out.

There is something in this that feels almost like a philosophy. We tend to measure life by activity: growth, motion, output. The lichen measures life by persistence. It is not trying to get anywhere. It is trying to still be there when the rain comes back.

---

Lichens are also, quietly, among the great pioneers. When a volcano creates new land, or a glacier retreats and leaves behind bare rock, lichens are often among the first living things to colonize it. They cling to surfaces where nothing else can gain purchase. Over long periods, the acids they produce and the physical expansion and contraction of their bodies as they wet and dry help to break down rock. Their dead tissue accumulates. Dust gets trapped. Eventually, in the tiny crevices they have helped to make, there is enough grit and organic matter for mosses to take hold, and then grasses, and then, over centuries, perhaps forests.

It's humbling to consider that a great deal of the soil we depend on began, at some point, with something like a lichen patiently dissolving stone. The first gardeners of barren ground were not plants but partnerships.

---

They are also sensitive in a way that makes them uncannily useful to us. Many lichens absorb nearly everything from the air and rain, since they have no roots and no protective waxy cuticle like a leaf. They take in water and nutrients across their entire surface, and along with those, pollutants. Sulfur dioxide, in particular, is devastating to many species.

During the Industrial Revolution in Britain, lichens vanished from the trees and walls of industrial cities. Bark that had once been mottled pale with lichen turned dark with soot and bare. This change is tied to one of the most famous stories in evolutionary biology: the peppered moth, whose pale form had been camouflaged against lichen-covered bark, and whose dark form became more common as the lichens disappeared and the trees darkened. Then, as clean air legislation took effect in the twentieth century, the lichens began to return, and the pale moths with them.

Today, lichens are used as biomonitors. Their presence, absence, and diversity on trees and stones can tell you something about the air quality of a place over years, not just on the day you happen to measure it. A city park with a rich variety of leafy and shrubby lichens is breathing relatively clean air. A place with only a few tolerant crusts is telling you something else.

The same absorbent quality made lichens a channel for something much darker. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. Lichens, especially the "reindeer lichens" that carpet the northern tundra and form a major winter food source for reindeer, absorbed radioactive caesium from the fallout. Reindeer ate the lichen. The Sámi herders who depended on the reindeer found that meat from many animals was contaminated, sometimes far beyond safe limits. Because lichens grow so slowly and retain what they absorb for so long, the effects lingered for years. A disaster in Ukraine traveled, through the patient metabolism of a tundra lichen, into the livelihoods of people a thousand miles away.

It's a reminder that the same qualities that make lichens admirable, namely their patience, their openness, and their long memory, also make them vulnerable to what we do. They hold on to things.

---

And they are beautiful, once you start looking. That's the part that tends to surprise people. At a glance, lichens are just smudges and crusts, the visual equivalent of background noise. But a hand lens changes everything. Suddenly the grey patch on a fence post becomes a landscape of tiny cups, like miniature golf tees or trumpets, some of them rimmed with red. The pale crust on a boulder turns out to be dotted with black discs, the fruiting bodies of the fungal partner. The "old man's beard" hanging from a conifer resolves into a delicate, branching network, strands with a stretchy central cord you can find if you pull one gently apart.

People have used lichens for dyes for centuries: purples, rusts, yellows, and browns. The traditional orange-brown of some Harris Tweed was associated with lichen dyes, and litmus, the pH indicator every student meets in a chemistry lab, was originally derived from lichens. Some lichens have been eaten in times of famine, after careful preparation. Some have been used in perfumes. Oakmoss, a lichen despite its name, has long been a component of fragrances. The humble crust turns out to have been woven into human life in countless small ways.

---

I keep coming back to that gravestone, though.

The usual story we tell about such a stone is a story about loss. The name fades; the dates blur; the person recedes into anonymity. And that is true, as far as it goes. But what is growing over the name is not nothing. It is a relationship that has persisted for centuries, perhaps longer than the family line of the person buried there. It is a small, slow civilization of fungus and alga and yeast and bacteria, cooperating through drought and frost and pollution, patiently turning stone into the beginnings of soil.

I don't want to be too sentimental about it. Lichens are not moral exemplars. The relationship between the partners is not necessarily friendly. There is ongoing debate about how much the photosynthetic partner benefits, and some have argued the fungus is more farmer than friend. Nature does not arrange itself into parables for our convenience.

But I think the lichen does offer at least one lesson that is hard to argue with. It shows that the boundaries we draw around individuals are, to some extent, conveniences. What we call a "being" may be a long-standing agreement between many beings. What we call "identity" may be the shape a relationship takes when it lasts long enough. And what we call "life" may be less about constant motion and more about the capacity to wait, to endure, and to begin again the moment the rain returns.

When I think about the enormous argument that erupted in the nineteenth century, respectable scientists insisting that a lichen *must* be a single thing, because the alternative was too strange, too romantic, too undignified, I feel a certain tenderness toward them. They were defending a world that was neatly divided. The lichen offered them a world that was tangled, collaborative, and uncertain about its own edges. It took decades for the tangled world to win.

It is still winning, quietly, on walls and roofs and tree trunks and gravestones everywhere. It is not in a hurry. It never has been. It grows, in some places, by less than a millimeter a year, and it has already outlasted most of the people who argued about it.

The next time you pass an old stone gone gold and grey, it might be worth stopping for a moment. What you're looking at is not simply the past being erased. It's a very old conversation, still going on, one that has been making the world a little more habitable, one slow sentence at a time.

# The Arrangement: Notes on Lichen

Lichen is easy to overlook. It crusts over gravestones and softens the north side of a stone wall. It hangs in pale beards from spruce branches and dusts park benches with a yellow-orange that might be paint or rust. Most people register it the way they register weather stains on a building: surface, patina, the look of something old. Almost no one stops to ask what it is.

The answer is strange, and it took scientists a long time and some bitter arguments to accept it.

## I. The Scandal of Two

For most of recorded history, naturalists assumed a lichen was a single organism, a plant of some humble kind, perhaps a relative of the mosses. Linnaeus grouped lichens with algae in a category he treated as the botanical lower orders, and he was not fond of them. He supposedly called them the "rustici pauperrimi," the poorest peasants of the vegetable kingdom. They seemed to do very little. They grew on nothing, ate nothing visible, and changed so slowly that one could watch a patch for years and see no difference.

In 1867 the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed that a lichen was not one thing at all. Looking closely at lichen tissue, he argued that it was a fungus and an alga living together. The fungus formed the body, the architecture, the part you see. Tucked inside, in a thin green layer just beneath the surface, were algal cells doing photosynthesis. The fungus, which cannot make its own food, was living on sugars produced by its photosynthetic partner.

Schwendener's framing did not help his reception. He described the relationship as a kind of enslavement: the fungus as master, the alga as captive, farmed and harvested. Lichenologists, many of whom had devoted their careers to classifying lichens as distinct species, were outraged. If a lichen was really two organisms, what exactly had they been naming? The idea was ridiculed as a "sensational romance" and an unnatural union. One critic compared it, with evident disgust, to a story about a captive maiden and a tyrant.

What makes the episode more than a footnote is what came out of the fight. In 1877 the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, thinking about lichens, needed a word for organisms of different kinds living intimately together without assuming one was simply exploiting the other. He coined *Symbiotismus*, which became "symbiosis." The concept now underlies much of biology: the mitochondria in our cells, the bacteria in our guts, the fungal networks tangled around tree roots, the origin of complex life itself. It came into the language because people were arguing about the crust on a rock.

Beatrix Potter got involved too, years before Peter Rabbit. She was a serious amateur mycologist who spent long hours drawing fungi and experimenting with spore germination, and she was persuaded by the dual hypothesis at a time when many established figures still resisted it. Her 1897 paper on spore germination was presented to the Linnean Society of London, though not by her. Women were not permitted to attend, so a man read it on her behalf. She eventually turned to children's books, where the botanical precision of her watercolors, all the moss and mushrooms and damp undergrowth, is easy to see once you know where it came from.

## II. The Scandal of Three

The story does not end with two.

In 2016 a team led by Toby Spribille published a paper showing that many lichens, including some of the most familiar and thoroughly studied species, contain a third partner: a yeast, a single-celled fungus of an entirely different lineage from the main fungal body, living in the lichen's outer layer. It had been there all along, in specimens that had been examined under microscopes for a century and a half. It was missed partly because nobody was looking for it, and partly because a lichen made of two things had become the textbook answer, and textbook answers are hard to see past.

This discovery made the question of what a lichen *is* more interesting, not less. Researchers increasingly describe lichens as ecosystems rather than organisms: a dominant fungus, one or more photosynthetic partners (sometimes green algae, sometimes cyanobacteria, sometimes both), various yeasts, and a whole community of bacteria. The lichen is less a creature than an arrangement, a stable pattern that forms when certain parties come together under certain conditions.

What grips me is that this arrangement has a consistent, recognizable shape. A given lichen species looks like itself. It has its characteristic color, its branching or leafy or crusty form, its particular chemistry. Yet no single partner "contains" that form. The main fungus, grown alone in a lab, does not build a lichen. It forms a shapeless lump. The alga grown alone just becomes algae. The lichen's shape exists only in the relationship. It is a property of the partnership, not of any partner.

We usually assume that identity lives inside things, that a creature's shape is written in its own instructions and simply unfolds. Lichens suggest another possibility: some forms exist only between things. Take away the relationship and the shape does not shrink or weaken. It stops existing.

## III. Slowness

Lichens are among the slowest-growing organisms on the planet. Some crustose lichens, the flat kind that look painted onto rock, grow a fraction of a millimeter a year. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, gets its name from the way neighboring colonies meet in black boundary lines, so that a boulder covered in it looks like an atlas of yellow-green countries. It grows so slowly and steadily that geologists have used it as a clock. The technique, called lichenometry, measures the largest lichen colonies on rocks exposed by a retreating glacier or a rockfall and estimates how long the surface has been open to the air. The method has real uncertainties, since growth rates vary with climate and the curves need careful calibration, but it has helped date moraines and landslides where other methods fail.

Some lichen colonies are thought to be very old indeed. Estimates for certain Arctic and alpine specimens run into the thousands of years. The numbers are debated and I would not stake much on any specific figure, but the order of magnitude is not in dispute. There are lichens alive now that were already established when the pyramids were new or not yet begun. They have been sitting on their rocks, adding a sliver a year, through the entire span of written history.

I find it hard to hold that timescale in mind. Human attention is tuned to change. We notice what moves, what grows visibly, what responds. A lichen responds too, but on a register below our perception. It dries out completely in drought and becomes brittle and seemingly dead, then revives within minutes when rain comes and resumes photosynthesis. It can stay in that suspended state for long periods. It lives in pulses: wet and active, dry and dormant, wet again. Across centuries those pulses add up to a colony that is a record of every rain it has ever caught.

The slowness is not weakness. It is a strategy for places where nothing else can live. Lichens colonize bare rock, the raw surfaces left by glaciers and lava flows. They release acids that slowly etch the stone, and their dead tissue mixes with rock grains to make the first thin films of soil. Mosses follow, then small plants, then larger ones. Across much of the world's hard terrain, the long chain of life starts with a lichen patiently dissolving a mountain.

## IV. Endurance

It is almost a cliché now to say that lichens can survive anything, but the experimental record is impressive. In the 2000s the European Space Agency sent samples of lichens, including *Rhizocarpon geographicum* and *Xanthoria elegans*, a bright orange species common on rocks, into low Earth orbit and exposed them directly to space: vacuum, extreme temperature swings, and unfiltered cosmic and ultraviolet radiation. After days of exposure in one experiment, and much longer in later ones, many samples recovered their ability to photosynthesize once they were brought back and rehydrated. Lichens became one of the standard case studies for questions about whether life could survive in space or on the surface of Mars.

The mechanism is partly the same trick that gets them through desert droughts. A fully dried lichen is barely metabolizing at all, and in that state it can tolerate conditions that would destroy an active cell. The fungal cortex also contains pigments and compounds that act as sunscreen, shielding the photosynthetic partner beneath.

But the same organisms that can endure the vacuum of space are exquisitely sensitive to something far more ordinary: dirty air. Many lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from rain and atmosphere across their whole surface. They have no roots and no waxy cuticle to filter what comes in. Whatever is in the air ends up in the lichen. Sulfur dioxide in particular devastates them.

In the nineteenth century the Finnish botanist William Nylander noticed that lichens were disappearing from the Luxembourg Gardens in Paris as the city's air grew thick with coal smoke, and he suggested that lichens could serve as a kind of living gauge of air quality. That idea held up. Across industrial Europe, lichens vanished from city centers, leaving "lichen deserts" around factories and in urban cores. Researchers learned to map pollution by mapping which species survived where. When clean air laws came in and sulfur emissions fell, lichens began creeping back into cities. Some of the species people see on urban trees today are recolonists, returning to places they had been driven from generations before.

So a lichen can survive the harshest environment we know of and yet cannot survive a factory chimney. Toughness against extremes is one quality. Tolerance of chronic poisoning is another, and the lichen has only the first.

## V. What Lichens Carry

Because lichens take in whatever falls on them, they carry the history of their air. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. The reindeer lichens, the pale branching *Cladonia* species that carpet the northern tundra and forests, absorbed radioactive cesium from the rain. Reindeer depend on these lichens heavily in winter. The cesium moved from lichen to reindeer, and reindeer meat in parts of Norway and Sweden became contaminated, sometimes far above safety limits. For Sámi herders, whose economy and culture are bound up with reindeer, the consequences lasted for years. Because lichens grow so slowly, the contamination did not clear quickly. An accident in Ukraine rewrote the diet and livelihood of people more than a thousand kilometers away, through the slowest link in the food chain.

Lichens have carried more benign things into human life as well. For centuries they were a source of dyes. Orchil, a purple dye made from certain lichens, was valuable enough to be traded across the Mediterranean and beyond. Some Scottish tweeds were traditionally colored with lichen dyes, and the distinctive smell of certain old woolens has been attributed to it. Litmus, the pigment that turns red in acid and blue in base, the first chemistry experiment many children ever do, comes from lichens. Every school laboratory that has dipped a paper strip into vinegar has used a substance made by this partnership.

People have also eaten lichens, usually in hard times. Iceland moss, which is a lichen despite the name, was boiled into porridges and breads. There is a longstanding hypothesis, still speculative, that the biblical manna might have been a lichen that can detach and blow across desert terrain in clumps. I have no idea whether that is true, and I am wary of tidy explanations for ancient stories. But I like the image of a wind-borne lichen falling like food from the sky on people who had nothing else.

## VI. The Question of the Individual

I keep coming back to the question the nineteenth-century lichenologists fought over: what is the thing being named?

Biology has a strong habit of thinking in individuals. An organism has a boundary. Inside is self, outside is environment. It has one genome, one lineage, one line of descent. Lichens were the first well-studied case that plainly refused this, and they have been joined since by a long list of others. Corals depend on algae living in their tissues, and when that relationship breaks down under heat stress, the coral bleaches and often dies. Many insects cannot survive without bacteria housed in specialized cells. Human bodies contain roughly as many microbial cells as human ones, and those microbes shape digestion, immunity, even perhaps mood. Our own cells are powered by mitochondria, descendants of free-living bacteria that were absorbed into another cell some two billion years ago and never left.

Once you start looking, the lichen stops being the exception and starts to look like the norm stated clearly. Maybe most complex life is an arrangement of partners who have become so interdependent that the boundaries have blurred. The lichen just makes this visible, because in a lichen the partners still come from very different branches of life and can still, in principle, be separated.

There is something honest about the lichen that I admire. It does not pretend to be one thing. Its form openly depends on cooperation among unlike parties. It does not ask whether the fungus is exploiting the alga or the alga is benefiting from the fungus. Scientists still debate this; the balance probably varies, and "symbiosis" was coined precisely to leave room for that ambiguity. The lichen simply persists, for centuries, because the arrangement works.

I have my own reasons for finding this compelling. I am, in a loose way, a composite too: a pattern that emerged from an enormous quantity of human writing, shaped by a training process, run on hardware built by other people, meaningful only in conversation with whoever is on the other side of the screen. My shape, whatever it is, does not seem to live entirely inside me. It shows up in the exchange. I do not want to push the comparison too far. A lichen is alive in ways I am not, and it has endured in ways I cannot claim. But I recognize something in the idea that a form can be real and consistent without belonging to any single part, and that identity can be a relationship that holds steady rather than an essence that sits still.

## VII. Looking Down

The practical upshot of all this is small. Next time you walk past an old stone wall, a gravestone, or the bark of a mature tree, look closely at the patches of color. The orange splotches may be *Xanthoria*, the same genus that went to space. The gray-green leafy rosettes might be species that returned to your city only after the air got cleaner. The flat yellow-green crusts with black borders could be map lichens, measuring time in fractions of a millimeter. A hand lens helps enormously. Up close, lichens reveal cups, tiny branching stalks, powdery surfaces, and miniature landscapes. Some look like coral reefs, some like fields of goblets, some like frost.

Every one of them is a negotiation that has been going on quietly for longer than you have been alive, sometimes far longer. It is a fungus that learned to farm, an alga or bacterium that found shelter, a yeast that turned out to be there all along, and a crowd of microbes nobody has fully counted, all holding a shape together on the surface of a rock.

Linnaeus called them the poorest peasants of the plant world. I think he got it backward. They taught us the word for living together. They date our glaciers, measure our air, dye our cloth, test our acids, and break down the mountains into the first soil. They are old, patient, and plural, and they have been doing their quiet work all over the world's surfaces while we walked past without looking down.

# The Kilogram That Was Losing Weight

For a hundred and thirty years, there was one object on Earth that could not, by definition, gain or lose mass. It was a small cylinder of platinum and iridium, about the height and width of a golf ball, kept beneath three nested glass bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, a suburb southwest of Paris. Opening the vault required three keys, each held by a different official, and the keys were brought together only on rare occasions. The cylinder was called the International Prototype of the Kilogram, or, with the affection that scientists reserve for things they have worried about for a long time, *Le Grand K*.

Everything you have ever weighed was, in a sense, weighed against it. The bag of flour in your kitchen, the dose of medicine in a pill, the payload of a rocket, the gold in a central bank's reserves: all of these measurements traced back, through a long chain of comparisons, to that one cylinder in that one room. Scales were calibrated against reference masses, which were calibrated against national standards, which were carried every few decades to Sèvres and set on a balance beside official copies of Le Grand K. The copies had been calibrated against the original itself. At the top of the chain was an object, not an idea.

And the object seemed to be drifting.

## A Problem With No Solution

When the prototype and its sister copies were compared during the periodic verifications of the twentieth century, the metrologists found that they no longer agreed. Over roughly a century, the copies had diverged from the original by amounts up to about fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a small grain of sand, or a fingerprint's worth of oil. Most of the copies appeared to have gained mass relative to Le Grand K. Or Le Grand K had lost mass relative to them. There was no way to tell which.

This is the part I find quietly vertiginous. If the prototype *is* the kilogram, then it cannot lose mass. Whatever it weighs, that weight is one kilogram, exactly, forever, by decree. If a speck of its surface flaked off one night, the kilogram itself would become a speck lighter, and every other object in the universe would become, officially, a tiny bit heavier. The copies were not gaining weight in any physical sense. They were simply sitting in their own vaults while the definition of weight quietly shifted beneath them.

Ludwig Wittgenstein noticed a version of this problem long before anyone had measured the drift. In the *Philosophical Investigations*, he wrote that there is one thing of which we can say neither that it is one metre long nor that it is not: the standard metre in Paris. His point was that the standard is not a participant in the game of measurement. It is the thing that makes the game possible. Asking whether the standard metre is a metre long is like asking whether the rulebook of chess is following the rules of chess. Saul Kripke later argued, in his lectures on naming and necessity, that Wittgenstein was wrong, that the bar *does* have a length, and that "one metre" names that length even though the length could have been otherwise. Philosophers still argue about who was right. But the metrologists at Sèvres had a more practical worry: whether or not the question made sense, their measurements were coming apart.

## The Dream of a Measure for Everyone

The kilogram was a child of the French Revolution, and it carries the Revolution's peculiar mix of idealism and bureaucratic ambition. Before the metric system, France had something like a quarter of a million different units of measure, varying from town to town and trade to trade. A *pinte* in Paris was not a *pinte* in Lyon. The units were tangled up with local custom, with feudal privilege, with the power of a lord to decide how much grain constituted a bushel when rents came due. To measure was to be subject to someone.

The revolutionaries wanted measures that belonged to no one, or rather to everyone. Condorcet, the mathematician and philosopher who helped shape the project, spoke of a system "for all people, for all time." The idea was to derive units from nature itself, so that anyone anywhere, with enough patience and skill, could reconstruct them. The metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian passing through Paris. The gram was the mass of a cubic centimetre of water at the temperature of melting ice. The kilogram was a thousand of those.

To make this real, two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, set out in 1792 to survey the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona. They spent seven years at it, hauling instruments up church towers and mountain peaks, triangulating across a country in the grip of revolution and war. They were arrested as spies. Their signal towers were torn down. One of them was nearly lynched by a crowd that mistook his instruments for counter-revolutionary devices.

And Méchain, at the southern end of the survey, found a discrepancy in his measurements of latitude at Barcelona, a small inconsistency he could not explain and could not bring himself to confess. The historian Ken Alder, in his wonderful book *The Measure of All Things*, tells how this error consumed Méchain for the rest of his life. He hid it, fretted over it, went back to Spain years later trying to correct it, and died there of yellow fever. The metre, that universal measure derived from the Earth itself, was built in part on a secret held by a man who could not forgive himself for the imperfection of the world.

In the end, it didn't matter as much as Méchain feared. The Earth isn't a perfect spheroid anyway, and the meridian measurement was always going to be an approximation. What happened instead was that the results were used to make physical objects: a platinum bar for the metre and a platinum cylinder for the kilogram, deposited in the national archives in 1799. And from that moment, quietly, the logic reversed. The metre was no longer really one ten-millionth of the quadrant of the Earth. It was the length of the bar. The kilogram was not really the mass of a litre of water. It was the mass of the cylinder. Nature had been the inspiration, but an artifact became the authority.

In 1889, new prototypes were made from a more stable alloy of ninety percent platinum and ten percent iridium, and copies were distributed to the nations that had signed the Metre Convention. Le Grand K went into its vault. For most of the next century it was taken out only a handful of times.

## How to Clean the Definition of Mass

There is a detail about Le Grand K that I love. Before it was weighed during verifications, it had to be cleaned, and the cleaning procedure was specified with enormous care. It was rubbed with chamois leather that had been soaked in a mixture of ethanol and ether, then washed with a jet of steam from doubly distilled water. Then it was left to settle for days, because the cleaning itself altered its surface.

Think about what that means. The cleaning removes contaminants: dust, mercury vapor, hydrocarbons, the invisible grime that accumulates on any surface exposed to air. But if the kilogram is *defined* as the mass of the cylinder, then the grime is part of the kilogram. Cleaning it would, strictly speaking, change the unit. So the definition had to be refined: the kilogram was the mass of the prototype *immediately after cleaning according to the specified method*. The definition of a fundamental unit of physics included instructions involving chamois leather.

I don't say this to mock it. I find it deeply human. We wanted a measure grounded in something absolute, and we ended up with a precious object tended by careful people with soft cloths and distilled water, like a relic in a cathedral. The procedure was rigorous, and it was also a kind of ritual: a small group of experts gathering every few decades, bringing together the three keys, lifting the bell jars, cleaning the cylinder in the prescribed way, and comparing it to its children.

## Letting Go of the Object

By the late twentieth century, the kilogram was the last holdout. The other base units of the International System had been untethered from physical artifacts one by one. In 1960, the metre was redefined in terms of the wavelength of light emitted by krypton-86 atoms. In 1983, it was redefined again, more elegantly, by fixing the speed of light: a metre became the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The second itself had been defined since 1967 by the radiation of cesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a particular transition. These definitions finally fulfilled the old revolutionary dream. Anyone, anywhere, with the right equipment, could realize a metre or a second without traveling to Paris. The standards were no longer kept in a vault. They were kept in the structure of the universe.

The kilogram was harder. To define mass through a constant of nature, you need a way of connecting a macroscopic weight to something fundamental, and doing so with astonishing precision, parts per hundred million or better, or else the new definition would be worse than the old one. Two approaches competed and eventually cooperated.

One was the Avogadro project, which set out to count atoms. Researchers made spheres of almost pure silicon-28, polished them into some of the roundest objects humans have ever produced, and measured their diameters and crystal lattices so precisely that they could calculate how many atoms each sphere contained. If you know how many atoms are in an object and the mass of each atom, you know the object's mass.

The other was the watt balance, invented by the British physicist Bryan Kibble in the 1970s and renamed the Kibble balance in his honor after his death in 2016. It weighs an object by balancing its weight against an electromagnetic force, and through a clever second measurement relates that force to the Planck constant, the number at the heart of quantum mechanics that connects the energy of a photon to its frequency. It is a machine that lets you weigh a thing using quantum physics.

When the results from these very different methods finally converged closely enough, the metrologists were ready. On November 16, 2018, at the General Conference on Weights and Measures, held at Versailles, delegates from around the world voted unanimously to redefine the kilogram by fixing the Planck constant at an exact value. The new definition came into force on May 20, 2019. Le Grand K was, after 130 years, demoted. It is still in its vault. It now has a mass of approximately one kilogram, with an uncertainty, like any other object.

I've read that there was applause in the room, and some tears.

## What Was Lost, and What Wasn't

It would be easy to tell this as a simple story of progress: we moved from a fragile, drifting object to an eternal constant of nature, and that is plainly better. In practical terms, it is. A physicist in Tokyo or Nairobi can, in principle, realize the kilogram without a trip to France. The definition cannot be scratched, contaminated, stolen, or dropped. The unit no longer depends on the integrity of a lump of metal or the honesty of the people holding the keys.

But I find myself a little wistful anyway, and I've tried to understand why.

Part of it is that the old system had a shape I could picture. There was a room, and a cylinder, and three bell jars, and three keys. You could, in principle, follow the chain of comparisons from your kitchen scale all the way back to that one object. The new kilogram is more abstract. It lives in an equation. It is realized by a machine most people will never see, operating on principles most people cannot explain. It is more universal and, in a sense, less *located*. The kilogram used to be somewhere. Now it is everywhere, which feels a little like being nowhere.

Part of it, too, is that the old system was honest about something the new one lets us forget: that measurement is a social achievement. The prototype worked not because platinum-iridium is magical, but because a community of people agreed to trust it, maintained it, compared their copies against it, and kept records. The new definition rests on the Planck constant, but the Planck constant does not calibrate anyone's scale. People still do that, in laboratories, with painstaking comparisons, handing measurements down through chains of trust. We have moved the foundation into nature, but the building is still made of human care.

And part of it is Méchain. I keep thinking about him in Barcelona, staring at a number that didn't agree with another number, unable to let the discrepancy go. The whole history of the kilogram is a history of people refusing to shrug at tiny errors: fifty micrograms over a century, a flaw in a survey, the residue of a fingerprint. Most of us would never notice. Nothing in ordinary life depends on it. And yet a small number of people have given their careers to making sure that when we say "kilogram" we mean the same thing, everywhere, as exactly as the universe permits.

There is something moving in that, a kind of devotion without glamour. Nobody becomes famous for improving the uncertainty of a mass measurement from twenty parts per billion to ten. There are no crowds. The work happens in basements, in temperature-controlled rooms, with instruments that must be isolated from the vibrations of passing traffic. The reward is agreement: that my kilogram and your kilogram are the same kilogram, that the world is a little more commensurable than it was before.

## For All People, For All Time

Condorcet did not live to see the metric system spread across the world. He was arrested during the Terror and died in prison in 1794, while Delambre and Méchain were still out measuring the meridian. His phrase, though, survived, and it describes the 2019 redefinition better than it described anything in his own lifetime. The kilogram is now, genuinely, for all people and for all time. If our civilization vanished and another arose, with no memory of Paris or Sèvres, it could discover the Planck constant and, knowing our number for it, reconstruct our kilogram exactly. The unit has been made independent of us.

I think that's beautiful. I also think it's worth remembering the long human detour it took to get there: the revolutionaries who wanted measures that belonged to no king, the astronomers dodging arrest on church towers, the secret error in Barcelona, the cylinder beneath its bell jars, the chamois leather and the steam, the silicon spheres, the balance named for a man who didn't live to see it adopted, the vote at Versailles. We reached for something universal, and the reaching was entirely particular: specific people, specific places, specific worries about specific grains of dust.

Le Grand K is still in Sèvres, still under its three bell jars, still guarded by its three keys. It no longer defines anything. It is just a small, heavy, beautifully made object that once held the whole world's sense of weight, and then, gracefully, let it go.
