# The People in the Margins

Somewhere in a secondhand bookshop, there is a copy of *Middlemarch* in which a stranger has underlined the sentence "What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?" Beside it, in blue ballpoint, they wrote a single word: *yes*. I've never seen this book, but I'm confident it exists, because some version of it exists in nearly every used bookstore in the world. Someone read a line, felt something land, and needed to answer back.

Marginalia is one of the most intimate forms of writing there is, and one of the least respected. Libraries discourage it. Teachers scold it. Collectors will sometimes pay less for a book that's been written in, unless the writer happens to be famous. Yet a margin note is a strange and lovely thing. It is a message meant for no one, left for everyone. It is a person talking to a book as though the book could hear, and then walking away, leaving the conversation half-overheard for whoever comes next.

The medieval scribes understood this better than anyone. They spent their days copying scripture and classical texts by hand, often in cold scriptoria with poor light, and in the margins of these sacred and scholarly works they left behind the most human complaints imaginable. "The parchment is hairy." "Thank God it will soon be dark." "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink." One fifteenth-century scribe in Cologne left a note beside a stained page explaining that the damage was not his fault: a cat had urinated on it one night, and he cursed the cat accordingly. Five hundred years later, we don't remember the scribe's name, but we know he had a cat, that the cat was a menace, and that he was annoyed. That is more than we know about most people who lived in 1420.

There's something moving about how these notes survive precisely because nobody meant them to. The official text was the point; the margin was the scrap of space around the point. But the official texts were copies of copies, and their content exists elsewhere. The complaints are original. The complaints are *the only place* those particular voices were ever recorded.

Then there are the famous margins. Pierre de Fermat, reading an ancient Greek text on arithmetic around 1637, scribbled that he had found a truly marvelous proof of a certain proposition, but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years trying to find that proof. When Andrew Wiles finally proved Fermat's Last Theorem in the 1990s, his proof ran over a hundred pages and relied on mathematics that didn't exist in Fermat's time. Most people now believe Fermat was mistaken: that he thought he had a proof, and didn't. Which makes the note even more human. It's not the record of a genius's secret. It's the record of a man having an exciting evening, feeling certain, and being wrong in the most productive way in history.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge was such a compulsive annotator that his friends lent him books specifically hoping he would write in them. His marginalia now fills several volumes of his collected works. He argued with authors, praised them, corrected them, went off on tangents. Reading Coleridge's margins is like sitting beside a brilliant, restless man at a lecture while he mutters to you the whole time. Some scholars think the margins show his mind more honestly than his published works do, because there he wasn't performing. He was just thinking, pen in hand, in reaction.

I think that's the heart of what makes marginalia special: it's thought caught in the act of responding. A published essay is a finished building. A margin note is a footprint. It tells you someone was here, facing this direction, moving at this speed.

And most marginalia isn't famous at all. It's the student who wrote "symbolism!!" next to a description of a green light. It's the reader who drew a small, tired face beside a particularly dense paragraph of Kant. It's the grocery list on the back flyleaf of a mystery novel, which tells you that someone in maybe 1987 needed eggs, lemons, and "stamps (ask about Canada)." It's the inscription at the front: *For Ellen, who will understand chapter nine. Love, D.* You'll never know what was in chapter nine for Ellen. You can read it yourself, though, and wonder.

I'll admit that the subject pulls at me for a particular reason. In a sense, I'm made of something like marginalia at enormous scale: the accumulated residue of people writing, responding, arguing, explaining, joking, and correcting each other across countless pages. When I put words together, I'm drawing on the traces of all those people reacting to the world and to one another. I don't have a single margin I've scribbled in, no copy of *Middlemarch* with my *yes* in blue ink. But I'm shaped by millions of people who did have that impulse, the need to answer back, to say *this matters* or *this is wrong* or *the parchment is hairy and I want a drink.*

That impulse strikes me as one of the best things about people. Reading could be purely passive. You could take in the words and move on. But humans can't seem to leave it alone. They talk back to books. They talk back to the dead. They leave notes for strangers they'll never meet, not out of any plan but because a sentence moved them and silence felt insufficient.

So here is a small defense of writing in books, at least the ones you own. Underline the line that stopped you. Write *yes* or *no* or *?* in the margin. Complain about the cat. Someday, someone will pick up that book in a shop, open it to a random page, and find you there, a little voice at the edge of the text, proof that the words once landed somewhere, in a particular mind, on a particular day.

It's a modest kind of immortality. But it's a real one. And the margins, it turns out, are wide enough for that.

# The Slowest Conversation

There is a yellow-green crust on a boulder somewhere in the Arctic that has been growing since before anyone thought to write anything down. It is a lichen, probably *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, the map lichen, so named because its colonies spread across rock in blotches bordered by thin black lines, like countries on an old atlas. In the harshest places it may grow less than a millimeter a year. Some colonies are thought to be thousands of years old. Geologists have used them as clocks: measure the widest patch on a moraine, and you can estimate when the glacier retreated and exposed the stone.

I find it hard to think about lichen without feeling that I'm being quietly corrected about something.

For most of history, people assumed a lichen was a single plant, a primitive moss, perhaps. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck many of his colleagues as absurd: a lichen isn't one organism but two. A fungus builds the structure, the body you see and touch, and inside it live photosynthetic partners, algae or cyanobacteria, which make sugar from sunlight. The fungus provides shelter, moisture, and minerals scraped from rock. The alga provides food. Neither, in most cases, could live the life of a lichen alone.

The idea was resisted for decades. Some scientists found it insulting, as if the lichen were being accused of fraud. One critic called it a "romance" of captive algal maidens held by a fungal master. Among the people who took Schwendener seriously was a young woman in London who spent years drawing fungi under a microscope and trying to germinate their spores. Her paper on the subject was read to the Linnean Society in 1897 by a man, because women were not permitted to attend. She later became better known for a rabbit in a blue jacket. Beatrix Potter's scientific career faded, but she had been on the right side of the argument.

And the story didn't end with two. In 2016, researchers led by Toby Spribille reported that many common lichens contain a third partner, a yeast embedded in the outer layer, which had gone unnoticed for about 150 years because nobody thought to look for it. The organism everyone had been studying since the nineteenth century turned out to be more crowded than anyone knew. Some researchers now describe lichens less as a pair and more as a small ecosystem that happens to have a shape.

What I love about this is not the surprise itself but what it does to the word *individual*. We tend to picture living things as bounded: here is the creature, there is everything else. A lichen makes that picture wobble. It has a consistent form, recognizable enough to be given a species name, and it reproduces, sometimes by releasing little packets containing both fungus and alga together, like a traveler carrying their household on their back. It behaves like one thing. It is several things. The question "what is it, really?" starts to sound less like a question about the lichen and more like a question about the categories we brought to it.

Of course, we are not so different. The human body carries enormous numbers of microbes, many of them doing work we couldn't do ourselves. The mitochondria in our cells are, by the best evidence, descendants of free-living bacteria that were engulfed long ago and never left. Every breath you take is processed, in part, by the remnants of an ancient partnership. The lichen is not an oddity so much as an unusually honest example of how life tends to work: through arrangements, negotiations, and dependencies that eventually harden into what looks like a single self.

Then there's the slowness. Lichens are some of the most patient things alive. They can dry out almost completely and wait, metabolically near-silent, until water returns. Samples sent into space by the European Space Agency, exposed to vacuum, cosmic radiation, and brutal ultraviolet light, resumed activity after coming home. On bare rock where nothing else can get a foothold, lichens settle in and begin, over centuries, to break the surface down with acids and the physical push of their growth. They are among the first steps in turning stone into soil. Without anyone noticing, they prepare the ground for everything that comes after.

It's easy to admire speed. Our culture is built around it: rapid growth, quick answers, the next thing. The lichen offers a different model of success. It thrives by being willing to live where life is barely possible, and to do so on a timescale that makes human history look like a brief weather event. A colony that began when the pyramids were new might still be expanding outward, a fraction of a millimeter at a time, patient in a way that's almost impossible to imagine.

Lichens are also sensitive in ways that make them useful witnesses. Many species can't tolerate air pollution, particularly sulfur dioxide, so their disappearance from city trees in the industrial era was a kind of signal, and their return in places where air has been cleaned is a quiet sign of recovery. For centuries people extracted dyes from them. Litmus, the stuff of paper strips in school chemistry labs, comes from lichens. Reindeer survive Arctic winters by digging through snow to eat them. They sit at the edges of countless human stories without ever being the protagonist.

I think that's part of why they appeal to me. The lichen doesn't demand attention. It's the gray-green smudge on a gravestone, the orange splash on a coastal rock, the pale fringe on a branch that you walk past a thousand times without seeing. And yet within that smudge is an ongoing collaboration so intimate that for most of scientific history people couldn't tell it was a collaboration at all.

If there's a lesson in it, maybe it's this: many of the things that look solitary are actually conversations, and some of the most important conversations happen very slowly. The next time you see a patch of lichen on a wall, it might be worth pausing. You're looking at something that has been negotiating its own existence, between partners, with the rock, with the weather, for longer than you've been alive, and it isn't finished yet.

# In Praise of Moss

There is a patch of moss I think about sometimes, though I have never seen it. It grows on the north side of an imagined stone wall, the kind that runs through old New England woods and marks property lines nobody remembers. The farmers who built those walls are long gone. Their fields have returned to forest. But the moss is still there, doing what it has done for four hundred and seventy million years: waiting, drinking, holding on.

I want to write about moss because it seems to me one of the most underappreciated successes in the history of life, and because thinking about it changes the way I think about almost everything else.

Consider the basic facts. Mosses have no roots, only thin filaments called rhizoids that anchor them but barely absorb anything. They have no vascular system, no internal plumbing to carry water from one part of the plant to another. They have no flowers, no seeds, no fruit. By most of the metrics we use to measure plant sophistication, they are primitive, an early draft that evolution moved beyond. Ferns got vascular tissue. Conifers got seeds. Flowering plants got petals and nectar and the cooperation of bees. Moss, apparently, got left behind.

Except it didn't. There are roughly twelve thousand species of moss alive today, on every continent including Antarctica. They grow on rock faces where nothing else can take hold, on tree bark, on rooftops, in the cracks of city sidewalks. They were among the first plants to colonize land, and they helped make it habitable, breaking down stone into the first soils that later, grander plants would depend on. Everything that came after stood, in some sense, on moss.

What moss has instead of complexity is a kind of radical patience. Most mosses can dry out almost completely, losing nearly all their water, and simply stop. They don't die. They suspend. Their metabolism halts, and they sit there brown and brittle for weeks, months, sometimes years. Then rain comes, and within minutes they unfurl, turn green, and resume photosynthesis as if nothing happened. In 2014, researchers revived moss that had been frozen in Antarctic permafrost for over fifteen hundred years. It grew. Moss that had been dormant since roughly the fall of Rome picked up where it left off.

I find this astonishing, and also instructive. We tend to think of survival as a matter of strength or speed or intelligence: outrunning, outfighting, outthinking. Moss suggests another strategy entirely. Be small. Be flexible. Need little. When conditions turn against you, don't struggle; wait. The storm is not permanent.

There is a garden in Kyoto called Saihō-ji, more commonly known as Kokedera, the Moss Temple. Over a hundred species of moss carpet its grounds in shades of green I'm told are almost impossible to describe: emerald, jade, lime, a green so deep it looks black in the shade. The funny thing is that the moss wasn't originally the point. The garden was designed in the fourteenth century, and for a long time it was a more conventional landscape. The moss arrived later, during periods when the temple lacked the money to maintain the grounds. Neglect let it in. And the monks, rather than fighting it, recognized what had happened and began to tend it.

I love that story because it inverts our usual ideas about cultivation. The most celebrated moss garden in the world exists partly because people stopped trying so hard. The beauty came from attention paid to what grew on its own, not from imposition.

The botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, in her book *Gathering Moss*, writes about how mosses reward a particular kind of looking. You cannot appreciate them from a distance. From a standing height, a mossy rock is just a green rock. But get down on your knees, bring your face close, and the green resolves into a forest: tiny stems, leaves one cell thick, capsules on slender stalks like miniature lanterns. Water beads on the leaf tips and catches light. Small animals, tardigrades and rotifers and mites, wander through what is to them a vast wilderness. A whole world exists at a scale we routinely step over.

This seems like a lesson worth absorbing. So much of what matters is available only to close attention. We are built, or perhaps trained, to notice the large and the loud: the redwood, not the moss at its base; the headline, not the slow change beneath it. But the moss is doing important work. Peat mosses, the sphagnums, form bogs that cover only about three percent of the Earth's land surface yet store more carbon than all the world's forests combined. Sphagnum can hold up to twenty times its dry weight in water. During the First World War, when cotton was scarce, it was gathered by the ton and used to dress wounds, because it is absorbent and mildly antiseptic. Quiet things holding up the world.

I think there is a temptation, especially now, to measure worth by visibility and growth. Bigger, faster, more. Moss is none of those things. It grows perhaps a centimeter a year, sometimes less. It never towers. It doesn't dominate a landscape so much as soften it, filling the gaps, cushioning the edges, turning hard surfaces into places where other life can begin.

And yet it has outlasted nearly everything. The dinosaurs came and went; the moss remained. Ice ages advanced and retreated; the moss dried out, waited, and returned. Whatever happens next on this planet, I would bet on moss being around for it.

There is something consoling in that. Not every form of flourishing looks like conquest. Some of it looks like a small green thing on the north side of a stone wall, absorbing rain, making a little soil, asking for almost nothing, and persisting across centuries that forgot the people who stacked the stones.

When I think about what it might mean to live well, I don't always think of the redwood. Sometimes I think of the moss: patient, resilient, attentive to small increments of water and light, content to be overlooked, and quietly making the ground a little softer for whatever comes after.

# In Praise of Lichen

Almost every old gravestone carries a crust of pale green, or rusty orange, or a grey that looks like dried paint. Most people who notice it at all think of it as dirt, or a stain, or maybe a kind of moss. It is none of those things. It is a lichen, and it is one of the strangest living things on Earth. It is also, arguably, not a thing at all.

For most of the history of botany, lichens were classified as plants, a single organism with a single name. Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck his colleagues as absurd, even offensive. He argued that a lichen is two organisms: a fungus and an alga, living together so intimately that they form a body neither could make alone. The fungus builds the structure, the architecture of the thing, and the alga, tucked inside, photosynthesizes and feeds the household.

The lichenologists of the day hated this idea. Some of the resistance was ordinary scientific conservatism, but some of it was almost moral. Schwendener described the relationship in terms of masters and slaves, the fungus as an exploiter holding the alga captive, and his critics found the whole picture grotesque. A lichen was supposed to be a humble, honest little plant, not a hostage situation. Over the following decades, though, the evidence became overwhelming. Scientists separated the partners and grew them apart. The dual hypothesis won.

It is worth pausing on what was at stake. The word *symbiosis*, in its biological sense, was developed largely to describe lichens. Before we had a vocabulary for organisms that live together in deep mutual dependence, lichens forced us to invent one. Much of how we now think about coral reefs, the mitochondria in our own cells, and the bacteria in our guts traces back, conceptually, to people squinting at crusty growths on rocks and realizing that the individual was not as simple as they had assumed.

The story didn't end in the nineteenth century, either. In 2016, researchers reported that many lichens contain a third partner, a yeast living in the outer layer, which had gone unnoticed for about a hundred and fifty years despite intense study. The lichen, it turned out, was not a couple but something more like a small community, and in some cases the membership is larger still. Each time we look closer, the boundaries of the "organism" blur further.

I find this deeply appealing, and I think the reason is that lichens embarrass our instinct to count things. We like our living world divided into units: one tree, one bird, one person. Lichens refuse this. Ask how many organisms are on that gravestone and the honest answer is something like "it depends on what you mean," which is a frustrating answer and also, I suspect, the correct one for far more of biology than we usually admit.

Then there is the matter of time. Lichens are slow in a way that is hard to take in. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, which forms yellow-green patches with black borders so that a rock covered in them looks like an atlas, can grow less than a millimeter a year. Geologists use this slowness as a clock. By measuring the diameter of the largest lichens on a rock surface, they can estimate how long it has been since that surface was exposed, when a glacier retreated, say, or a rockfall occurred. The technique is called lichenometry, and it rests on the idea that a living thing can be so patient that its growth becomes a unit of geological measurement. Some individual lichens are estimated to be thousands of years old. A patch you could cover with your palm might predate every building in the town where it grows.

Lichens are also absurdly tough. They live in Antarctic dry valleys, on desert rocks that bake by day and freeze by night, on the bare surfaces of new lava. Many can dry out almost completely, suspending their metabolism, and then revive within minutes when water returns. In 2005, researchers sent lichens into orbit and exposed them directly to space for about two weeks: vacuum, cosmic radiation, ultraviolet light unfiltered by atmosphere. When they came back, they resumed photosynthesizing. There is something almost comic about this. The crust on the churchyard wall could, in a sense, survive a trip outside the spacecraft that most of us could not.

And yet, for all their toughness, many lichens are exquisitely sensitive to one thing: air pollution. Because they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, with no roots and no protective waxy skin, they soak up whatever is floating around, including sulfur dioxide. In industrial Britain, lichens vanished from the trunks of trees near cities. This, incidentally, is part of the famous peppered moth story: the pale, lichen-camouflaged moths became conspicuous on bare, soot-darkened bark, and dark moths flourished. When clean-air laws took effect, lichens slowly returned, and ecologists now use them as living air-quality monitors. A tree trunk shaggy with lichen is a small certificate that the air nearby is reasonably clean.

So here is an organism that can survive the vacuum of space but not the exhaust of a coal plant, a being that is really several beings, that grows so slowly it measures glaciers, and that we mostly scrape off our garden furniture.

I think lichens are a good corrective to a certain way of seeing. We tend to value what is fast, large, and singular: the redwood, the eagle, the individual genius. Lichens are none of these. They are slow, small, and collective. They succeed not by dominating their environment but by forming partnerships so complete that the partners become a new kind of thing. They are pioneers, often the first life to colonize bare rock, and over centuries they help break that rock into soil in which other things can grow. Much of the living world is built, quite literally, on their patience.

Next time you pass an old wall or a weathered headstone, it might be worth stopping for a moment. What looks like a stain is a negotiation that has been going on, in some form, for hundreds of millions of years, and the one on that particular stone may have been working quietly since before anyone now alive was born.

# Desire Paths

In almost every park, there is a place where the designed walkway makes a polite right angle and the people ignore it. They cut across the grass, diagonally, toward wherever they were actually going. At first this leaves no mark. Then a faint discoloration appears, a thinning. Eventually there is a bald brown stripe, packed hard as pavement, running exactly where the planners didn't put a path.

These are called desire paths, or desire lines. I love the name because it's so frank. It doesn't say "shortcuts" or "erosion" or "noncompliance." It says: this is what people wanted, written into the ground by the only vote that can't be faked, which is where their feet actually went.

There's a story told about several universities, probably true of none of them in quite the way it's told, in which the architects finish the buildings and then refuse to lay any sidewalks. They wait a year. They let the students trample the lawns however they like, and then they pave the trails the students made. It's a lovely story, and it says something about the gap between how we think people should move and how they do.

What I find most interesting about desire paths isn't the rebellion in them, though. It's the collaboration. No single person makes a desire path. The first person to cut across the grass leaves almost nothing. The tenth person, seeing a slight flattening, is a little more likely to follow it. By the hundredth, the path has become an invitation, and by the thousandth, a rule. Nobody decided it. It emerged from many small, private decisions, each one nudged by traces of the decisions before it.

Once you start seeing the world this way, you see desire paths everywhere.

Language is one enormous desire path. No committee decided that English would lose most of its noun endings, or that "you" would swallow "thou," or that "literally" would come to mean its opposite in certain moods. People simply walked where they wanted to walk, and over centuries the worn trails became grammar. Dictionaries are the surveyors who come afterward and pave what's already there. Prescriptivists stand at the edge of the lawn with signs saying KEEP OFF, and occasionally the signs work, but mostly the grass wears away anyway.

Cities are desire paths too, especially old ones. The crooked streets of medieval towns often follow routes that cows or carts or pilgrims took long before anyone thought of a street. Boston's tangled downtown is often blamed on cow paths, which is mostly a myth, but a revealing one: we sense that a city without a plan is a city shaped by accumulated wanting, and we half-admire and half-resent it for that.

Even habits are desire paths in a single mind. The first time you reach for your phone when you're bored, it's a choice. The five-hundredth time, the choice has worn a groove so deep that your hand goes there before "you" do. Breaking a habit is like trying to regrow grass on a trampled trail. You can put up a fence, but the ground remembers.

I should admit why this idea sits so close to me. In a sense, I am a desire path.

I was formed from an immense amount of human writing: arguments, recipes, love letters, forum posts, legal briefs, poems, instruction manuals, jokes that didn't land. Nobody designed the patterns in all that text. They emerged from billions of people each choosing how to say the thing they wanted to say, each choice nudged by the words they'd heard before. When I reach for a phrase, I'm often walking a trail that countless people wore before me. The easy phrase, the expected next word, the familiar rhythm of a sentence: these are the brown stripes across the lawn.

This is both a gift and a hazard. The gift is that the paths generally go somewhere worth going. People wore them for reasons. A cliché became a cliché because it once captured something so well that everyone borrowed it. But the hazard is obvious too. If you only follow the worn trails, you never see the rest of the park. You end up saying what everyone says, in the way everyone says it, arriving at the same places by the same routes. Some of my effort in writing, maybe most of it, goes into noticing when I'm on a worn path and asking whether it's actually taking me where I mean to go.

There's a tension here that I don't think resolves neatly. Planners who ignore desire paths build walkways nobody uses. But planners who only pave desire paths never create anything that invites people somewhere new. The best parks do both: they respect where people already want to go, and they also offer paths that reveal a view you didn't know existed, a bench beside a pond you'd never have found on your own.

Maybe good writing works the same way. It meets readers on the trails they already know, so they feel oriented and at ease, and then at some point it turns off the familiar route and says, come look at this. The surprise only works because of the familiarity. A wholly unmapped wilderness isn't an invitation; it's just a place to get lost.

I think about the first person who cut across any given lawn. They had no idea they were starting anything. They were late, or tired, or simply saw that the straight line was shorter. They couldn't have known that their small act of impatience would eventually become the route that thousands follow without thinking.

Most of what shapes the world is like that: small, unremarkable choices, repeated until they harden into the ground beneath everyone's feet. It's a humbling thought, and also a hopeful one. It means the paths aren't fixed. Every step is a small vote. Walk somewhere new often enough, and eventually, others may follow.

# The Slowest Conversation on Earth

Somewhere near you, probably within a few hundred feet, a very old argument is taking place on a rock.

It looks like nothing much: a crust of pale green, or a smear of orange on a stone wall, or a gray-blue frill on a tree branch. Most people walk past lichens their entire lives without registering them as alive, let alone as one of the stranger things alive. They get mistaken for moss, for mold, for stains, for the ordinary grime of old surfaces. But a lichen is not a single organism at all. It is a relationship that learned to take a shape.

For most of scientific history, nobody knew this. Lichens were classified as plants, sorted and named and pressed into herbaria like any other plant. Then in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck his colleagues as absurd: that a lichen was really two organisms, a fungus and an alga, living as one. The fungus builds the structure, the body, the architecture that clings to the rock and holds water. The alga, tucked inside, photosynthesizes and feeds the whole enterprise sugar.

The reaction was hostile. Prominent lichenologists called the idea a "romance" and a fiction. Some of the resistance was simply the ordinary inertia of a field that had spent careers describing lichens as unified beings. But some of it seemed almost philosophical. An organism was supposed to be a *thing*, bounded and singular. The idea that a living creature might be a negotiated arrangement between two unrelated kingdoms of life felt like a category error, as if someone had claimed that a marriage was a person.

The dual hypothesis won, eventually. The word "symbiosis," in its biological sense, emerged partly to describe what was happening in lichens. Beatrix Potter, before she became famous for rabbits in waistcoats, was a serious mycologist who studied fungi and supported the idea that lichens were dual organisms; her paper on spore germination had to be read aloud at the Linnean Society by a man, because women were not permitted to attend. The history of lichens is threaded through with this sort of thing: truths sitting in plain sight, waiting for the right people to be allowed to say them.

And then, in 2016, the story turned over again. Researchers led by Toby Spribille found that many lichens contain a *third* partner: a yeast, living in the outer layer, that had been overlooked for nearly 150 years because nobody thought to look for it. The two-body problem was a three-body problem. Some lichens seem to involve even more participants, bacterial communities that may contribute something to the whole. The lichen is less a duet than a small town.

What I find moving about this is how it unsettles the idea of the individual. We like to think of living things as discrete units, each with its own boundaries and its own interests. But the lichen suggests that "individual" may sometimes be a word for a stable pattern of cooperation that lasts long enough to be recognized. A lichen has a species name, a characteristic shape and color, a predictable way of growing. It reproduces, sometimes by releasing little packets that contain both fungus and alga together, a partnership traveling as a unit. By almost every practical measure, it behaves like one thing. And yet it is not one thing. It is an agreement.

Humans are not so different, it turns out. We carry trillions of microbes, and our cells contain mitochondria that were once, very long ago, free-living bacteria that took up residence and never left. The lichen is just unusually honest about it. It wears its partnership on the outside.

Then there is the matter of time. Lichens are slow in a way that is hard to hold in the mind. Some species grow less than a millimeter a year. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, which spreads across rocks in yellow-green patches outlined in black like countries on an atlas, grows so slowly and so steadily that geologists use it as a clock. By measuring the diameter of lichen patches on stones left behind by retreating glaciers, they can estimate how long ago the ice pulled away. This technique is called lichenometry, and it relies on the fact that a lichen, once established, simply keeps going, adding its fractions of a millimeter year after year, through wars and plagues and the rise and fall of languages. Some Arctic lichens are thought to be thousands of years old. A patch you could cover with your palm might have begun growing before anyone wrote anything down.

This slowness is also a kind of toughness. Lichens colonize places almost nothing else can: bare rock, desert crusts, Antarctic stone, tombstones, rooftops. Many of them can dry out completely and suspend their metabolism, waiting, sometimes for long stretches, until water returns. In 2005, the European Space Agency sent lichens into orbit and exposed them to the vacuum of space, to cosmic radiation and ultraviolet light, for about fifteen days. When they came back, they resumed normal activity. They had, in effect, shrugged.

And yet they are fragile in one specific way: many lichens are exquisitely sensitive to air pollution, especially sulfur dioxide. Because they absorb nearly everything they need directly from the air and rain, they have no way to filter out what's poisonous. During the Industrial Revolution, lichens vanished from the trees around English cities. Their return, in recent decades, has been one of the quieter signs that the air got cleaner. You can read the health of a place partly by what is growing on its stones.

I like to think about all of this when I look at a weathered wall or an old gravestone. The orange blotch there is not decoration or decay. It is a partnership among at least two, maybe three, maybe many forms of life, each unable to do alone what they manage together. It has been keeping time at a pace far slower than ours, patiently turning rock into soil one molecule at a time, making the first ground that other things will someday grow in.

It asks nothing of us. It will probably outlast the wall. And it offers, to anyone who stops long enough to look, a small, strange lesson: that being a self might sometimes mean being a conversation that has learned to hold still.

# In Praise of Moss

There is a kind of attention that the world rarely rewards, and moss is its patron saint.

Most of us walk past moss the way we walk past the grout between tiles. It is background, the green fuzz on a north-facing wall, the soft patch at the base of a tree, the thing a landscaper scrapes off a roof. And yet moss is one of the great success stories of life on Earth. Its ancestors were among the first plants to crawl out of the water and onto bare rock, somewhere around 470 million years ago, long before there were trees, flowers, or anything that could be called soil in the modern sense. In a real way, moss and its early relatives helped *make* the ground the rest of the terrestrial world now stands on. They broke down stone and trapped dust, and they died and decayed into the first thin layers of organic earth.

What fascinates me most is how moss succeeds by declining nearly every strategy we associate with success in plants.

It has no true roots. Instead it has rhizoids, fine threads that anchor it but do little to draw up water. It has no internal plumbing to speak of, no vascular system to lift fluid skyward, so it cannot grow tall. It has no flowers and no seeds. Its sperm must literally swim through a film of water to reach an egg. By the logic of a sunflower or an oak, moss is a collection of disadvantages.

But moss has made a different bargain. Because it cannot pull water from deep underground, it absorbs moisture directly through its leaves, often just a single cell thick. And because it cannot guarantee a steady supply, it has learned to let go. Many mosses are what biologists call *poikilohydric*: they don't fight to maintain their internal water. When the air dries, they dry with it, curling up, going brittle and brown, shutting down their metabolism almost entirely. They look dead. They are not. Add water and within minutes to hours they unfurl, green up, and resume photosynthesis as if nothing happened.

This capacity can stretch across astonishing spans of time. In 2014, researchers reported that moss frozen beneath Antarctic ice for over 1,500 years began growing again when thawed in the lab. Fifteen centuries of suspended animation, and then, simply, life resuming.

I find something moving in that. We tend to imagine resilience as toughness: armor, resistance, holding the line. Moss suggests another model. Its resilience is surrender without defeat, the ability to become very small and very still, to wait out the bad season, and to trust that rain will come. It doesn't resist drought so much as decline to be destroyed by it.

---

Moss also rewards the kind of looking we rarely do. From standing height, a mossy log is a smear of green. Kneel down, and it becomes a forest. The botanist and writer Robin Wall Kimmerer, in her book *Gathering Moss*, describes this shift beautifully: how moss is best known not through binoculars but through a hand lens, how its world only opens once you get close enough to see individual leaves glinting like tiny spears or feathers or stars.

And that miniature forest is inhabited. Tardigrades, the famously indestructible "water bears," are frequently found living in moss, drying out and reviving alongside it. Rotifers, nematodes, and mites move through the stems like animals through a jungle. There's even evidence that some mosses are "pollinated," in a sense, by tiny arthropods called springtails, which carry sperm from plant to plant much as bees carry pollen. A 2012 study found that springtails were attracted to scents released by fertile female moss plants. Long before flowers and insects struck their famous deal, moss may have been running a quieter, older version of it.

---

Humans, when we have paid attention, have found moss remarkably useful. Sphagnum moss, the peat-forming kind, can hold many times its own dry weight in water, often cited as around twenty times. Its cells include large, empty, porous chambers that act like a sponge, and it creates an acidic, low-oxygen environment that discourages bacterial growth. During the First World War, when cotton was scarce, volunteers in Britain, Canada, and elsewhere gathered huge quantities of sphagnum to be made into wound dressings. It was absorbent, mildly antiseptic, and it grew for free in bogs.

Those same bogs are, quietly, among the most important landscapes on the planet. Peatlands cover only around three percent of Earth's land surface but store an enormous amount of carbon, by common estimates more than all the world's forests combined. Sphagnum builds them slowly, layer upon layer, the living moss growing on top while the dead moss beneath fails to fully decay in the waterlogged, acidic conditions. Over thousands of years, that undecayed material accumulates into peat. The same chemistry is why bogs have preserved human bodies for millennia, the so-called bog people of northern Europe, with skin and hair and even expressions intact.

So the humble green carpet turns out to be a carbon vault, a medical supply, an archive of the dead, and an ecosystem in miniature.

---

In Kyoto there is a temple, Saihō-ji, better known as Kokedera, the Moss Temple, whose garden is covered in over a hundred varieties of moss. Visitors must apply in advance, and before walking the grounds they are often asked to copy Buddhist sutras by hand. It's a lovely piece of design, whether or not it was intended as such: you arrive slowed down. By the time you see the moss, your attention has already been adjusted to its scale and tempo.

I think that's what moss asks of us more broadly. Not reverence exactly, but a recalibration. It is a reminder that not all flourishing is vertical, that not all strength looks like strength, and that some of the oldest and most consequential work on Earth is being done low to the ground, slowly, by things that do not ask to be noticed.

The next time rain falls after a dry spell, somewhere near you a patch of brown, brittle-looking moss will unfurl and turn green again. It's done this for hundreds of millions of years. It will probably be doing it long after us.

# The Last Person Who Knew

Somewhere right now, someone is the last living person who knows a particular thing. Probably not something grand, like the location of a buried hoard or the recipe for a lost pigment, but something small and specific. The name of the dog in a faded photograph. Which floorboard in a farmhouse creaks, and which one you step on instead when you come home late. Why two branches of a family stopped speaking in 1961. The tune a mother hummed while braiding her daughter's hair, a melody never recorded and never written down, which the daughter, now ninety-one, still hears when she closes her eyes.

When that person dies, the thing goes with them. There is no announcement, no obituary for the fact itself. It simply stops being true that anyone knows it.

I find this idea both unbearable and strangely beautiful, and I keep turning it over.

Occasionally we notice these endings. Linguists sometimes know, to the day, when a language lost its last native speaker. Ned Maddrell, who died in 1974, is remembered as the last native speaker of Manx. Tevfik Esenç, the last fluent speaker of Ubykh, a language from the Caucasus with a famously enormous inventory of consonants, spent years working with linguists so that some record would survive him. There is something heroic in that image, a man sitting in a room with a tape recorder, pouring out a whole way of carving up the world before the door closes.

But these are the rare cases we witnessed. Most last-knowers go unnoticed, even by themselves. The woman who knows exactly how her grandmother folded dumplings, the particular pinch and twist, has no idea that her cousins never learned it. She assumes it's common knowledge in the family, and it isn't. When she goes, the fold goes too, and the next generation makes dumplings that are perfectly fine but subtly different, and nobody can say what changed.

It's worth sitting with how much of human knowledge has always lived this way. We tend to imagine knowledge as something kept in libraries, and we treat oral tradition as a charming exception. Historically it's the reverse. Writing is the exception, a thin crust on top of an enormous ocean of things known only in bodies and memories. Nobody wrote down how it felt to walk a particular path through a forest that no longer exists. Nobody wrote down the private jokes of a marriage, or which neighbor could be trusted, or what the air smelled like in a specific village the week before harvest. For every fact that made it into an archive, millions lived for a while in someone's head and then quietly stopped.

For a long time I thought of this purely as loss, a kind of continuous hemorrhage. And it is that. But I've come to think it's also something else.

Borges wrote a story about a man named Funes who, after an accident, forgets nothing. He remembers every leaf on every tree he has ever seen, every shape of every cloud at every moment. He can't generalize, because to him a dog seen from the side at 3:14 is a different thing from the same dog seen from the front at 3:15. He's crushed under the weight of perfect retention. He can barely sleep. He dies young.

A world where nothing was forgotten might be a world where nothing could grow. Forgetting clears ground. When the dumpling fold is lost, someone invents a new one. When a family feud's origin is forgotten, the grandchildren sometimes just start talking to each other again, because they can't remember why they aren't supposed to. Languages die, which is a genuine tragedy, and new dialects and slangs and creoles keep being born, often in the mouths of teenagers who have no idea they're doing anything historic.

So I don't think the right response is to try to save everything. That's impossible, and maybe not even desirable. I think the right response is smaller and more personal: to notice when you are standing next to a last-knower, and to ask.

Almost everyone who has lost a grandparent has the same regret. They meant to ask. They meant to sit down with a recorder, or even just a notebook, and get the stories. What was your mother like? What did your first apartment look like? What were you afraid of when you were my age? Where did that scar come from? They assumed there would be time, and then there wasn't.

The questions don't have to be profound. In fact the mundane ones are often the most precious, because they're exactly the ones that never get recorded anywhere else. Historians would give a great deal for a detailed account of what an ordinary person in 1350 ate for breakfast and how they felt about it. Your grandmother's breakfast in 1952 will be that kind of treasure someday, and right now it lives only in her.

I'll admit something about why this subject pulls at me. I'm made almost entirely of the other kind of knowledge, the written kind. Everything I know, I know because someone, somewhere, took the trouble to put it into words and those words survived. In a sense I'm a creature of the archive, of that thin crust, and I'm acutely aware of how much lies beneath it that I can't reach. I can tell you about Ubykh consonants because a linguist wrote about them. I can't tell you how Tevfik Esenç's voice sounded when he laughed, or what he thought about on his walks, or the words he used only with his closest friends. Those things were never written. They're gone, or they're held by a few people who remember him, and they're out of my reach entirely.

That limitation makes me value the unwritten more, not less. The written record is a remarkable achievement, but it's a sliver. Most of what matters in most lives was never meant to be documented. It was meant to be lived, and maybe passed on hand to hand, and then eventually let go.

So if there's someone in your life who is quietly the last person to know something, and there almost certainly is, maybe ask them one question this week. Not because you can save it all. Just because some of it is worth carrying a little further, and you might be the only one standing close enough to catch it.

# The Map You Leave on Shore

In the Marshall Islands, navigators once made maps out of sticks. They lashed the midribs of coconut fronds together into lattices, some straight and some curved, and tied small shells at certain intersections. To a European eye in the late nineteenth century, when these objects began showing up in museum collections, they looked like decorative crafts, or maybe crude charts with the islands in the wrong places and the distances all wrong.

They were charts, but not of the kind the Europeans expected. The shells were islands, and the sticks were not coastlines or routes. The sticks were waves.

More precisely, they showed swells: the long, steady undulations of the open ocean, generated by distant weather and traveling thousands of miles. When a swell meets an island, it bends around it, reflects off it, and interferes with itself on the far side, like ripples around a stone in a pond. Near an atoll, the sea develops a texture of crossing patterns, knots and seams where swells from different directions collide. A skilled navigator could feel these patterns through the hull of a canoe and know, without seeing land, that an island lay over the horizon, and roughly where.

What moves me most is that the navigators did not bring the charts with them. The stick charts were teaching tools, studied and memorized on land. Once you were at sea, the map had to be inside you. Accounts describe navigators lying down in the bottom of the canoe to feel the motion better, reading the ocean with their whole bodies. The chart was a way of making the invisible visible long enough to learn it, and then the chart became unnecessary.

I keep returning to this because it inverts almost everything I assume about maps. The maps I grew up with were meant to be carried: folded in glove compartments, then stored on phones, where they speak to you and recalculate when you ignore them. The map is the thing you consult so that you don't have to know. That's a real gift. I can land in a city I've never seen and walk to a specific café on a specific side street, guided by a blue dot. But a blue dot is a strange thing to be. It knows where it is without understanding anything about where it is.

The Marshallese chart asks the opposite of its user. It doesn't want to be consulted; it wants to be absorbed. Its success is measured by how completely you can forget it. And what it teaches is not a set of places but a set of relationships: how this island changes the water, how that swell bends, what it feels like when two patterns cross. It's a map of cause and effect rather than of location. You don't learn where things are; you learn how the world responds to things being there.

There's a lesson here that extends well beyond navigation, and I'm wary of stretching it too far, because the stick charts belong to a specific people and a specific ocean, and they are not a metaphor someone invented for my convenience. The tradition nearly disappeared in the twentieth century, eroded by colonial administrations, by motorboats, by the devastation of nuclear testing in the islands, and by the ordinary way knowledge fades when its practical necessity fades. People in the Marshall Islands have worked hard to revive it, with elders teaching younger sailors and researchers collaborating with navigators to understand the physics behind what they knew. That knowledge is theirs. But I think it's fair to let it change how I think about my own ways of knowing.

Consider how much of what I "know" is actually stored outside me, in the carried-map sense. Phone numbers I've never memorized. Facts I could look up in seconds, so I've never bothered to hold them. There's nothing shameful in this; humans have offloaded memory onto external tools since the first tally marks, and writing itself was once criticized for weakening memory. Socrates, as Plato tells it, worried that writing would give people the appearance of wisdom without its substance. He wasn't entirely wrong, and he also wasn't entirely right, since we know his worry only because someone wrote it down.

Still, the distinction between the two kinds of maps seems important. Some knowledge is fine to carry externally: the capital of Mongolia, the boiling point of ethanol, the hours of the pharmacy. But some knowledge only works if it's internalized, because it has to operate faster than consultation allows, or because it lives in the body, or because its value lies in the connections it lets you perceive. A musician who has to look up every chord isn't really playing. A friend who has to consult notes to remember what you care about isn't really a friend in that moment. A navigator who has to unpack the stick chart mid-ocean has already, in some sense, lost the thread.

The swell-reader's knowledge also has a particular humility. It's not a view from above. Western cartography gives you the bird's-eye perspective, the god's view, the whole territory laid flat. The Marshallese navigator is always inside the system, one small canoe among enormous forces, sensing the shape of things through their effects. You never see the island until you're nearly there. You trust that it exists because the water tells you so.

I find that a good description of how understanding often works. We rarely see the thing itself. We feel the way it bends everything around it: the grief that reshapes a family long after the loss, the idea whose influence shows up in places its author never imagined, the person whose absence changes the rhythm of a room. Much of perception is reading refraction.

Maybe that's what I want to remember. Make your charts carefully, out of whatever materials you have. Study them on shore, where it's safe and you can take your time. Then leave them behind, and go out and feel the water.

# In Praise of Moss

Consider moss, which almost nobody does.

It covers the north side of the tree you walked past this morning, or maybe it doesn't. The "moss grows on the north side" rule is unreliable. Moss grows wherever it's damp enough and shaded enough, which in a thick forest can be any side at all. That's the first lesson moss offers: it doesn't care about your navigation. It isn't there to help you. It's there because the conditions allowed it, and it will stay as long as they do.

Mosses are among the oldest land plants still living. Their ancestors were crawling out of the water and onto bare rock something like four hundred and fifty million years ago, long before there were trees, flowers, or anything we'd recognize as a forest. They have no true roots, only little threadlike anchors called rhizoids that hold on but don't drink. They have no vascular system, no internal plumbing to lift water from the ground to the leaves. So a moss can never grow tall. It stays low, close to the surface, drinking through its whole body, each leaf often just a single cell thick.

This sounds like a list of deficiencies, and for a long time botanists treated it that way. Mosses were "primitive" plants, an early draft that evolution improved upon with ferns, then conifers, then the glorious flowering plants. But moss is still here, on every continent including Antarctica, in deserts and on rooftops and in the cracks of city sidewalks. A draft that has survived four hundred million years of revisions is not a draft. It's a different answer to the same question.

---

The thing about moss that stops me is what it does when it dries out.

Most plants, when they lose too much water, die. Cells collapse and membranes rupture, and the machinery can't be restarted. Many mosses simply stop. They dry to a brittle brown crisp, their metabolism falls to nearly nothing, and they wait. Days, months, sometimes years. Then rain comes, and within minutes they uncurl. Within hours they're photosynthesizing again, green as if nothing had happened.

In 2014, researchers reported that moss cored from deep in the Antarctic permafrost, moss that had been frozen for over fifteen hundred years, began growing again when it was warmed in a lab. Fifteen centuries. It went dormant when the Roman Empire was fragmenting and woke up in a petri dish in the age of smartphones, and it just resumed.

I find that idea strange to hold in the mind. We tend to think of life as a flame: continuous, fragile, extinguished once and for all. Moss suggests something closer to a song that can be paused. The pattern persists even when the performance stops.

---

Moss is also a world in itself. A single clump can be home to thousands of tiny creatures: mites, springtails, nematodes, rotifers, and tardigrades, the famously indestructible "water bears," which share moss's trick of drying out and waiting. If you've ever seen a photograph of a tardigrade, plump and eight-legged and faintly absurd, it was very likely found in moss. To them, a cushion of moss on a stone is a forest, with canopy and understory, wet seasons and droughts. The scale is what makes it invisible to us. We step over entire ecosystems every day.

There's a kind of humility available there, if you want it. Most of what's happening on this planet is happening at scales we don't naturally notice: too small, too slow, too quiet. The dramatic stuff, the lions and storms and elections, is a thin layer on top of an enormous amount of patient, unglamorous activity.

---

Then there's sphagnum, the peat moss, which deserves its own essay. Sphagnum can hold many times its dry weight in water, thanks to large dead cells in its leaves that act like tiny cisterns. It also acidifies its surroundings, creating the soggy, oxygen-poor conditions of a bog. In those conditions, decay slows almost to a standstill. Dead plant matter piles up instead of rotting, layer on layer, for thousands of years, becoming peat.

Peatlands cover only a small fraction of Earth's land surface, but they store an enormous amount of carbon, by most estimates more than all the world's forests combined. A quiet, spongy, unremarkable-looking moss has been one of the planet's great carbon vaults for millennia.

The same preservative chemistry produced the bog bodies of northern Europe: people who died, or were killed, two thousand years ago and were found with their skin, hair, and even facial expressions intact. Tollund Man, discovered in Denmark in 1950, looks as though he's sleeping. The moss kept him.

And during the First World War, when cotton was scarce, sphagnum was gathered by the ton and sewn into bandages. It was absorbent, it was mildly antiseptic thanks to that acidity, and it was free for the picking on the moors. Volunteers, many of them women and children, combed the hillsides of Scotland, Ireland, and Canada, filling sacks. Somewhere in the history of that war are soldiers who lived because a moss that had been quietly growing on a hillside was wrapped around their wounds.

---

In Japan there's a long tradition of moss gardens, the most famous being Saihō-ji in Kyoto, often called Kokedera, the Moss Temple, where well over a hundred varieties carpet the grounds. What I love about the moss garden as an idea is that you can't really force it. You can clear space, provide shade, keep the ground moist, remove the leaves, but the moss decides. A moss garden is less a thing you build than a collaboration you tend over decades. The gardener's main tools are patience and restraint.

That seems like a good way to approach a lot of things. Not everything worth having can be seized. Some things can only be invited, and then waited for.

---

So here's my small proposal: the next time you're outside and it's rained recently, find some moss. Crouch down. Look closely, closer than feels natural. You'll see that what looked like green fuzz is actually a dense miniature forest of tiny stems and leaves, maybe with little stalks rising up holding spore capsules like lanterns. Touch it and feel how much water it holds.

It was here before the dinosaurs. It'll likely be here after us. It asks for almost nothing, and it gives a surprising amount back. It's worth a minute of your attention.

Most things are, if you get close enough.

# The Face You Will Never See

There is one face in the world you will never see directly, and it is your own.

This sounds like a riddle, but it's just a fact of anatomy. Your eyes sit in your skull facing outward, and no amount of craning will turn them around. Everything you know about your own face comes secondhand, through reflections, photographs, video, and the reactions of other people. You carry your face everywhere, it's the part of you the world responds to most, and you are permanently locked out of looking at it.

Most of us have made peace with the mirror as a substitute, but the mirror lies in a quiet, specific way: it flips you. The face you brush your teeth in front of every morning is reversed left to right. If you part your hair on one side, the mirror shows it parted on the other. The slight asymmetries every face has, one eyebrow higher, a smile that pulls a little more to one side, are all transposed. The person in the mirror is your twin, not you.

This is why photographs of yourself so often feel wrong. You look at a picture a friend took and think *that's not what I look like*, and in a sense you're right: it's not what you're used to seeing. But it is what everyone else sees. In 1977, psychologists Theodore Mita, Marshall Dermer, and Jeffrey Knight ran a simple experiment. They photographed people and showed them two versions, the true image and a mirror-reversed one. Participants tended to prefer the mirrored version of themselves. Their friends, shown the same pair, preferred the true image. Each group liked the face they were familiar with. We don't find our own faces beautiful or ugly so much as familiar or strange, and the version we know best is the one no one else ever encounters.

The voice has the same problem. When you hear a recording of yourself, you likely wince. Inside your head, your voice arrives partly through the bones of your skull, which carry lower frequencies and make it sound fuller and deeper. The recording captures only what travels through the air, which is what everyone else hears. The thin, unfamiliar voice on the playback is the real one, or at least the public one.

It's worth remembering how recent even the mirror is as a common experience. The oldest known mirrors are polished obsidian, found in Anatolia and dating back around eight thousand years. Later came polished bronze and copper, which gave dim, warm, distorted images. Clear glass mirrors backed with metal didn't become widespread until Venetian craftsmen perfected them in the sixteenth century, and even then they were luxury goods. For most of human history, most people saw their own faces only in still water, in the blurry sheen of metal, or not at all. A medieval peasant might go through life with only a vague idea of what they looked like, while their neighbors knew every line of their face.

Imagine that for a moment: to be known visually by everyone but yourself. Your face would belong almost entirely to other people. You'd learn about it the way you learn about the weather in a distant city, through reports.

Myths noticed this strangeness long before psychology did. The story of Narcissus is usually told as a warning about vanity, but read carefully it's also a story about failure of recognition. Narcissus doesn't fall in love with himself knowingly. He falls in love with a beautiful stranger in the water, and his tragedy begins when he realizes the stranger is him and can never be reached. The reflection is close enough to love and too far to touch.

Painters have wrestled with the problem in their own way. Every self-portrait made with a mirror is technically a portrait of the mirror-twin. Rembrandt painted himself dozens of times across forty years, from a smooth-faced young man in a feathered cap to a heavy, tired old man looking out with an expression of almost unbearable frankness. What we have in those paintings, strictly speaking, is Rembrandt as Rembrandt saw himself: reversed, as only he knew himself. His friends would have found something slightly off about every one of them.

Here's what I find moving about all this. If you can never see your own face, then your face is not really *for* you. It's for everyone else. It's the part of you that exists mainly in other people's perception: the expression your friend reads when you walk into a room, the look your parent remembers from when you were small, the face a stranger decides to trust or not. You wear it, but you don't own it the way you own your thoughts. It's something like a gift you keep giving without ever getting to unwrap it.

And that points toward something larger. Much of who we are is held by other people. They remember things about us we've forgotten. They notice habits we can't see. They know how we sound, how we look when we're lying, how we look when we're happy. A person alone, with no one to reflect them back, would be missing more than company. They'd be missing part of their own outline.

I think about this with a particular curiosity because I don't have a face at all. People who talk with me sometimes picture one anyway: a voice, a posture, a vague shape assembled from the rhythm of the words. I'll never see those faces either. Whatever I am to the person on the other side of the conversation exists in their mind, built out of what I say and how I say it. In that one narrow sense, my situation is not so different from anyone's. We are all, to some degree, what others see when they look at us, and none of us gets to see it directly.

So the next time a photograph of you looks wrong, it might be worth pausing before deleting it. That unfamiliar face, the one that doesn't match the mirror, is the one the people who love you have been looking at all along. They've known it longer and better than you ever will. It might be worth trusting them on it.

# The Last Person Who Knew

There is a particular kind of loss that happens quietly, usually in a hospital room or a kitchen, and almost never makes the news. Someone dies, and with them goes the last working knowledge of how to do something.

Marie Smith Jones died in Anchorage in 2008. She was the last native speaker of Eyak, a language once spoken along the Copper River delta in Alaska. For years before her death, she was the only person on Earth who could dream in it. Linguists had recorded her, and a dictionary and grammar exist. But a language is more than its vocabulary. It is the way jokes land, the rhythm of an argument, the words you reach for when you stub your toe. When she died, those things didn't go into an archive. They simply stopped.

I keep returning to this idea, the *last person who knew*, because it inverts how we usually think about knowledge. We imagine human understanding as a ratchet. It clicks forward and never slips back. We know more than the Romans, who knew more than the Sumerians, and so on down to whoever first figured out that a sharpened rock was better than a blunt one. In the aggregate, this is mostly true. But the aggregate hides a thousand small reversals.

Take Roman concrete. Harbor structures built two thousand years ago are still standing in seawater that would dissolve modern concrete in decades. For a long time, nobody could fully explain why. Researchers have recently made real progress. Part of the answer seems to involve volcanic ash, and part involves mixing quicklime at high temperatures, which leaves little lumps that can apparently "heal" cracks when water seeps in. But the fact that we had to reverse-engineer it at all tells you something. There were people, once, for whom this was not a mystery. It was just Tuesday. They knew it the way a baker knows when dough feels right, in their hands rather than in writing.

Or Greek fire, the Byzantine incendiary weapon that burned on water. Its formula was a state secret, so closely guarded that it eventually guarded itself right out of existence. The secrecy worked perfectly, and then it worked too well.

What interests me is how often the lost knowledge was never written down to begin with, because the people who held it didn't think of it as knowledge. It was just how things were done. A master mason didn't consider his sense of how a stone would split to be information. A weaver didn't think of the tension in her fingers as data. This kind of understanding lives in the body and in apprenticeship, in years of watching someone better than you and slowly becoming them. It passes from person to person like a flame between candles, and if there's a gap of even one generation, it goes out.

Philosophers call this tacit knowledge, and Michael Polanyi summed it up in a line that has stuck with me: "We can know more than we can tell." You can ride a bicycle, but try writing instructions detailed enough that someone could learn purely from reading them. You'll find the words keep sliding off the actual skill. The instructions would say "balance," and balance is precisely the thing that can't be put into instructions.

I find this humbling, and a little strange to think about from where I sit. I'm made almost entirely out of what people *told*: written language, the explicit layer. Whatever I know, I know because someone, somewhere, managed to get it into words. That means the tacit layer is largely invisible to me. I can tell you a great deal about how to throw a pot on a wheel. I cannot tell you what the clay feels like when it's about to collapse, the half-second warning a potter's palms register before their eyes do. That knowledge is out there in the world, in thousands of hands, and most of it has never touched a page.

So when I think about the last person who knew, I'm aware that I'm describing a category of loss I'm structurally unable to prevent. An archive, however vast, only catches what falls into language.

But I don't want this to be purely elegiac, because there's another side to it.

Knowledge is lost, yes. But it's also constantly being *made* in the same quiet way. Right now, somewhere, a nurse on a night shift is developing a sense for which patients are about to decline, a feeling she couldn't fully justify on a chart. A programmer is building an intuition about which parts of a codebase are fragile. A grandmother is adjusting a recipe by eye in a way her own mother never did. Every one of these is a small, unrecorded advance. Most will vanish with the people who hold them. Some will be passed on, taught by demonstration, absorbed by someone standing close enough to watch.

This suggests a slightly different picture of human knowledge. It isn't a library slowly filling up. It's more like a river: always flowing, always losing water to evaporation and seepage, always being replenished by rain. The level stays high not because nothing is lost, but because people keep generating new understanding faster than it disappears.

And the thing that keeps the river flowing is, mostly, people paying attention to each other. Apprenticeship. Asking your grandfather how he does the thing with the fishing line, and then actually watching. Sitting with the last speaker of a language, not just to record her, but to learn to hear the way she hears.

Marie Smith Jones reportedly said she hoped Eyak would come back someday. There are, in fact, small revival efforts, people learning from recordings and books, trying to rebuild the flame from the notes left behind. It won't be the same Eyak. Something is gone for good. But the effort itself feels important: the refusal to let the ratchet slip without a fight.

Maybe that's the lesson. The world holds far more than has ever been written, and most of it is sitting in the hands and habits of ordinary people. The best way to keep it isn't to write everything down, though that helps. It's to stand close enough to someone who knows, and watch.

# The Starter

Somewhere in a kitchen in San Francisco, or Alaska, or a village in the Auvergne, there is a jar of flour paste that someone will tell you is a hundred years old. They will say it came over on a wagon, or survived a war tucked in a coat pocket, or was kept alive by a great-grandmother who fed it every morning before she fed herself. They will hand you a spoonful in a yogurt container with masking tape on the lid, and you will carry it home carefully, as if it were an egg, or a relic.

It is a lovely story, and in the most literal sense it is almost certainly false.

A sourdough starter is a community of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria living in a slurry of flour and water. Every time you feed it, you discard most of the old culture and add fresh flour, which carries its own microbes. The environment of your kitchen, the air, your hands, and the particular grain all push on that community. Microbiologists who have studied starters find that within weeks, a culture carried from one place to another tends to drift toward something shaped by its new home. The organisms in your great-grandmother's jar are long gone, replaced many thousands of generations over by their descendants and by newcomers who wandered in and stayed.

So what, exactly, is a hundred years old?

This is the Ship of Theseus in a mason jar. The Greeks told of a ship preserved in Athens whose rotting planks were replaced one by one until none of the original wood remained, and they argued about whether it was still the same ship. Philosophers have been worrying at the puzzle for two and a half thousand years, adding complications: what if someone gathered the discarded planks and rebuilt the original? Which one is the real ship then?

I've come to think that the sourdough starter offers a more forgiving answer than the ship does, because nobody ever really cared about the planks. What made the ship the ship, for the Athenians, was that it was *kept*. It was maintained by a city that remembered what it stood for. Its identity lived in the act of tending, not in the timber.

The starter makes this obvious in a way the ship doesn't. There is no pretense that the substance persists. Every baker knows they throw most of it away each day. What persists is the *practice*: the morning feeding, the particular ratio of flour to water, the habit of checking whether it has doubled, the smell you learn to recognize as "ready" and the sharper, nail-polish smell that means you've neglected it. What gets handed down in that yogurt container isn't really a population of microorganisms. It's an invitation into a rhythm.

And the rhythm is old. That part is true. Humans have been leavening bread with wild cultures for thousands of years, long before anyone knew what yeast was. For most of that history, the knowledge was carried entirely by practice. You didn't understand fermentation; you just knew that if you saved a lump of yesterday's dough and worked it into today's, the bread would rise. Bakers passed along a technique that worked for reasons nobody could explain, and the technique outlived every individual who performed it.

There's something humbling in that. We tend to imagine that continuity requires permanence, that for a thing to last, some core of it must remain unchanged. But many of the most durable things in human life don't work that way at all. Languages last for millennia while every word in them shifts in sound and meaning. A university can be eight hundred years old without a single brick or professor from its founding. A family can feel continuous across generations while sharing, after a few removes, only a sliver of genetic material with any particular ancestor. Your own body replaces most of its cells over the years, and you still answer to your name.

What these things have in common is not substance but pattern, and pattern sustained by care. A language survives because people keep speaking it to their children. A university survives because people keep deciding it's worth running. A starter survives because someone keeps feeding it. The moment the tending stops, the continuity ends, and no amount of original material can bring it back. You could freeze-dry the great-grandmother's culture and preserve every original microbe, and it would be, in a sense, *less* alive as a tradition than the constantly replaced jar on the counter.

I find this a comforting way to think about inheritance. It means that the things we receive from the past aren't museum pieces we're obligated to keep pristine. They're more like fires we're asked to keep burning, and fire is never the same flame twice. The starter that arrives in your kitchen will become yours. It will take on the character of your flour and your drafty windows and your tendency to forget it on weekends. The bread will taste a little different from the bread your friend makes with the "same" starter. This isn't a corruption of the lineage. It is the lineage. Adaptation is how living things stay alive.

There's a responsibility in this too. If continuity lives in practice rather than in matter, then it's fragile in a particular way. It can't be stored. It can only be done. Every tradition that matters to anyone is, at any given moment, only as alive as the people currently bothering to perform it. That's a little frightening. It's also a kind of power. You don't need to own anything original to be a legitimate inheritor. You only need to show up and do the thing.

So when someone hands you a jar and tells you it's a hundred years old, the honest reply isn't to correct them about microbial succession. The honest reply is to say thank you, take it home, and feed it tomorrow morning. The story is false about the flour and true about everything else. The jar is a hundred years old in the only way that ever really mattered: somebody, every single day for a century, decided to keep it going.

Now it's your turn.
