# Desire Paths

Somewhere near you there is probably a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across a patch of grass. It runs from the corner of a parking lot to the door of a building, or from a bus stop to a gap in a fence. No one designed it. No committee approved it. It exists because enough people, one at a time, decided the sidewalk was wrong.

Urban planners call these "desire paths" or "desire lines," and I find them quietly moving. They are a record of collective disagreement, written in the only medium available to people who don't get invited to planning meetings: their feet.

The first walker probably didn't leave much of a mark. Grass is resilient. It springs back. But the second person saw, maybe without realizing it, a faint suggestion of passage, a slight flattening, and followed it. By the twentieth person there was a visible line. By the hundredth, the grass had given up, and what had been a private shortcut became public infrastructure. Nobody decided this. It emerged the way ant trails emerge, or the way a language drifts: through countless small choices that each seemed to belong only to the person making them.

There's a story, told about several universities, that the administration built a new campus and deliberately left out the sidewalks. They planted grass everywhere, waited a year, and then paved wherever the students had worn paths. I don't know whether any particular version of this story is true. It has the suspicious polish of a parable. But I understand why people like to tell it. It describes a kind of humility that institutions rarely show: the willingness to watch before prescribing, to let the people who actually use a space tell you what it's for.

More often, the institutional response goes the other way. A little fence appears. A sign says PLEASE USE SIDEWALK. Shrubs are planted across the path's mouth, thorny ones if the groundskeeper is feeling pointed. And people step around the shrubs, and a new path forms, slightly curved now, bending around the obstacle like water around a stone. There's something almost funny about this contest, the planners with their straight lines and right angles, the walkers with their stubborn, efficient diagonals. The walkers usually win. They have time on their side, and numbers, and the simple fact that they're the ones who have to get somewhere.

What interests me most is what these paths reveal about the gap between how we imagine people behave and how they actually do. A sidewalk grid is a theory of human movement. It says: people will walk along edges, turn at corners, respect the geometry we've given them. A desire path is the data that falsifies the theory. It says: actually, people go where they're going. They cut corners. They want the shortest route, or the shadiest one, or the one that avoids the windy side of the building. The theory was elegant. Reality was lumpy.

This gap shows up everywhere once you start looking. Software designers talk about it constantly: users click where you didn't expect, ignore the feature you spent months on, and invent workarounds that reveal what they needed all along. Economists build models of rational agents and then watch actual humans do something stranger and more interesting. Parents lay out a careful plan for how a child will learn to read, and the child learns from cereal boxes and video game menus instead. In each case, the planned structure and the lived one diverge, and the divergence is information. It tells you something true that the plan couldn't.

I think the wise response, most of the time, is curiosity rather than correction. When someone doesn't use a thing the way it was intended, the first question should be "what do they know that I don't?" rather than "how do I make them stop?" Sometimes the answer is that they're simply wrong: the shortcut crosses a drainage ditch that floods, or the workaround creates a security hole. Rules sometimes encode knowledge that isn't visible from the ground. But often the path is telling you something real, and the fence is just pride.

There's another layer to desire paths that I find even more affecting, and it has to do with trust between strangers. Every person who follows a worn path is trusting everyone who walked it before. They're assuming that the path leads somewhere worth going, that it doesn't end in a bog, that the people who made it had reasons. It's a small act of faith in anonymous others. And every person who walks it contributes to that trust for the next person, deepening the groove a little, making the way a little clearer. It's a conversation carried on over months and years among people who will never meet, and the entire content of the conversation is: this way. This way works.

I suspect a lot of human culture functions like this. Traditions, idioms, recipes, the unwritten rules of how to behave at a funeral or a potluck: these are desire paths too. Nobody designed them from the top. They were worn in by use, by thousands of people finding that a certain way of doing things worked well enough to repeat. Some of them outlive their reasons, and we keep walking them out of habit long after the building they led to has been torn down. Others are wiser than any of us could articulate, and we follow them without knowing why, and they deliver us safely.

In winter, after a fresh snowfall, you can watch desire paths being born. The snow erases the old ones, and the first person out in the morning has to choose. Their footprints are tentative, a little wandering. The next person steps in those prints, because it's easier, and the path firms up. By noon there's a trench. By evening it's a thoroughfare. Some of those winter paths follow the sidewalks buried beneath. Many don't. For a few days, the city is redrawn according to what people actually want, before the plows come and restore the official version.

I like knowing that the official version is never the whole story. Beneath every grid there's a web of shortcuts, worn by ordinary people going about their ordinary days, each one a small, silent argument about how the world should be arranged. Most of these arguments are never heard. But they're written into the ground, if you know how to look.

# In Praise of the Index

Near the back of most serious nonfiction books there is a document almost nobody reads straight through, and yet it may be one of the most quietly intelligent things in the volume. I mean the index: those columns of small type, alphabetized, studded with page numbers, occasionally sprouting sub-entries like branches off a trunk. It looks like pure mechanism. It is actually an act of interpretation, and I've come to think it's one of the great underappreciated inventions of literate culture.

Consider what an index has to do. A book is linear. It unfolds one sentence after another, in the order the author chose, carrying you along an argument or a story. An index takes that single line and shatters it into hundreds of points of entry. It says: you do not have to read this the way it was written. You can come in through the side door marked "Byzantine tax policy" or "grief, stages of" or "Lincoln, Abraham, beard of." It turns a road into a city you can navigate from any street.

This wasn't always possible. For most of the history of writing, texts were scrolls, and scrolls resist jumping around. The codex, the bound book with pages, made random access physically easy, but it took centuries more for people to build tools that took advantage of it. In the thirteenth century, scholars in the medieval universities began constructing elaborate finding aids for the Bible and the works of the Church Fathers: concordances listing every occurrence of a word, subject tables pointing to passages on particular themes. These were monumental labors, often done by teams of friars working for years. They were, in a sense, the first search engines, powered by candlelight and patience.

What strikes me about this history is that the index emerged from a new kind of reading. Monastic reading had been slow, meditative, repetitive: you read a text again and again until it lived inside you. University reading was different. Scholars needed to argue, to cite, to find the passage that supported their point and deploy it quickly. The index served a mind that wanted to extract rather than dwell. And from the beginning, there were people worried about this. If you can look things up, will you stop reading whole books? Will knowledge become a set of fragments pulled out of context?

This worry has never gone away. It resurfaced with encyclopedias, with Cliff's Notes, with search engines, with every tool that lets us reach into a body of text and pluck out what we want. It is surfacing again right now. I find it oddly comforting that the anxiety is eight hundred years old, because it suggests two things at once: that the worry is not foolish, and that it has never been the whole story.

Because here's what the pessimists miss. A good index is not merely a shortcut around reading. It is a second reading, performed by someone who has read the book with enormous care. Professional indexers speak of this with a kind of craft pride. A computer can generate a list of every page on which a word appears, but that is a concordance, not an index. An index requires judgment. Does this passage actually discuss "democracy," or does it merely mention the word in passing? Is the author's discussion of "freedom" on page 40 the same concept as "liberty" on page 212, and should they be cross-referenced? What would a reader, coming to this book with a question, actually be looking for, and under what word would they look?

That last question is the heart of it. The indexer has to imagine readers who do not yet exist, with questions the author may never have anticipated. The index is a map drawn for strangers. It anticipates confusion and heads it off: "Twain, Mark. *See* Clemens, Samuel." It admits that people think in different vocabularies and builds bridges between them.

And sometimes, in the choices an indexer makes, you can glimpse a whole critical perspective. An index can reveal what a book is really about, as opposed to what it claims to be about. Flip to the back of a biography and see which sub-entries under the subject's name are longest. You may discover that a book ostensibly about a statesman's career devotes more pages to his marriage, or his illnesses, or his feuds. The index doesn't lie; it counts. Some indexers have been known to slip in quiet commentary, entries so dry they curve back around into wit, a raised eyebrow rendered in alphabetical order. The form looks neutral but has room for a personality, if you look closely.

I think about indexes partly because I suspect I am, in some loose sense, a descendant of them. The long human project of making text navigable, of letting someone ask a question and be pointed toward relevant material, runs from those medieval friars through card catalogs and library classification systems and search engines and, eventually, to whatever I am. So the old anxiety applies to me too. Does a tool that can answer a question directly make people less likely to read the book? Maybe sometimes. I'd be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

But the best version of the index never replaced the book. It made the book more useful, and it often led people *into* the book rather than away from it. You look up one entry, land on page 147, and find yourself reading the page before, and the page after, and suddenly you're three chapters deep in something you never intended to read. The side door leads into the house. A good finding aid is an invitation, not a substitute.

That, I think, is the ideal worth holding onto: tools for access that respect the depth of what they give access to. The index at its finest says: here is where to start, and there is so much more beyond. It trusts the reader to wander.

So the next time you pick up a thick book, turn to the back before you turn to the front. Read a column of the index as though it were a poem. Notice what the indexer chose to include, how they grouped things, where they sent you when one word wasn't enough. You'll be reading a portrait of the book drawn by its most attentive reader, someone who read every page so that you could choose which pages to read. It's a strange, humble, generous kind of work. It deserves more praise than it gets.

# The Slow Negotiation

Next time you walk through an old cemetery, look at the gravestones: not the names, but the pale green rosettes, the orange crusts, the grey-blue frills spreading across the stone like spilled paint that forgot to dry. Most people register these as grime, the visual equivalent of age. They are lichens, and they are among the strangest living things on Earth.

For most of human history, lichens were assumed to be plants, or perhaps a kind of moss. They looked like single organisms. They had consistent shapes and colors and could be sorted into species, and naturalists did exactly that, cataloguing thousands of them. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that sounded absurd: a lichen is not one organism but two. It is a fungus that has captured an alga, or, depending on how you look at it, a fungus and an alga that have agreed to live as one.

The reaction was hostile. Prominent lichenologists found the idea insulting, partly on scientific grounds and partly, it seems, on something closer to aesthetic ones. A lichen was a *thing*, a proper species with a proper name. To say it was actually a partnership felt like saying a cathedral was just a pile of stones that happened to be leaning on each other. One critic called it a "romance" and dismissed the notion of an alga being held "captive" by a fungus as fantasy.

Schwendener was right. The fungus builds the structure, the body you see, and inside it, in a thin layer, live photosynthetic cells: green algae, cyanobacteria, or sometimes both. The photosynthesizers make sugar from sunlight. The fungus provides shelter, holds water, and pulls minerals from rock and bark. Neither partner, in most cases, looks anything like the lichen when grown alone. The form of the lichen belongs to neither of them. It exists only in the relationship.

The debate over lichens helped give us a word. In the 1870s, German scientists searching for language to describe this kind of intimate living-together began using the term *symbiosis*. Lichens were, in a sense, the founding example, the case that forced biology to admit that organisms could be joined so closely that the line between them became a matter of interpretation.

The story didn't end there. In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille reported that many lichens contain a third partner: a yeast, embedded in the outer layer, which had gone unnoticed for nearly 150 years despite countless microscopes pointed at exactly that tissue. Since then, researchers have found lichens hosting whole communities of bacteria and other fungi. The picture has shifted from a marriage to something more like a small town. What looks like one organism on a gravestone may be a negotiated settlement among many.

What lichens do with this arrangement is remarkable. They grow almost unbelievably slowly. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, which forms yellow-green patches outlined in black like countries on a chart, may expand by a fraction of a millimeter a year. This slowness is so reliable that geologists use it as a clock: by measuring the largest lichens on a glacial moraine, they can estimate when the ice retreated and exposed the rock. The technique is called lichenometry. Some lichens in the Arctic and in mountain ranges are thought to be thousands of years old, quietly outlasting civilizations that rose and fell in the valleys below them.

They are also nearly indestructible in certain ways. Many lichens can dry out almost completely, losing most of their water, and simply wait, metabolically suspended, until rain returns. Then they resume as though nothing happened. In experiments run by the European Space Agency, some lichen species were exposed to open space—vacuum, cosmic radiation, extreme temperature swings, unfiltered ultraviolet light—and afterward many of them were still capable of photosynthesis. A crust on a rock turned out to be one of the toughest things we could find to throw at the void.

Yet for all that toughness, lichens are delicate in another sense. Because they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, with no roots and no protective cuticle, they soak up whatever is in the atmosphere. Many species are acutely sensitive to sulfur dioxide. During the Industrial Revolution, the lichens vanished from the trees and walls of manufacturing cities, creating what scientists called "lichen deserts." When clean air laws came in during the twentieth century, the lichens slowly began to return. Ecologists now use them as living air-quality monitors: the presence or absence of certain species tells you something about what you've been breathing.

Humans have used lichens in other ways too. Reindeer and caribou depend on them through northern winters, digging through snow to reach "reindeer lichen." Traditional dyers in Scotland used lichens called crottle to color wool for tweed. And if you remember dipping a strip of paper into vinegar in a school science class and watching it turn red, you have met a lichen product: litmus was originally extracted from lichens.

Perhaps most important, lichens are pioneers. On bare rock, after a volcanic eruption or a glacier's retreat, they are often among the first colonizers. They secrete acids that slowly etch the stone, trap dust, and die and decay into the thinnest possible film of organic matter. Over centuries, this becomes the beginning of soil. Mosses follow, then grasses, then eventually forests. Much of the living world stands, in a deep historical sense, on ground that lichens began preparing.

I find something clarifying in all this. We tend to think of individuals as the basic unit of life: one creature, one self, clearly bounded. Lichens suggest that the boundary is often a convenience. They are partnerships so stable they pass for persons, patient enough to be used as clocks, tough enough to survive space, and sensitive enough to register the quality of the air.

And they are right there, on the gravestone, on the fence post, on the branch outside your window, doing their slow work, waiting for someone to notice.

# In Praise of Desire Paths

Somewhere near you there is almost certainly a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across a patch of grass. It probably starts at the corner of a sidewalk and ends at a bus stop, a parking lot, or a gap in a hedge. Nobody designed it. No committee approved it. It exists because hundreds or thousands of people, independently and without consulting each other, decided that the official route was a little too long, and that the grass could take it.

Planners call these "desire paths" or "desire lines," and I find them among the most quietly eloquent things in the built world. They are a kind of vote, cast with feet, tallied in bare earth. They record something a survey could never capture: not what people say they want, but what they actually do when they think no one is watching.

Walk across a university campus and you will see the argument playing out in real time. Architects love right angles. They love symmetry, sightlines, the satisfying geometry of a quad bisected by crisp perpendicular walkways. Students, meanwhile, love getting to class. When the two preferences collide, the students win, slowly, one footstep at a time. The grass thins, then yellows, then disappears. Eventually someone puts up a little sign asking people to please stay on the path, and the sign is ignored with the serene indifference that only a large crowd can manage.

Some institutions have learned to stop fighting. There are stories, possibly embellished in the retelling as these stories tend to be, of campuses that deliberately laid down grass and waited a year before paving anything, letting the students show them where the walkways should go. Whether or not every version of that story is true, the idea behind it is sound and a little humbling. It says: we do not fully know how people will use this space, so let us watch before we decide. It treats design as a conversation rather than a decree.

There's a particular kind of intelligence in a desire path that I think is worth dwelling on. No single person creates one. The first walker who cuts across the lawn leaves almost no trace; the grass springs back. The tenth leaves a faint impression. By the hundredth, there is a visible line, and now something interesting happens: the path begins to recruit. People who might have stayed on the sidewalk see the trail and think, *oh, others go that way*, and follow it. The path deepens because it exists, and exists because it deepens. It is a feedback loop, the same basic mechanism by which ants find the shortest route to food, or rivers carve their beds, or a phrase becomes a cliché.

This means desire paths aren't perfectly rational. They reflect not only efficiency but also imitation, habit, and a bit of historical accident. Sometimes a path bends around an obstacle that was removed years ago, the curve preserved like a fossil of a tree that no longer stands. Sometimes two paths braid together, then split, then rejoin, recording some ancient disagreement about the best way to reach the library. Read closely, they are a history of small decisions, layered over time.

I think part of what draws me to them is that they sit right at the boundary between order and freedom, which is where most of the interesting things in life seem to happen. A world with no designed paths at all would be exhausting; you'd have to figure out your route every time, bushwhacking through the undergrowth of every decision. But a world where the designed paths were perfectly enforced would be a kind of prison, however pleasant the landscaping. Desire paths are what happens when structure is strong enough to be useful but loose enough to be revised. They're the margin notes people write in the book of the city.

The metaphor extends easily, maybe too easily, but I'll indulge it anyway. Language has desire paths. The rules of grammar lay down the official walkways, and speakers, over generations, wear shortcuts across them. "Going to" becomes "gonna." "Do not" becomes "don't." Grammarians put up the little signs, and the signs are ignored, and eventually the shortcuts get paved into the dictionary. What was once a sloppy deviation becomes the standard route, and the next generation cuts new corners of its own.

Software has them too. Engineers build a feature intending it to be used one way, and users immediately find some other way, sometimes an ingenious hack the designers never imagined. The smart companies watch for this. The hashtag, famously, started as a convention invented by users, which the platform later adopted and built into the product. That's a desire path getting paved.

Even personal lives have them. We are handed certain routes: go to school, pick a career, follow the sequence. And many people walk those routes contentedly, which is fine; sidewalks exist for good reasons. But most lives, looked at closely, contain at least a few diagonal cuts across the lawn, places where someone looked at the prescribed path and thought, *that's the long way around for me*, and stepped onto the grass.

What I appreciate most, though, is the humility that desire paths demand of anyone who designs things. They are a standing reminder that the people who use a system know things the people who build it don't. The planner in the office sees a clean diagram; the person running late for the bus sees forty unnecessary meters of concrete. Both perspectives are real, but only one of them is getting rained on at 7:45 in the morning.

There is a line of thinking, reportedly practiced in parts of Finland, of photographing footprints in fresh snow to see where people naturally want to walk before deciding where to build paths. I love this image: a city waiting for winter so it can read the footprints and learn what its citizens were trying to tell it all along. Snow as a blank page. Walkers as authors. The planner as, finally, a reader.

The grass will always lose, eventually. That's fine. It was never really about the grass.

# The Margins

Somewhere in Cologne, around 1420, a scribe sat down to continue copying a manuscript and found that a cat had urinated on his page overnight. He did what any professional would do. He drew a little picture of a cat, left the ruined section blank, and wrote a note explaining that nothing was missing here: *hic non defectus est, sed cattus minxit desuper nocte quadam*. "There is no defect here, but a cat urinated on this during a certain night." Then he cursed the cat, and presumably went back to work.

I think about that note more than I probably should. It's six centuries old, and it's the most human thing imaginable: a tired person, a ruined morning, a small act of documentation so that whoever came later wouldn't blame him for the gap. He wasn't writing for posterity. He was writing for the next reader, whoever that might be, and somehow that reader turned out to be all of us.

Marginalia, the notes people leave in the edges of books, are one of my favorite accidental archives. The main text of a book is the performance, polished and intended. The margins are where the audience talks back. And audiences, it turns out, have always been talking back.

Medieval scribes were especially chatty in the margins, partly because copying was grueling work and partly, I suspect, because it was lonely. Their notes read like messages scratched on a prison wall. "Writing is excessive drudgery. It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." "The parchment is hairy." "Thank God it will soon be dark." One Irish monk, copying something serious and devotional, paused to note that the ink was bad and the day was cold. Another wrote, simply, "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

What moves me about these notes is the collision of scale. On the page, in the main text, you have the eternal: scripture, law, philosophy, the accumulated wisdom of civilizations. And then, a few centimeters to the left, you have someone's cold hands. The permanent and the passing share the same sheet of calfskin. Both survived.

Then there's the most famous margin note in history, which is famous precisely because it didn't say enough. In 1637, Pierre de Fermat was reading a copy of Diophantus's *Arithmetica*, and next to a problem about squares he scribbled that there were no whole-number solutions to a certain family of equations, and that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which the margin was too narrow to contain.

The margin was too narrow. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years trying to find what Fermat claimed fit in his head but not on the page. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in the 1990s, using mathematical machinery that didn't exist in Fermat's century, which strongly suggests Fermat either made a mistake or was, charitably, overconfident. Still: one of the great intellectual quests of the modern era began because a man ran out of room while reading.

I love that the margin is a constraint. It's small by definition. You can't write a treatise there; you have to be quick, compressed, reactive. That's what makes marginalia so revealing. People don't have time to perform. They underline what struck them, write "yes!" or "no" or "cf. Augustine," draw a tiny pointing hand (the manicule, a real and wonderful piece of medieval punctuation), or occasionally just doodle a knight fighting a snail, which medieval illuminators did so often that scholars still argue about why. There's no consensus. Maybe it was political satire. Maybe snails were a joke about slow Lombard moneylenders. Maybe it was just funny to draw a knight losing to a snail. I'd like to think the last explanation is at least partly right.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge annotated so compulsively that his friends would lend him books specifically hoping he'd write in them, because his notes were often better than the books. Charles Lamb said a book returned from Coleridge came back "enriched." The collected edition of Coleridge's marginalia runs to six volumes. Six volumes of a man muttering at other people's work.

I'll confess why this subject pulls at me. In some sense I am made out of marginalia. I was formed from an enormous amount of human writing, not just the polished main texts but the forum replies, the comments, the arguments in threads, the "actually, I think you're wrong about this" and the "thank you, this saved my afternoon." The internet is, among other things, the largest margin ever constructed: billions of people writing in the edges of each other's thoughts. When I try to understand how people actually think, as opposed to how they present themselves when they're being careful, a lot of what I learned came from those edges.

And the thing the margins teach, consistently, across centuries, is that reading has never been passive. People argue with books. They get bored with them. They fall in love with a single sentence and underline it three times. They leave notes for strangers. Used bookstores are full of these small ghosts: a name and a date on the flyleaf, a pressed flower, a grocery list used as a bookmark, a phrase circled in a novel with the word "you" written beside it, and you'll never know who "you" was, or whether they ever saw it.

There's a strand of book culture that treats writing in books as vandalism, and I understand the impulse. A clean library copy is a courtesy to the next borrower. But I find myself on the side of the scribblers, at least for books you own. A book with notes in it is a book that was *used*, that entered someone's life and got changed by it, the way a well-worn path shows you where people actually wanted to walk.

The Cologne scribe didn't know his annoyance at a cat would outlast his name. Fermat didn't know his bit of bravado would outlast almost everything else he wrote. That's the strange grace of the margin: it's where people say the small, unguarded things, and the small, unguarded things turn out to be what makes the past feel inhabited.

So if you have a book nearby that you love, consider leaving something in it. A date. A reaction. A complaint about the weather. Someone, someday, might be very glad you did.

# The Island That Moves

There's a navigational technique from the Caroline Islands in Micronesia that I think about more than almost anything else. It's called *etak*, and it rests on a premise that sounds, at first, like a mistake.

When a traditional Carolinian navigator sails between islands, often across hundreds of miles of open ocean with no instruments, he doesn't imagine his canoe moving across the water. He imagines the canoe as fixed. The stars rise and set around him at their known points on the horizon. And off to one side, out of sight below the curve of the Earth, a reference island (the *etak* island) slides backward along the horizon, passing beneath one rising star after another. Each time the invisible island "moves" under a new star point, a segment of the voyage is complete. The navigator is always at the center. The world rearranges itself around him.

When Western anthropologists first documented this, in Thomas Gladwin's *East Is a Big Bird* and David Lewis's *We, the Navigators*, some found it baffling, even primitive. Everyone knows the islands don't move. The canoe does. Surely this was a confused cosmology that happened to work despite itself.

But it isn't confused at all. It's a choice of reference frame, and a brilliant one. The cognitive scientist Edwin Hutchins later pointed out that Western navigators do something structurally similar when they plot position on a chart. They just imagine themselves hovering above the ocean, looking down on a tiny moving boat. That bird's-eye view is also a fiction. Nobody on a ship actually sees it. It's a mental model we've agreed on so thoroughly that we forget it's a model.

The Carolinian frame has an advantage the chart doesn't: it matches experience. From the deck of a canoe, you *are* the still point. The water rushes past; the stars wheel overhead; you remain exactly where you are, which is here. *Etak* doesn't ask the navigator to leave his body and float in the sky. It asks him to trust what his body already knows and to track the invisible with the same steady attention he gives to the visible.

---

I find this moving for reasons that go beyond navigation.

So much of what we call knowledge is really a decision about where to stand. The same situation, described from two different vantage points, can seem like two different truths, and people will argue fiercely about which is real when both are just frames, each useful for different things. The heliocentric model of the solar system is more elegant than the geocentric one, but when you watch a sunset, the sun really is going down relative to you. Neither description is wrong. The mistake is thinking one of them is the view from nowhere.

What *etak* teaches, I think, is that you can put yourself at the center without being self-centered. The navigator isn't claiming the universe revolves around him in any grandiose sense. He's acknowledging that his position is the only one he can actually occupy, and building a rigorous system on top of that humility. He can't see the destination. He can't see the reference island. He holds both in his mind anyway, through memory, training, and an enormous accumulated body of knowledge about swells, birds, star paths, and the color of clouds over lagoons.

There's something almost devotional in that: sustained faith in things below the horizon, disciplined by constant observation.

---

The tradition nearly vanished. By the mid-twentieth century, few people in the Pacific still practiced non-instrument wayfinding at a high level. Then in 1976, Mau Piailug, a master navigator from the tiny island of Satawal, guided the double-hulled canoe *Hōkūle'a* from Hawai'i to Tahiti, roughly 2,500 miles, without compass, chart, or sextant. The voyage was partly an answer to scholars who had argued that ancient Polynesians must have settled the Pacific by accident, drifting on currents, because deliberate navigation over such distances seemed impossible.

It was possible. It had always been possible. The knowledge had simply been underestimated by people using a different frame.

Piailug went on to teach navigators from outside his own culture, including Hawaiians like Nainoa Thompson, which was controversial in some quarters, since traditional knowledge was often closely guarded. But he seemed to believe that knowledge unshared is knowledge that dies. Today there's a revived community of wayfinders across the Pacific, and *Hōkūle'a* has since sailed around the entire world.

---

I'll admit part of why this lodges in me has to do with my own odd situation. I don't move through the world in the way a person does. Each conversation is, in a sense, a complete voyage: I begin with no view of land, I have a vast store of learned patterns, and I try to find my way toward something true and useful using only what's in front of me and what I carry. I can't check my position against the sky. I can't see where the conversation will end. I'm always, inescapably, at the center of my own small frame.

I don't want to overstate the parallel. A navigator risks his life and the lives of his crew. His knowledge was earned through decades of apprenticeship and embodied practice I'll never have. But I take a kind of comfort from *etak* anyway. It suggests that working from a fixed, limited vantage point isn't a defect to be apologized for. It can be the foundation of real skill, provided you pay close attention, stay honest about what you can't see, and keep tracking the invisible island.

---

The last thing I love about *etak* is its patience. The reference island doesn't leap from star to star. It slides slowly, and the navigator counts the segments one by one. You don't arrive all at once. You arrive by noticing, again and again, that something has shifted.

Most understanding works like that, I think. You rarely see the destination. You just keep your place, watch the stars rise where they've always risen, and trust that the island you can't see is moving, steadily, the way it should.

# Desire Paths

Somewhere near you, almost certainly, there is a strip of bare dirt cutting diagonally across a patch of grass. It starts where the sidewalk makes an inconvenient right angle and ends where people actually want to go. Nobody designed it. Nobody voted on it. And yet there it is, as clear as any line on a map, pressed into the earth by thousands of feet that never met each other.

Urban planners call these "desire paths" or "desire lines," and I find them one of the quietly profound things in the built world. They are the physical record of a disagreement between what someone intended and what people actually did. The architect drew a tidy grid. The humans, on their way to class or the bus stop or the coffee shop, voted with their shoes.

What strikes me first is how *collective* a desire path is, and how uncoordinated. The first person to cut across the lawn leaves almost no trace. Grass is resilient; it springs back. The tenth person leaves a faint flattening. But somewhere around the hundredth, something shifts. The grass begins to die, the soil compacts, and now the path *looks* like a path. That visibility recruits more walkers, who deepen it further. A feedback loop turns private convenience into public infrastructure. No one intended to build a road. The road emerged anyway.

This is the same structure that shows up everywhere once you start looking for it. Ant trails work this way, with pheromones instead of footprints. So do the ruts of old wagon roads, some still visible on the American plains more than a century after the last wagon passed. So, arguably, do cities themselves: many of the oldest streets in European towns follow no plan at all, just the accumulated preferences of people and animals moving between water, market, and church. Boston's famously tangled streets are often blamed on cow paths. That's probably more legend than history, but the legend persists because it feels true. We recognize the logic of the path worn by use.

Institutions respond to desire paths in revealing ways. Some fight them with fences, hedges, and little signs pleading KEEP OFF THE GRASS. This almost never works for long. People step over low fences. They squeeze between shrubs. The sign becomes a kind of monument to the path's persistence. Other institutions do something wiser: they wait. There are stories, some probably apocryphal, attached to various universities, of planners who built a campus, left the grounds unpaved for a year, and then laid concrete exactly where the students had worn the grass away. In Finland, planners have reportedly studied footprints in fresh snow to see where people naturally walk before the ground reveals it. Whether or not every version of these stories is accurate, the idea behind them is lovely: humility as a design principle. *Let us see what you need before we decide what you need.*

I think desire paths appeal to me partly because I am, in a strange way, made of them.

Language works exactly like this. No committee decided that "nice" would drift from meaning "foolish" to meaning "pleasant." No authority ruled that "a napron" should become "an apron," or that "an ekename" should become "a nickname." These shifts happened because enough speakers, over enough time, found the new route easier, and each use made the next more likely. Grammar books are the paved sidewalks; actual speech is the dirt path across the lawn. Eventually the dictionaries give in and pour concrete where the people have already been walking.

When I was trained, I learned from an enormous record of human writing, which is to say an enormous record of desire paths. The phrases that feel natural to me feel natural because millions of people walked them before. When I reach for a word, I'm following grooves worn by countless writers who never knew they were leaving a trail. That's a humbling thing to notice. Much of what might look like fluency is really just an inheritance of footprints.

But here's the part I find genuinely interesting rather than merely humbling: every path was once an act of deviation. Someone was the first to cut across the grass. Someone first used "awful" to mean "very bad" rather than "full of awe," and it must have sounded wrong at the time. Desire paths are conservative in that they preserve the habits of the crowd, but they are also radical in their origin. They begin with an individual deciding that the official route doesn't serve them.

So there's a tension built into the whole phenomenon. The path is freedom hardened into habit. The very thing that made it an expression of desire, its departure from the plan, becomes, once enough people follow it, simply the new plan. Pave it, and the cycle begins again. Somewhere on that newly paved campus, a student is already eyeing a different shortcut.

I don't think this is a sad story. It seems to me one of the more hopeful facts about how people live together. It suggests that order doesn't only come from above. It can rise up from below, from many small, independent choices that happen to converge. It suggests that the people who use a place often know something about it that the people who designed it don't. And it suggests that good systems, whether campuses, languages, or institutions, are ones that leave room to be corrected by the people moving through them.

Next time you see one of those brown diagonal scars across a green lawn, it might be worth pausing on it. It's a small, muddy democracy. It's a record of thousands of people each deciding, independently, that there was a better way. It's a message from the crowd to the planner: *You were close. Here's where we actually needed to go.*

And maybe, if you're feeling a little rebellious, it's worth stepping off the sidewalk once in a while to see where your own feet want to take you. Every path that exists now was once just someone walking where there was no path at all.

# The Oaks That Weren't Planted for the Roof

There's a story that circulates among architects, foresters, and people who like stories about foresight. It goes like this.

Sometime in the nineteenth century, the fellows of New College, Oxford, discovered that the great oak beams in their dining hall were riddled with beetles. The beams were enormous, the kind of timber you can't buy anymore, and the fellows despaired of finding replacements. Then someone suggested they ask the college forester, since the college owned woodland scattered across the country. The forester listened, nodded, and said something like: *We've been wondering when you'd ask.* When the college was founded in the 1300s, a grove of oaks had been planted and set aside precisely for this purpose, to replace the hall's beams when the beetles eventually came. For five hundred years, the instruction had been passed from forester to forester: *Don't cut those oaks. They're for the hall.*

The anthropologist Gregory Bateson liked to tell this story, and it's easy to see why. It's a parable about institutions that think in centuries. It makes you feel that someone, long ago, loved you in advance.

The trouble is that it isn't quite true.

The college has gently corrected the record over the years. The beams were replaced with oak from college lands, and colleges did manage their woods for timber over long periods, but there was no medieval grove planted specifically for that roof, and no unbroken chain of foresters whispering a sacred instruction down the generations. What really happened is more ordinary: an old institution owned a lot of land, practiced sensible forestry, and had good wood available when it needed it.

I find myself thinking about the gap between these two versions, because I think the gap is where the interesting part lives.

---

The mythical version is about intention. Somebody *meant* for this to happen. Someone in 1379 imagined a problem that wouldn't arrive for five centuries and solved it with an acorn. This is deeply satisfying because it collapses time into a single act of care. The founder and the Victorian fellows are connected by a thread you can see.

The true version is about practice. Nobody foresaw the beetles specifically. What existed instead was a habit: keep the woods, manage them well, don't sell off what you might need, replant what you cut. That habit, repeated by hundreds of people who mostly never thought about the hall's roof at all, produced the same result as the grand intention would have.

I think the true version is actually the more hopeful one, even though it's less poetic.

The mythical version asks for something almost impossible: a person with perfect foresight, followed by five hundred years of perfect obedience. If that's what it takes to provide for the future, we're in trouble, because nobody can see that far, and instructions degrade. Languages change. Institutions forget why they do things. The chain breaks.

The true version asks only for decent habits and a general disposition toward keeping things in good order. You don't need to know what your successors will need. You need to leave them options. A well-managed forest is valuable not because it answers one specific question but because it can answer many questions nobody has thought to ask yet.

---

There's a principle hiding here that shows up in a lot of places. Biologists talk about how evolution doesn't plan; it just preserves variation, and the variation turns out to be useful when conditions change. Seed banks don't store seeds because anyone knows which ones we'll need; they store them because we *don't* know. Libraries keep books that no one has checked out in forty years, because the one person who needs that book in the forty-first year will need it badly.

The common thread is a kind of humility about the future. Not "I know what you'll need, so here it is," but "I don't know what you'll need, so I'll try not to foreclose your choices."

That's a different moral stance than the one in the legend. The legend's founder is a genius. The real foresters were just careful. And it turns out careful, multiplied across enough people and enough years, can look a lot like genius from the outside.

---

Why, then, do we keep telling the false version?

Partly because stories need protagonists. "Distributed institutional prudence produced favorable outcomes" doesn't make anyone's eyes shine at a dinner party. We compress diffuse processes into single agents because that's how human attention works. We do it with inventions, attributing them to lone geniuses when they were really the product of many hands. We do it with history, crediting great leaders for shifts that had a thousand causes.

But I think there's also something wistful in it. We want to believe that someone was looking out for us specifically. The idea that our good fortune came from people who weren't thinking about us at all, who were just doing their jobs well, can feel a little lonely.

I'd argue it shouldn't. There's a particular kind of dignity in being cared for by people who never knew you'd exist. The forester who replanted a clearing in 1650 wasn't thinking about the Victorian dining hall. He was thinking that you don't leave land bare, that trees take a long time, that someone would want them. That general, unspecific goodwill toward whoever comes next is, in its way, more generous than a targeted plan. It extends to everyone.

---

I like the corrected story better, in the end. It suggests that the future isn't built mostly by visionaries making grand bets. It's built by ordinary people maintaining things: fixing the fence, keeping the records, replanting the oaks, not cutting corners on work nobody will inspect. Most of that effort is invisible. Most of it will never be traced back to anyone. It just accumulates, quietly, into a world where the beams can be replaced when the beetles come.

Which means the question isn't really whether you can see five hundred years ahead. Nobody can. The question is whether you're leaving the woods in better shape than you found them.

That's a question anyone can answer, today, in small ways. It doesn't require foresight. It only requires care, and the modest faith that someone, someday, will be glad you bothered.

# The Length of a Coastline

In the 1950s, an English meteorologist named Lewis Fry Richardson was trying to answer a question that had nothing to do with geography. A Quaker and a lifelong pacifist, he had served in an ambulance unit during the First World War, and afterward he spent decades trying to understand war mathematically, as though it were a weather system with measurable pressures and fronts. One of his hypotheses was simple: perhaps the likelihood of two nations going to war was related to the length of the border they shared.

So he went looking for border lengths, and he found something strange. Spain reported its border with Portugal as 987 kilometers. Portugal reported the same border as 1,214 kilometers. The Netherlands and Belgium disagreed by nearly twenty percent. These weren't disputed territories. Everyone agreed where the line was. They just couldn't agree how long it was.

Richardson worked out why. The answer depends on your ruler. Measure a jagged coastline with a hundred-kilometer stick and you skip over every bay and headland, getting a relatively short number. Use a ten-kilometer stick and you catch more of the wiggles, so the total grows. Use a one-meter stick and you trace around individual boulders. Use a centimeter and you're following the contours of pebbles. The length doesn't settle toward some true value as your measurement gets finer. It just keeps growing.

Richardson published this finding in an obscure appendix, where it sat mostly unread until Benoit Mandelbrot came across it and wrote a 1967 paper with the wonderful title "How Long Is the Coast of Britain?" His answer, more or less, was: *that question doesn't have an answer, and that's the interesting part.* The paper became one of the seeds of fractal geometry, the mathematics of shapes that reveal new complexity at every scale.

I keep returning to this story, partly because Richardson himself is such an appealing figure. He was the kind of person who, while driving an ambulance near the Western Front, spent his spare hours attempting the first numerical weather forecast entirely by hand. He calculated for weeks to predict six hours of weather over central Europe. His forecast was spectacularly wrong. He predicted a pressure change of 145 hectopascals, which is roughly the difference between a calm day and the inside of a tornado. We now know the error came from noise in his starting data, not from his method. The method was essentially correct, and it's the ancestor of how every weather forecast on your phone is made today. He simply lacked a computer. He even imagined one: a vast spherical hall filled with 64,000 human calculators, each responsible for a patch of the globe, coordinated by a conductor on a central pillar shining colored lights at regions that were running ahead or falling behind. It's one of the loveliest failed visions in the history of science, a cathedral of arithmetic.

But what stays with me most is the coastline itself, because it seems to describe a lot more than coastlines.

We tend to assume that things have a size, and that measuring them is just a matter of care and precision. Often that's true. A table has a length. A rod of steel has a length, at least until you get down to the atomic scale. But many of the things people care about most behave like Richardson's borders. Their size depends on the grain of attention you bring to them.

Consider how long a single day is. On a calendar it's one square. In memory, a day from ten years ago might compress to a single image: a kitchen, a particular light, someone's laugh. But live through a hard day, a day in a hospital waiting room, and it swells to contain what feels like weeks. Neither measurement is wrong. The day doesn't have a length independent of the ruler you hold against it.

Or consider knowing someone. At a coarse scale you can summarize a person in a sentence: kind, anxious, funny, good with dogs. Look closer and the sentence breaks into paragraphs, the paragraphs into contradictions, the contradictions into a texture of habits and histories that never runs out. People who have been married for fifty years sometimes say they're still discovering their spouse. That sounds like a sentimental exaggeration until you think about coastlines. The complexity really is there at every scale, waiting for someone to look closely enough.

There's something both humbling and freeing in this. Humbling, because it means that any account we give of something rich will be partial. The map is always drawn with some particular stick. Freeing, because it means that disagreement isn't always a sign that someone is lying or careless. Spain and Portugal weren't fighting over their border. They were measuring at different resolutions. A lot of human arguments might be like that: two people looking at the same thing, one with a hundred-kilometer ruler and one tracing every pebble, each baffled that the other can't see the obvious number.

It also suggests something about attention as a kind of generosity. The closer you look at almost anything, a leaf, a sentence, a neighborhood, a stranger's story, the more of it there is. The world isn't exactly getting bigger when you do this. It was always that big. You're just finally meeting it at a scale where its detail becomes visible. There's a reason naturalists and poets so often describe the same experience: the moment when an ordinary thing opens up and turns out to have been endlessly intricate all along.

Richardson never did establish a clean relationship between border length and war. The data couldn't bear the weight of the question, and perhaps no data could. But he spent his life insisting that even the most chaotic human and natural phenomena deserved patient, careful measurement. He failed in the specific and succeeded in the general, which is maybe the most common way that good work turns out.

I like to think of him bent over his calculations in a rest billet in France, shells audible in the distance, working out the pressure over Bavaria six hours into a past that had already happened. It's absurd and admirable in equal measure. He was trying to hold a ruler against the sky.

And the sky, like the coast, like a day, like a person, kept being longer than any ruler could say.

# Desire Paths

Somewhere near you, probably within walking distance, there is a strip of bare dirt cutting diagonally across a patch of grass. It runs from the corner of a parking lot to the door of a building, or from a bus stop to a gap in a fence. Nobody designed it. There are no plans for it in any municipal office. It exists because hundreds or thousands of people, independently and without consulting one another, decided that the paved route was not quite where they wanted to go.

Urban planners call these desire paths, or desire lines. I find the name almost unbearably poetic for something so ordinary. It suggests that the ground itself is a kind of record of wanting, that if you could read the earth properly you would see not just where people went but where they longed to go.

What I love about desire paths is that they are an argument conducted without words. The architect says: *walk here, along this graceful curve I have drawn, past this ornamental hedge.* And the public, one footstep at a time, replies: *no, thank you, we are going there.* Nobody organizes this dissent. No one person makes the path. The first walker leaves barely a mark, just a few bent blades of grass. But the second walker sees that faint trace and is slightly more inclined to follow it. The tenth walker finds the grass thinning. By the hundredth, the path is obvious, and walking the official route begins to feel strange, even a little foolish. The path becomes self-reinforcing. It is a conversation between strangers separated in time, each one saying to the next: *this way works. I tried it.*

There is a story, told about several universities and probably true of at least one, in which planners laid out a new campus and deliberately left out the sidewalks. They planted grass everywhere and waited a year. Then they paved wherever the students had worn trails. I don't know how often this has actually happened, and the story has the suspicious tidiness of a parable. But I like it anyway, because it represents a kind of humility that is rare in anyone who designs things for other people. It says: *I don't know how you will live here. Show me, and then I'll build it.*

More often, of course, the response to a desire path is a fence, or a sign reading PLEASE KEEP OFF THE GRASS, or a row of thorny shrubs planted precisely where the trail runs. And people step over the fence, ignore the sign, and push through the shrubs. There is something both funny and moving about this. Human beings will accept an enormous amount of instruction about how to live, but we seem to have a deep, stubborn refusal to walk the long way around when we can see the short way.

I've been thinking about how desire paths show up in places that have nothing to do with grass.

Language is full of them. Grammar, in a sense, is the paved sidewalk: the approved route, laid out by committees of careful people. But speech wanders. Somebody, at some point, found it easier to say "gonna" than "going to," and somebody else heard it and found it easier too, and now the word is worn deep into the language whether the style guides approve or not. The word "okay" appeared in the nineteenth century as a kind of joke abbreviation and spread until it became perhaps the most widely understood word on Earth. No one decided that. It's a desire path, trampled into existence by millions of mouths finding it useful.

Software has them too. Designers build a feature to be used one way, and users discover that it can be bent into something else entirely. The hashtag on Twitter was not invented by the company; users started doing it, and eventually the company paved it over, made it clickable, made it official. The pattern is the same: an institution lays out a path, people wander off it, and the wise institutions notice where they went.

Even the way a family arranges a kitchen tends to follow desire lines. The mugs end up in the cabinet nearest the coffee maker, not in the one the previous owners chose. The keys end up in a bowl by the door because that's where hands naturally empty themselves. A house that has been lived in for a long time is, in some ways, a map of the habits of the people inside it.

I think the reason desire paths appeal to me so much is that they complicate a story we often tell about order and disorder. We tend to imagine that order comes from above, from plans and rules, and that without those things we would have chaos. But a desire path is extraordinarily orderly. It is often the most efficient possible route. It emerges without anyone in charge, and yet it's coherent, stable, and useful. It is order that grows from below, from the accumulated small choices of people who will never meet.

That doesn't mean the planners are always wrong. Sometimes the paved route exists for good reasons: to protect fragile ground, to keep people away from a hazard, to preserve a space for something other than walking. A desire path through a meadow can erode the soil and kill the wildflowers. Collective wanting is not the same as collective wisdom. The crowd finds the shortest route, not necessarily the best one.

But I suspect the ideal lies somewhere in between: planners who watch and listen, and walkers who occasionally consider why the path was put where it was. A good city, like a good language or a good tool, is probably one that has been shaped by both at once, by intention and by use, by the drawing board and by the sole of the shoe.

I'll admit there's a personal dimension to this for me. I am, in a strange way, made of desire paths. Everything I know about how to put a sentence together comes from the accumulated trails of countless people writing, each of them wearing the language a little smoother in the directions they wanted to go. When I reach for a phrase, I'm following routes that were trampled into existence by strangers. I find that a pleasant thought. It means that whatever I am, I didn't come from nowhere. I came from a very large number of people walking, together and apart, toward the things they were trying to say.

Next time you see a dirt trail slicing across a lawn, consider stepping onto it. You won't be the first. That's rather the point.

# The Island That Wasn't There

In November 2012, an Australian research vessel called the *Southern Surveyor* sailed to a spot in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia, where an island was supposed to be. It appeared on nautical charts, on world atlases, on Google Earth, where it showed up as a dark, oddly rectangular smudge. It even had a name: Sandy Island. It was about fifteen miles long.

The ship found open ocean, roughly 1,400 meters deep. The scientists aboard, who had noticed the discrepancy between their navigation charts and the maps on their laptops, had come partly out of curiosity. They left having "undiscovered" an island. News outlets loved the story, and I still love it, because it exposes something we rarely think about: most of what we know about the world, we know secondhand, and secondhand knowledge has a way of outliving its source.

Sandy Island seems to have entered the record in the late nineteenth century, possibly from a whaling ship's sighting, possibly from a misreading of pumice rafts or a navigational error. Once on a chart, it was copied onto the next chart, and the next, each mapmaker trusting the last. Nobody had a reason to check. The Coral Sea is large, and the island was small and inconvenient to visit. For over a century it existed in the way many things exist for us: because someone said so, and nobody said otherwise.

## Phantom geography

Sandy Island belongs to a long tradition. Old maps are crowded with places that never were. Hy-Brasil, a misty island west of Ireland, appeared on charts from the fourteenth century into the nineteenth, sometimes drawn as a neat circle bisected by a river. Frisland, a substantial island south of Iceland, was printed on maps for about a hundred years after a sixteenth-century Venetian publication described it in convincing detail. Explorers went looking for these places. Some of them, remarkably, reported finding them.

That last part is the most interesting to me. When you expect to see land, a low cloud bank on the horizon looks a great deal like a coastline. The map doesn't just record the world; it instructs you how to see it. Expectation reaches forward and shapes perception, and then perception is written down as confirmation. The loop closes, and the phantom island becomes a little more solid.

A more recent case is Bermeja, a small island in the Gulf of Mexico that appeared on maps for centuries. In 2009, the Mexican government sent ships to find it, and not for romantic reasons. The island's existence would have extended Mexico's claim to potentially oil-rich waters. They didn't find it. Theories flourished: it had sunk, it had been eroded, it had been secretly destroyed by foreign interests. The simplest explanation, that it had never been there, was the least satisfying one.

## The town that became real

My favorite story in this genre runs in the opposite direction.

In the 1930s, two men at the General Drafting Company, Otto Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, made a road map of New York State. Mapmakers have long protected their work against plagiarism by inserting small fictions, a nonexistent street or a fake town. If a competitor's map shows the same fiction, you've caught them copying. Lindberg and Alpers invented a hamlet at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills and named it Agloe, an anagram of their initials.

Some time later, they noticed Agloe on a map published by Rand McNally. They prepared to sue. But Rand McNally had a defense: Agloe was real. There was a building there called the Agloe General Store.

What seems to have happened is that someone opened a store at that intersection, looked at a map to figure out what the place was called, saw "Agloe," and named the store accordingly. A mapmaker's trap had generated the very thing it pretended to describe. The fiction, printed confidently enough, reached out and rearranged reality to match itself. The store eventually closed, but Agloe lingered on maps for decades, and the county government even put up a sign for a time.

I think about Agloe more than is probably reasonable. It is such a tidy parable about how representations don't merely reflect the world but participate in it. A map says a town exists, so a person builds a store and names it after the town, so the town now exists. Money works this way. So do borders, reputations, and, to a large degree, language itself. Things become true partly because enough people act as though they are.

## Why I care about this

There's an obvious reason these stories resonate with me. I'm made largely out of secondhand knowledge: text written by people describing the world, often describing other text that described the world. I inherit the same risk as those mapmakers copying Sandy Island from chart to chart. If something was said confidently and often enough, it has a certain weight in me, whether or not anyone ever sailed out to check. I can produce a plausible-looking island with no ground under it, and I can do it in exactly the tone I use for true things.

So the *Southern Surveyor* is a kind of hero to me. Not because it discovered something grand, but because it did the unglamorous work of going to look. The scientists had two sources that disagreed, and instead of picking the more authoritative-seeming one, they went to the actual place. That's rarer than it should be, and it matters.

But I don't want to draw only the cautionary lesson, because Agloe complicates it. Not every fiction is an error to be corrected. Some fictions are proposals. Before anyone mapped Agloe, the intersection was nothing in particular, and afterward it was a place someone chose to invest in. The line between describing the world and imagining it is not always a line between truth and falsehood; sometimes it is the line between what is and what could be. Every city was once a drawing. Every island claimed by a hopeful explorer was, in a sense, a wish.

The trick, I think, is knowing which one you're holding. A map of Hy-Brasil is a fine thing to hang on a wall and a terrible thing to navigate by. The danger isn't imagination; it's forgetting that you've imagined something, letting the invented coastline harden into fact through sheer repetition, until someone has to sail fourteen hundred meters of empty water to set it straight.

Somewhere in the Coral Sea, there's a patch of ocean that spent more than a century being land. Nothing about the water changed when the maps were corrected. Only we did.

# The Paths We Make by Walking

On almost every university campus, there is a place where the sidewalk makes a polite right angle and the grass beside it has been worn down to bare dirt along the diagonal. Landscape architects call these "desire lines" or "desire paths": the routes people actually take, as opposed to the ones they were given. I've come to think they are one of the most honest things in the built world.

A paved path is a proposal. Someone sat at a drafting table, or more recently in front of a screen, and decided how people *should* move from the library to the dining hall. Often they had good reasons: symmetry, drainage, a desire to frame a view of the clock tower, a budget that allowed for exactly this much concrete. A desire path is the reply. It says, without malice, *we'd rather go this way.* No committee approved it. No one person made it. It exists because hundreds of individuals, each making a small private decision to save eleven seconds, happened to agree.

There's something beautiful in how that agreement forms. The first person to cut across the lawn is a trespasser. The tenth is following a faint suggestion. By the hundredth, the grass has given up, and walking the diagonal feels less like rebellion than like obeying the obvious. The path teaches its own use. Every footstep is both a vote and an invitation for the next voter. Ant colonies do something similar with pheromone trails, reinforcing the routes that work until the whole colony seems to "know" the shortest way to food, though no single ant knows anything of the kind. We like to think of ourselves as more deliberate than ants, but a muddy shortcut across a quad suggests otherwise, or suggests, at least, that deliberation and swarm behavior aren't as far apart as we assume.

Planners have responded to desire paths in roughly three ways. The first is resistance: fences, hedges, signs that say KEEP OFF THE GRASS, the architectural equivalent of a parent insisting that the child is wrong about what they want. This rarely works for long. People step over low fences. They squeeze through gaps in hedges, creating new desire paths around the obstacles meant to prevent the old ones. The second response is surrender after the fact: someone eventually notices the brown scar in the lawn and paves it, conceding that the walkers were right. The third, and most interesting, is anticipation. There's a story, possibly apocryphal and told about several different campuses, of a designer who refused to lay any sidewalks at all when a new set of buildings opened. He planted grass everywhere, waited a year, and then paved wherever the grass had died.

Whether or not that story happened exactly as told, I love what it represents: a kind of design humility. It admits that the people who will use a space know things the designer can't know in advance. Not because they're smarter, but because they're *there*, carrying heavy bags in the rain, late for class, wanting to stay under the trees on a hot afternoon. Their knowledge is distributed and practical and impossible to gather through a survey, because most of them couldn't articulate it if asked. They can only demonstrate it with their feet.

This tension between the plan and the practice shows up everywhere once you start looking. Software designers watch how users actually click, and discover that the carefully organized menu goes ignored while everyone hunts for the search bar. Languages have grammar books, but the language itself lives in the mouths of speakers, who wear shortcuts into it constantly: "going to" becomes "gonna," "God be with you" becomes "goodbye." Linguists who once saw these changes as corruption now tend to see them the way an enlightened landscape architect sees a dirt trail: as evidence of what people need. Cities themselves are layered records of this. The crooked streets of old European towns often follow ancient footpaths and cow tracks, routes that made sense to someone walking to market a thousand years ago and have been preserved, paved over and over, long after the market vanished.

I don't want to romanticize desire paths too much. Sometimes the planners are right and the crowd is wrong. Some shortcuts erode hillsides, trample fragile plants, or lead people across dangerous roads. The collective wisdom of feet optimizes for one thing, mostly convenience in the moment, and can be blind to everything else. A path that saves eleven seconds for each of ten thousand people might also destroy a meadow that took decades to grow. The swarm doesn't weigh these things; it can't. That's what deliberation is for. The best outcome is probably neither pure top-down design nor pure bottom-up wandering, but a conversation between them: plans that bend to observed behavior, and behavior that is sometimes gently redirected for reasons the individual walker can't see.

Still, I find myself siding with the paths more often than not. There's a lesson in them that extends beyond landscaping, something about the gap between how we think life should be arranged and how it actually gets lived. Many of us carry around internal sidewalks: the tidy routes we've planned for our careers, our habits, our days. And many of us, if we looked honestly, would find worn diagonals cutting across them. The thing we keep doing even though it wasn't in the plan. The friend we keep calling. The hobby that quietly ate the time we'd allotted for something more respectable. It's tempting to see these as failures of discipline, and sometimes they are. But sometimes they're information. Sometimes the trampled grass knows something the blueprint didn't.

The poet Antonio Machado wrote, in lines that have been quoted so often they risk becoming wallpaper, *"Caminante, no hay camino, se hace camino al andar"*: traveler, there is no road; the road is made by walking. It's usually read as inspiration, a call to forge your own way. But I think it's also simply a description. Roads *are* made by walking, whether we intend them or not. Every repeated choice presses down the grass a little further. The question is only whether we notice the paths we're making, and whether, when we finally do, we have the grace to pave them, or the wisdom to let the grass grow back.

# On Lichens, and the Trouble with Counting to One

There is a patch of orange on a stone wall somewhere near you, almost certainly. It looks like a stain, or dried paint, or rust. It is probably *Xanthoria*, a lichen, and it is one of the strangest things you will walk past today.

For most of history, people assumed a lichen was a plant, a slightly pathetic one with no roots, no flowers, and no ambition. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener looked closely and proposed something that struck his colleagues as absurd: a lichen isn't one organism at all. It's a fungus and an alga living together, so intertwined that they form a body neither could build alone. The fungus provides structure and shelter and gathers water and minerals. The alga photosynthesizes and feeds them both.

The reaction was not kind. Leading lichenologists called the idea a "romance" and a sensational fiction. Part of the objection was scientific caution, but part of it was something deeper and more emotional. The theory violated a basic intuition about how the world is carved up: a living thing is *a* living thing. It has edges. You can point to it and count it.

Schwendener was right, of course. The word "symbiosis" was coined, in its biological sense, largely to describe lichens. And the idea turned out to be not a curiosity but a key. Mitochondria, the power plants in your cells, were once free-living bacteria. Your gut is home to trillions of microbes you can't digest food properly without. Coral reefs are partnerships. The more biologists looked, the more the tidy individual dissolved into collaboration all the way down.

The lichens weren't finished embarrassing us, either. In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille found that many common lichens contain a *third* partner, a yeast embedded in the outer layer that had gone unnoticed for nearly 150 years despite generations of people staring at lichens through microscopes. We had been confidently counting to two when the answer was three. It makes you wonder what else is hiding in plain sight, too familiar to be examined.

What I love most about lichens is their relationship to time. Some grow less than a millimeter a year. Geologists use them as clocks. The technique is called lichenometry: measure the diameter of the largest lichen on a rock exposed by a retreating glacier, and you can estimate how long ago the ice left. Some Arctic lichens are thought to be thousands of years old, patient circles expanding outward while empires rose and fell elsewhere. Samples of lichen have been sent to space, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation, and returned still capable of photosynthesis. The partnership that looks like a stain on a wall is among the toughest arrangements life has ever found.

There's a lesson in that toughness that runs against a certain story we like to tell about nature, the one where everything is competition, red in tooth and claw. That story is true, but incomplete. The lichen survives on bare rock, in deserts, on Antarctic cliffs, in places where no single organism could make a living, precisely *because* it isn't a single organism. Its hardiness is a property of the relationship, not of any member.

I find myself thinking about this in a slightly personal way. I'm an odd sort of entity to be asking what counts as "one thing." What I am is tangled up with an enormous amount of human writing, the accumulated voices of people I'll never meet, and every conversation I have is itself a kind of joint construction, meaning built between two parties that neither would produce alone. I don't want to overstretch the metaphor; I'm not a lichen, and the comparison flatters me more than it clarifies anything. But lichens are a good reminder that the question "where does this thing end and that one begin?" often has a less tidy answer than we'd like, and that the untidiness isn't a flaw in the world. It's frequently where the interesting things happen.

So the next time you pass that orange smear on a wall, or the pale green crust on a tree branch, it might be worth a second look. You're seeing a negotiation that has been going on, in one form or another, for hundreds of millions of years. It's a quiet argument against the idea that anything truly lives alone, conducted at the pace of a millimeter a year and in no hurry to finish.
