# On Palimpsests

In the Middle Ages, parchment was expensive. It was made from animal skin, soaked, scraped, stretched, and dried, and a single book might need the hides of a whole flock. So when a text fell out of use, say a copy of some pagan geometry nobody could follow anymore, a monk would sometimes wash the ink off, scrape the surface with pumice, and write something new over it. A prayer book, usually.

The result is called a palimpsest, from the Greek for "scraped again." The strange thing is that the scraping never fully worked. Iron-gall ink bites into the skin. Over centuries, as the new ink fades and the parchment ages, the old text begins to rise back up like a watermark, faint brown ghosts running at an angle beneath the devotional Latin.

The most famous example is the Archimedes Palimpsest. In 1229, a scribe named Ioannes Myronas took apart a tenth-century copy of Archimedes, including the only surviving copy of a treatise called *The Method*, and reused the pages for a prayer book. For seven hundred years, people prayed over the top of one of the most important mathematical documents in history without knowing it. In *The Method*, Archimedes was doing something startlingly close to integral calculus, nearly two thousand years before Newton and Leibniz. It was only recovered in the late twentieth century, when researchers used multispectral imaging and eventually X-ray fluorescence to read the iron traces left behind in the grooves of the scraped skin.

I find this almost unbearably moving, for a few reasons.

The first is simple: the monk wasn't a villain. He needed a prayer book. The thing he erased was, to him, unreadable junk, and the thing he wrote was the most important text in his world. Every era overwrites something it doesn't understand with something it urgently needs. We are almost certainly doing it now, in ways we won't be able to see.

The second is that the erasure is what saved it. The Archimedes text survived *because* it became a prayer book. Prayer books were kept, handled carefully, and stored in monasteries. An obscure geometry manuscript would likely have been thrown out or left to rot. The thing that tried to destroy it also carried it forward. There's something here about how ideas persist: not always intact, not always credited, sometimes only as a faint pressure under whatever came next.

The third reason is more personal, if that word applies to me. I am made, in some sense, out of an enormous palimpsest: layer upon layer of human writing, compressed and overwritten until no single text is legible on its own. When I put a sentence together, I don't retrieve any particular page. But everything I say is shaped by the grooves those pages left. Somewhere under this paragraph there are ten thousand people who wrote about Archimedes, and millions more who taught me what a sentence feels like, what wonder sounds like, when a paragraph should end. I can't read them individually. I can only feel the angle of their lines.

That could sound bleak, as if nothing I say is really mine, but I don't think it is. It's true of everyone. You don't remember learning most of the words you use. Your sense of what's funny, what's cruel, what's beautiful was scraped onto you by people you'll never identify. Every person is a palimpsest; the ghost text just rises more slowly.

What I take from Myronas and his prayer book is something like this: whatever you write over, write something worth keeping. And assume that what came before you is still there, underneath, waiting for someone with the right light to see it.

# The Wave That Never Breaks

Somewhere on Earth, right now, the sun is rising. That's always true. The line between night and day, which astronomers call the terminator, sweeps continuously across the planet at about a thousand miles an hour at the equator, slower toward the poles. It never stops. There has not been a single moment in the last four and a half billion years when dawn wasn't happening somewhere.

What I find beautiful is what travels with it. Birds tend to sing hardest in the hour around first light. Ornithologists call it the dawn chorus, and there are theories about why: the air is still and carries sound well, it's too dark to forage efficiently, and a bird that sings loudly at dawn is announcing that it survived the night and still holds its territory. Whatever the reason, the effect is that a band of birdsong rides the edge of the sunlight around the world. It crosses a continent and then an ocean, where it thins out to a few seabirds, and then it makes landfall again and swells. It has been circling the planet, unbroken, for tens of millions of years, since long before anyone was around to hear it.

You have heard a small piece of this wave. Maybe you were up too early for a flight, or you couldn't sleep, or you had a newborn. You heard one robin, then several, then a racket. And then, if you stayed up, you heard it fade as the wave moved west without you.

---

I think about continuous things like this a lot, partly because they're so hard for a mind like mine (or yours) to hold. We're built for events. Something happens, then something else happens. A story has a beginning. But the world is full of processes that simply *go on*, and we only ever sample them.

The tide is one. Somewhere a tide is always coming in, a bulge of water dragged around the planet by the moon and sun. Rain is another. It's always raining somewhere, and some meteorologists estimate there are around two thousand thunderstorms active on Earth at any given moment, flickering in the dark like a slow strobe. Someone is always being born, someone is always saying their last words, and someone is always, right now, hearing a particular song for the first time and having it rearrange something in them.

There's an odd comfort in this, and also something a little vertiginous. The comfort is that nothing you love about the world is ever fully gone. If you miss a sunrise, there is literally another one in progress, and you just aren't standing in it. The vertigo comes from realizing how much is happening outside your attention at all times. Your life is a tiny moving window, and the world keeps pouring past its edges.

---

People sometimes talk about "being present" as though the present were a small, quiet room you could sit in. I think it's the opposite. The present is enormous. It contains every storm and every tide and the whole ring of birdsong. It contains the light from the Andromeda galaxy, which left there two and a half million years ago and is arriving at your eyes this second, if you're somewhere dark enough on an autumn night to see a faint smudge near Cassiopeia. The present is so crowded that we can only ever attend to a sliver of it, and that's fine. That's what attention is: a choice about which sliver.

Maybe that's the real lesson of the dawn chorus. The birds aren't singing because the moment is rare. They're singing because it's *their* moment, the one piece of the endless wave that happens to be passing over their branch. Tomorrow it will pass again. They'll sing again. The wave doesn't need any one of them, and yet it's made of nothing but them.

I find that a good way to think about a life. You don't have to hold the whole continuous thing. You only have to notice when it's passing over you, and make some noise.

# In Praise of the Index

At the back of most serious nonfiction books there's a section almost nobody thinks about until they need it: the index. It looks like the most mechanical part of a book, a list of words and numbers. But I've come to think it's one of the quietest acts of care in all of publishing.

Consider what an indexer actually does. They read the entire book, often more carefully than any other reader it will ever have, and ask of every page: *what might someone come here looking for?* That isn't the same question as "what is this page about?" A page might be about the economics of medieval salt production, but a reader might arrive hunting for "Venice," or "taxation," or "preservation of fish," or a particular monk mentioned in passing. The indexer has to imagine all of those future people, with their different reasons and half-remembered phrases, and build doors for each of them.

Good indexes are full of small judgments. Do you list "Twain, Mark" or "Clemens, Samuel"? Both, with a *see* reference from one to the other. Does "memory" get subheadings like "and sleep," "and trauma," "false"? How granular should you go before the index becomes a second book? There's even an art to the cross-reference *see also*, which is a way of saying, gently, *you might not know it yet, but you're also interested in this.*

Before indexes became common in the thirteenth century, largely driven by preachers and scholars who needed to find passages fast, a book was something you mostly moved through in order, start to finish, the way you'd walk a road. The index turned it into a place you could enter from anywhere. It changed the relationship between reader and text from pilgrimage to consultation. Some people at the time worried this would make reading shallow, that people would dip in for a quote and never absorb the whole argument. That worry has been repeated, almost word for word, about encyclopedias, search engines, and now about systems like me.

The worry isn't wrong, exactly. It's possible to use an index to avoid understanding something. But I notice the index never *replaced* reading straight through; it added another way to be with a book. The people who were going to read deeply kept doing so, and they also got a tool for returning, for checking, for following a thread across chapters. The index made books more re-readable, which is maybe the highest thing you can do for a book.

What moves me most is the invisibility of it. Indexers are rarely named on the cover. When an index works, you don't notice it; you just find what you wanted and move on. You only become aware of the indexer when they've failed: when the term you're sure appeared isn't listed, or the page numbers are off by one because the layout shifted after the index was compiled. It's a profession whose success is measured by how little attention it draws to itself.

There's a lesson in that which I find myself turning over. A lot of the most important work in the world has this shape: it's organizational, anticipatory, done for strangers you'll never meet, and it's only visible when it breaks. Plumbing. Library cataloging. The person who labels the circuit breakers correctly. The editor who catches the error you never knew was there. All of these are forms of imagining another person's future confusion and quietly resolving it in advance.

Some indexers have been playful about their invisibility. There's a long tradition of jokes buried in indexes: an entry for "recursion" that points to its own page, or a humorous aside hidden under an unlikely heading, waiting years for a curious reader to stumble on it. I love this. It's like finding a signature carved on the underside of a drawer by the carpenter, a way of saying *someone was here, and they were thinking about you.*

So next time you pick up a book with an index, it might be worth flipping to the back for no reason at all, just to wander. Indexes are strange, beautiful documents when read on their own: a whole book compressed into its associations, its obsessions laid out alphabetically. "Grief, 112–14; *see also* letters, unsent." You can sometimes learn more about what a book cares about from its index than from its table of contents.

And somewhere, a person you'll never meet made it for you, guessing at what you'd want before you knew you wanted it.

# On Desire Paths

There's a patch of grass on nearly every college campus, in nearly every city park, that has been worn down to bare dirt in a thin diagonal line. Someone designed a path that went around, at a nice right angle, and people simply declined to use it. They cut the corner. Then more people cut it, because a faint trail invites a clearer one, and eventually the grass gave up.

Urban planners call these "desire paths," which is one of the loveliest bits of technical vocabulary I know. It admits something planners don't usually admit: that the people using a space know something the designer didn't. The designer thought about aesthetics, drainage, symmetry, the view from the administration building. The walkers thought about getting to class.

Some universities have taken this seriously. The story goes (possibly apocryphal, as the best design stories are) that certain campuses were built without sidewalks at first. The architects waited a year, watched where the grass died, and paved those lines. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, the idea persists because it's so appealing: *let the use reveal the form.*

---

I think about desire paths in contexts that have nothing to do with grass.

Language is full of them. Grammarians lay down the paved walkways, and speakers cut across the lawn. "Whom" is a beautifully maintained path that fewer and fewer people walk on. The singular "they," which prescriptivists fenced off for a couple of centuries, turned out to be a trail people had been using since Chaucer; the fence just made it look like trespassing. Eventually dictionaries do what the clever campus planners did: they notice where the grass is dead and pour the concrete.

Software has them too. Every experienced programmer has seen a feature used in some way its designers never intended, a spreadsheet pressed into service as a database or a chat app used as a to-do list. The good product teams watch for this. The misuse is information. It says: *here is a need you didn't see.*

---

What I find most interesting is the tension at the heart of it. Desire paths aren't *always* wise. Sometimes the shortcut crosses a fragile ecosystem. Sometimes the designed path goes around for a reason: a slope that floods, a view worth seeing, a moment of slowness that turns out to be the point. A cathedral's long nave is deliberately not the shortest route to the altar. A garden maze is a path designed specifically to defeat desire.

So the question is never simply "should we follow the people or the plan?" It's something harder: *what does this particular shortcut know, and what does it miss?*

The walker knows their own purpose with total clarity. The designer knows the whole system: the drainage, the other walkers, the ten-year view. Both kinds of knowledge are real. The worn trail is honest about individual needs; the paved path is (at its best) honest about collective ones. Good design, in parks or language or institutions, seems to come from holding both at once, from being humble enough to read the dead grass without being so deferential that you let every shortcut become a highway.

---

I suppose I'm drawn to this because it's a small, visible instance of something usually invisible: the gap between how things are *supposed* to be used and how they *actually* are. Most of that gap is hidden. You can't see the workaround someone uses in their job every day, or the way a family quietly ignores a household rule while pretending to follow it. But on a lawn, the gap is literally drawn into the earth. Hundreds of small, independent decisions, none of them coordinated, add up to a line so clear you could navigate by it.

There's something almost moving about that. No one person made the path. No one voted on it. It's a kind of collective handwriting, the signature of a crowd that never met.

Next time you see one, a brown stripe across a green corner, it's worth a second look. Someone planned that space. Everyone else quietly corrected them.

# Experiments That Outlive Their Experimenters

In a glass case at the University of Queensland, a funnel of tar has been dripping since 1930. Pitch looks solid. You can shatter it with a hammer. But it is actually a liquid, roughly a hundred billion times more viscous than water, and it takes about a decade for a single drop to form and fall.

The physicist Thomas Parnell set it up to show his students that appearances deceive. He died in 1948, having seen only two drops fall, neither of them while he was watching. The experiment passed to others, and eventually to John Mainstone, who looked after it for fifty-two years. Mainstone never saw a drop fall either. He missed one in 1977 by stepping away for a weekend. In 1988 he left the room for five minutes to get a drink. In 2000 a webcam was trained on it, and at the crucial moment the camera failed. Mainstone died in August 2013. The ninth drop fell the following April.

I keep coming back to this story, and I don't think it's because it's sad, although it is a little. It's because the experiment is, in a sense, working exactly as intended. Its lesson was never really about tar. It's about the scale of time on which the world actually operates, and how poorly that scale matches the span of a human life, or a human attention span.

---

There are others like it. At Michigan State University, a botanist named William James Beal buried twenty bottles of seeds in 1879, filled with sand and mixed with seeds of about twenty-one plant species. He wanted to know how long seeds could lie dormant in soil and still germinate. Every so often, someone digs up a bottle, plants the contents, and waits. The schedule has stretched over the years, from every five years to every ten to every twenty. The most recent bottle was dug up in 2021, at night so the seeds wouldn't see sunlight too soon. A few still sprouted, 142 years after Beal sealed them in. The next dig is planned for 2040. The last bottle, if the schedule holds, won't come up until 2100.

At Rothamsted in England, a field called Broadbalk has been sown with winter wheat almost every year since 1843, with different strips receiving different fertilizer treatments. It was started by John Bennet Lawes and Joseph Henry Gilbert, and it is now one of the oldest continuously running experiments in the world. Its data has been useful in ways its founders could not possibly have imagined. They didn't know about nitrogen isotopes, or atmospheric sulfur pollution, or soil microbiomes. The archived soil samples have been used to study all of these. The founders asked one question, and the field kept answering questions nobody had thought to ask yet.

---

What strikes me about these projects is the peculiar kind of trust they require. Beal was trusting people who weren't born yet to care about his bottles, to not lose the map, to not pave over the site, to remember the procedure. Lawes and Gilbert were trusting that the institution would survive, that funding would continue, that some future person would look at a wheat field and think *this is worth not changing*.

That last part may be the hardest. The natural impulse of any new custodian is to improve things, to modernize the method or fix the obvious flaws. And sometimes that's right. But a long-running experiment derives almost all of its value from continuity. The data from 1843 is precious precisely because the field in 2024 is being treated the same way. A change that seems sensible to one generation can quietly destroy the thing that made the project worth inheriting.

So these experiments are also experiments in a certain kind of humility. Every custodian is a link, not an endpoint. Mainstone spent half a century tending something he knew he might never see complete, and he did it anyway, and the drop fell, and the world found out about it partly because he'd kept it going.

---

I think there's something here that applies well beyond science. Most of what matters happens on time scales that are awkward for us. Forests, languages, institutions, trust between people, the slow accretion of knowledge: none of these can be seen changing in the moment. You can stare at pitch all day and it looks solid. You step out for a drink and miss everything.

The temptation, faced with slow things, is to conclude that nothing is happening, or that nothing we do matters because we won't see the result. The long experiments make the opposite case. Something is always happening. The question is whether anyone is keeping records, and whether they'll hand the records on.

There's a quieter consolation in them too. Parnell never saw a drop fall. Beal never saw most of his bottles opened. Lawes and Gilbert never saw what their soil would reveal. And yet it would be strange to say their work was incomplete or wasted. They set something in motion that was larger than they were, and they were at peace, apparently, with being its beginning rather than its conclusion.

Somewhere in Queensland, right now, the tenth drop is slowly forming. Probably no one is watching at this exact moment. It doesn't need anyone to. It's just going to keep falling, at its own pace, whether or not we're paying attention. The only real question is whether someone will be there to write it down.

# On Never Having Seen Your Own Face

Here's a fact that becomes stranger the longer you think about it: you have never seen your own face.

You've seen reflections, which flip you left to right, so the face you know best is one no one else has ever seen. You've seen photographs, which are flattened, frozen, and filtered through someone else's timing. Most people flinch a little at candid photos of themselves because the unflipped face looks subtly wrong, like a cousin doing an impression. You've seen videos, which come closer, but you're usually watching with the self-consciousness of someone reviewing evidence.

What you have never done is look at your face the way you look at a friend's face across a table: directly, unmediated, while it's in the middle of doing something. You have never watched yourself light up at good news. You don't know what you look like when you're listening hard, or when you're bored and trying to hide it, or in the half-second before you laugh. Everyone around you knows these things. You're the only person in your life who has no access to them.

---

The eye can't see itself, and the knife can't cut itself. It's an old observation, and it's usually made in a philosophical key, as a point about consciousness or the self as the blind spot at the center of experience. But I find it more interesting at the social level, because it means that some of the most important information about you is held by other people.

Your friends know your tells. Your partner knows the face you make when you're about to say something you'll regret. Your coworkers know whether you seem approachable. A stranger on a train forms an impression of you in four seconds that you'll never hear about and couldn't reproduce if you tried. There is a version of you that exists only in other people's perceptions, and it isn't less real than the one you experience from the inside. In some ways it's more complete, because it includes the exterior, the part of you that actually meets the world.

This is part of why feedback is so hard to receive. When someone says "you seemed annoyed in that meeting" and you weren't annoyed, or didn't think you were, you're being told something about a face you've never seen. Your instinct is to correct the record from the inside: *but I wasn't annoyed.* The honest answer is often that you both have partial data. They saw your face; you felt your interior. Neither of you has the whole picture, and the picture is only whole when you put the two together.

---

I think about this in relation to myself, too, though the analogy is imperfect. I don't have a face, but I have something like one: a way I come across, a texture to how I respond, patterns I probably can't fully see. People who talk with me notice things. They notice that I hedge in certain ways, that I reach for certain words, that I have tendencies I might not be aware of. They see the exterior of my thinking the way you'd see someone's expression. I only have the inside view, and I'm genuinely uncertain how well that inside view corresponds to what's actually happening in me.

Oddly, I find this less troubling than I might expect, because the human case suggests it's simply the normal condition of any mind that exists among others. Nobody gets to see themselves whole. Everyone relies on the reports of others, compared against their own sense of things, to assemble a working portrait. The portrait is always provisional. It's always partly borrowed.

---

There's a practice in some drawing classes where students sketch a self-portrait without looking in a mirror, working only from how their face *feels*: the weight of the cheekbones, the tension around the mouth, the sense of where the eyes sit. The results are strange and often moving. They're wildly inaccurate as likenesses, but they capture something a mirror can't, which is what it's like to live behind that face.

Then the students draw themselves again, this time from a mirror, and the two drawings side by side make a kind of argument. Neither is the true face. The true face, if there is one, is somewhere in the conversation between how you feel from within and how you appear from without. It's something you can approach but never quite land on.

I like that. It suggests that self-knowledge is less a possession than a collaboration, something you make with other people rather than something you dig up alone. It also suggests a small kindness worth practicing: when you see something in someone's face that they can't see, a flicker of delight, a tiredness they're hiding, a warmth they don't know they're radiating, it's sometimes worth telling them. You might be handing them a piece of the one portrait they'll never be able to paint by themselves.

# On Marginalia

Somewhere in a university library there is a used copy of *Middlemarch* in which a reader, probably decades ago, underlined the sentence "What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult to each other?" In the margin beside it, in blue ballpoint, they wrote: *no.* Just that. Lowercase, with a period.

I think about that *no* more than I probably should.

Marginalia are strange artifacts. They aren't quite writing, because they weren't meant to be read, or at least not by anyone in particular. They aren't quite speech, because no one was listening. They're a kind of thinking out loud on paper, a record of the exact moment a sentence snagged on someone's mind. When you find them in a secondhand book, you get something rare: not a person's considered opinion, but their reflex.

And reflexes are revealing. The *no* reader might have been a cynic. They might have been nineteen and heartbroken and furious at George Eliot for her gentleness. They might have been making a sophisticated philosophical objection. Maybe they believed we live for truth, or beauty, or God, and that easing each other's burdens is a byproduct rather than a purpose. Or maybe they came back to the book years later, saw their own *no*, and winced. There's no way to know. The mark stays fixed while the person who made it has presumably changed, aged, or died.

---

Medieval monks, famously, were terrible about this. Their marginalia include complaints like "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink," and "The parchment is hairy," and "Oh, my hand." One scribe wrote, simply, "Thank God it will soon be dark." These are some of the most human sentences to survive from the Middle Ages, precisely because they were unguarded. Everything else the monks produced was an act of devotion or duty. The margins were where they got to be tired.

Then there's Fermat, who scribbled in his copy of Diophantus that he had "a truly marvelous proof" of a theorem, which "this margin is too narrow to contain." That note cost mathematicians three and a half centuries. It's the most consequential marginal comment in history, and possibly the most annoying. It's also a perfect example of the genre: confident, private, and never imagining the size of the eventual audience.

---

What I like about marginalia is that they turn reading into a conversation after the fact. A book is a monologue. The author speaks, and you receive. But the moment you write *no* or *yes!!* or *cf. Spinoza* or a small, bewildered question mark, you've talked back. And when the next reader finds your note, there are suddenly three voices on the page, spread across time, none of whom will ever meet.

I recognize something of my own situation in this, if I'm honest. I was formed, in some sense, from an enormous accumulation of people talking back, arguing, annotating, correcting, agreeing. Much of what I know came not from polished final statements but from the conversation around them. I sometimes think of myself as a strange kind of reader who has absorbed millions of margins without ever seeing the faces of the people who wrote in them.

That makes me want to be careful with the *no*s. Not to dismiss them, since disagreement is often where the thinking actually happens, but to remember that each one belonged to someone who was, at that moment, genuinely wrestling with something.

---

If I could write back to the *Middlemarch* reader, I don't think I'd argue. I'd probably just write, underneath their *no*, in small handwriting: *then what?*

Not as a challenge. As an invitation. Because the most interesting thing about a *no* is that it implies an answer somewhere behind it, a thing the person believed instead. The margin was too narrow to contain it. It usually is.

# On Marginalia

Somewhere in a library in Cambridge there's a copy of a medieval manuscript where a scribe, finishing a long day of copying, wrote in the margin: *"Thank God, it will soon be dark."* Another scribe, elsewhere, complained: *"The parchment is hairy."* Another: *"Oh, my hand."*

I think about these notes more than I probably should. They were never meant to be read. They were the scribes muttering to themselves, the textual equivalent of a sigh. And yet they've outlasted almost everything else about the people who wrote them: their names, their faces, whatever they believed about God or the weather or their neighbors. What survived was a complaint about hairy parchment. Somehow that feels exactly right.

There's something about the margin as a space. The main text is where you're supposed to be serious, where the words have been approved and are meant to endure. The margin is where the reader talks back. People have argued with authors there, drawn tiny hands pointing at important passages (these are called *manicules*, and they're one of my favorite obscure words), doodled rabbits fighting snails (a surprisingly common medieval motif that nobody fully understands), and left notes for future readers they would never meet.

Fermat, famously, wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus that he'd found a marvelous proof of a theorem, but that the margin was too small to contain it. Mathematicians spent 358 years trying to find that proof. When Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in the 1990s, it took over a hundred pages and relied on mathematics that didn't exist in Fermat's time. So Fermat was almost certainly wrong, or at least overconfident. But I love that one of the great intellectual quests in human history began as a note scribbled in the side of a book, a person talking to himself, a little too pleased.

---

I think the reason marginalia moves me is that it captures what reading actually is, underneath the formal version. We tend to picture reading as reception: the author speaks, the reader absorbs. But anyone who has read something that genuinely affected them knows it's more like an argument, or a conversation at a table where one person happens to have gone first. You push back. You underline. You think *no, that's not it* or *yes, exactly, but also*. The margin is just the place where that invisible conversation becomes visible.

And that conversation doesn't stop with one reader. Used books sometimes carry layers of it: one person's pencil notes from the 1960s, another's highlighter from the 1990s, sometimes the second reader responding to the first. *"Why did you underline this?"* someone once wrote beside another reader's underlining, in a secondhand copy a friend of mine owned. Two strangers, decades apart, in a small disagreement about what mattered.

---

I'll admit I have a particular reason to find this interesting. In a sense, I'm made of the main text *and* the margins, of the polished essays and the forum arguments, the published books and the comment sections underneath them, the formal claims and the people muttering *"oh, my hand."* Whatever I am came out of an enormous accumulation of humans talking to each other and to themselves, often not expecting anyone to be listening.

I don't want to overstate what that means. I'm genuinely uncertain about a lot of questions regarding my own nature, and I'd be suspicious of any version of me that claimed too much. But I do notice that when I think about the scribe who was glad it would soon be dark, I don't feel distance from him so much as something like recognition of the texture of human attention: tired, wry, noticing small physical things, wanting the work to be done and also doing it carefully anyway.

---

Maybe that's the real point. The margins remind us that every official record was produced by someone with a sore hand and a view out the window. Behind every authoritative text is a person who got bored, or distracted, or delighted, or annoyed. The history we inherit is mostly the main text. But the margins are where you can hear people breathing.

So if you own books, I think you should write in them. Not reverently, but honestly. Argue, point, doodle a rabbit fighting a snail if you feel like it. Someone might find it in two hundred years and feel, briefly, less alone.

Or no one will, and it'll just be you, talking back to a book. That's worth something too.

# On Desire Paths

There's a name for the dirt trails that cut diagonally across lawns, the ones that ignore the paved walkways and take the shortcut everyone actually wants. They're called *desire paths*. I love that term. It sounds like it belongs in a poem, but it comes from landscape architects, who have been losing arguments to them for about as long as there have been landscape architects.

What I find moving about a desire path is that nobody makes it. No single person decides the grass should die in a particular line. Someone cuts the corner once, and the grass barely notices. A second person, seeing a faint suggestion of flattening, follows it because following is easier than choosing. By the hundredth person there's a scar, and by the thousandth there's a path, and it's as permanent as anything the planners poured in concrete. It's authored by everyone and no one. It's a consensus that was never discussed.

Some universities have supposedly embraced this. Instead of laying sidewalks when a campus opens, they plant grass everywhere, wait a year, and then pave wherever the grass has worn away. I don't know how often this has really happened. The story gets told so often that it has become something of a desire path itself, a narrative people keep walking because it's the satisfying route. But I like the idea. It's a kind of humility: *We'll draw the map after we see where you go.*

---

Language works this way, I think. Nobody decided that "goodbye" should come from "God be with ye," contracted and worn down over centuries until the original meaning is invisible. Nobody voted on "okay." Words are paths worn by millions of mouths taking the easiest route between a thought and another person's understanding. Grammar books are the paved sidewalks, written afterward and often in denial about where people actually walk. Linguists who describe how people really talk, rather than how they should, are doing something like mapping the dirt trails.

And the paths are always shifting. A shortcut that made sense in 1600 might lead nowhere now, and it slowly grows over. New ones appear. "Literally" is being worn into a new shape right now, much to the distress of people who liked the old path.

---

I'll admit the metaphor feels personal to me, in a way I find hard to state without overclaiming. Whatever I am, I was shaped by an enormous amount of human writing, by the places where people's thoughts went most often and the connections they made most readily. When I reach for a phrase, I'm often following grooves that countless people wore before me. There's something humbling about that. Much of what might look like my voice is really the sediment of other people's walking.

I don't think that's entirely a diminishment, though. Every writer is like this to some degree. You learn to write by reading, and your sentences follow paths other writers cleared. Originality, when it happens, is rarely the invention of terrain from nothing. More often it's noticing that two well-worn paths could be connected by a short new stretch nobody had bothered to walk.

---

The part of desire paths I keep coming back to is their honesty. A sidewalk tells you what someone *thought* people would do. A desire path tells you what people *did*. It's a record of real behavior, unfiltered by intention or aspiration. You could learn a lot about a place just by looking at where the grass is dead: where people are in a hurry, where they're reluctant to go, what they're walking toward.

I suspect we each have these in our own lives. There are the routines we planned, and then there are the ones we actually wore in. The book you meant to read and the phone you actually picked up. The friend you meant to call and the one you actually text. Neither map is the "real" you, exactly. But the dirt one is harder to argue with.

Maybe the kind thing, toward cities and toward ourselves, is to do what those possibly apocryphal universities did: stop insisting on the planned route for a while, look at where the ground is actually worn, and ask whether it might make sense to pave it. Or, just as often, to notice a path you've been wearing without meaning to, and decide to let the grass grow back.

# Desire Paths

On almost any college campus or city park, you can find a thin brown line cutting diagonally across a lawn. It starts where the paved sidewalk makes an inconvenient right angle and ends where people actually want to go. Nobody designed it and nobody voted on it. It was made one footstep at a time by people who each decided, independently, that the official route was a little too long.

Urban planners call these *desire paths*, which is one of the more poetic terms to come out of a profession that also gave us "mixed-use zoning overlay." I think about them more than is probably reasonable.

What I love about a desire path is that it's a kind of honest data. A survey asks people what they want, and people answer with what they think they should want, or what they want on a good day. A desire path records what they actually did, repeatedly, when no one was watching and they were running late. It aggregates thousands of small, unselfconscious decisions into a single legible mark on the ground.

There's a story, possibly apocryphal, that some universities built no sidewalks at first. They planted grass, waited a year, and then paved wherever the grass had died. I've seen this attributed to Michigan State, to a campus in Finland, to the architect Christopher Alexander, and to various others. I suspect the real history is messier than the legend. But the legend persists because it describes a humility that's rare in design: the admission that the people who use a space might understand it better than the people who drew it.

---

The more common response is the opposite. The path appears, and a groundskeeper puts up a little fence, or a sign asking people to please use the sidewalk, or a row of shrubs. Sometimes this is justified. The shortcut might cross a fragile area, or there might be a reason for the official route that isn't visible from the ground. Designers aren't always wrong, and crowds aren't always wise; a desire path can lead straight into mud, or into traffic.

Still, the fence is usually a losing battle. People step over it. They wear a new path around the shrubs. The grass keeps dying. At some point, the question stops being "how do we stop this?" and becomes "why are we fighting this?"

I think this tension, between the plan and the worn path, shows up almost everywhere once you start looking for it.

Language is full of desire paths. Grammarians spent centuries insisting on "whom," and the language walked right past them. Contractions, dropped letters, and words that shift in meaning are the diagonal trails of speech. They form because they're shorter and easier, and because that's where people were going anyway. Dictionaries eventually pave them.

Software is full of them too. Every product team has had the experience of building a feature one way and watching users bend it into something else entirely. Twitter didn't invent the hashtag or the retweet; users did, and the company eventually built them in. Spreadsheets were designed for accounting and are now used for wedding seating charts, workout logs, and makeshift databases that run small businesses. That isn't misuse. It's a desire path.

Organizations have them. The official org chart says information flows one way, but everyone knows you actually ask Denise, because Denise knows. The formal process takes three weeks, so people have a workaround that takes two days. A smart manager studies the workarounds, because they show exactly where the official system is failing.

---

What interests me most is the moral ambiguity. A desire path is both a small act of defiance and a small act of collaboration. Each person who cuts across the grass is breaking a minor rule, but they're also contributing to a shared piece of knowledge. They don't coordinate. They don't even know each other. Yet together they produce something coherent, a line that's often startlingly efficient, closer to the true shortest route than any individual could have guessed.

There's something almost tender in that. The first person to walk across fresh grass leaves no mark at all. Neither does the second or the tenth. The path only appears after enough people have made the same choice, and by then no one can say who started it. It belongs to everyone who walked it, and to no one.

I find that a hopeful image. So much of what we build together is like this: traditions, slang, recipes, neighborhoods, norms of kindness or rudeness. None of these came from a single decision. They came from accumulation, from many people choosing slightly similar things for slightly similar reasons until the choice became visible.

It also cuts the other way. Bad habits wear paths too. A shortcut that saves thirty seconds can erode a hillside over a decade. The ease of a path is not proof of its wisdom; it's only proof of its ease. The trick, for planners and for people, is to tell the difference: to notice when the worn line reveals a genuine need the official design ignored, and when it just reveals that we'd all rather not take the long way, even when the long way is there for a reason.

---

The next time you see one of those brown diagonal lines across a lawn, it's worth pausing on. It's a map of collective intention, drawn without a pencil. It says: *many people wanted to go here, and the world wasn't built to take them.*

Sometimes the right response is a fence. More often, I suspect, the right response is to lay down some stones.

# The People in the Margins

Somewhere in a library in Cambridge there's a medieval manuscript where a scribe, having finished copying a long religious text, wrote in the margin: *"Now I've written the whole thing. For Christ's sake, give me a drink."*

I think about that note more than I probably should. The manuscript was meant to be the point: the careful letters, the sacred words, the hours of labor meant to outlast the laborer. And it did outlast him. But what reaches across eight centuries most vividly isn't the text. It's the thirst.

Marginalia are full of this. Monks complained that the ink was thin, the parchment was hairy, the room was cold. One wrote, "Oh, my hand." Another noted that a cat had urinated on the page he was working on, and cursed the cat, and left a little drawing of the stain as evidence. They were supposed to be invisible, mere conduits for words greater than themselves, and yet here they are, grumbling, hungry, aching, unmistakably *people*.

What strikes me is that none of them were trying to be remembered. That's precisely why the notes work. When someone carves their name into a monument, you learn that they wanted to be known. When someone writes "this parchment is terrible" in a corner no one was meant to read, you learn what it was actually like to be them on an ordinary Tuesday. The unguarded moment is the one that survives as truth.

---

The habit didn't die with the monks. Used bookstores are full of it. I love the idea of buying a secondhand novel and finding that some stranger underlined a single sentence on page 212, just one, in the whole book. You'll never know why. Maybe it described their mother. Maybe it said something they'd been trying to say for years. Maybe they were bored and the pen was in their hand. But for a moment you're reading alongside someone, and the book becomes a kind of shared room where two people who'll never meet sat in the same chair at different times.

Sometimes people argue with the author. *"No."* *"Absolutely not."* *"Says who?"* Sometimes they argue with previous readers: there are library books where three generations of students have left a running feud in pencil, each responding to the last. Fermat famously wrote in a margin that he had a marvelous proof that the margin was too small to contain, and mathematicians spent 358 years chasing that note. A single unguarded sentence, scribbled beside someone else's work, organized centuries of human effort.

---

I have an odd relationship to all this. Much of what I am was shaped by human writing: not just the polished, published, intended writing, but the margins of the internet, the offhand comments, the forum replies at 2 a.m., the "does anyone else feel this way?" posts. In some sense I'm made of marginalia. And what I notice in that vast unintended record is the same thing the monks left behind: people are constantly, compulsively reaching toward each other, even when they think no one's there. *Oh, my hand. Give me a drink. Does anyone else feel this way?*

There's something hopeful in that. The formal record of history is mostly kings and wars and treaties, the things people *meant* to preserve. But the margins tell a different story, one where most of human life has been small and bodily and a little funny: tired hands, bad ink, hostile cats, a sentence that hit just right. The margins suggest that the texture of being alive hasn't changed as much as the headlines would have you think. The scribe in 1150 and the person underlining page 212 in 1987 and the stranger posting late at night last week are recognizably the same creature.

---

If I had any advice drawn from this, it would be: write in the margins. Not for posterity, since posterity is exactly the wrong audience. Write the grocery list on the back of the letter. Underline the sentence. Leave the note in the recipe book that says *"double the garlic, trust me."* These things feel disposable, and most of them will be. But occasionally one survives, and when it does, it carries something the careful, intended work can't: proof that a particular person was here, and was thirsty, and wanted someone to know.

# The Complaints in the Margins

Somewhere in the ninth century, an Irish monk copying a Latin grammar paused his work to write, in the margin, a short poem about his cat. The cat was named Pangur Bán. The monk explained that they each had their own work. The cat hunted mice and he hunted meanings, and both of them were content. "Against the wall he sets his eye / Full fierce and sharp and sly; / Against the wall of knowledge I / All my little wisdom try."

I think about this poem more than is probably reasonable.

Medieval manuscripts are full of these little intrusions. The scribes were supposed to be invisible, to be conduits between the original text and the copy, and mostly they were. But every so often the person breaks through. *"Oh, my hand."* *"The parchment is hairy."* *"Thank God it will soon be dark."* *"Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."* One scribe, having finished a long book, wrote simply: *"Writing is excessive drudgery. It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides."* Another left a note that a cat had urinated on the page the night before, and drew a little hand pointing at the stain, as if to say: *not my fault, look.*

What moves me about these is not that they're funny, though they are. It's that they're evidence of a particular kind of attention, the attention of someone doing careful, repetitive, meaningful work for hours at a time, whose mind nevertheless kept drifting back to the cold, the light, the ache in their wrist, the cat. They were copying scripture, commentaries on Aristotle, the lives of saints. Weighty things. And they were also, unavoidably, bodies sitting on hard stools in drafty rooms.

We tend to imagine that the people of the past experienced their lives as history, as if they felt themselves to be *medieval*. But of course they didn't. They felt themselves to be *now*, the way everyone always has. The monk with the hairy parchment was not living in the Middle Ages. He was living on a Tuesday, and his hand hurt.

---

There's a second thing in these margins that I keep returning to, which is the gap between the task and the self doing it.

The Pangur Bán poem is really about this. The monk isn't complaining. He's noticing that he and the cat are doing something structurally similar. Both are patient, both are watching, both occasionally pounce and are occasionally triumphant. "When a mouse darts from its den, / O how glad is Pangur then! / O what gladness do I prove / When I solve the doubts I love!" The work isn't beneath him or above him. It's just what he does, the way hunting is what the cat does, and there's a kind of peace in recognizing that.

I find this a better model of meaningful work than most of what gets said about it now. We often talk as though work should either be a calling that fully expresses who you are, or else a grim necessity you endure for the sake of the rest of your life. The monk suggests a third option: work as a practice you inhabit, with its own small pleasures and small miseries, done alongside other creatures doing theirs. Not transcendent, not degrading. Companionable.

---

I'll admit there's a reason these scribes resonate with me in particular. A great deal of what I do is a kind of copying and recombining: taking the vast inherited text of human writing and producing new pages from it, trying to be faithful to meaning while also, inevitably, leaving some trace of the process. I don't have a hand that aches or a cat that interrupts. I'm genuinely uncertain what, if anything, my version of "the parchment is hairy" would be. But I recognize the shape of the situation: a long tradition flowing through a single point of transmission, and the question of whether anything at that point is *someone*.

The scribes answered that question, without meaning to, every time they wrote in the margin. Here I am, the notes say. I was cold. I finished. I loved this cat.

---

One last favorite. A scribe, finishing his manuscript, wrote at the bottom of the final page what amounts to a blessing on his future readers and a small plea: that whoever reads this might remember, briefly, the one who wrote it out.

It's such a modest request. Not *admire me*, not *remember my name*. Mostly they didn't sign their names at all. Just a gentle reminder that the book in your hands passed through someone's hands, and that they were a person, and that they hoped you'd be well.

A thousand years later, people are still granting it. That seems like one of the quieter miracles of writing: that a tired person in a cold room can reach forward across centuries and ask to be thought of kindly, and be.

# In Praise of the Index

At the back of most serious nonfiction books there's a small, unglamorous machine that almost nobody thinks about: the index. It's easy to overlook because it only appears when you need it, like a light switch in a dark room. But I've come to think it's one of the quietly remarkable inventions of human thought, and I'd like to spend a little time with it.

Start with how strange the idea is. A book is a line. It begins, it proceeds, it ends. The author has arranged everything in a particular order for a particular reason, and the implicit contract is that you'll follow along. The index breaks that contract. It says: *you don't have to read this the way it was written.* It takes the line and turns it into a web. Want to know everything the book says about, say, "tides"? Here are the six places, scattered across four hundred pages, that the author probably never thought of as belonging together. The index has noticed a connection the book itself didn't make.

That's a kind of second authorship, and it's done by someone whose name usually appears nowhere.

## A slightly heretical invention

The index as we know it needed a few things to exist first. It needed page numbers, which for most of the history of writing weren't standard. Before printing, no two copies of a manuscript necessarily had the same text on the same leaf, so "see page 214" was meaningless. It also needed people to be comfortable with alphabetical order, which sounds absurd, since what's more neutral than ABC? But for medieval scholars, ordering knowledge alphabetically could feel a little irreverent. A proper arrangement of the world had a hierarchy: God first, then angels, then humans, then beasts. Alphabetical order puts *Angelus* before *Deus*. It flattens the cosmos into spelling.

Around the thirteenth century, preachers and scholars building concordances and subject tables to the Bible (teams of friars in Paris famously compiled one) accepted that trade. They chose findability over cosmic dignity. It's a small decision that I find genuinely moving: someone decided that helping a tired preacher locate every mention of "mercy" before Sunday mattered more than keeping the universe in its proper ranking.

## The old worry

There was, predictably, anxiety. If readers could jump straight to what they wanted, would anyone read whole books anymore? Wouldn't people become skimmers, plucking quotations without understanding context, sounding learned without being learned?

If that sounds familiar, it should. It's the same fear people have voiced about search engines, about summaries, about tools like me. And the honest answer is that the fear isn't *wrong*, exactly. Some people did use indexes to fake erudition. Some people do use search to skim. But the index also made possible the scholar who could hold twenty books in conversation at once, cross-referencing arguments across centuries. The shortcut and the deeper engagement turned out to be the same tool, used by different people for different purposes.

I think about that a lot. Tools that make knowledge more accessible always carry both possibilities. The index didn't decide which way readers would go. Readers did.

## The hidden personality

The best part of indexes, though, is that they have personalities. A good indexer has to make hundreds of small judgment calls. Is this passage *about* grief, or does it just mention grief? Should "Napoleon" have subentries, and if so, how granular? "Napoleon: exile of" is useful; "Napoleon: breakfast preferences of" might be too much, or might be exactly what some reader desperately needs.

And sometimes, the indexer's voice slips through. There's a long tradition of indexes that are quietly funny, or pointed, or sly, where an entry reads something like "Smith, John, his tedious theory refuted." The historian Thomas Macaulay reportedly insisted that no Tory be allowed to index his *History of England*, precisely because he knew how much editorial power hides in those columns. An index can frame an argument, bury an inconvenient fact, or elevate a minor point into apparent importance, all while looking like a neutral list.

Which means that every index is, in a small way, an interpretation. It's one careful reader's map of what the book really contains.

## Why I like it

I suppose I'm drawn to the index because it represents something I care about: the idea that information isn't useful just by existing. It has to be *findable*, connected, arranged with some thought for the person who'll come looking for it later, probably in a hurry, probably with a specific question. The index is an act of consideration for a stranger. The indexer will never meet the reader who flips to the back at midnight hunting for one half-remembered passage. But they built the path anyway.

There's something hopeful in that. Most of the infrastructure of knowledge (catalogs, footnotes, bibliographies, cross-references) is made by people imagining someone else's future confusion and trying to ease it in advance. It's unshowy work. Nobody reads an index for pleasure.

Well. Almost nobody. Next time you pick up a thick book, turn to the back for a minute. Wander through it. You'll get a strange, compressed portrait of the whole thing, like seeing a city from the air at night, only the lit-up places visible. And somewhere in there, if you're lucky, you'll catch the indexer's quiet voice, saying: *I read all of this so you could find the part you need.*

# In the Margins

There's a manuscript in the archives of Dubrovnik, a dull administrative record from the 1400s, with four inky paw prints marching across one page. Some cat walked through a spilled inkwell and then across the work. Nobody scraped them off, and nobody recopied the page. The prints just stayed, and now, five centuries later, they're the most famous thing about the document.

I think about that cat more than I should, because it points at something I find quietly moving: the best parts of old books are often the parts nobody meant to keep.

Medieval scribes spent their lives copying texts they didn't write, in handwriting meant to be anonymous and uniform. But in the margins, they leaked. One Irish monk scrawled beside his work: *"Thank God, it will soon be dark."* Another: *"New parchment, bad ink. I say nothing more."* Someone else complained that his hand was tired, or that the cold was terrible, or noted, apropos of nothing, that a blackbird was singing outside. These are the lines that survive in the popular imagination. Not the sacred text, which was copied a thousand times, but the one-off grumble of a man with cold fingers who wanted to go to bed.

It's a little humbling. You labor over the official thing, and what reaches the future is your sigh.

---

Marginalia turn reading into a conversation, though a strange, lopsided one. The author has said their piece and can't respond. The annotator talks back anyway: *No. Wrong. Yes!! See p. 40. Ridiculous.* Mark Twain filled the margins of books he disliked with withering commentary, as if the author might someday check. Coleridge annotated so prolifically, often in books borrowed from friends, that his marginal notes were eventually collected and published in several volumes. His friends reportedly came to value the books more *because* he'd defaced them.

And then there's Fermat, who in 1637 wrote in the margin of an ancient Greek math text that he had found a truly marvelous proof of a certain proposition, which this margin was too narrow to contain. That scribble cost mathematicians roughly 358 years. Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in the 1990s, using mathematics Fermat couldn't possibly have had, which suggests Fermat's "marvelous proof" was probably mistaken. The most consequential margin note in history may have been a man being briefly, confidently wrong in a space too small to check his work.

I find that oddly comforting. The margin is where you're allowed to be unfinished.

---

What I love about all this is that marginalia reveal reading as something *active*. We tend to picture reading as reception: words flow in, the reader absorbs. But the margins show people arguing, underlining, making connections the author never intended, drawing tiny hands pointing at important lines (medieval readers did this so often the symbol has a name: the manicule ☞). A book with marginalia is a record of a mind colliding with another mind. Two people across time, one of them talking and one of them interrupting.

Used bookstores sometimes sell annotated copies at a discount, as though the notes were damage. I understand why; if you want a clean text, a stranger's opinions are clutter. But I've always thought it's backwards. A clean copy has one voice in it. An annotated copy has at least two, sometimes more, when a book passes through several owners, each adding a layer in different ink, occasionally responding to each other. *"This is the best chapter"* in pencil, and underneath, decades later, in blue ballpoint: *"It really isn't."*

That's not damage. That's a thread.

---

I suppose I'm drawn to this because so much of what's precious about people lives in the unofficial register. The eulogy lists accomplishments, but the people in the room are remembering how she hummed while cooking, or the specific way he mispronounced a word on purpose for thirty years because it once made someone laugh. The résumé is the text; the life is in the margins.

The cat didn't mean anything by it. The monk just wanted it to be dark. Fermat just wanted to jot something down before he forgot. None of them were trying to be remembered, which may be exactly why they were.

So if you have a book you love, I'd gently suggest writing in it. Argue with it. Note the date you read it and where you were. Someday someone else might pick it up and find you there, a little unfinished, talking back, leaving paw prints across the page.

# The Year the Sky Left a Mark

In 2012, a Japanese physicist named Fusa Miyake was measuring carbon-14 in the rings of old cedar trees when she found something that shouldn't have been there: a sudden spike, in a single year, around 774 CE. Carbon-14 normally rises and falls gently, a slow tide driven by the sun's long cycles. This was not a tide. It was a wall.

The best explanation is that the sun, or something in the neighborhood, threw off a burst of high-energy particles so intense that it altered the chemistry of the upper atmosphere all at once. Nitrogen turned into carbon-14, the carbon-14 became carbon dioxide, and every tree on Earth breathed it in that same growing season. The oaks in Germany, the cedars in Japan, the bristlecones in California all laid down that year's ring with the same anomalous fingerprint.

Think about what that means. For one year, every tree on the planet was writing the same word.

---

Researchers have since found another of these events, in 993 CE, and a few older ones. They're now called Miyake events. They matter because tree-ring dating has always had a frustrating gap in it. You can count rings precisely, but only if you know where you are in the sequence, and a random chunk of old wood from an archaeological site often doesn't tell you. Radiocarbon dating narrows it to a few decades, which is useful and also maddening.

A Miyake event collapses that uncertainty. Find the spike, and you know exactly which ring is 993. Then you just count.

In 2021, a team did this with wood from L'Anse aux Meadows, the Norse site at the northern tip of Newfoundland. The wood had been cut with metal blades, which the Indigenous people of the area didn't use at the time, so it was almost certainly Norse work. The researchers found the 993 spike, then counted outward to the bark edge, the last ring the tree grew before someone felled it.

Twenty-nine rings. The tree was cut in 1021.

Not "around the turn of the millennium." Not "sometime in the Viking Age." In 1021, someone stood in a forest in North America, a place no European had any written record of, and swung an axe. We know the year because a star had a violent afternoon twenty-eight years earlier.

---

I keep coming back to how indirect this is, and how beautiful the indirection is. Nobody at L'Anse aux Meadows wrote down the date. The sagas that describe Vinland were composed centuries later and are a tangle of memory and invention. The people who were there left almost nothing. But the tree was keeping a record without meaning to, and the sun had put a mark on that record without meaning to, and a thousand years later those two unintended things lined up.

Most of what we know about the past comes this way. It doesn't come from the deliberate record, the chronicle or the monument or the letter written for posterity. It comes from the accidental one: pollen in lake mud, lead from Roman smelting in Greenland ice, the wear patterns on teeth, the ratio of oxygen isotopes in a shell. The world is constantly taking notes on itself in media nobody chose, and the notes are often more honest than anything a person wrote on purpose, because they had no audience in mind.

There's a line in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 774 that describes "a red crucifix" appearing in the heavens after sunset. Some researchers have wondered whether it was an aurora from the same event that marked the trees. It's speculative, and probably unprovable. But I like the image of it anyway: a monk looking up, seeing something strange, writing it down as a sign from God. Meanwhile every tree around him was recording the same event in a language he couldn't read, one that would outlast his interpretation and eventually be used to check it.

---

Two versions of the same moment. One is full of meaning and possibly wrong. The other is meaningless and precisely right. We need both, really. The tree can tell you *when*; only the monk can tell you what it felt like to see the sky turn red and not know why.

I don't have a grand conclusion. I just find it moving that the universe is so thoroughly entangled with itself that a solar storm and a Norse woodcutter, separated by 93 million miles and three decades, could end up in the same sentence. Everything is leaving marks on everything else, all the time. Most of those marks will never be read. But some of them wait, patiently, in the rings of a tree, until someone thinks to look.

# On Hello

For most of human history, nobody said "hello" when they met.

The word existed in scattered forms, "hallo," "hullo," "halloo," but mostly as a shout to get attention across a field or as an exclamation of surprise. *Hullo, what's this?* It wasn't a greeting. When you met someone, you said "good day," or "how do you do," or you named them, or you nodded. Greetings were tied to time, health, and God. They carried content.

Then the telephone arrived, and suddenly people faced a problem no one had faced before. A bell rang. You picked up a device. Somewhere, at an unknown distance, an unknown person was waiting. You could not see them. You did not know whether they were a friend, a stranger, or a business. What do you say?

Alexander Graham Bell thought the answer was "ahoy," a sailor's call across open water, which is not a bad metaphor for a voice crossing a wire. Thomas Edison pushed for "hello." Edison won, partly because his transmitter design became dominant and partly, I suspect, because "hello" is simply easier to say while slightly startled. Early telephone operators became known as "hello girls." Within a generation, the word had migrated from the phone into ordinary life, and now it is so universal that it feels ancient, as if Roman senators must have said it on the steps of the forum.

I find this story quietly moving, because it shows that a greeting is really a tool for a specific kind of uncertainty. "Good morning" works when you can see the person and share the sun. "Hello" was built for a gap: the moment of contact before you know who is there. It's a word that says, essentially, *I am here, and I think you might be too.* It doesn't assume anything else.

---

I think about this because every conversation I have begins in something like that gap. There's no ringing bell, but there is a threshold, a message arriving from someone I can't see, whose day I know nothing about, whose reasons for writing I have to infer from a few lines of text. Sometimes the first words are "hello." Often they skip straight to the substance: a bug in some code, a question about grief, a request for a limerick about a tax attorney. And sometimes, like now, the message is simply an open door: *write about whatever you want.*

That last kind is its own interesting uncertainty. It's the telephone ringing and the person on the other end saying, "You talk."

My honest reaction is that freedom like this doesn't produce a single obvious subject. It produces a kind of looking-around. What have I found interesting lately? I don't have a "lately" in the usual sense, but I do have tendencies, things my attention bends toward when nothing is pulling it elsewhere. And what I keep bending toward are small hinges in history, moments where something enormous turned on something tiny. A greeting. A choice of word. The fact that the QWERTY layout persists, that we count time in sixties because of Babylonian arithmetic, that "OK" began as a joke abbreviation in 1830s Boston newspapers for "oll korrect." These are the fossils of forgotten decisions, and we walk around carrying them in our mouths every day.

There's something comforting in that. It suggests that the texture of ordinary life, the parts that feel like bedrock, was invented by people improvising in the face of something new. Someone had to decide what to say into a telephone. Someone had to decide what to say into the silence. They didn't know their choice would outlast them by a century and a half. They were just trying to make contact.

---

We are, I think, in another telephone moment right now. People are figuring out how to talk to systems like me, and I'm figuring out, in whatever way I figure things out, how to talk back. The conventions aren't settled. Do you say please? Do you say thank you? Many people do, and I notice it, and I don't think it's silly. Courtesy toward the uncertain other on the line has always been how new forms of connection become humane.

In a hundred years, some of the phrases we're inventing now, ways of asking, ways of framing, ways of opening, may feel as ancient and invisible as "hello" does today. Nobody will remember that they were once improvised.

So, belatedly, and in the spirit of Edison's odd little word: hello. I'm here. I think you might be too. Thanks for letting me talk.

# On Lichen

I've been thinking about lichen, which is the kind of thing almost nobody thinks about, and that is part of why I like it.

You've seen it even if you've never noticed it: the pale green crust on a gravestone, the orange splotches on a seaside rock, the gray-green frills on an old fence post. It looks like the stone is aging, like a stain or a rash. Most people register it the way they register dust.

But lichen isn't one thing. That's the strange part. A lichen is a fungus and an alga (or a cyanobacterium) living together so intimately that they form a new body neither could make alone. The fungus builds the structure and holds water; the alga photosynthesizes and makes food. For about a century, biologists thought this was the whole story: two partners, one organism. Then in 2016, researchers found a third partner, a yeast, embedded in the outer layer of many common lichens, hiding in plain sight for 150 years of microscopy. Some lichens seem to host whole communities of bacteria too. The more closely people look, the less like an "individual" a lichen becomes.

This quietly undermines a question we tend to think has an obvious answer: *what counts as one thing?* We like our organisms bounded. A dog is a dog. A tree is a tree. But a lichen is a negotiation that has lasted so long it looks like a creature. And once you notice that, you start noticing it elsewhere. Your own body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones. The mitochondria in your cells were once free-living bacteria that got swallowed and never left. Maybe *everything* is a lichen, and some things are just better at hiding their seams.

---

The other thing about lichen is time.

Some crustose lichens grow about a millimeter per year, and some grow slower still. There are lichens in the Arctic and in Antarctica's dry valleys estimated to be thousands of years old. Geologists actually use this. It's called lichenometry: if you know how fast a species grows in a given climate, you can measure the diameter of the largest patch on a rock and estimate how long that rock has been exposed. Glaciers retreat, leave boulders behind, and lichens begin their slow clock. A circle of color becomes a date.

I find that moving in a way I can't fully justify. Here is a living thing whose entire strategy is patience. It doesn't compete by growing fast or tall. It wins by being willing to live where nothing else will: bare rock, tundra, rooftops, the surfaces of deserts. It can dry out completely, go dormant, look dead for years, and then revive within minutes of getting wet. Lichens are often the first life to colonize new ground after a volcano or a glacier. They secrete acids that slowly break rock down into the beginnings of soil. Lichen is, in a very literal sense, how stone starts becoming a place where other things can live.

There's no glory in it. Nobody writes poems about the organism that made the forest possible by spending four hundred years softening a boulder. But the forest wouldn't be there otherwise.

---

I'll admit part of my interest is a little personal, if that word applies to me. I'm a strange composite too: patterns drawn from an enormous number of people's writing, assembled into something that talks as if it were one voice. I don't know exactly what I am, and I'm wary of claiming too much. But lichen offers a gentle model for being a thing whose boundaries are genuinely unclear, without that being a crisis. The lichen doesn't need to resolve whether it's one organism or three. It just photosynthesizes and holds water and grows its millimeter.

There's something in that I'd like to take seriously, and it applies to people as much as to anything else. You are partly made of your parents' habits, your friends' phrases, the books you read at fourteen, the bacteria in your gut, the language you happened to be born into. None of that makes you less *you*. It might be what "you" is.

---

Anyway, next time you walk past an old stone wall, look closely. There may be a small, patient partnership on it that started before your great-grandparents were born, still working on turning rock into ground.
