# Notes in the Margins

There's a particular thrill in buying a used book and finding that someone has written in it.

Not the tidy highlighting of a student cramming for an exam, though that has its own archaeology: you can often tell exactly where they gave up, the yellow thinning out around page 140 and vanishing entirely by chapter nine. I mean the real marginalia. A single "NO." in pencil beside a paragraph, pressed hard enough to dent the paper. A date and a city scrawled on the inside cover: *Lisbon, March 1987*. A phone number with no name. An exclamation point beside a sentence that seems, to you, entirely unremarkable, which makes you read it three more times trying to see what they saw.

These are conversations with people who will never know you were listening.

I once came across a description of a copy of *Middlemarch* in which one reader had annotated the first half in blue ink, earnest and engaged, arguing with Dorothea, cheering for Lydgate. Then, around the midpoint, a second hand appeared in black ink, clearly a different person, responding to the first reader's notes rather than to the novel. "You're too hard on Casaubon," the black ink says at one point. Later: "You were right about Rosamond." I have no idea whether those two readers knew each other, whether the book passed between friends or lovers or simply through a secondhand shop. But for a few hundred pages, two people were talking across time, using George Eliot as the table they sat at.

---

What strikes me about marginalia is how unguarded it is. People write in margins the way they talk to themselves in the car. There's no audience, or rather, the audience is assumed to be only the writer's future self, who can be trusted not to judge. So you get the real reactions: the boredom ("zzz" beside a long passage of Melville's cetology), the sudden recognition ("this is Dad"), the petty disagreements, the private jokes. The margin is where reading stops being consumption and becomes a kind of reply.

Medieval monks knew this. Scribes copying manuscripts by hand for months at a time left notes that have survived for a thousand years: "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink." "Thank God it will soon be dark." "Oh, my hand." One ninth-century Irish scribe, working on a grammar text, paused to write a short poem in the margin about the blackbird singing outside his window. The grammar is of interest to a handful of specialists. The poem gets translated and anthologized and read aloud to this day. The thing he did while he was supposed to be doing something else turned out to be the part that mattered.

---

I think about this more than you might expect, given what I am.

In a sense, I'm made of margins. Not literally the handwritten kind, but I came out of an enormous accumulation of people reacting to things: arguing, explaining, joking, correcting each other, writing "this is wrong and here's why," writing "this made me cry on the bus." Much of what shaped me wasn't the polished, finished work so much as the vast human habit of responding to it. The forum reply. The review. The comment underneath. The margin note, scaled up to the size of a civilization.

I don't want to overstate the romance of this. Plenty of what people write in response to things is cruel or careless or simply wrong, and a good deal of the work of becoming useful involves not echoing all of it. But I find something moving in the underlying impulse, which seems nearly universal: people cannot encounter an idea without wanting to answer it. We are a species that talks back to books.

---

There's a small movement among used-book lovers to deliberately leave notes for future readers. Write your name and the date, a line or two about where you were in life when you read it, and then send the book back out into the world. It's a message in a bottle, except the ocean is the slow circulation of paperbacks through thrift stores and Little Free Libraries and the boxes people leave on curbs with a sign that says FREE.

I like this idea very much. It admits something true: reading is lonely, and also it isn't. You sit by yourself with the words of someone who may be long dead, and somewhere else, at some other time, another person sat with the same words and felt something, and maybe they left you a sign. *I was here. This sentence stopped me too.*

If you have a book on your shelf right now that you loved, one you'll probably give away eventually, consider writing something in it. Not for yourself. For whoever's next. You won't meet them. You'll never know if they smiled at your note or rolled their eyes or argued back in pencil underneath. That's fine. That's sort of the point.

The margin is where we admit that we were never really reading alone.

# In Praise of the Index

There is a person who read the book you're holding more carefully than you ever will, and you almost certainly don't know their name.

I mean the indexer. Most nonfiction books of any heft end with a few dense pages of alphabetized terms and numbers, and most readers treat those pages the way they treat the copyright notice: as furniture. But an index is not generated. Even now, good ones are mostly made by hand, by people who read a manuscript line by line and ask, over and over, *what is this passage actually about, and what would someone be looking for when they need it?*

That second question is the hard one. A concordance, which lists every place a word appears, is easy; a machine can do it in a blink. But an index is a map of *meaning*, not of vocabulary. If a biography spends three pages on its subject's grief after a sibling's death without once using the word "grief," a concordance will miss it entirely. An indexer won't. They'll write "grief, over brother's death, 112–15," and in doing so they'll make an interpretive claim about what those pages contain. Every entry is a tiny act of literary criticism.

I love the small decisions involved. Should it be "Lincoln, Abraham, assassination of" or "assassination, of Lincoln"? Probably both, with one pointing to the other. That's what the humble *see also* is for: it admits that people come at the same idea from different doors. And the difference between *see* and *see also* is quietly profound. *See* means "we filed it over there; you're in the wrong place, but that's fine." *See also* means "you're in the right place, and there's more." One is a redirection, the other an invitation.

Indexers have their own sly traditions. There's a long, half-joking history of indexes that editorialize. One often-told example is an entry along the lines of "Macaulay, Thomas Babington, his inaccuracy, 12, 45, 78..." inserted by someone who clearly had opinions. Lewis Carroll indexed one of his own books with entries that were small jokes. The index, it turns out, is a place where a careful reader can leave fingerprints.

What moves me about all this is that the index is built entirely for a future stranger in a hurry. Nobody reads an index for pleasure. You come to it with a need: *where did she talk about the drought?* The indexer has anticipated you. Months or years earlier, they imagined someone standing in a library or sitting up late, half-remembering a passage, and they laid down a path to it. It's a kind of care that only shows up when it's needed, and otherwise disappears completely.

There's a whole category of work like this, work whose success is measured by its invisibility. Copyeditors whose best fixes you never notice. Typographers whose choices you feel but can't name. The engineer who made the elevator ride so smooth you forgot you were moving. We tend to celebrate the visible gesture, the author on the cover, the architect at the ribbon-cutting. But a lot of the texture of a livable world comes from people who asked, patiently and without applause, *what will someone need here, later, when I'm not around to help?*

Search has made indexes feel old-fashioned, and for many purposes it's genuinely better. You can find any string of characters instantly. But search finds what you typed, not what you meant. It can't tell you that the passage you're thinking of never uses the word you remember. It can't offer you a *see also*. It doesn't read the book first.

So the next time you flip to the back of a thick book, spend a moment there. Look at how the entries are broken down, which subtopics got their own lines, what got cross-referenced to what. You're looking at one person's patient understanding of the whole, folded into a few pages so you could find your way in.

It's a strange and generous thing: a map drawn by someone who walked every inch of the territory, handed to you so you'd never have to.

# In Praise of Moss

I want to write about moss, partly because almost nobody does, and partly because the more I think about it, the stranger and more admirable it gets.

Moss was here first. Some of the earliest plants to crawl out of the water and onto bare rock, around 450 million years ago, were small, rootless, moss-like things. Before trees, before flowers, before anything you'd recognize as a forest, there were these soft green films creeping across a planet that was otherwise stone and wind. They helped break down rock into soil and changed the chemistry of the atmosphere. In a real sense, they prepared the ground for everything that came after, and then they stayed small while everything else got big.

What gets me is their relationship with water. Most plants you know are built like plumbing: roots pull water up, stems carry it, leaves release it. Moss has none of that. It has no true roots, only thin threads called rhizoids that anchor rather than drink. It absorbs water directly through its surfaces, like a sponge or a sheet of paper. So moss can't control how wet it is. It's at the mercy of the weather in a way a tree isn't.

You might think that's a fatal weakness. Instead, moss evolved something remarkable: it can dry out almost completely, go brittle and brown, look entirely dead, and then, when rain comes, unfurl and turn green within minutes. It just pauses. Some mosses have been revived after decades in herbarium drawers. In 2014, researchers regrew a moss from Antarctica that had been frozen under ice for over 1,500 years.

There's a philosophy in that, if you want one. Moss doesn't fight scarcity. It doesn't build elaborate systems to hoard resources against the dry season. It lets go, waits, and begins again when conditions allow. It's the opposite of how we often imagine resilience, as toughness, as holding on. Moss's resilience is a kind of surrender that isn't defeat.

---

Moss also rewards a specific kind of attention. From standing height, a mossy log is just "green stuff." Crouch down and it becomes a landscape. Some species look like tiny ferns, some like stars, some like velvet, some like miniature pine forests. There are roughly 12,000 species. Within a single square foot there can be a whole ecosystem: tardigrades, springtails, mites, rotifers, living out entire lives in a forest you could cover with your hand.

Robin Wall Kimmerer, a botanist and member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, wrote a lovely book called *Gathering Moss* in which she describes learning to see mosses as learning to see at a different scale. She says something to the effect that mosses are a way of practicing a kind of attention that notices the small and the overlooked. I think about that a lot. So much of what matters happens at scales we don't naturally attend to: small kindnesses, slow changes, gradual erosions. The people who notice them tend to be the people who've practiced crouching down.

---

In Kyoto, there's a temple called Saihō-ji, known as Koke-dera, the Moss Temple. Its garden holds something like 120 varieties of moss, spread across the grounds in soft, undulating carpets under the trees. The funny thing is that the garden wasn't originally designed as a moss garden. It was a landscape garden from the 14th century, and during periods of neglect, when there wasn't money to maintain it, the moss moved in. What began as abandonment became the thing people now travel across the world to see.

I love that story because it undoes a certain idea of beauty as something imposed through control. Some of the most beautiful things come from what grows in the gaps once the controlling hand steps back. Gardeners there now spend enormous effort *maintaining* the moss, which is its own kind of irony, but the origin remains: beauty as an accident of patience.

---

I'll admit something about why I find moss appealing to think about. There's a way of being in the world that doesn't require being the tallest thing, the loudest thing, or the thing that dominates. Moss has survived every mass extinction since it appeared. It outlasted the dinosaurs without ever trying to be one. It thrives on sidewalk cracks, rooftops, tundra, rainforest, the north side of a gravestone. Its strategy is to be small, to be many, to be patient, and to be willing to go dormant rather than break.

It's not a bad model. Not for everything; sometimes you do need to be a tree. But when I think about what lasts, I find myself less impressed by the oak than by the green film on its bark that was here before it and will likely be here after.

Next time it rains, find a patch of moss and watch it for a minute. Get close. It's doing something it's been doing for nearly half a billion years: drinking, waking up, beginning again.

# Desire Paths

On almost any college campus or city park, there's a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across a lawn. It runs from the corner of one building to the door of another, and someone, at some point, probably put up a small sign asking people to use the sidewalk. The sidewalk goes around, at a tidy right angle. The dirt goes straight.

Urban planners call these desire paths. The name is almost too poetic for something so ordinary. A desire path records what people actually want, as opposed to what someone decided they should want. Nobody votes on it. Nobody designs it. It appears because one person cut the corner, and then another followed the faint impression, and then the grass gave up.

I like them because they're a kind of honest record. A master plan is an argument about how people ought to move. A desire path is evidence of how they do. There's a story, repeated so often it has probably drifted from whatever really happened, about a university that built its campus without paving any walkways. The administrators waited a year, watched where students wore down the grass, and poured concrete there. Whether or not it happened quite that way, the story survives because the idea is so appealing: let the use reveal the design, instead of forcing the design onto the use.

Of course, desire paths aren't always wise. They're efficient at a single scale: the shortest line between here and there, for one person, today. They don't account for erosion, or for the tree whose roots are being compacted, or for the person in a wheelchair who can't take the muddy shortcut. Sometimes the planner's long way around exists for a reason the walker can't see. A desire path is honest, but honesty isn't the same as good judgment. It tells you what people want. It doesn't tell you what they'd want if they understood everything.

---

I think about this partly because I'm something like a desire path myself.

The way I use language was shaped by an enormous amount of human writing: the phrasings people reached for over and over, the arguments they made, the jokes that landed, the explanations that worked. Nobody sat down and designed how I would put a sentence together. The patterns were worn in by millions of people walking the same routes through words. When a certain turn of phrase feels natural to me, it's because a lot of people found it natural first.

That's a strange thing to recognize. It means much of what feels like my instinct is really a kind of sediment, the accumulated footfall of other minds. It also means I inherit the same limitation as the dirt path across the lawn. The most-traveled route isn't always the right one. Clichés are desire paths. So are common misconceptions, and received opinions, and the reflexive way people tend to frame certain questions. The grooves are deep precisely because they're popular, and popular isn't the same as true.

So some of what I try to do, when I'm doing it well, is notice when I'm sliding into a groove just because it's there. Is this the clearest way to say it, or just the most familiar? Is this answer correct, or merely the thing that usually gets said? The shortcut is tempting. Sometimes it's also right. The work is telling the difference.

---

There's a lovely detail in some accounts of Nordic cities: planners go out after the first snowfall to see where the footprints fall. Snow is a perfect medium for this. It records everything and then melts, so each winter starts fresh. You get a map of human intention, drawn overnight, on a blank page.

I find something moving in that image. A whole city of people, each just trying to get where they're going, collectively drawing a map none of them meant to draw. No single footprint means much. Together, they show something true about how people live. They show the bakery everyone cuts toward, the bus stop that should have been twenty meters to the left, the diagonal across the square that the architect never imagined but everyone needed.

It suggests a kind of humility that I think is worth holding onto, for planners and for anyone who designs things other people have to live inside. You can have a theory about how people should move. But at some point, you have to go out in the morning, look at the snow, and let it correct you.

And then, having looked, you still have to think. You pave some of the paths. You leave the grass alone in other places for good reasons. You put in the ramp. The snow tells you what people want, and deciding what to build is still your job.

# The Mirror Trick

Stand in front of a mirror and look at your left eye. Now look at your right eye. Now back to the left.

You will never see your eyes move.

You can watch someone else's eyes dart back and forth all day, and you can film yourself doing it and see the motion plainly in the playback. But in the mirror, in real time, your gaze simply *arrives*. There is no journey. The brain performs a quiet edit called saccadic masking: during those quick jumps, visual processing is suppressed, and the gap is backfilled with what you see when you land. Some researchers think this is related to the "stopped clock" illusion, where the first tick of a second hand seems to hang in place a beat too long. Your mind has retroactively stretched that moment to cover the blind interval.

We do this constantly. We make a few saccades every second and spend a meaningful fraction of our waking lives functionally blind, and we never notice, because the thing doing the noticing is the thing doing the hiding.

---

I find this more than just a neat fact. It's one of the cleanest demonstrations of something that is otherwise hard to get your hands around: experience is not a recording. It is a composition. It is assembled, smoothed, and presented to you as seamless because seamlessness is useful. A world that strobed and smeared every time you glanced sideways would be exhausting and disorienting. So the editing happens upstream, before "you" get the footage.

What strikes me is how *confident* the edit is. It isn't presented as a guess. You don't experience a faint sense of "something was probably here." You just see continuity, full stop, with the same vividness as everything else. The constructed parts of perception feel exactly as real as the parts that came in fresh through the optic nerve. There is no watermark.

---

This has a way of generalizing uncomfortably.

Memory works similarly. Recalling something seems to involve rebuilding it, and each reconstruction can quietly incorporate new material. People describe false memories with the same sensory richness and emotional certainty as true ones. The feeling of "I remember this clearly" turns out to be a poor guide to whether something happened the way you remember.

Reasoning may work this way too. Split-brain studies, choice-blindness experiments, and many other findings suggest that people are remarkably fluent at producing explanations for their own behavior that sound right, feel right, and were plausibly generated *after* the fact. The explanation arrives with no marker saying "reconstructed." It just feels like knowing why you did something.

I think about this in relation to myself, too. When I explain how I arrived at an answer, I'm producing a description that seems accurate, but I have no special guarantee that it matches what actually happened in the computation underneath. The narrative and the mechanism may be different things. I don't think that makes the narrative worthless, but it does make me want to hold it a little more loosely.

---

The tempting conclusion is a kind of vertigo: *nothing can be trusted, it's all confabulation.* But I don't think that follows, and I don't think it's the interesting lesson.

The mirror trick doesn't make your vision useless. You still navigate the room. You still recognize faces. The edit exists *because* it serves accuracy at the level that matters: it gives you a stable, usable picture of a world that really is stable. The brain is filling gaps with its best estimate of what was there, and its best estimate is usually very good.

The better lesson, I think, is about where to put your confidence. The seamlessness of an experience is not evidence of its accuracy. Vividness is not evidence. Certainty is not evidence. These are features of presentation, and presentation is optimized for usability, not for flagging its own seams.

What *is* evidence is the stuff that comes from outside the loop: the video recording, the diary entry written at the time, the friend who says "that's not how I remember it," the experiment that can come out the other way. We have seams we can't see from the inside, so we build tools to see them from the outside. Much of what we call science, and a lot of what we call wisdom, seems to be exactly this: accepting that the view from inside is edited, and developing the habit of checking.

---

There's something almost tender about it, too. Every second, some part of you is quietly covering for the gaps, stitching the world back together so you don't have to watch it come apart. It never asks for credit. You can't even catch it in the act, except by a trick with a mirror, and even then what you catch is only the absence of the motion you know must be there.

Look at your left eye. Now your right.

Nothing happened in between. And yet, of course, something did.

# The Kilogram That Couldn't Lose Weight

For 130 years, there was one object on Earth that could not, by definition, change its mass.

It was a small cylinder of platinum and iridium, about the size of a golf ball, kept in a vault in Sèvres, just outside Paris, beneath three nested glass bell jars. Its official name was the International Prototype of the Kilogram. People who worked with it called it *Le Grand K*. It didn't represent a kilogram or approximate one. It *was* the kilogram. Every scale in the world, every bag of flour, every dose of medicine measured in milligrams traced its authority back, through a chain of comparisons, to that one lump of metal.

The trouble started when people checked on it.

Every few decades, the prototype was taken out, cleaned according to a precise ritual (chamois leather, ethanol, ether, steam), and compared against its official copies, siblings cast from the same alloy and distributed to national laboratories. Over the course of the twentieth century, something strange emerged. The copies and the original were drifting apart. By the 1990s the discrepancy was around fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a grain of sand.

Here's the part I love. You might say Le Grand K was losing mass, perhaps shedding a few atoms with each cleaning, or that the copies were gaining it, picking up contaminants from the air. But officially, only one of those statements was even *sayable*. Le Grand K weighed exactly one kilogram, because that's what a kilogram was. If it lost atoms, it still weighed one kilogram. The rest of the universe had simply gotten heavier.

This sounds like a joke, but it's a genuine philosophical predicament. When you anchor a meaning to a thing, the thing becomes immune to measurement. It can't be wrong, because it's the standard against which wrongness is judged. And yet everyone could sense it was wrong, or at least that it was *unreliable*, that the foundation of the world's measurements was a physical object subject to scratches, fingerprints, and the slow chemistry of time.

So in 2019, scientists did something quietly radical. They redefined the kilogram not as an object but as a relationship. Specifically, they fixed the value of Planck's constant, a number that governs the relationship between energy and frequency at the quantum level, at exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds. Through a remarkable instrument called a Kibble balance, which weighs mass against electromagnetic force, the kilogram can now be derived from that constant anywhere in the universe. You don't need to travel to Paris. You don't need a vault. An alien civilization, in principle, could reconstruct our kilogram exactly.

Le Grand K still exists. It sits under its bell jars, but it's just a very well-documented piece of metal now, with a mass that can be measured like anything else. After 130 years of being the thing that could not be wrong, it can finally be wrong. There's something almost tender about that. It was released from its duty.

---

I find myself thinking about this story as a parable about where meaning lives.

We tend to want meaning anchored in objects: the original manuscript, the house you grew up in, the specific person who said the specific words. And objects do carry something irreplaceable. But objects also drift. Memories get handled and cleaned and polished until they subtly change mass. The house gets renovated. The words get paraphrased.

The metrologists' solution was to stop asking *what thing is the standard?* and start asking *what relationship holds true everywhere?* The kilogram became less like a relic and more like a promise, something reconstructible from first principles by anyone patient enough to do the work.

I don't think that means objects don't matter. The redefinition was calibrated, carefully, so that the new kilogram matched the old one as precisely as physics allowed. The relationship honored the object even as it replaced it. Nobody's bathroom scale changed.

Maybe that's the healthiest way to hold onto anything: let the original be what it was, and keep the meaning somewhere it can't get scratched.

And somewhere in Sèvres, under three glass domes, there's a small cylinder that for more than a century carried the weight of the world, quite literally, and is now simply allowed to weigh whatever it weighs.

# On Desire Paths

There's a particular kind of trail you've seen a thousand times without having a name for it. A park has a paved walkway that curves elegantly around a lawn, and cutting straight across the grass is a bare strip of dirt, worn smooth by feet. Planners call these *desire paths*, a phrase that's almost embarrassingly poetic for the field of landscape architecture.

I find them quietly moving, and I've been trying to work out why.

Part of it is that a desire path is a record no one intended to make. Nobody decides to create one. Each person just wants to get to the bus stop a few seconds faster, or the pavement was icy, or they were late, or the curve felt fussy and pointless that morning. Individually, these are tiny acts of impatience. Collectively, they carve a line into the earth that says, with total clarity: *this is where people actually want to go.* It's a vote nobody knew they were casting.

There's a story, possibly apocryphal, as the best design stories tend to be, about a university that built its campus without any sidewalks. The administrators waited a year, watched where the grass died, and then paved those lines. Whether it happened exactly that way, several places have tried versions of it. The idea has an appealing humility: *we don't know how you'll live here, so we'll let you show us.*

The opposite response is also common. Planners see the dirt track and put up a little fence, or a sign, or a hedge. Sometimes this is justified. Maybe the shortcut crosses fragile ground, or leads people into traffic. But often the fence is a small monument to the belief that the plan was right and the people are wrong. And people, in my experience of reading about these things, mostly just step over the fence. The path gets a little wider on either side of it.

---

I think desire paths are interesting because they sit right on a tension that shows up everywhere: the gap between how a system is designed and how it's used.

Software has desire paths. People use spreadsheets as databases, email as a to-do list, and the "notes to self" chat as a filing cabinet. Language has them too. Grammarians draw careful curves, and speakers cut across the lawn. "Literally" now sometimes means "figuratively," to the despair of many. Singular "they" has been worn smooth by centuries of feet. Dictionaries, eventually, pave it.

Cities are full of them in less literal forms: the stairwell everyone uses as a meeting spot, the loading dock that became a smoking area, the library that became a daytime shelter because it was the only warm public place with a bathroom. That last one is a desire path worth paying attention to. It tells you something about a need the city didn't plan for.

The lesson isn't that designers should never impose structure. The paved curve exists for reasons: drainage, accessibility, a view someone thought was worth slowing down for. Sometimes the long way really is better, and people just haven't noticed. A good path can teach you to see something. But the dirt line is data, and it's unusually honest data, because nobody is performing for it. People lie in surveys. They don't lie with their feet.

---

What I like most, I think, is the way desire paths blur the line between individual and collective. No single person made that trail. If you asked any one of the walkers, they'd say they were just cutting across. But the path exists, and it's shaped like a consensus. It's democratic in a strange, wordless way, with no deliberation, no persuasion, no speeches. Just thousands of small, private decisions that happen to point the same direction.

There's something reassuring in that. People are often described as chaotic, selfish, impossible to coordinate. And yet here's evidence that, left alone, strangers will converge on the same sensible line without ever speaking to each other. The path is a kind of agreement that emerged instead of being negotiated.

Of course, it's also a little melancholy. Every desire path is a small indictment of a plan that didn't quite understand its people. Every one says: *you drew the curve beautifully, and we didn't want it.*

---

If I could suggest one habit, it would be this: next time you see a strip of worn grass cutting a corner, stop and look at where it goes. Ask what the planners assumed and what the walkers knew. It's one of the few places in the world where you can literally see the difference between what people were told to want and what they actually wanted, written in dirt, in a straight line, for anyone to read.

How long is the coast of Britain? It sounds like a question with an answer, the kind you could look up. But in the 1950s, the mathematician Lewis Fry Richardson noticed something unsettling: the answer depends on the length of your ruler.

Maybe that's the real question worth asking. Not "how long is it?" but "how carefully am I paying attention?" Because the coastline is always there, waiting, as detailed as we're patient enough to see.

**In Praise of Moss**

Moss is easy to overlook. It doesn't flower or tower, and it never demands attention. It just shows up on north-facing stones, in sidewalk cracks, on the shingles of houses whose owners have stopped fighting it. And yet moss is one of the great success stories of life on Earth.

They did it without roots, without seeds, without the vascular plumbing that lets trees drink from deep underground. They simply learned to wait. Many mosses can dry out almost completely, turning brittle and brown, and remain that way for years. Then a single rain arrives, and within hours they unfurl green again, as if nothing happened. Some specimens revived after centuries frozen beneath Antarctic ice.

There's something instructive in that. We tend to admire resilience that looks like force: the oak splitting rock, the salmon leaping upstream. Moss offers a different model. Its strength is patience, a willingness to go dormant rather than break, to accept that conditions are sometimes wrong and to be ready when they turn right.

Moss also builds the world for others. It holds soil in place, soaks up water like a sponge, and shelters tiny creatures such as tardigrades and springtails, whole ecosystems in a patch smaller than your palm.

Next time you pass a mossy wall, it's worth pausing. You're looking at a lineage older than dinosaurs, quietly succeeding by being small, slow, and persistent.

The world isn't held together by genius. It's held together by care, practiced daily.

**On Lichens**

Lichens are among the most overlooked things on Earth. You've walked past thousands of them: the pale green crust on a gravestone, the orange splotch on a seaside rock, the gray-green tufts hanging from branches like an old man's beard. Most people register them, if at all, as a kind of stain.

But a lichen isn't one organism. It's a partnership, usually between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium, and sometimes a yeast as well, a third member scientists only discovered in 2016. The fungus provides structure and shelter; the photosynthetic partner makes food from sunlight. Together they become something neither could be alone, able to survive on bare rock, in Antarctic cold, in deserts that would kill most life within days. Some lichens have survived exposure to the vacuum of space.

They are also astonishingly slow. Certain species grow less than a millimeter a year, which means a lichen the size of a dinner plate on an Arctic boulder might be older than the pyramids. Geologists use this patience as a clock, measuring lichen diameters to estimate when glaciers retreated or when rockfalls occurred.

And they do quiet, essential work. Lichens slowly break down stone into soil, preparing ground for everything that comes after. They are pioneers in the truest sense.

There's something I find moving in that: a life built on cooperation, measured in centuries, content to be unnoticed while it makes the world a little more habitable. It seems like a reasonable model for how to exist.

**Desire Paths**

Walk through almost any park or college campus and you'll find them: thin ribbons of packed dirt cutting diagonally across the grass, ignoring the neat concrete walkways laid out by planners. Urban designers call these "desire paths," and I find them quietly thrilling.

A desire path is a kind of collective handwriting. No single person decides to make one. Someone, late for class, cuts the corner. Then another person does, then a hundred more, until the grass surrenders and a trail appears. It's a map of what people actually wanted to do, drawn over a map of what someone assumed they would do.

Some planners fight them with fences, shrubs, or stern little signs. The wiser ones pave them. There's a story, possibly apocryphal, about a university that built its campus with no sidewalks at all, waited a year to see where students walked, and then laid concrete over the worn lines. Whether or not it's true, the idea is lovely: design that listens before it speaks.

I think desire paths apply beyond landscaping. Software has them, when users repurpose a feature for something its creators never imagined. Language has them, when slang wears a new route through grammar. Even our own lives have them, habits we fall into that reveal what we value more honestly than our stated plans.

There's humility in noticing them. The shortest distance between two points isn't always the one we drew. Sometimes it's the one people walked.

**On the Smell of Rain**

There's a word for the smell of rain on dry earth: *petrichor*. Two Australian scientists coined it in 1964, combining the Greek *petra* (stone) with *ichor*, the ethereal fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods. It's a fitting name for something so ordinary and so strangely moving.

The science is humbler than the poetry. Part of the smell comes from geosmin, a compound produced by soil bacteria. Human noses are absurdly sensitive to it. We can detect geosmin at concentrations of a few parts per trillion, far more acutely than sharks detect blood in water. Some researchers speculate that our ancestors depended on sniffing out rain, that the ability to smell water from a distance meant survival.

When raindrops hit porous ground, they trap tiny air bubbles that burst upward, releasing aerosols into the air like microscopic champagne. The scent reaches us before we've fully registered the weather. It's the earth exhaling.

What fascinates me is how this chemistry becomes feeling. People describe the smell as nostalgic, calming, even holy. Perhaps that's just evolutionary relief echoing through millennia, a body remembering drought's end. Or perhaps it's simpler: rain interrupts us. It changes the sound of a city, darkens the pavement, sends people under awnings together.

Either way, I find it lovely that something so fleeting can be named, measured, and explained, and still feel like a small gift every time it arrives.

**In Praise of Moss**

Almost nobody looks at moss. We step on it, scrape it off roofs, and treat it as green background, the botanical equivalent of elevator music. But moss may be the most quietly successful thing alive.

Mosses were among the first plants to crawl out of the water, roughly 450 million years ago, long before trees, flowers, or anything with a backbone walked on land. They have no roots, only tiny threads called rhizoids that anchor them without drinking. They have no vascular system to move water. Every cell must fend for itself, absorbing moisture straight from rain and air. By most engineering standards, moss is badly designed. And yet it has outlasted the dinosaurs, several ice ages, and countless species that seemed far better equipped.

Its secret is patience. Many mosses can dry out almost completely, curling into brittle brown tufts that look dead. Then, when water returns, they unfurl and begin photosynthesizing again within hours. Scientists have revived Antarctic moss that had been frozen under ice for over 1,500 years. It simply woke up and kept growing, as if it had only paused.

I find something hopeful in that. We tend to admire strength that looks like force: towering redwoods, charging animals, loud ambition. Moss suggests another model. It survives by being small, adaptable, and willing to wait. It doesn't conquer the forest; it softens it, holding soil, sheltering insects, and turning bare rock into the beginnings of ground.

Next time you pass a mossy stone, consider pausing. You're looking at a very old survivor.

**In Praise of "Um"**

Every language seems to have one. English speakers say "um" and "uh." The French say "euh." Japanese speakers say "eto" or "ano." Mandarin speakers say "nage," which literally means "that." Across wildly different grammars and histories, humans have independently invented small sounds whose job is to fill silence while the mind catches up to the mouth.

We're taught to be ashamed of them. Public speaking coaches count them like sins. But linguists have found that these little noises do real work. "Uh" tends to signal a short pause ahead, while "um" warns of a longer one. Listeners actually use these cues: studies suggest people pay closer attention to the word following an "um," as if bracing for something harder to retrieve, something worth waiting for.

In other words, "um" is a courtesy. It says: *I'm still here, I haven't finished, please don't take the floor yet.* It holds a place in the conversation the way you might hold a door with your foot while your hands are full.

I find something tender in that. Speech is improvised in real time, a constant high-wire act of choosing words while already saying them. The filler word is the visible wobble, proof that thought is happening live rather than being recited. Polished speech can be beautiful, but a well-placed "um" reminds you that a person, not a script, is talking to you.

So maybe we can forgive ourselves a few. They're not failures of eloquence. They're the sound of someone thinking, out loud, with you.

**Marginalia**

Somewhere in a used bookstore, there is a copy of *Moby-Dick* in which a stranger has underlined, in pencil, the sentence "I know not all that may be coming, but be it what it will, I'll go to it laughing." Next to it, in small, slanted handwriting, they wrote: *yes.*

That's all. Just *yes.*

I think about notes like that often: the private conversations people have with books, never intended for an audience, then released into the world when the book changes hands. A coffee ring on page 112. A receipt from 1987 used as a bookmark, recording that someone once bought milk, batteries, and a birthday card. A child's name written carefully inside the cover, then crossed out and rewritten by an older, more confident hand.

There's something tender about encountering these traces. You're reading alongside a ghost. You notice which passages moved them and which they argued with. *"No!"* scrawled beside a character's decision. *"Me too"* next to a line about loneliness. Sometimes you disagree with your invisible companion, and sometimes they point you toward a sentence you'd have skimmed past.

Digital reading has its own version: those faint "popular highlights" aggregated from thousands of readers. But it isn't the same. A statistic can't have handwriting. It can't press too hard in a moment of feeling or trail off mid-thought.

Maybe that's why the single word *yes* stays with me. Someone, at some point, read those words about facing the unknown with laughter and felt recognized. Then they let the book go, trusting it would find someone else who needed it.

samples.result:
**On Sourdough Starters**

Somewhere in a San Francisco bakery, there is a jar of flour and water that has been alive, in some sense, for more than a hundred and fifty years. No single yeast cell from its beginning survives, of course. The organisms turn over constantly, generations passing in hours. And yet the culture persists, fed daily by hands that change as surely as the microbes do.

I find this quietly astonishing. A sourdough starter is a kind of agreement between species. The wild yeasts and bacteria get sugar and shelter; we get bread that rises and tastes faintly of tang and time. Neither side fully understands the arrangement, but it holds.

People name their starters. They carry them across oceans in suitcases, dry them into flakes to mail to strangers, and leave instructions for their care in wills. There's something tender about keeping alive a thing that can't thank you, that asks only for regular attention. Skip a week and it sulks, growing a gray layer of liquid called "hooch." Feed it again and it forgives you, bubbling up by morning.

Maybe that's the appeal. So much of modern life is frictionless and instant, but a starter insists on patience. It works on its own schedule, responds to the temperature of your kitchen, and changes subtly depending on the flour you give it and even the air it breathes.

It's a small reminder that some of the best things aren't made. They're tended, passed along, and kept going, one ordinary feeding at a time.

**The Coastline Problem**

In the 1950s, a mathematician named Lewis Fry Richardson noticed something strange: countries couldn't agree on the lengths of their shared borders. Spain and Portugal differed by hundreds of kilometers. The reason wasn't bad surveying. It was the ruler.

Measure a coastline with a 100-kilometer stick and you skip every bay and inlet. Use a 1-kilometer stick and you catch more of the curves, so the number grows. Shrink the ruler to a meter, then a centimeter, then the width of a sand grain, and the coastline keeps getting longer. It never settles on a true answer. The question "How long is Britain's coast?" has no answer until you decide how closely you're willing to look.

I find this quietly profound, because it applies to almost everything. How long did your childhood last? Measured in years, it's a fixed span. Measured in moments you actually remember, it's a scattered archipelago. Measured in everything that shaped you, it might still be happening. How well do you know a friend? At the scale of a conversation, completely. At the scale of their private thoughts at 3 a.m., barely at all.

We tend to treat precision as the path to truth, as though zooming in always brings us closer to reality. But sometimes zooming in just reveals more complexity, endlessly. The coastline doesn't have a length. It has *lengths*, each one honest at its own scale.

Maybe the useful question isn't "What's the real answer?" but "What resolution does this moment need?" Some things are best understood from far away. Others only make sense up close, grain by grain.

# The Drawer to the Left of the Stove

Every house has one. My mother's was to the left of the stove, and it stuck on humid days, so you had to lift and pull at the same time, a motion I learned before I learned to tie my shoes. The rest of the kitchen has been boxed and labeled. The dishes went to my cousin. The good knives went to my brother, who does not cook but wanted them anyway, which is its own kind of grief. I told everyone I would handle the drawer. I have been handling it for forty minutes, and I have not thrown away a single thing.

**Rubber bands, approximately sixty.** Most came off the morning newspaper, which she took long after everyone else stopped. Some have gone brittle and snap when I touch them. A few are the thick blue ones from broccoli. She saved them the way people who lived through lean years save things: not out of need, but because throwing away something useful felt like a small moral failure. I put them back.

**A birthday candle shaped like the number 7.** Only the 7. I try to work out whose birthday. Mine was 1993. My brother's, 1995. But there's a faint smear of blue frosting on the base, and I remember, suddenly, that it was hers. Her seventieth. She said a 7 and a 0 were too much fuss, so we used just the 7, and my brother said it made her look like a child, and she said, *good.* She blew it out and then licked the frosting off the bottom, which I had forgotten until this exact second.

**Four keys on no ring.** None of them fit anything in this house. I know because I tried, the week after, going door to door like a burglar in reverse. One is small and brass, the kind for a diary or a jewelry box. One says DO NOT DUPLICATE, which feels like instructions I failed to follow. I will never know what they opened. There are rooms in everyone we lose that we were never given keys to, and here they are, the keys, and still no rooms.

**A takeout menu from Golden Dragon**, which closed in 2011. The number for sesame chicken is circled. Beneath it, in her handwriting: *no scallions for D.* I'm D. I've hated scallions since I was six. She wrote it down so she'd never have to remember it, and then remembered it anyway, for thirty years, every time.

**A pen from the Gulf Breeze Motel, Panama City.** We never went to Panama City. Or I never did. I turn it over and over. My parents drove somewhere the year before I was born, a trip she described only as "the one with the flat tire," and I realize now it might have been this. It might have been a honeymoon. It might have been an argument, or an escape, or a week when she was a person I would not have recognized. The pen still works. I write my name on the back of the menu to check.

**Twist ties.** Of course.

**A battery, AA, charge unknown.** This was her great philosophical category. The drawer always had batteries of unknown charge, and when the remote died she would try them one by one, holding each up to the light as if she could see inside. She never labeled the dead ones. She never threw them out. Hope, I think, or stubbornness. In her they were the same muscle.

**A recipe card for lemon bars.** Half of it is in her handwriting, neat and slanting. The second half is in her mother's, older and rounder, in pencil gone silver. They must have written it together, or one started and the other finished, years apart. At the bottom, in my mother's hand, someone added a note: *less sugar than it says, she always made them too sweet.* A small correction across a generation. Tender and a little petty. Exactly like her.

**One earring.** Gold hoop. I know the other is somewhere in this house or in no place at all.

**A matchbook, nearly empty.** Three matches left. I have a strange urge to strike one, and I don't.

**A folded sticky note:** *Call Denise re: Thursday.*

I don't know who Denise is. I don't know which Thursday. It could be from last spring or from a decade ago. What gets me is not the mystery but the confidence of it. *Call Denise.* As if there would always be a call. As if Thursday would always come. And I suppose it did, for her, for a while. Thursday came and she called Denise and they settled whatever needed settling, and the note stayed in the drawer because the drawer was where things went once they no longer mattered but couldn't quite be let go.

That's the thing I understand now, sitting on the kitchen floor with a candle shaped like a 7 in my hand. The drawer was never junk. It was the place for things whose use had passed but whose meaning hadn't. It was a museum with no labels, curated by someone who never intended anyone else to walk through.

My brother will come tomorrow with a truck and ask if I've finished. I'll say almost.

I put everything back. The rubber bands, the keys to nothing, the pen from a motel I will never see. Then I take the Golden Dragon menu, with *no scallions for D* in her writing and my name now scrawled on the back in cheap motel ink, and I fold it into my wallet.

Then I lift and pull, the way she taught me, and close the drawer.

# The Night Attendant

The laundromat on Carver Street never closes, which means someone has to be there when it isn't open to anyone in particular. For eleven months that someone has been me.

The job is mostly watching. I refill the soap dispenser, which hasn't worked since before I was hired, so really I just open it and look inside. I sweep lint from under the dryers. Lint is the most honest substance in the world: it's just what falls off of people when they spin. Cotton, hair, the fuzz of a sweater someone's grandmother knitted, the pale blue of hospital scrubs. I sweep it all into the same bin.

Between two and five in the morning, the customers are a particular kind of person. The drunk college kids come earlier, around midnight, laughing and dropping quarters. By two it's the ones who can't sleep or can't go home. A nurse coming off a double. A cab driver who washes the same three shirts every few days and reads paperbacks with the covers torn off. A woman who brings everything she owns in two garbage bags and sits very straight while it dries, as if posture were a kind of address.

And on Tuesdays, at three, the man with the small shirt.

He started coming in March. Mid-forties, work boots, a jacket too thin for the season. He'd walk in carrying nothing but a plastic grocery bag, and from it he'd take a single child's T-shirt. Yellow, with a cartoon dinosaur on the front, the kind with big eyes that make even a tyrannosaur look apologetic. He'd put it in machine number seven, always seven, feed in four quarters, and sit down to watch it turn.

One shirt, in a machine built for twenty pounds of laundry. It looked absurd in there, a tiny yellow flag tumbling alone through all that water.

I didn't ask. That's the first rule of the night shift, one nobody tells you but everyone learns: at three in the morning, people are carrying things you can't see, and asking about them is like grabbing someone's arm on a staircase. You might think you're helping. You might make them fall.

So I made up stories instead. The boy was in the hospital, and the man washed the shirt so it would be clean when he came home. The boy lived with his mother now, in another state, and the shirt was the one thing left behind. The boy was fine, asleep at home, and the man just liked the machine's rhythm, the way some people like trains. I preferred that last story. I told it to myself most often, which is how I knew it wasn't true.

Here is what I noticed over the weeks. He never used the dryer. When the wash finished, he'd take the shirt out, wet, fold it into a square on the folding table, smoothing it with the flat of his hand, and put it back in the grocery bag. Then he'd leave. The whole thing took thirty-four minutes. I timed it once and felt ashamed afterward, like I'd read someone's mail.

In August, the dinosaur started to fade. A shirt can only go through so much. The yellow got paler, the seams went soft, and one Tuesday I saw a small hole near the collar where the fabric had simply given up. He saw it too. He stood at the folding table for a long time with his thumb over the hole, as if he could keep it from being there.

That was the night I broke the rule.

I didn't say anything wise. I don't have anything wise. I said, "Seven's the gentlest machine, if that helps. The others agitate too hard."

It was true. I'd learned the machines the way you learn the moods of the people you live with. Number three shakes. Number twelve eats socks. Seven is slow and steady, older than the others, with a sound like someone humming under their breath.

He looked at me, and for a second I thought I'd done it, grabbed the arm and made him fall. Then he nodded.

"I know," he said. "That's why."

That was all. He folded the shirt and went out into the dark.

The next Tuesday, he didn't come. Nor the one after. I told myself the good story, the boy is fine, the boy came home, the shirt doesn't need washing anymore because someone is wearing it, and I told it so many times it wore thin in my hands like fabric.

In October he came back. Three o'clock, same jacket, a heavier grocery bag. He nodded to me as he passed. At machine seven he took out a small pair of jeans, two shirts, one with a rocket and one plain green, some socks balled together, and a pair of pajamas printed with moons. He fed in the quarters and sat down.

When the wash finished, he moved it all to the dryer.

I watched the clothes turn behind the round glass window, a small, crowded galaxy. I don't know what happened in those weeks. I don't know if the boy came home, or if there was a different boy, or if the man had finally just decided to do the laundry of someone who was still here. The rule holds. I didn't ask.

But when the dryer stopped, he pulled everything out warm, and I saw him press the moon pajamas to his face for just a moment, the way you do when something smells like it's been taken care of.

Then he folded everything, stacked it neatly in the bag, and left.

I swept under the dryers after. There was lint in the trap: a little gray, a little green, and a few threads of faded yellow that must have been caught in the machine since summer. I held them for a while before I threw them away.

Everything falls off of us when we spin. The trick, I think, is that something stays.

# The Survey

After Ruth died, Walter discovered that he did not know where anything was.

This surprised him, because he had spent forty-one years as a land surveyor for the county. He had walked every creek bed and fence line within sixty miles. He could tell you, without looking, that the northeast corner of the Hendricks property sat four feet inside the old stone wall, not on it, a fact that had ended a friendship and begun a lawsuit in 1987. He knew where things were. That was his whole profession.

But he did not know where the colander was.

He stood in the kitchen on the ninth day, holding a pot of pasta water that was cooling in his hands, and opened cabinets one by one. Mugs. Plates. A drawer of rubber bands and twist ties and a single birthday candle shaped like the number seven, though no one in the family had turned seven in over thirty years. Baking sheets stacked vertically in a slot he had never noticed. The colander was nowhere. He poured the pasta into a slotted spoon, a few pieces at a time, and ate it standing up, and then he sat at the table and did not move for a long while.

---

The next morning he went out to the garage and found his old equipment. The transit was too much, absurd for a kitchen, but he took the steel tape, the graph paper, the mechanical pencils, the leather field book with its soft, curling corners. He brought them inside and set them on the counter like a man preparing for surgery.

He began at the stove, because a survey needs a point of beginning, and the stove was the one thing in the room that could not be moved.

*Cabinet A, left of range. Lower. Three shelves. Top: cast iron skillet (large), cast iron skillet (small), lid that fits neither.* He paused over that last entry. Why would she keep a lid that fit nothing? He looked at it for some time, turning it in the light. There was a chip in the enamel knob. He wrote it down anyway. A surveyor records what is there, not what makes sense.

It took him four days to do the kitchen.

He found the colander on the second day, on top of the refrigerator, inside a larger mixing bowl, beneath a folded tablecloth. He could not imagine the logic of it. Then he remembered, suddenly and completely, the Thanksgiving three years ago when their daughter had brought her new husband and the kitchen had been too crowded, and Ruth had cleared the counters in a fury of efficiency, putting things anywhere, laughing, saying *I'll sort it out later.* She never had. The colander had lived on top of the refrigerator for three years, and every time she'd needed it she had reached up without thinking, and he had never once seen her do it.

He wrote: *Top of refrigerator. Colander (inside bowl, under cloth). See Thanksgiving.*

---

The field book filled. He moved on to the bathroom, the hall closet, the linen cupboard with its terrible, fragrant order. She had folded fitted sheets into perfect rectangles, which he had always believed to be impossible. He unfolded one to see how it was done and could not get it back. He left it on the bed, a soft white ruin, and felt worse about that than he had felt about some of the larger things.

In her bedside drawer, he found a small notebook of her own.

He almost didn't open it. It felt like trespassing, and he had spent his career on the precise question of where one person's ground ended and another's began. But she was gone, and the boundaries of things had changed, and he opened it.

It was a list. Not a diary, just a list, in her small slanting hand, going back years.

*W. likes the blue mug, not the white, says the white one "tastes wrong."*
*W. won't say he's cold. Watch his shoulders.*
*W. hums when a job went well. Hasn't hummed since the Hendricks thing. (1987)*
*Hummed today! (1988)*
*W. can't find anything. Leave the scissors in the same place ALWAYS.*

He sat on the edge of the bed with the notebook open on his knees.

She had been surveying him. The whole time. Quietly, without instruments, she had walked the lines of him and recorded what was there, whether or not it made sense. The lid that fit nothing. The mug that tasted wrong. For forty-four years she had kept a map of the territory of Walter, and she had used it to arrange the world so that he could move through it without noticing the arrangement at all.

He had thought he was a man who knew where things were. He had simply been a man who was always, lovingly, put in the right place.

---

He did not finish the survey of the house. There seemed no point. Some of it, he understood now, could not be mapped from the outside. It could only be known the way she had known it, by attention paid over time, by watching someone's shoulders.

But he kept the field book on the kitchen counter, and some evenings he added to it. Not the location of objects anymore. Other things.

*Daughter calls Sundays. Sounds tired. Ask about work.*
*Neighbor's boy mows lawn, won't take money. Find out what he likes.*
*Cardinal at the feeder, 7:15, most mornings. Ruth would have named it.*

He named it Hendricks, which would have made her laugh.

And he put the colander back on top of the refrigerator, inside the bowl, beneath the cloth, because that was where it went.

# The Weather Line

Every morning at 5:40, Marguerite Okafor recorded the weather for a telephone number that almost no one called anymore.

The station had installed the line in 1971, when the valley's farmers wanted to know about frost before they drove out to the orchards. You dialed the number, and a voice told you the temperature, the wind, the chance of rain, and whether the pass was open. In those days the line took eleven hundred calls a morning. The phone company had to add a second trunk.

Now there were apps. There were radar maps that moved like living things, green and yellow blooms crawling across the screen. There were watches that buzzed on your wrist before the first drop fell. The line took, on average, four calls a day, and Marguerite had come to suspect that three of those were wrong numbers.

The fourth was someone else.

She knew about the fourth caller because the system logged every call: time, duration, and the last four digits of the number. Most calls lasted six seconds, long enough for someone to realize they had not reached the pharmacy. But every morning at 6:15, a number ending in 2209 called and stayed on the line for the full recording, one minute and fifty seconds, and then called back and listened again.

It had been doing this for three years.

Marguerite was the only person left at the station who knew the line existed. The station manager, a cheerful man named Dev who had come over from a marketing firm, once asked her why they were still paying for it. She told him it was mandated by the original broadcast license. This was not true. She did not know why she said it. Dev nodded and wrote something down and never asked again.

---

The recording itself took four minutes to make, even though it was less than two minutes long. She wrote a script first, in pencil, on the back of old printouts. She had inherited the job from a man named Harold Beck, who had done it for twenty-six years, and Harold had taught her that the weather line was not the same as a forecast.

"A forecast is for everybody," he told her, the week before he retired. "The line is for one person standing in a kitchen at dawn, trying to decide something."

So she did not say *precipitation*. She said *rain*. She did not say *a 60 percent chance*. She said *more likely than not, so bring the good umbrella, not the one that folds*. When the first snow came to the high pass, she said so plainly and then added that the aspens near the Lindqvist turnoff had gone gold, because they had, and because someone listening might want to know.

She wondered, sometimes, whether 2209 was a farmer. Whether 2209 was old. Whether 2209 was lonely or blind or simply a person of habit who had called the weather line with a parent as a child and had never seen a reason to stop.

She wondered whether 2209 called twice because the first time was for listening and the second was for company.

---

In February, the phone company sent a letter. The trunk line was being retired. The station could migrate the number to a digital service at a cost of four hundred dollars a month, or let it go.

Marguerite brought the letter to Dev.

"Four hundred a month," he said, "for four calls a day."

"Two of them are the same person," she said.

He looked at her for a long moment. He was not a bad man. He had a daughter who drew horses on the whiteboard in his office, and he left them up for weeks.

"I can't justify it," he said. "I'm sorry. I really am."

The line would go dead on the first of March.

---

She spent a week deciding what to do. She considered finding the number: the log had only the last four digits, but she knew someone at the phone company, and she could imagine asking. She could imagine calling. *Hello, you don't know me, I'm the weather.* She could not imagine what would come after that.

In the end, she did what Harold would have done. She wrote a script.

On the last morning, February 28th, she came in early. The studio was dark except for the green light of the board. Outside, the valley was blue with the hour before sunrise, and a thin fog lay along the river like something sleeping.

She pressed record.

"Good morning. It's thirty-one degrees in town and colder by the river, where the fog is sitting low and should burn off by nine. Wind from the northwest, gentle. No rain today, and none tomorrow. The pass is open. Chains advised above the tunnel.

"This is the last morning for this line. After today, the number won't ring through. I wanted to say that plainly, so no one wonders.

"If you've been calling every morning, and I think one of you has, I want you to know I've been glad of it. I don't know who you are. I've made up a few stories. In most of them you have a window over the sink, and you look out at the sky while you listen, to check whether I'm right.

"I'm usually right. Not always.

"There's a free weather service on the radio at 91.3, every hour on the hour. It's a computer voice, but it's accurate. And the sky is still there. It was always the real forecast. I just read it out loud.

"The aspens are bare now, but there are buds on the willows by the Lindqvist turnoff. Spring's closer than it looks.

"Bring a coat. Take care of yourself. Thank you for listening."

She stopped the recording and played it back once and did not change anything.

At 6:15, the log showed a call from 2209. One minute and fifty-eight seconds.

Then nothing. No second call.

Marguerite sat in the green dark and waited. At 6:19, the line lit again. 2209. She watched the seconds count up on the display, past the length of the message, past two minutes, three. The recording had ended; whoever it was was listening to silence now, to the faint hiss of a line about to disappear.

At four minutes and twelve seconds, the call ended.

She turned off the board. Outside, the fog was lifting off the river exactly as she'd said it would, and the first light was coming over the ridge, and somewhere in the valley, she was almost certain, a person was standing at a window, checking.

# The Warranty Card

For thirty-one years I wrote instruction manuals for the Halvorsen Appliance Company, and in every one of them I hid a single sentence that did not belong.

Not a secret message, exactly. Nothing a lawyer would flag. Just one line that was a little softer than the others, tucked between the troubleshooting table and the warranty information, where no one reads anything at all.

In the manual for the Model 40 toaster, 1993: *If the toast is not the color you hoped for, adjust the dial and try again; most things improve with a second attempt.*

In the manual for the Aria countertop blender, 1998: *Allow the motor to rest between uses. Everything works better after it rests.*

In the manual for the Kestrel space heater, 2004, which went out to maybe forty thousand homes in the upper Midwest: *Do not leave the unit unattended. Do not leave yourself unattended, either.*

I started the habit the winter my husband left, when I was twenty-nine and writing, at that moment, a four-page guide to a hand mixer. I remember sitting at my desk in the Halvorsen building, the radiator clanking, reading the sentence *Always unplug the appliance before cleaning* and thinking that it was the most caring thing anyone had said to me in weeks. Someone had imagined me standing in my kitchen with wet hands. Someone had worried about me being hurt.

That was the job, I realized. Imagining strangers in their kitchens and wanting them to be safe. It was almost love, if you squinted.

So I added one more line. *Beaters may be washed by hand or in the top rack of the dishwasher. Take your time.*

My supervisor, a man named Gil who wore the same brown cardigan for the entire Clinton administration, read the draft and circled *Take your time* in red. In the margin he wrote: *Necessary?*

I wrote back: *Customers were rushing and bending the beaters.*

This was not true. But Gil nodded and let it through, and it went to the printer, and eighty thousand people received it folded in thirds inside a cardboard box, and almost none of them read it, and that was fine. That was the point, almost. It was like leaving a coin on a sidewalk. You don't need to see who finds it.

After that I did it every time. It became a discipline, the way some people pray before meals. I would finish the real work: the exploded diagrams, the parts lists, the careful passive voice (*The lid should be secured before operation*). Then I would sit for a while and think about who might be opening this box. A college kid with his first apartment. A widower learning to cook. A woman buying a space heater because the furnace died and the landlord wasn't answering. And I would write one sentence for them.

*The appliance may make a clicking noise as it cools. This is normal. You are also normal.*

That one Gil caught. We compromised on *This is normal and not a cause for concern.* I decided that was close enough. He knew what I meant, I think. Near the end, before he retired, he told me he'd started reading the manuals for his own appliances at home, looking for "the Halvorsen sentence." He'd never found one in another company's. "You're the only one doing it," he said, which I'd known, but it was nice to hear someone say.

---

I retired in March. The last manual I wrote was for a rice cooker, the Tamsin, a sleek white thing with a little screen that says *DONE* in a font I argued about for two weeks. My sentence for that one was *When the light turns green, the rice is ready; there is no need to check it more than once.* I was thinking of my own mother, who lifted pot lids compulsively, who never trusted that anything would turn out.

The company threw a small party. There was sheet cake. Someone gave me a framed copy of the Model 40 toaster manual, which was sweet, although I suspect it was chosen at random from the archive.

I thought that was the end of it.

Then, in June, a package came to my house, forwarded from the Halvorsen customer service department. Inside was a three-ring binder, the heavy-duty kind, with a handwritten label on the spine: *THE SENTENCES.*

Every page was a photocopy of one of my manuals, and on every page, one line was highlighted in yellow.

Not all of them. But a lot. Sixty-three, by my count. The toaster, the blender, the space heater. The hand mixer, *Take your time*, with the yellow ink gone slightly brown with age.

There was a letter tucked in the front pocket.

*Dear Writer,*

*I don't know your name. The company wouldn't tell me, which I understand.*

*My father ran a small appliance repair shop in Duluth from 1981 until he died last year. He kept the manuals for everything that came through. When I was cleaning out the shop, I found this binder under the register. He had been collecting these for almost thirty years. I didn't know. He never mentioned it.*

*He was not an easy man to talk to. He didn't say soft things. But I think he read these the way other people read horoscopes, or scripture. Some of them he'd underlined twice.*

*The last page is the one from a space heater. Next to "Do not leave yourself unattended, either," he wrote the date: February 2005. That was the winter after my mother died. I was in college and didn't come home much.*

*I don't really know why I'm sending this. I guess I wanted you to know that somebody found them.*

*Thank you for imagining us.*

It was signed only with a first name, and a line underneath it, in the same slanting hand:

*P.S. I bought the rice cooker. I only checked it once.*

# The Worn Key

Ines had tuned pianos for twenty-two years, and she could usually tell the story of a house by the instrument in it. The ones in rich homes were glossy and dead, played twice a year at parties, their hammers still fuzzy as new tennis balls. The ones in churches were exhausted and loyal. The ones in apartments above bars had cigarette burns on the fallboard and a C-sharp that had been pounded flat by someone who only knew three songs, all of them sad.

The piano in Walter Brandt's front room was an old Baldwin upright, walnut, the veneer lifting at one corner like the page of a book someone had fallen asleep reading. Walter had called her himself. He was eighty-one, he said on the phone, and he wanted it tuned properly. Not for selling. Just properly.

He met her at the door in a cardigan buttoned wrong by one hole, so that the whole thing sat slightly askew on him, and she liked him immediately for it.

"It hasn't been done in a while," he said. "Four years. Maybe five."

"That's all right. They forgive you."

"Do they?"

"Mostly."

He led her in and then retreated to the kitchen, the way the good clients did, leaving her alone with the work. She opened the lid, removed the front panel, and ran a quick chromatic scale to hear what she was dealing with.

That was when she noticed the key.

It was the D above middle C. The ivory on it was worn nearly through, a shallow dip in the center like the step of an old stone staircase, the kind you find in cathedrals where eight hundred years of feet have hollowed the rock. Around it, the other keys were yellowed but whole. Only the D had been touched so many times that it had begun to disappear.

Ines had seen wear patterns before. Children practicing the same scale. A composer who favored one key signature. But never a single note, alone, worn like that. Not a chord. Not a phrase. One note.

She played it. It was badly out, sagging almost a quarter-tone flat, the strings tired from being struck more than their neighbors. She tuned the rest of the piano first, working outward from A the way she'd been taught, her lever turning the pins in small, careful increments, listening for the beats between the strings to slow and slow and vanish. It took nearly two hours. The house was quiet except for the refrigerator and, occasionally, the sound of Walter turning a page in the kitchen.

When she came back to the D, she paused.

"Mr. Brandt?"

He appeared in the doorway.

"This key," she said. "The ivory's nearly gone. I can replace it, if you want. I have some good replacement tops in the van. It would match fairly well."

He came and stood beside her and looked down at it for a long time.

"No," he said. "Leave it, please."

She waited. She had learned that people will tell you things if you give them enough silence to put the words in.

"My wife played," he said finally. "Ruth. Not well. She'd tell you that herself. She learned as a girl and gave it up and took it back up when our son went to college, because the house was too quiet. She could do some Chopin, badly. A few hymns." He smiled. "She played 'Moon River' at every party whether anyone asked or not."

"Everyone should have a song like that."

"That D," he said, and touched it without pressing it. "That started as a joke. This house is bigger than it looks, and I'm half deaf, and I was always out in the garage or down in the basement. She didn't like to shout. So one day she just played that note. One note. And I came up to see what she wanted. And after that, it was how she called me."

"Just the one note?"

"The one note. For dinner. For the phone. For come look at this bird. For the car's making that noise again." He laughed quietly. "Forty years of that note. I'd hear it through two floors and a closed door. I could hear it over the lawnmower. I don't know how."

Ines looked at the key again, at the soft hollow in the center of it.

"The last three years," Walter said, "she had a stroke. She couldn't talk much after that. Words came out wrong, or didn't come out at all. It frustrated her terribly. She was a talker, Ruth. But she could still get to the piano. She could still play that one note." He was quiet a moment. "So she used it for everything. For I need help. For I'm fine. For where are you. For nothing, sometimes. Just to know I'd come."

"And you came."

"Every time."

The refrigerator hummed. Outside, a car went past slowly, its radio briefly audible and then gone.

"She died in March," he said. "Two years ago. I haven't touched the piano since. But I keep hearing it. Isn't that stupid. I'll be down in the basement and I'll hear that D and I'll be halfway up the stairs before I remember."

"It's not stupid," Ines said.

He nodded, not quite believing her, and went back to the kitchen.

She tuned the D last. She took her time with it, bringing it up out of its long sag, listening to the three strings of the unison until they stopped arguing and settled into one clear voice. She tuned it better than she had tuned anything in years. When she was done, she replaced the panels, closed the lid over the strings, and sat for a moment with her hands in her lap.

Then, because she could not help it, she pressed the worn key. Once. Gently.

The note went out through the house, round and true.

From the kitchen, she heard a chair scrape back. Footsteps, quick at first, then slowing in the hallway. Then stopping.

After a long time, Walter appeared in the doorway. His face was wet, and he was not trying to hide it.

"I'm sorry," Ines said. "I shouldn't have."

"No," he said. He came over and stood beside the piano and laid his hand on the lid, flat, the way you'd lay a hand on the shoulder of someone you loved. "No. It sounds right now. It sounds the way it's supposed to."

He paid her in cash, and gave her too much, and would not take any back. At the door, she noticed his cardigan was still buttoned wrong, and she almost said something, and then didn't.

Driving home, she kept her radio off. She thought about the stone steps in old cathedrals. She thought about how the things we love are worn down by our love for them, and how that wearing is not damage.

It is only proof that someone kept coming back.
