# The Bridge Over Nothing

The river left our town in the spring of 1987, and the bridge stayed behind.

It happened the way these things happen, which is to say slowly and then all at once. Three weeks of rain. A levee upstream that nobody had inspected since Eisenhower. One morning the Calloway River was where it had always been, brown and patient under the iron trusses of the Main Street Bridge, and the next morning it was a mile and a quarter east, cutting a new path through the Hendricks soybean fields as if it had been planning the move for years and was only waiting for an excuse.

The engineers came out from the capital. They walked the old channel in rubber boots and pointed at things. They said the river would not be coming back, that the new course was lower and the water would prefer it now, the way water always prefers the easiest way down. They said the bridge was structurally sound but functionally obsolete, which my grandmother said was the most honest description of a retired person she had ever heard.

There was talk of tearing it down. There was talk of selling the iron for scrap. A man from a city I had never heard of offered to buy the whole thing and reassemble it over a creek on his property, and for a while it seemed like that might happen. Then the town council met in the Methodist fellowship hall and voted, eleven to two, to keep it.

Nobody could quite say why. The minutes from that meeting, which I have read, contain only the vote and a note that the coffee urn was malfunctioning.

---

So the bridge stayed. It still stands over the old riverbed, which filled in over the years with grass, then wildflowers, then a scattering of cottonwoods whose seeds must have been waiting in the mud all along. In June the meadow beneath the bridge goes white with Queen Anne's lace. Deer bed down in the long grass where the catfish used to lie. Children who were born after 1987 have never known it as anything but a bridge over a field, and they find nothing strange in it, the way children find nothing strange in anything that was already there when they arrived.

Every four years the town paints it. The same green, a dark bottle green that the hardware store has to special-order. It costs more than you would think. There is a line in the municipal budget, between road salt and the library's large-print collection, that says *Bridge Maintenance*, and every year someone at the budget meeting asks what it's for, and every year someone else explains, and the line stays.

---

My grandmother crossed the bridge every day until she died.

She lived on the east side of Main, and the post office was on the west side, and she could have walked around. The street runs right up to the abutments now; you can step off the curb and cross the meadow in the same number of steps. But she took the bridge. Up the gentle incline of the deck, past the plaque from 1911, over the middle span where the river had been deepest, and down the other side. Every day. Rain or snow.

When I was twelve I asked her why. I had just learned the phrase "a waste of time" and was eager to apply it to everything.

She stopped in the middle of the bridge and leaned on the rail. Below us a meadowlark was sitting on a fence post someone had planted in the old channel.

"Your grandfather proposed to me right here," she said. "In 1954. The water was high that year. I could hardly hear him."

I said something about how the water wasn't there anymore.

"No," she agreed. "And he isn't either." She looked down at the grass for a while. "But I'm not going to start walking around things just because they're gone."

I didn't understand what she meant. I thought I did, for years, and then later I understood that I hadn't, and I suspect there are still layers to it I haven't reached.

---

Here is what I think now, at forty-one, having moved away and come back, having lost some things of my own.

We are told to move on. We are told that the healthy thing is to adapt, to take the new path, to prefer the easiest way down like water does. And there is wisdom in that. The river was right to move. It didn't owe us anything.

But people are not rivers. We are the things rivers leave behind. We are bridges, built at great expense for a particular crossing, and when the crossing is gone we remain, shaped exactly to the absence. You can tear down a bridge like that, and some people do, and I don't blame them. Or you can keep it painted. You can keep walking over it. You can let the meadow grow underneath and learn the names of the flowers that come up where the water used to be.

I don't think my grandmother was clinging to the past. I think she was keeping faith with it, which is different. Clinging is when you refuse to let the meadow grow. Faith is when you walk over the meadow every morning, and notice the Queen Anne's lace, and remember the sound of the water, and hold both at once.

---

I walked the bridge this morning. They painted it last fall, so the green is still bright, and the rivets catch the early light. At the middle span I stopped where she used to stop and leaned on the rail.

A girl of maybe seven was down in the meadow with her father, picking something—clover, I think. She looked up and saw me and waved, the uncomplicated wave of a child who has never once wondered why a bridge would cross a field.

I waved back.

Then I went on across, down the other side, and went about my day, the way you do. Carrying the river with me. Not walking around it.

# The Sock Museum

Walt had worked the overnight shift at the Suds-N-Go on Fremont for eleven years before he started the museum.

It began with a single sock, a child's, pale yellow with a cartoon duck whose one eye had been worn away by washing. It sat on top of dryer number six for a week. Walt moved it to the folding table, then to the windowsill, then back to the dryer. Nobody claimed it. On the eighth night he found an index card in the drawer under the register, and in careful block letters he wrote:

*DUCK SOCK, LEFT (PROBABLY). Belonged to a child who was learning to dress himself and insisted on doing it without help. Lost during the great hurry of a Tuesday morning. His mother still thinks about it sometimes, for no reason she can name.*

He propped the card against the sock and felt, for the first time in a long while, that he had done something correctly.

---

By the second year there were forty-one exhibits. Walt had cleared a shelf by the vending machine and lined it with a strip of green felt from the craft store. Each sock had its card.

*ARGYLE, MAROON AND GRAY. Worn to a job interview in 1997 and every important occasion after, as a kind of charm. The job did not work out. The charm, its owner maintains, did.*

*BLACK ATHLETIC, NIKE, SIZE 10–13. One of approximately four hundred identical socks owned by a man who bought them in bulk so he would never have to match them. He did not notice this one was gone. This is the saddest card in the museum.*

*WOOL, HAND-KNIT, BLUE WITH A CROOKED HEEL. The knitter was ninety-one. She got the heel wrong on purpose so her grandson would know it was hers.*

Walt didn't know if any of it was true. That wasn't the point. The point was that someone had worn these things, had pulled them on in the cold dark of some ordinary morning, had walked around inside them, and then one day they were simply gone, into the gap between the drum and the door, into the lint, into the vast quiet country where missing things go. Somebody ought to write it down.

---

The regulars got used to it. A nurse named Priya, who came in at 3 a.m. after her shifts, started bringing him socks from the hospital laundry that had lost their mates. A college kid wrote a card of his own once, taped it up without asking, and Walt left it there because it was good:

*STRIPED, RAINBOW. Bought ironically. Worn sincerely.*

Nobody ever claimed a sock. That was the strange part, or maybe it wasn't. Maybe people understood that once something had a card, it belonged to the museum now. It had become a story, and you can't put a story back in your drawer.

---

The girl came in on a February night when the snow had turned the parking lot into a blank page. She was maybe nineteen, with a trash bag of clothes and the particular stillness of someone who has been crying in a car. She loaded two machines, sat down, and stared at nothing.

After a while she got up and wandered to the shelf. Walt watched her read the cards, one by one, down the whole row. It took her twenty minutes. Near the end she laughed once, a short surprised sound, at the Nike card.

Then she went back to her bag and dug through it and came up holding a single sock. Gray, men's, a hole in the toe.

"Can you do one for this?" she asked.

Walt looked at it. "Where's the other one?"

"He took it." She shrugged, badly. "He took everything. That's the only thing of his that's still in my stuff. I don't even know why I brought it. I was going to throw it out."

Walt took the sock carefully, as if it might be warm. He found a fresh card and a pen and sat at the folding table for a long time, while the dryers turned and turned.

Finally he wrote:

*GRAY CREW SOCK, MEN'S, HOLE IN TOE. Left behind by someone who was not careful with things. It was here for a while and then it wasn't needed anymore. Its former owner is fine. She is going to be fine. She did her laundry in a snowstorm, which is exactly the kind of thing a person does when they have decided to keep going.*

He handed it to her. She read it, and her face did something complicated, and she set the card and the sock on the felt herself, at the very end of the row, straightening it twice.

"Thanks," she said.

"It's a museum," Walt said. "That's what it's for."

---

He thinks about that sometimes, what museums are actually for. Not the grand ones with marble stairs, but the idea underneath them: that the lost things deserve a place. That the ordinary objects of ordinary lives, the ones that slipped away without anyone noticing, might still be worth a card and a strip of felt and a moment of someone's attention at three in the morning.

Everything goes missing eventually. The duck socks and the job-interview socks and the crooked heels knitted by hands that are gone now. The people too, in their way. What you can do, Walt figures, is notice. Write it down. Say: this was here. Someone wore it. It mattered, at least a little, at least to someone.

The girl never came back, which Walt chooses to take as a good sign.

The gray sock is still there, at the end of the row. Every so often, when he's wiping down the shelf, he straightens it.

# Equal Temperament

The piano had not been played in eleven years, and Ines could tell before she lifted the lid. There is a particular silence that settles into an unplayed instrument, a dust not of the surface but of the wood itself. She pressed middle C and the note came out tired, a half-step lower than it had any right to be, like a man answering the door in his bathrobe at noon.

"It's bad," said Mr. Adair. It was not a question.

"It's asleep," she said. "Bad is different."

He was perhaps eighty, thin in the way of men who had once been broad, and he stood in the doorway of his own living room as if he needed permission to enter it. The room was clean. Someone dusted. But the chairs were arranged to face the television, and the piano sat against the far wall like a guest nobody had introduced.

"My wife played," he said. "I don't."

Ines nodded and opened her case. She had heard this sentence, in one form or another, perhaps two hundred times. *My daughter played. My mother played. We bought it for the grandchildren.* Pianos outlived their reasons. They were too heavy to move and too expensive to throw away, so they stayed, accumulating photographs on their tops like barnacles.

This one had no photographs. That was unusual.

She removed the fallboard and the music desk and looked in at the strings, the long bronze-wound basses and the bright steel trebles, the hammers lined up in their felt like a choir waiting for a downbeat. She set her tuning hammer on the first pin and began.

Mr. Adair did not leave. Most people left. They offered coffee and then retreated to the kitchen, because the sound of tuning is not music. It is the same note, over and over, bending slowly toward itself. But he sat on the arm of the sofa and watched.

"How do you know," he said after a while, "when it's right?"

She played two strings of the same note together and held up a finger. "Listen. Hear that wobble? Wah-wah-wah?"

He tilted his head. "Yes."

"That's called a beat. When two strings are almost the same pitch but not quite, they interfere with each other. The closer they get, the slower the beat." She turned the pin a hair's width. The wobble slowed, slowed, and vanished into a single clean tone. "When it's gone, they agree."

"So you just get rid of all the beats."

"No," she said. "That's the strange part."

She had explained this to very few people, because very few people asked, and because it sounded, when said aloud, like a small heartbreak built into the physics of the world.

"If you tune a piano perfectly, every interval pure, with no beats at all, it only sounds right in one key. You could play in C and it would be gorgeous. But move to F-sharp and it's a disaster. The math doesn't close. You go around the circle of fifths and you come back to where you started and you're not where you started. You're a little off."

"So what do you do?"

"You make every interval a little bit wrong. Evenly. On purpose. Every fifth slightly narrow, every third slightly wide. So that nothing is perfect, but everything is usable. You can play in any key." She played a chord, and even on the half-tuned instrument he could hear it, a faint shimmer inside the harmony. "Those beats stay. That's what it costs to be at home everywhere."

Mr. Adair was quiet for a long time. Ines went back to work. The afternoon light moved across the carpet. She tuned through the middle octaves, then the treble, where the strings are short and stubborn and the notes ring like struck glass.

When she reached the high E, she paused. The key stuck slightly, came up slowly, and there was a small nick in the ivory, a sliver missing from the front edge.

"That one's always been like that," said Mr. Adair. He had come to stand behind her. "She dropped a glass on it. Nineteen seventy-something. Wine glass. She was playing and gesturing at the same time, telling me some story, and she knocked it right off the top." He almost smiled. "She said the key never forgave her. Every time she hit it she'd say *sorry, sorry.* Out loud. Forty years."

Ines touched the chipped edge. "I can replace the key top. And fix the sticking. It'd take another visit."

"No," he said, quickly. Then, more slowly: "No. Leave that one."

She nodded. She tuned the string and left the key alone.

It was almost five when she finished. She played a scale up the full length of the keyboard, then a few chords, then, because it seemed the piano deserved it, the first page of a Chopin nocturne she had memorized at fourteen and never forgotten. The instrument woke up under her hands. It had a warm, slightly veiled tone, the sound of old felt and good spruce. Somebody had chosen it carefully once.

When she stopped, Mr. Adair was sitting on the bench beside her. She had not noticed him sit.

"Why did you call me?" she asked. "If nobody plays."

He looked at the keys. "I don't know. I kept walking past it. It felt like leaving someone on hold." He lifted one hand, hesitated, and pressed the high E. It came up slow. The note rang clean and bright into the room.

"Sorry," he said softly, and she understood that he was not speaking to her.

She packed her tools. At the door he paid her in cash, counted twice, and asked whether pianos needed tuning even if they weren't played.

"Twice a year," she said. "The wood moves with the seasons. It drifts."

"Then come back in the spring."

Driving home, she thought about the beats she had left in his piano, hundreds of them, tiny deliberate imperfections tucked inside every chord, so small that most people would never hear them. The price of being able to go anywhere. The shimmer that proves two notes are trying to agree and cannot quite, and are beautiful anyway.

She thought she might tell him about it in the spring. Or she might not. Some things you only understand by sitting next to them for a while, and listening.

# Four Hundred and Twelve

I have seen her four hundred and twelve times.

I know because I started counting in the second week, when I realized she was going to be a fixture, like the cracked tile at the Delmore stop or the driver who hums show tunes on Thursdays. I keep the count in the notes app on my phone, under a file labeled "Groceries" in case anyone ever looks. Nobody ever looks.

She gets on at Fairview, three stops after me, at 7:22. She sits in the fourth row on the left if it's open, which it usually is, because the fourth row on the left has a heater vent that runs too hot and most people learn to avoid it. She doesn't seem to mind. She carries a green umbrella every single day, including the cloudless ones, including the August week when the pavement softened and the whole city smelled like tar. She reads paperbacks with the covers torn off. I have never been able to tell what they are.

I want to be clear that this is not a romance. I'm fifty-three. I've been married, and then not married, and I have a daughter in Portland who calls on Sundays and tells me about her sourdough starter, which she has named Gerald. I'm not looking for anything. It's just that when you take the same bus for two years, at the same hour, in the same gray light, you start to need the landmarks. You start to organize your mornings around them. The humming driver. The tile. The woman with the green umbrella.

In November, she stopped getting on.

The first day, I didn't think much of it. People get sick. People take vacations. On the third day, I found myself leaning forward at Fairview, watching the doors fold open onto nobody, and I felt something I can only describe as a skipped stair. That small, stupid lurch of the body expecting something solid and finding air.

By the second week I was making up stories. She had moved. She had changed jobs. She had bought a car, finally tired of the heater vent. She had died — I didn't let myself think that one for long, but it came around, the way those thoughts do at 7:22 in the morning when the sky hasn't decided what it's going to be.

The ridiculous thing is that I didn't know her name. I didn't know where she went after the bus. She got off at Harmon Street, near the hospital and the community college and a dozen office buildings, any one of which could have been hers. I had spent four hundred and twelve mornings with her, and I could not have described her to a police officer beyond "fifties, maybe, gray coat, green umbrella, reads books without covers."

I told my daughter about it on a Sunday. I don't know why. She was telling me that Gerald had developed a strange smell and she was worried he'd gone bad, and I just said it, in the middle of her sentence: "There's a woman on my bus who stopped coming."

There was a pause on the line.

"Did you know her?"

"No," I said. "Not at all."

"Then why does it matter?"

I didn't have an answer. I still don't, really. The best I could do was: "Because I was keeping track."

My daughter, who is kinder than I raised her to be, didn't laugh. She said, "Dad, that's kind of beautiful," and then, "also kind of weird," and then she went back to Gerald.

What I didn't tell her was that I'd started getting off at Harmon Street. Just walking around for ten minutes before catching the next bus to my actual stop and arriving late to work. I'd walk past the hospital entrance. The college. The coffee place with the chalkboard sign that always had a pun on it. I told myself I was getting exercise. I did this for six days and felt like a fool on every one of them.

On the nineteenth day, she got on at Fairview.

She had a cast on her right arm, bright blue, the kind they give children. The green umbrella was hooked over her left wrist. She paid awkwardly, fumbling her card with the wrong hand, and the driver — it was a Thursday, the humming one — said something to her I couldn't hear, and she laughed. She walked to the fourth row on the left and sat down beside the too-hot vent and let out a breath, like she'd come home.

I don't know what came over me. I've gone over it many times since. I think it was the cast — the evidence that something had happened, that she had a life with falls in it, with emergency rooms and X-rays and people who signed their names on plaster. I stood up. I walked two rows forward, holding the rail, and sat across the aisle from her.

"You were gone," I said.

She looked at me. She had gray eyes, which I hadn't known. I'd only ever seen her in profile.

"Nineteen days," she said.

I must have looked startled, because she smiled — not unkindly — and lifted the blue cast an inch off her lap.

"Ice," she said. "Front steps. Very undignified." Then: "You're the man in the second row on the right. With the brown scarf. You always get on before me."

"Yes," I said.

"You check your phone at Delmore. Every day. Like you're writing something down."

I thought of the file labeled "Groceries." Four hundred and twelve.

"I suppose I was," I said.

She nodded, as if this were perfectly reasonable, as if everyone kept records of the people who sat around them on the bus, as if that were simply what you did to stay tethered to a morning.

"I'm Ruth," she said.

"Walter."

We didn't say much else. The bus hummed and the driver hummed and the heater vent pushed its dry, too-warm air over both of us. At Harmon Street she stood, and hooked the umbrella over her good wrist, and said, "See you tomorrow, Walter," the way you'd say it to someone you had known for years.

That night I opened the file on my phone. I looked at the number for a long time. Then I changed the title from "Groceries" to "Ruth," and I added one more.

Four hundred and thirteen.

# Count Week

Every year on the Saturday before Christmas, Walter Pruitt counted birds in a circle fifteen miles across, and every year he got the worst part of it: the sewage lagoons, the Methodist cemetery, and a quarter mile of frozen ditch behind the Tractor Supply.

He didn't mind. Thirty-eight years ago he'd asked for it, because the lagoons never froze all the way over, and where there's open water in December there are ducks, and where there are ducks there are sometimes surprises. Ruth used to say he had a talent for loving the places nobody else wanted. She meant it as a compliment, mostly. She'd said it about herself, too, the first year they were married, when he took her to the lagoons on a date and she stood in the smell with her hands in her coat pockets and laughed until she had to sit down on the hood of the car.

This was the first year he did the count without her.

He arrived at 7:10, before full light, and sat in the truck with the heater running and his clipboard on his knee. The tally sheet was the same one they'd always used, printed from the regional compiler's email, species listed in taxonomic order. Canada Goose. Mallard. American Black Duck. Ruth had kept the sheet; Walter had kept the binoculars. She had the better handwriting and he had the better eyes, and between the two of them they were one competent birder. That was the joke. They'd told it at the compilation dinner for three decades, and people had laughed politely at it for most of them.

He got out. The cold went straight through his jeans.

The lagoons gave him what they usually gave him. Forty-one Mallards. A dozen Buffleheads, bobbing and diving like wind-up toys. Six Ring-necked Ducks. A single Pied-billed Grebe, which he was glad to see, because some years there wasn't one and the absence felt personal. He wrote the numbers down in his own cramped hand, which slanted badly and which Ruth had once described as "a man falling down stairs."

By nine he'd moved to the cemetery. It sat on a rise above the river, and the old cedars along its northern edge held robins in winter, and juncos, and in a good year a Hermit Thrush skulking low in the hedge. Ruth was not buried here. Ruth was buried forty miles away, next to her parents, which had been her wish and which he had honored. But he found that he walked the rows more slowly than usual anyway, reading names he'd read a hundred times.

He was standing by the Hollenbeck family obelisk when the bird landed.

It dropped out of a cedar onto the frozen grass maybe thirty feet from him, and for a second his brain simply refused it. It was robin-shaped but wrong. Slate-gray back. Throat and eyebrow a deep, burning orange, like a coal someone had blown on. A dark band across the chest, clean as a necklace. Orange bars on the wings.

He knew what it was. He had known what it was since he was nine years old, paging through his grandfather's Peterson guide, when he'd stopped on that plate and thought it was the most beautiful bird in the book and also the one he would never see, because it lived in the dark wet forests of Oregon and Washington, two thousand miles from here.

Varied Thrush.

It hopped twice. It flipped a leaf with its bill. It looked at him, or seemed to, with one black eye.

Walter did not move. He did not raise his binoculars, because he was afraid the motion would flush it, and because he didn't need them. He just stood there in the cold among the Hollenbecks and the Garveys and the infant Mary Louise Strand, 1911–1912, and looked.

Later he would think about how long it lasted. Forty seconds? A minute? It felt longer, the way certain moments in a marriage feel longer, the way a hospital night does, or a first kiss. Then a truck downshifted out on Route 9 and the thrush was gone, up and over the cedars and down toward the river, and Walter was an old man standing alone in a cemetery with his mouth open.

He knew what would happen next. He'd seen it happen to other people.

A Varied Thrush in this county would be a first record, or close to it. The compiler would want documentation. A photograph, ideally. At minimum, a detailed written description and a second observer. The records committee would review it. They would be polite. They would ask whether he'd considered an aberrant robin. They would note, gently, his age, and the lack of corroboration, and maybe, if they'd heard, his recent loss. And the sighting would go into the database with an asterisk, or it would not go in at all.

Ruth had carried the camera. Ruth would have gotten the photo; she was fast, she was always fast. And if she hadn't, she'd have been his second observer, and her word had always been worth more than his in rooms full of people, because she was calm and precise and did not get excited about things.

He stood there a long time.

Then he walked back to the truck, got in, and turned the heater up. He took out the clipboard. He found the thrushes on the tally sheet — Eastern Bluebird, Hermit Thrush, American Robin — and he wrote *robins, 23*, which was true, and *Hermit Thrush, 1*, which was also true, from the hedge on the way out.

He looked at the blank margin for a while.

At the compilation dinner that night, over chili in the basement of the Lutheran church, people would go around the table and report their highlights, and someone would ask about the lagoons, and he would say the grebe was back. And they'd say good, good. And somebody who knew would squeeze his shoulder.

He didn't write it down. Not because they wouldn't believe him. Because for thirty-eight years, everything he'd seen, he'd seen with someone, and every bird had belonged to both of them, and every count had been a thing they made together, and now here was one sighting, the most beautiful one of his life, that belonged only to him.

He thought she would have understood that. He thought she would have laughed.

He put the truck in gear and drove to the Tractor Supply, where the ditch was frozen solid and there was, as usual, nothing at all.

# Screws That Fit Nothing

My father labeled everything. I knew this the way you know the weather of the house you grew up in, but I didn't understand it until the week after the funeral, when I opened the door to his workshop and found forty years of masking tape looking back at me.

*Washers, small.* *Washers, smaller.* *Hinges (good).* *Hinges (someday).* The handwriting was all capitals, blocky and slanted slightly left, the same hand that had signed my report cards and written *DRIVE SAFE* on the back of every envelope he ever mailed me, as though the post office might deliver the warning faster than I could get into a car.

My brother said we should hire someone. There are people, apparently, who come and clear out the houses of the dead. They sort, they haul, they sell what can be sold and throw away the rest, and you never have to touch any of it. He sent me a link. The company's logo was a sun rising over a clean horizon, which struck me as either very kind or very cruel.

I told him I'd do the workshop myself. He didn't argue. He'd never liked that room. It smelled of sawdust and machine oil and something sharper underneath, a scorched smell from the time in 1994 when Dad tried to fix the toaster and the toaster won. My brother associated the room with being asked to hold things. Hold this steady. Hold this light. No, *here*. I associated it with the same thing, but I'd liked it. There's a particular trust in being asked to hold the light. It means someone believes you'll keep it where it needs to be.

So I started on a Saturday with a roll of contractor bags and a thermos of coffee and every intention of being ruthless.

I lasted about twenty minutes.

The problem wasn't sentiment, exactly. The problem was that everything had been *decided*. My father had already looked at every object in that room and determined what it was and what it was for. Throwing something away meant overruling him, and I found I couldn't do it casually. A coffee can marked *Nails, bent, straighten later* was not trash. It was a promise he'd made to himself, and the fact that he'd never kept it didn't make it less of one.

I began making piles instead. Keep. Donate. Brother. Undecided. Undecided grew fastest.

Around noon I found the jar.

It was on the highest shelf, behind a row of paint cans so old their labels had faded to the color of weak tea. A pickle jar, the big kind, full nearly to the lid with screws. Brass and steel, flat-head and Phillips, long and stubby, some with threads so fine they looked etched, some so coarse they could have held a boat together. On the lid, in the familiar capitals:

*SCREWS THAT FIT NOTHING.*

I sat down on his stool and laughed until I had to put the jar on the floor.

Because of course. Of course he had kept them. Every time he'd taken something apart and found a screw left over, every time he'd bought a pack of twenty and used nineteen, every time a mystery screw had turned up in a drawer or a pocket or the lint trap of the dryer, he had tried it against every hole he could find, and when it fit none of them, he hadn't thrown it away. He'd put it here. And then he'd labeled the jar, which meant he'd known. He'd understood exactly what he was doing. This wasn't a jar of screws waiting to be sorted. This was a jar of screws that had been sorted, thoroughly and finally, into the category of *useless*, and kept anyway.

I thought about what my mother would have said. She'd died eleven years before him, and she had been a thrower-out, a clearer of surfaces, a woman who believed that anything you hadn't touched in a year was simply taking up the space where something better might go. They'd fought about the workshop for as long as I could remember. Not cruelly. It was the kind of argument that becomes a sort of song a couple sings together, the same verses every time. *What are you keeping that for?* *You never know.* *I do know. I know you'll never use it.* *Then I'll never use it here, where it's not bothering anybody.*

I unscrewed the lid and poured a handful into my palm. They were cold and heavier than I expected. A few were rusted. One was bright gold, tiny, the kind that holds the arm of a pair of glasses. I wondered whose glasses. I wondered if they'd been mine.

Here's what I think now, though I didn't think it all at once.

I think my father knew perfectly well that most things in the world don't fit. That you spend your life with pieces left over: conversations that never found their place, apologies that arrived after the hole they were meant for had closed up, love shaped wrong for whatever it was aimed at. And I think he decided, in his quiet, capital-lettered way, that not fitting wasn't the same as not mattering. That a thing could be useless and still be worth keeping. That you could look at something clearly, name it honestly, *this fits nothing*, and still put it on the high shelf where it would be safe.

I didn't hire the people with the sunrise logo. I did, eventually, get ruthless. The bent nails went. The paint cans went. Most of the hinges, good and someday, went to a man from the church who builds cabinets for families who've lost their houses to fire.

But the jar is on a shelf in my kitchen now, between the flour and the good olive oil. My daughter asked me what it was for, and I told her the truth: nothing. She considered this with the seriousness of a seven-year-old and asked if she could add to it.

Last week she brought me a screw she'd found on the sidewalk outside school. We tried it in everything, the cabinet doors, the back of the radio, the battery panel of her flashlight. It didn't fit.

She held the jar steady while I dropped it in.

# Notes for the House-Sitter

Thank you again for doing this on such short notice. I know two weeks is a long time, and I know Priya told you it was "basically just a dog," which is true, but there are a few things.

**1. The dog.** His name is Biscuit. He will tell you he hasn't been fed. He has been fed. He eats one scoop in the morning and one at night, and the scoop is the red one, not the blue one, because the blue one is bigger and he knows it. If you use the blue one he will look at you with enormous gratitude and then throw up on the stairs around 2 a.m.

He is not technically my dog. I'll explain that further down, or I won't. Either way, feed him.

**2. The front door** sticks in humid weather. Lift the handle up while you turn the key. There's a knack. You'll get it by the second day. It took me four years, but I was married to someone who always got to the door first, so I never had to learn.

**3. The thermostat** is set to 68. Please leave it at 68. There is a sticky note on it that says "DON'T TOUCH – M." You can ignore the M part. The M part is not relevant anymore. But leave it at 68 anyway, because I've gotten used to it, which is its own kind of problem.

**4. The plants.** The fern in the kitchen needs water every other day. The snake plant in the living room needs water approximately never. You could leave for a year and come back and it would still be there, looking at you, faintly disappointed. I admire it very much.

There is a third plant on the upstairs landing. It is dead. Please don't water it, and please don't throw it out. I know how that sounds.

**5. Trash** goes out Tuesday night. Recycling is every other Tuesday, and I have never once known which Tuesday. I usually just look at what the neighbors do. The Hendersons on the left are reliable. The man on the right puts his bins out on random days, possibly as a form of protest. Follow the Hendersons.

**6. Mail.** Just stack it on the counter. If anything comes addressed to Michael Okafor, please put it in the shoebox by the door. He's coming by to pick it up at some point. He has a key. He may also take the dog for an afternoon; that's fine; that's arranged. If he comes, he'll probably be polite and a little too friendly, and he may ask how I'm doing. You don't have to answer. You can say you don't know me that well, which is true, and which will be a relief to both of you.

**7. The upstairs room at the end of the hall.** You don't need to go in there. It's not locked or anything. It's not a Bluebeard situation. It's just that it was going to be something, and then it wasn't, and there's still a can of paint in there in a color called "Morning Oat," which I picked because I thought it was a funny name, and he picked because he thought I would like it, and it turns out we both just wanted the other person to be happy with the paint. That's not nothing. I think about that more than I think about the other stuff.

Anyway, the Wi-Fi router is in there, so if the internet goes out you'll have to go in and unplug it and plug it back in. Sorry.

**8. Wi-Fi password** is on the fridge. Don't judge it. It was chosen in a different era.

**9. Biscuit, continued.** He sleeps at the foot of the bed, on the left side. If you're in the guest room, he will cry at the door for about ten minutes and then give up and sleep in the hallway. If you want to let him in, let him in. For the first month after Michael left, Biscuit slept by the front door every night, waiting, and I didn't know how to explain to him that the thing he was waiting for was not going to happen in the way he wanted. Then one night he came upstairs and got on the bed on the left side, where he'd never been allowed, and I didn't stop him. So now that's where he goes.

We decided he'd stay here because the house has a yard and Michael's new apartment doesn't. That was the reason we said out loud. I think the real reason is that Michael knew I would need something to feed twice a day. He was always good at knowing what I needed, just not at being it. Those turn out to be different skills.

**10. Where I'll be.** I'm going to my sister's, on the coast. She says I need to "get out of the house," as if the house were the problem. The house is fine. The house is great, actually. The door sticks and the Tuesdays are a mystery, but it holds up.

My number is on the fridge, under the Wi-Fi password. Call if anything catches fire, including metaphorically.

**11. One last thing.** The dead plant on the landing was the first thing we bought together, the week we moved in. A little lemon tree. We had big ideas about lemonade. It never fruited, not once, and in March it just quietly stopped. I haven't been able to throw it out. I think I'm waiting until throwing it out means something smaller.

If, while I'm gone, you look at it and think, *that's just a dead plant in a pot*, then maybe you're right. Maybe when I get back, I'll see it that way too.

But leave it for now.

Help yourself to anything in the fridge. The good coffee is in the freezer. Biscuit will try to convince you otherwise, but he's already eaten.

Thank you. Really.

— D.

# Inventory

The lost property office at Harrow Street Terminal has no windows, and Odile likes it that way. Windows would mean weather, and weather would mean time passing, and the whole point of the office, as far as she can tell, is that time stops here. Things arrive and then they wait. Some are claimed. Most are not. After ninety days they're auctioned, donated, or thrown away, but for ninety days they exist in a kind of suspension, belonging to no one and still, technically, to someone.

She has worked the night shift for eleven years. The ledger is her invention. The railway has a computer system, and she uses it, but she also keeps a green clothbound book in which she writes a description of every object that comes through. Not the official description, which is always something like *UMBRELLA, BLACK, COLLAPSIBLE*, but the real one.

*Umbrella, black, one spoke bent inward like a broken finger. Handle worn pale where a thumb rested. Someone held this through a lot of rain.*

*Glove, left hand, child's, purple with a cartoon cat. The cat is missing an eye. The right glove is somewhere else, with the child, being useless.*

*Prosthetic leg, below-knee, carbon fiber. How? How do you forget this?*

She doesn't know why she does it. Her supervisor, when he found the ledger years ago, flipped through it with an expression she couldn't read and then handed it back and said, "Carry on." That was the most anyone had said to her about it until the night of the scarf.

---

He came in at 2:40 a.m., which was unusual. The last train arrives at 1:15, and after that the terminal belongs to cleaners and pigeons and the occasional person with nowhere else to be. He was old, maybe eighty, in a tweed coat too heavy for September. He stood at the counter and took a long time to speak, and when he did, his voice was careful, as if he'd rehearsed.

"I lost a scarf," he said. "Blue. Wool. It had a fringe on each end, and my wife knitted a small white *H* in one corner."

Odile pulled the keyboard toward her. "When did you lose it?"

"March," he said. "1971."

She looked at him. He looked back, entirely serious.

"Sir, we only keep items for ninety days."

"I know." He nodded. "I know that. I asked at the time. It hadn't been turned in. I asked every day for two weeks, and then I stopped asking." He placed both hands flat on the counter. "My wife died in June. Of this year, I mean. And I've been going through things. And I realized she never made me another one. She made scarves for everyone. The grandchildren, the neighbors, the postman one year. But never for me again. And I never asked why. And now I can't."

Odile said nothing. There's a skill to saying nothing, and she has it.

"I don't expect you to have it," he said. "I suppose I just wanted to ask one more time. So that I'd have asked."

---

Here's what Odile knows about the storeroom: there are, at any given moment, somewhere between forty and sixty scarves in it. Scarves are among the most frequently lost objects, after umbrellas, phones, and single gloves. People take them off on warm trains and forget them, because a scarf is the kind of thing you only remember when you're cold.

She told him to wait. She went into the back.

She was not planning to lie to him. She wants that to be clear, at least to herself. She went back there because it seemed cruel to simply type something and say *no*, and because walking to the storeroom gave her a minute to think about what she would say instead.

The scarves were in bin fourteen. She went through them. Red, grey, tartan, a sequined thing, a Manchester United one, black, black, black. And then, near the bottom, a blue one. Wool. Fringed.

No *H*. She checked both ends twice.

She stood there holding it for a long time.

---

When she came back out, he was looking at the ceiling, at nothing.

"I'm sorry," she said. "It isn't here."

He nodded. He'd known. He started to thank her, and she lifted the blue scarf onto the counter between them.

"But this one's been here eighty-nine days," she said. "It goes out tomorrow. Nobody's coming for it."

He looked down at it. He touched the fringe.

"It isn't mine," he said.

"No."

"There's no *H*."

"No." She paused. "I think maybe that's all right. I think maybe some things get lost so they can end up somewhere else."

She had no idea if that was true. It sounded like something printed on a mug. But he picked up the scarf and held it for a while, and then he wrapped it around his neck, over the heavy tweed coat, and it suited him. It genuinely did.

"She'd say it was the wrong blue," he said, and laughed, and then something happened in his face that she looked away from, out of respect.

He thanked her. He left. She never learned his name.

---

After he was gone, she opened the green ledger and turned to the entry, eighty-nine days old, for the blue scarf. She had written:

*Scarf, blue wool, fringed. Smells faintly of cedar and cigarettes. Someone wore this for years. Someone will miss it when it gets cold.*

She took out her pen and added a line underneath:

*Claimed.*

Then she sat for the rest of the shift in the windowless room, where time doesn't pass, and thought about everything in the storeroom waiting for the right person to come asking for the wrong thing.

# Readings

My father kept a record of the weather every day for forty-one years.

I found the notebooks after the funeral, in the bottom drawer of the desk in the garage, the drawer I had always assumed held tax returns. There were sixty-three of them, the cheap kind with marbled covers, each one labeled on the spine in black marker with a start date and an end date. The earliest began in March of the year I was born.

Every entry followed the same format. Date. High and low temperature, taken from the thermometer nailed to the fence post by the tomato beds. Precipitation, measured in a plastic rain gauge I remembered knocking over with a soccer ball when I was nine. Wind, described rather than measured: *calm*, *light from W*, *gusty*, *strong, took the lid off the bin*. Sky. And then, at the end of each line, a single short remark.

The remarks were what undid me.

Most of them were about the weather itself. *Fog burned off by ten.* *First frost, lost the basil.* *Hail, small, didn't last.* But scattered among them, sometimes weeks apart, sometimes months, were other things.

*K. walked today. Four steps to the couch.*

K. is me.

*K. home from school sick. Watched cartoons together. Rain all afternoon, which suited us.*

*M.'s mother passed. Clear and cold. M. sat outside a long time.*

M. was my mother.

I sat on the concrete floor of the garage with the notebooks spread around me in a half circle and read for four hours. I read the year my parents almost separated, which I had not known about, and which I understood only from a stretch of entries in which the remarks disappeared entirely for eleven weeks, just numbers, and then returned with: *M. and I talked. Mild. Wind dropped in the evening.* I read the day I left for college: *Overcast. K. gone. House very quiet. 71/54.* I read the week my mother was diagnosed, and the long gray months after, the remarks getting shorter and shorter until they were single words. *Hospital.* *Hospital.* *Home.* *Better.* *Worse.*

The day she died, he wrote the temperatures, the rainfall, the wind, the sky, and then nothing. The next day, the same. He didn't write another remark for almost two years. But he never missed a reading. Not one day. I checked.

I don't know what to make of a man who could not skip measuring the rain the morning after his wife died. For a while I thought it was coldness, or a kind of avoidance, the engineer's retreat into numbers when feelings got too big. That's how I'd always thought of him: reliable, reserved, a man who expressed love by checking the tire pressure on your car before a long drive.

But I don't think that anymore.

I think the readings were how he stayed. I think going out to the fence post every morning, in his robe, in the dark, in the snow, was a promise he kept to the world that he would keep paying attention to it, even when paying attention was the hardest thing he could do. I think the weather was the one thing that kept arriving no matter what, and he wanted to be there to meet it.

The last entry was eight days before he died. His handwriting had gotten shaky by then, the numbers leaning into each other. *Sunny, warm for October. 68/49. Leaves turning on the maple. K. called.*

I did call. I remember it. We talked for maybe ten minutes, mostly about whether he'd been taking his pills, and I was distracted, making dinner, and I said I'd call again on the weekend. I didn't. Something came up. I don't even remember what.

*K. called.* That's all. No complaint that it was short. No note that I'd promised to call back. Just the fact of it, set down beside the leaves and the temperature, as though my voice on the phone were one more condition of the day worth recording. As though it counted.

---

I brought the thermometer home. I had to pry it off the fence post with a screwdriver, and the post was so old that a strip of gray wood came away with it. The rain gauge was cracked, so I bought a new one, glass this time. I mounted them both on the railing of my apartment balcony, which faces east, over a parking lot and a row of sycamores and, beyond that, the freeway.

I bought a notebook with a marbled cover.

It has been four months now. I take the readings in the morning before work, with my coffee going cold on the railing beside me. I am not as disciplined as he was. I've missed eleven days. On those days I leave the line blank rather than guess, because guessing seems like a kind of lie, and I think he would have agreed.

Mostly I just write the numbers. But some days I add something at the end.

*Rain overnight, 0.4 in. Sycamores dripping.*

*Cold. Saw my breath for the first time this year.*

*Called Aunt Ruth. She told me the story about Dad and the goat again. Still funny.*

*Clear. 52/38. Missed him.*

I don't know who I'm writing them for. There is no one to find these notebooks in a drawer someday. Maybe that's fine. Maybe the point was never to be found.

This morning it was foggy, the kind of fog that erases the freeway and makes the parking lot feel like the edge of the ocean. I stood on the balcony and couldn't see the sycamores at all, only hear them, the soft tick of water falling from leaf to leaf. It was quiet in a way the city almost never is.

I wrote it down. The temperature, the sky, the wind, which was calm. And then, after a while, because it was true:

*Paying attention.*

# The Holds Shelf

The first email came eleven days after the funeral.

*Hello MARGARET. The following item is ready for pickup at Eastside Branch: The Hidden Life of Trees. Please collect by March 14.*

Walter read it on the kitchen laptop, the one Margaret had used for everything: recipes, bank statements, her endless correspondence with a cousin in Leeds about a family tree that had, by the end, grown more branches than any real tree could support. He had meant to shut the account down. He had meant to do a great many things.

He sat with the email for a long time. Then he got his coat.

The Eastside Branch was a low brick building with a leaking skylight that had been leaking, as far as Walter knew, since the Carter administration. He had not been inside in years. Margaret had been the reader. He had been the man who waited in the car with the engine running, listening to the ballgame, watching her come out with her canvas bag pulled heavy against her shoulder like she'd been shopping for stones.

The holds shelf was near the entrance. Books wrapped in paper slips, organized by the last four digits of a library card number. He found hers without trying. 4471. She had written it on so many forms that he knew it better than his own phone number.

He did not know how to check it out. A young woman at the desk showed him. She had a silver ring through her eyebrow and very kind hands.

"Is this your card?" she asked.

"My wife's."

"She can come pick them up too, you know. Anytime."

"I know," Walter said.

---

He read the book about trees. It was not the kind of thing he read. He had worked thirty-four years as an insurance adjuster, and his reading had mostly been reports: water damage, fire damage, the particular grammar of catastrophe as recorded by people trying to get paid for it. But he read about how trees send sugar to one another through their roots, how a stump can be kept alive for centuries by the forest around it, fed by neighbors who have no obvious reason to bother.

He underlined nothing, because it wasn't his book. But he folded down the corner of one page, then felt guilty, then unfolded it and pressed the crease flat with his thumb for a long time.

---

The second email came in April. *Hello MARGARET. A Field Guide to Getting Lost.*

The third came in May. A cookbook, Persian, full of pomegranates and saffron and dishes that required a patience he did not possess. He tried one anyway. The rice burned onto the bottom of the pot in a thick golden crust, and he was about to scrape it into the trash when he read, three pages later, that the crust was the point. That people fought over it. That it had a name: *tahdig.*

He ate it standing at the counter. It was the best thing he had cooked in his life.

---

By summer, the young woman at the desk knew him. Her name was Priya. She did not ask about Margaret again, and he suspected she had figured it out, the way he suspected everyone could see it on him, the way you can see water damage even after the drywall's been painted.

"You've got another one," she'd say, and slide it across.

A novel set in Iceland. A history of salt. A slim book of poems by a woman he'd never heard of, in which he found a line he read eleven times in a row: *what we love, we will lose, and what we lose, we will keep.* He did not know if it was true. He wanted it to be.

He started to understand something about the holds. Margaret had placed them over months, maybe years. Some of these books had waiting lists fifty people long. She had put her name down knowing it might be a year before her turn came. She had been making appointments with her future self, a woman who would still be here, still curious, still wanting to know about salt.

He was keeping those appointments for her. He did not know what else to call it.

---

In October, the email said: *Hello MARGARET. This is a courtesy notice. You have 1 item remaining on hold.*

One.

He logged into her account for the first time. It had never occurred to him that he could. The list of holds was a single line: *Birds of the Pacific Northwest.* Position in queue: 3.

He sat back in the kitchen chair. They had talked about it, a long time ago, before her diagnosis, before the word *metastatic* entered their household like a boarder who never paid rent. A trip to Oregon. The coast. She wanted to see puffins. He'd said *someday*, the way you say it when you think someday is a place you can drive to.

He could cancel the hold. He could let it lapse. He could let this be the end of it: the last thread cut, the account closed, the laptop wiped and given to his nephew.

Instead he clicked on the search bar and typed, slowly, with two fingers: *Oregon coast travel.*

Seventeen results. He placed a hold on four of them.

Then, under the account settings, he found the field labeled *Name*. He looked at it for a while. MARGARET. The cursor blinked beside it like a small, patient heartbeat.

He did not change it. Not yet. But he added, under *Additional cardholders*, a second name. His own.

---

The bird book came in December. Priya slid it across the desk with a slip that said 4471, and beneath it, handwritten in her small tidy print, a note she must have added herself:

*Hope she likes it.*

Walter put the book in the canvas bag, the heavy one, and carried it out to the car, and before he started the engine he opened it to a page at random. Tufted puffin. *Fratercula cirrhata.* Orange beak, white face, a pair of pale golden plumes swept back from the eyes like an old man's eyebrows, or a woman's hair in the wind off the water.

"Someday," he said aloud, and this time he meant a date.

# Hand Lettering

The sign above Dot's Diner had been fading for eleven years, and nobody had noticed until Dot died.

Then everyone noticed at once. Walking past on the way to the funeral home, people looked up and saw what the weather had done: the red of *DOT'S* gone the color of a healed scar, the apostrophe entirely lost, so that the sign now read DOTS DINER, like a place that served punctuation.

Walt Kessler noticed from his kitchen window across the street, where he had been noticing things for most of his seventy-nine years. He had painted that sign in 1974. He remembered the day because Dot had paid him partly in cash and partly in pie, and he had argued with her about the ratio, and she had won.

He called her son.

"I'd like to repaint the sign," he said. "Before Saturday."

There was a pause on the line, the kind of pause that is really a man deciding whether to explain something. "Mr. Kessler, we're selling the building. Somebody's turning it into a vape place, I think. Or a phone store."

"I know."

"So the sign's coming down in a month anyway."

"I know," Walt said. "I'd still like to repaint it."

---

His hands were the problem. They had been the problem for a while. A sign painter's hand is supposed to be a steady thing, a tool that happens to be attached to a person, and Walt's had started to feel more like a person attached to a tool: opinionated, easily tired, occasionally trembling in a way that had nothing to do with fear.

He went to the garage and found his kit. The brushes were still good. He had cared for them the way some men care for guns. The quill of a lettering brush, long and soft, has to be cleaned in oil and shaped with the fingers and stored flat, and he had done all that for decades after anyone was paying him to. He unrolled the canvas wrap and there they were, laid out like a set of surgical instruments for an operation nobody performed anymore.

The paint was harder. One-Shot enamel had changed its formula since he'd last bought any, and the man at the hardware store, a boy really, had to look it up on a tablet. Walt stood at the counter feeling like a visitor from a country that had been dissolved.

---

Thursday morning, he set up the ladder.

A few people stopped to watch, which he'd expected. What he hadn't expected was that they'd stay. A woman with a stroller. Two teenagers who were supposed to be somewhere else. The man from the bank. Nobody said much. They stood the way people stand around a campfire, a little hypnotized by something happening slowly.

He started with the D.

There's a secret to hand lettering that he had tried to explain to his apprentices back when he had them: you don't paint the letter. You paint the stroke, and the letter emerges. A capital D is two decisions, a vertical and a curve, and the curve is where most people fail, because they try to draw it. You can't draw a good curve. You have to commit to it, load the brush, turn your wrist, and pull, trusting that your body remembers what your mind has forgotten.

His hand shook at the top of the curve. He stopped, lowered the brush, breathed.

"You okay up there?" called the man from the bank.

"Fine," said Walt, which was a lie, and then he loaded the brush again and made the curve, and it was not perfect but it was good, and it was his.

---

By noon he had DOT on the board, and his shoulders felt like someone had filled them with wet sand.

The woman with the stroller had gone and come back with a coffee, which she handed up to him without asking how he took it. Black. She'd guessed right. He wondered if he looked like a man who took his coffee black, and decided he probably did.

"Did you know her?" she asked.

"Fifty years," he said.

"Were you—" She didn't finish.

"No," Walt said. "Nothing like that. She was married to Frank, and I was married to Ellen, and then they were gone, and we were two old people who ate breakfast in the same place. She was my friend."

He didn't say the rest of it: that for the past six years, since Ellen, Dot's had been the only place he went where anyone expected him. That she kept his mug, an ugly brown one, on a hook behind the counter. That when he'd missed two mornings in a row last winter with the flu, she had shown up at his door with soup and a lecture, and he had been so happy to be scolded that he'd nearly cried.

---

He saved the apostrophe for last.

It was the smallest mark on the sign and the one that mattered. Without it, DOTS was just a word. With it, it was a person, a possession, a claim. *This belongs to someone.* He loaded the tip of the brush with the barest amount of red, touched it to the board, and flicked it down into a small tapered comma floating in the air.

When he climbed down, his knees objecting at every rung, there were maybe fifteen people on the sidewalk. Somebody started clapping, and then felt embarrassed about it, and stopped, and then somebody else started, and they all joined in, and Walt stood there holding his brush like a man who'd been caught doing something private.

---

The sign came down five weeks later. The new owners had a backlit plastic thing, blue, that said something he didn't bother to read.

But he'd asked for the old board, and the son had said yes, and now it leaned against the wall of Walt's garage, DOT'S DINER in fresh red over fifty years of older red, and every morning he went out with his coffee, black, in an ugly brown mug, and said good morning to it.

It never answered. That was fine. He knew what she'd say.

# The Freezer

My mother died in March and left behind a chest freezer full of soup.

I found it the second week, after the funeral casseroles had stopped arriving and I'd run out of excuses not to go through the house. It sat in the garage under a quilted cover she'd sewn for it, as if it were a birdcage or a sleeping animal. I lifted the lid expecting frost-burned peas and a turkey from some forgotten Thanksgiving. Instead: rows. Dozens of quart containers, stacked with the precision of a woman who had once alphabetized her spice rack and then, years later, re-alphabetized it by frequency of use.

Each lid had a strip of masking tape. Each strip had her handwriting.

*Split pea — Jan 2019 — snowed in, radio said 14".*

*Chicken & rice — Oct 2020 — D. called, sounds better.*

*Minestrone — Aug 2017 — too many zucchini again, never again (lie).*

I stood there with the cold pouring out over my shins and read them the way you'd read someone's diary if you were sure they'd never find out. D. was my brother. He had not sounded better in October 2020, not really, but I suppose she'd needed to write it down to make it so.

---

I should explain that my mother was not a sentimental person. She threw away birthday cards after a week. She said photographs were for people who didn't trust their memories, and she trusted hers completely, right up until the last year, when it began quietly abandoning her like a tenant slipping out before the rent was due. She kept no journal. When I asked her once, as a teenager, whether she'd ever been in love before my father, she said, "Of course," and went back to shelling beans, and that was the entire oral history.

So the labels undid me a little. Here was the record she swore she didn't keep, written in the one language she'd always been fluent in.

*Lentil — Mar 2016 — first robin. Knee bad.*

*Beef barley — Dec 2018 — made for Ruth, she won't eat it, froze rest.*

*Tomato — Sept 2021 — can't remember if I already made this year. Making anyway.*

That one I held for a long time.

---

I didn't know what to do with them. Throwing them out felt like burning letters. Giving them away felt worse, like letting strangers read the letters first. The freezer hummed along beside me, running up an electric bill for a dead woman, keeping her afternoons at zero degrees.

In the end, I decided to eat them.

Not all at once. One a week, maybe two. I took the oldest first, because that seemed like the proper order, the order she'd have wanted: first in, first out. *Vegetable — Feb 2015 — power out 2 days, cooked on the woodstove, tastes like smoke.* It did taste like smoke. It also tasted a bit like freezer, which after eight years was fair. I ate it at her kitchen table with the window open, and outside a cardinal kept flinging itself at its own reflection in the car mirror, and I thought, *She would have written that down.* So I did. I started a notebook.

---

This went on through spring. I learned things.

I learned she'd had a friend named Ruth who was dying slowly across most of 2018 and whom I had never heard of. I learned that the zucchini situation was a recurring crisis of her own making, which she acknowledged annually and addressed never. I learned that she listened to the Saturday opera broadcast on the radio, because three different labels mentioned what was on: *Tosca, too loud. Carmen. Something German, turned it off.* I learned the date my father's brother died, which I had known, and the date she stopped setting two places at the table, which I hadn't.

*Potato leek — Apr 2019 — one bowl.*

That was all it said. One bowl.

I learned, as the dates crept forward, what her decline looked like from the inside. The handwriting got larger. The notes got shorter. Some containers had two labels, the second one contradicting the first. One was marked only *soup* and the date, and it turned out to be applesauce, and I laughed out loud alone in her kitchen and then cried for twenty minutes, which is how most things went that spring.

---

By June there were four left.

I'd started rationing. I'd go a week, then two, without opening the freezer, telling myself I was busy, which I wasn't. It's a strange thing to be afraid of reaching the end of someone's soup. But every quart I ate was a quart she would never make again, and some stupid animal part of me believed that as long as there was one in the freezer, she was still, in some small refrigerated way, in progress.

My brother came up for a weekend in July. I told him about the labels. I thought he might find it morbid, or funny, or both. Instead he went quiet and asked if there were any left, and I said three, and he asked if he could have one.

We chose together. *Chicken & rice — Oct 2020 — D. called, sounds better.*

He read the label and didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "I wasn't better."

"I know," I said.

"She knew too."

"I know."

We heated it up and ate it on the back steps, passing the pot between us like teenagers with a bottle, and it was very good soup. It had a lot of pepper in it. She always said pepper was for people who were sick or sad, and that the two were basically the same thing.

---

There are two left. I've decided to keep them.

Not forever. I'm not building a shrine to legumes. But the freezer is mine now, and I've started filling the space around them. Last week I made split pea, badly, because I don't have her hands or her patience or her unshakable belief that a ham hock solves most problems. I let it cool, ladled it into a quart container, pressed down the lid, and tore off a strip of masking tape.

I stood there with the pen for a long time, trying to think what was worth saying.

*Split pea — Aug 2023 — too thick. Cardinal still fighting the mirror. Missing you.*

Then I put it in the freezer, next to hers, where it will keep.

# Colors, Named

Marguerite names paint colors for a living, which people find either delightful or ridiculous, and she has stopped trying to predict which.

The job is this: a chemist in Ohio mixes a new shade, a spectrophotometer turns it into numbers, and the numbers arrive in her inbox with a small square of the color itself, which never looks the same on two screens. She stares at the square and gives it a name. The company pays her by the batch. Forty colors, forty names, due Friday.

Most of the names are not hers. They belong to the catalog, to the voice the catalog has had since before she arrived: *Harbor Mist. Morning Oat. Quiet Birch.* Nouns that sound like a house you could afford if you made different choices. Her first year, she tried to name a gray *Parking Garage at Dusk*, and her editor, a kind man named Philip, wrote back: *Accurate. Devastating. No.*

So she learned the voice. She got good at it. She can produce *Soft Heron* in her sleep.

---

The year her marriage ended, something went wrong with the job, or possibly right.

It started with a brown. Warm, a little red underneath, the color of wet clay or a strong tea left too long. She looked at the square and thought, without meaning to, of the coffee table David had refinished the first summer they lived together. He'd done it in the driveway because the apartment had no garage. He'd sanded it for three weekends, shirtless, cursing, and when he finally stained it, the stain went on exactly this color. She'd brought him a beer and he'd said, *Well, it's ours now,* as if labor were the thing that made furniture belong to you.

She typed *Driveway Table*. Then she deleted it and typed *Summer Walnut*, because that was the voice.

But the next square was a pale green, and it was the green of the hospital curtain the night his father died, the curtain they had both stared at rather than at each other. She typed *Curtain* and let it sit there, just that one word, and felt something in her chest loosen.

She didn't send those names. Not at first. She kept a second column in the spreadsheet, the true names, and then a first column, the ones Philip would get. *Hospital Curtain* became *Celadon Whisper*. *The Blue of the Pool at Your Sister's Wedding When We Were Still Pretending* became *Poolside*. She was, she realized, translating. She had always been translating. She just hadn't known what from.

---

Here's a thing people don't know about paint colors: the names matter enormously. Customers will not buy a color called *Mud*, but they will buy the identical pigment called *Riverbank*, and they'll feel good about it. They'll put it on their bedroom walls. They'll wake up inside it.

Marguerite used to find this cynical. Now she thinks it might be the most human thing she knows. We don't want the color. We want the story the color lets us tell about ourselves. Nobody lives in a gray box. They live in *Coastal Morning*, and it is always about to be a good day.

---

In March, David came by to pick up the last of his books. She'd boxed them herself, which felt either generous or hostile, and she still wasn't sure which. He stood in the living room and looked at the walls.

"You painted," he said.

She had. Two weekends, alone, windows open, cursing. The walls had been white when he lived there, a builder's white so flat it seemed to absorb sound. Now they were a pale, warm yellow, not quite butter, not quite straw. It was a color from the catalog. She'd named it herself, three years ago, back when the job was only a job.

"What's it called?" he asked.

He used to do this. When she first started, he'd read the catalog aloud in bed in a mock-seductive voice, *Mmm, Sandy Linen*, until she laughed so hard she cried. She had forgotten that. She had forgotten a great deal, on purpose, and here it was anyway, walking back in.

"*First Light*," she said.

He nodded slowly. He looked at the wall for a long moment and she could see him deciding whether to say something, the small tightening at the corner of his jaw that meant a sentence was being drafted and revised. Then he picked up the box.

"It's good," he said. "It suits the place."

After he left, she stood in the living room and looked at the wall herself. She thought about what she had actually been thinking, three years ago, when she named that yellow. It came back all at once: a Sunday, early, David asleep, the sun just reaching the bed and lighting up the side of his face, and her thinking with a kind of terror, *I am going to lose this someday. Everyone loses this.* She had named the color for that moment, the good version, the version without the terror. *First Light.* She'd sent it to Philip and he'd written back, *Perfect.*

---

Friday, she opened the new batch. Forty squares. She went through them slowly, and for each one she wrote the true name first, the one only she would see, and then the other one, the one that would go out into the world and onto people's walls.

The last square was a deep, clean blue, the blue of a sky about an hour after sunset, when the streetlights have come on but the day hasn't fully given up. She looked at it for a long time.

In the true column she wrote: *After.*

In the other column, after some thought, she wrote the same thing.

She sent it to Philip. He wrote back within the hour.

*Unusual,* he said. *But I think people will want to live there.*

# Notes for the Next Owners

The realtor told me not to leave this. She said buyers want a blank slate, that a letter from the previous owner feels like a ghost standing in the kitchen. I'm leaving it anyway, in the drawer under the phone jack that no longer connects to anything. If you've found it, you're the kind of person who opens drawers, and I trust you already.

First, practical matters.

The third stair from the bottom creaks. Not the second, not the fourth. The third. You can step over it if you're trying to come home quietly, which my son learned at sixteen and which I pretended not to know for two years. The fourth stair also creaks, but only in winter, when the wood contracts. It sounds like someone saying "hm" in disagreement. You'll get used to it.

The kitchen window sticks in August. Don't force it. Take a butter knife and run it along the left side of the frame, where the paint has built up over forty years of people like me thinking one more coat would solve things. It won't. But the butter knife will.

There's a fig tree in the backyard that doesn't produce figs. I want to be honest about this because the listing described it as "a mature fig tree," which is technically true in the way that describing me as "a mature woman" is technically true. It has not given fruit since 1994. My husband believed it was waiting for something. He talked to it every spring, not in a whimsical way but in a stern, managerial way, like a foreman addressing a union holdout. It never gave in. I admired it for that, eventually.

You may cut it down. I would understand. But I'd ask you to give it one more spring. Not for sentimental reasons. I just have a feeling.

The basement floods when it rains more than two inches in a day. There's a sump pump. It works. It makes a sound like a large animal clearing its throat, and the first time you hear it at three in the morning you will sit bolt upright and wonder who is in your house. Nobody is in your house. It's just the pump, doing its job, being dramatic about it.

Now the less practical matters.

On the inside of the pantry doorframe there are pencil marks. Two children, measured every birthday from ages two to fourteen, and then, in different handwriting, two grandchildren measured on the occasional Thanksgiving. The lines are labeled with initials and dates. The highest one says *R, 14, finally taller than Mom*, and there's a small arrow pointing to a line slightly lower that says *Mom*, and next to that my own note: *temporarily*.

I know you'll paint over them. The realtor said I should do it myself before the showings, and I stood there with the brush for a while and then went and had a sandwich instead. I'm not asking you to preserve them. That would be unfair, like leaving you a pet you didn't agree to feed. I only want you to know what's under the paint, so that when you're standing in the pantry some night looking for the peanut butter, you might feel, without knowing why, that you are standing somewhere people grew.

And then, if you have children, I hope you'll start your own lines. There's room. The wood is good oak and takes a pencil well.

The bedroom at the end of the hall gets the best light in the house, between seven and eight in the morning. It comes in low and gold and lands on the wall opposite the window, and for about fifteen minutes the whole room looks like the inside of a peach. We used it as a guest room for years, which is a crime I can't undo. Sleep there. Or read there. Or just go in with your coffee and stand around. It's the only thing in the house I'd call magic, and it costs nothing, and it happens every clear day whether anyone is watching or not.

I've been thinking about that a lot lately, how much of what's beautiful just goes on without an audience. Every morning for twenty-some years that light filled that room and mostly nobody saw it. It didn't seem to mind.

A few more things.

The neighbor to the east, Dolores, will bring you a loaf of zucchini bread within your first week. It will be dense enough to use as a doorstop. Eat it anyway and tell her it's wonderful. She is eighty-one and has buried two husbands and a daughter, and the bread is how she says she's still here. You'll figure out what to say back.

The neighbor to the west has a dog named Pickles who barks at the mail carrier with a hatred that seems personal. There's no history there. Pickles just has convictions.

The hall closet has a light switch on the outside that turns on a light inside, but also, for reasons no electrician has ever explained, the porch light. You cannot have one without the other. My husband called it "the house's opinion" and stopped trying to fix it. I'd recommend the same approach to most of the house's opinions.

I'm moving somewhere smaller, closer to my daughter, with an elevator and a woman at the front desk who already knows my name. It's the right decision. I made it myself and I'd make it again. But I walked through every room this morning and touched the doorframes the way you'd touch someone's shoulder on the way past, and I want you to know that the house knows how to be lived in. It's good at it. It's had practice.

Be happy here. Be ordinary here, which is harder and better. Fight in the kitchen and make up in the kitchen, since that's where it always happens anyway. Let the stairs creak.

And watch the fig tree this spring.

I have a feeling.

— M.
