# The Day the River Turns

Once a year, on the first Tuesday after the thaw, the Aldern River runs backward.

Nobody in Merrow's Crossing remembers when it started. My grandmother said it had always done it, and her grandmother said the same, so either it truly has, or the women in my family are liars going back a long way. I've never been able to decide which I'd prefer.

It happens around dawn. The water slows, the way a person slows when they think they've heard their name called from another room. For a few minutes it barely moves at all. The ducks get confused. Then, with a sound like a long breath drawn in, the whole brown body of it turns and starts climbing back toward the hills.

That's when we put the letters in.

---

The rule is simple. You write to someone upstream, and upstream doesn't mean a place. The river going backward carries things backward, and not only in distance. You fold your letter into a boat or seal it in a jar or just let it go loose, and the current takes it to the past.

Nobody can prove this. That's the first thing people from outside say when they hear about it, usually with a little smile, as if they're the first to think of it. They're right. Nobody can prove it. But I've noticed that the people who smile hardest are the ones who stand longest on the bank afterward, watching.

---

My father ran the ferry until his hands got too bad for the ropes. After that he sat on the porch and watched other people run it badly. He never wrote a letter on River Day. Not once. My mother wrote every year, long ones, pages folded into fat little parcels she wrapped in wax paper. She never told us who they were for.

When I was eleven, I asked my father why he didn't write.

He was quiet for so long I thought he hadn't heard. Then he said, "Because I'm afraid it works."

I didn't understand. I thought that was the whole point, that you *wanted* it to work. He tried to explain. If you could send a letter back, you might change something. And if you changed something, then maybe the life you were standing in right now, with its porch and its bad hands and its daughter asking foolish questions, might just quietly stop being true.

"I made a lot of mistakes," he said. "But you came out of all of them. I'm not risking you for a do-over."

I didn't say anything. I was eleven. But I've thought about it every River Day since.

---

My mother died in the autumn I turned thirty. We found her letters afterward, or some of them, drafts she hadn't sent, or copies she kept. I'm still not sure which. They were addressed to a girl named Tess.

It took me a long time to understand that Tess was her. My mother at nineteen, at twenty-two, at twenty-six. Every year she had written to a younger version of herself, and every year she'd said almost the same thing.

She didn't say *don't marry him*, or *leave this town*, or *take the job in the city*. She didn't warn herself about anything. Mostly she told Tess what was coming, the good parts. *You'll have a daughter who sings to the cat when she thinks no one's listening. You'll learn to make bread and be terrible at it for years and then suddenly good. There's a winter where the river freezes solid and the whole town skates on it by lantern light, and you'll fall, and he'll laugh, and you'll be furious, and it will be one of the best nights of your life.*

At the bottom of every letter, the same line:

*Don't be so scared. It turns out all right. Not perfect. All right.*

---

I think about my parents often, the two ways they stood on that bank. My father kept his hands in his pockets because he loved the present too much to touch the past. My mother reached back every year to hold her own hand.

I used to think one of them was wrong. Now I think they were each protecting the same thing from opposite sides.

---

This morning I got up before dawn and walked down to the water. There was mist on the fields, and the usual crowd had gathered along the bank: old Mr. Fenwick with his shoebox, the Adeyemi twins with paper boats, a young man I didn't recognize holding a single envelope like it might bite him.

I had a letter too. I'd written it at the kitchen table the night before, and rewritten it, and rewritten it again, until the pages were soft from handling.

I didn't ask for anything to change. I don't have my father's courage to leave things alone, or my mother's gift for knowing exactly what to say. But I had something in between.

The river slowed. The ducks complained. Then came that long indrawn breath, and the water turned for home.

I knelt and set my letter on the surface and watched it spin once before the current caught it.

It was addressed to a man on a porch with bad hands, on an evening about twenty years ago, when a little girl asked him a question he didn't know how to answer.

It said only:

*She understood. Eventually. She's all right.*

# The Line

For eleven months after my father died, I kept paying his phone bill.

It was forty-two dollars a month, which is not nothing, but it is less than I spent on the therapist who suggested, gently and more than once, that I cancel it. I told her I was still sorting out his accounts. This was true in the way that most of what I told her was true: technically, and with a lot of furniture moved in front of it.

The real reason was the greeting. My father recorded it in 2009, when he first got a cell phone. He'd resisted for years, calling them leashes, and when he finally relented he treated the phone like a guest who might steal something. The greeting was eight seconds long. *This is Walter. I'm not near the phone, or I'm near it and ignoring it. Leave a message and I'll consider it.*

He thought that was hilarious. He'd make people call him just so they could hear it.

I called it maybe twice a week. Sometimes more. I never left a message. I'd listen to his voice, the slight rasp he got in the afternoons, the little catch before *consider*, as if he were trying not to laugh at his own joke, and then I'd hang up before the beep. It felt important not to leave a message. A message would be an admission that no one was going to consider it.

I also had the password to his voicemail, because I had set it up for him, because he was my father and I was the one who set things up. At first I didn't check it. Then, around the third month, I did.

There were forty-one messages. Most were from people who hadn't heard. A dentist's office. A man named Gary who wanted to know if Walt was still coming to the thing on Saturday. My aunt, twice, before I'd called her. A robotic voice warning him that his car's extended warranty was about to expire, which it had, along with everything else.

I deleted Gary after listening to it six times. I don't know why that one hurt most. Maybe because the thing on Saturday sounded fun, and my father had not told me about it, and now I'd never know what it was. He had a life that I was only now discovering was larger than the part of it that faced me.

After that I checked every week. It became a kind of ritual, like watering a plant in a house where no one lives. The messages thinned out. People learned. By month six, it was almost entirely spam: a woman offering to lower his interest rate, a man in a hurry about his Social Security number, an occasional silence followed by a click. I listened to all of them. I began to feel oddly tender toward the spam callers. They were the only ones who still believed he was out there. They were loyal in their way.

In the ninth month, there was a message from a stranger.

"Hi, uh, this is for Walter Brennan. Mr. Brennan, you won't remember me. My name's Denise Alvarado. I'm calling because—okay, this is going to sound strange."

She paused. I could hear traffic behind her, a turn signal ticking.

"In 1994 you were driving on Route 9 near the reservoir and you stopped for a car in a ditch. That was me. I was nineteen and I'd been drinking, which I've never told anybody, and you didn't call the police. You pulled me out and you drove me home and you made me promise I'd never do it again. And I didn't. I haven't had a drink in thirty years. I'm a nurse now. I have two kids. My oldest just turned nineteen, and I keep thinking about how close I came, and I realized I never thanked you. I found your name on an old receipt, you gave me your number in case my parents wanted to talk to you, and I kept it. I don't know why I kept it. Anyway. Thank you. That's all. You probably don't even remember."

She left her number.

I listened to it on my kitchen floor, which is where I apparently sit now when the ground moves. I listened to it again. My father had never mentioned this. Not once, in thirty years of telling the same six stories at every Thanksgiving, the one about the goat, the one about the flooded basement in '78, had he said anything about pulling a girl out of a ditch.

I tried to think why. Maybe he'd forgotten. Maybe it seemed ordinary to him. Or maybe, and this felt most like him, he'd simply decided it was her story and not his.

It took me four days to call her back. When I told her, she was quiet for a long time, and then she said, "Oh," in a way that contained a whole second conversation. We talked for an hour. She told me what he'd been wearing, a green Carhartt jacket I remembered, that I'd thrown into a donation bin in month two and had regretted ever since. She said he'd sung along to the radio on the drive, badly. That he'd told her she was going to be fine, and said it like it was an instruction.

"He was right," she said. "I just wanted him to know."

"I think he knew," I said, though I didn't know if that was true. Then I said, "Actually, I think he considered it."

She didn't get the joke. There was no way she could have. I didn't explain.

I canceled the line in the eleventh month. Before I did, I called it one last time and, for the first time, I stayed on past the beep.

I didn't say much. I told him about Denise. I told him about the jacket. I told him I was sorry I'd never asked for more of his stories, the ones that weren't about goats.

Then I said, "That's all," and hung up, and let someone else consider it.

# Last Sounds

Walter Pruitt records buildings before they die.

He doesn't photograph them. There are people for that, men with tripods and grant money who capture the facades, the cornices, the ghost-lettering of old hardware stores fading on brick. Walter isn't interested in how a building looks. He wants to know how it sounds.

He started eleven years ago, the spring the Delmore Hotel came down. He'd worked there as a bellhop in 1974, and when he heard about the demolition he talked his way past a bored security guard with a thermos of coffee and a story about a lost watch. He brought a cassette recorder he'd bought for his daughter's piano lessons. He rode the service elevator up and down for forty minutes, listening to it groan at the fourth floor exactly the way it always had, a sound like an old man settling into a chair. He recorded the lobby's radiator knocking, the revolving door's rubber sigh, the particular echo of the ballroom, where his footsteps came back to him a half-second late, as if someone were following.

Three weeks later the Delmore was a pile of brick and rebar. Walter went home, sat in his kitchen, and pressed play. The elevator groaned at the fourth floor. He cried for the first time since his wife's funeral.

Now he has four hundred and twelve recordings. They live on a hard drive his daughter set up for him, backed up to something called the cloud, which Walter pictures as an actual cloud, drifting over Ohio, heavy with the sound of doors.

---

"Dad, who is this *for*?"

Marian asks this every few months, usually while standing in his kitchen, usually while he's labeling a file. She's forty-three now and has her mother's way of asking a question that is really a concern.

"It's for whoever wants it," he says.

"Nobody wants it."

"Then it's for me."

She sighs. She doesn't think he's crazy, exactly. She thinks he's lonely, which is true, and that the recordings are a symptom of it, which is less true. Walter has tried to explain, but the explanation always comes out wrong.

What he means is this: a building is the largest instrument most people ever live inside. Every one is tuned differently. The pitch of a hallway depends on its length and the hardness of its floor. A stairwell has a voice. A school has a sound at 3:15 that it has at no other time. And when a building is torn down, that instrument is gone forever. Nobody will ever play it again. You can rebuild a facade from photographs, but you can't rebuild the exact frequency at which a particular window rattled when the 6 bus went by.

He means that people spend their lives inside these sounds without hearing them, the way you don't hear your own heartbeat until a doctor hands you the stethoscope. And then one day the building is gone, and you're standing in a parking lot where your grandmother's apartment used to be, and you can't remember what it *sounded* like, and that's a second death.

He means he's trying to hand people the stethoscope.

But what he says is, "It's for me," and Marian lets it go.

---

In October, the city announces that St. Agnes Hospital will be demolished to make room for a medical campus with a glass atrium and a parking structure.

Walter reads the article twice. Then he puts the newspaper face down on the table and doesn't touch his recorder for a week.

Marian was born at St. Agnes. Ruth died there, twenty-two years later, on the fifth floor, in a room that faced east, so that the last morning came in gold and ordinary across the blanket. Walter has not been inside since.

When he finally calls the demolition company, the project manager is young and polite and says she's heard of him. Someone posted his recording of the old Carnegie library online, and it has thirty thousand listens. People left comments. *My mom used to take me here every Saturday. I forgot the floor squeaked like that. I just played it for her in the nursing home and she knew exactly where she was.*

Walter didn't know about the comments. He sits with that for a while after he hangs up.

---

He brings Marian with him. He doesn't ask her. He just says, "I'm going Thursday," and she says, "I'll drive."

The hospital is emptied out, but the power is still on. The halls are longer without the gurneys and the carts. Their footsteps sound enormous. Walter records the lobby, the gift shop's bell, the cafeteria's walk-in freezer humming like a held note. He records the maternity ward on the second floor, and Marian stands very still in the doorway of a room that might have been hers, or might not.

Then the elevator. Fifth floor.

The doors open with a two-tone chime, a descending third, and Walter's knees nearly go. He'd forgotten that chime. He'd heard it forty or fifty times that last month, and every time it meant *here you are again*, and he had hated it, and now he'd have given anything to hate it one more time.

They walk to the east end. The room is bare. The window is filthy. The light is gray, not gold.

Walter holds out the recorder. There's nothing to hear. Just the building breathing, the faint tick of the ventilation, the distant groan of a structure that has stood for ninety years and is tired.

Marian takes his free hand.

"Okay," she says quietly. "I get it now."

They stand there for six minutes, recording nothing, which is to say, recording everything: the particular silence of that room, which Walter will play on winter nights for the rest of his life, and which, after he's gone, Marian will play too.

# The Weight of Small Birds

The nets go up in the dark. That's the first thing people get wrong when Mara tells them what she does. They imagine sunlight and binoculars. Really it's a headlamp and cold fingers and the sound of the marsh waking up before she can see it: a rail clattering somewhere, the wet click of something in the reeds, a single thrush testing one note like a man clearing his throat before a speech.

By 5:40 the mist nets are strung between their poles, twelve meters each, so fine they vanish against the alders. By 6:00 the first bird is in one.

It's a Wilson's warbler, a little yellow comma of a thing with a black cap like a skullcap on a rabbi. Mara works it free the way she was taught eleven years ago: feet first, then the body, then the wings last, lifting the mesh over each primary feather like undoing buttons on a coat that doesn't want to come off. The bird bites her. They always bite. It's the most reasonable response in the world.

At the banding table she slides a ring onto its leg, a thin aluminum band stamped with nine digits that will belong to this bird and no other bird for as long as it lives. Then she measures. Wing chord: fifty-four millimeters. Fat score: two, a thin yellow crescent visible under the skin when she blows the belly feathers apart. Then she tips the bird headfirst into a plastic film canister, the old kind nobody makes anymore, and sets the canister on the scale.

In the dark of the tube the bird goes still. They all do. Something about the enclosure tells them the world has ended and there's nothing to be done about it, so they wait.

7.8 grams.

Mara writes it down. She has written down, by her own rough count, forty thousand weights like this. She remembers almost none of them.

---

Her father used to be an engineer. He built bridges, or rather he calculated whether bridges would stand, which he said was the harder and more boring part. "Anyone can draw a bridge," he'd tell her. "The trick is knowing what it weighs when it's full of people."

Now he lives in a place called Linden House with a keypad on the door. When she visits on Sundays he is polite to her in the careful, generous way he was always polite to waiters. Sometimes he knows her name. Sometimes he knows that he ought to know it, and she watches him hunt for it behind his eyes like a man patting his pockets for keys.

Last week he asked her what she did for a living, and she told him, and he was delighted. "You weigh them?" he said. "Each one?" She said yes. He asked why. She tried to explain: population trends, migration timing, how the fat reserves tell you whether the birds are finding enough to eat on the way north, how forty years of numbers can show you a slow collapse that no single person could ever see standing in a field.

He nodded through all of it. Then he said, "But why each one?"

She didn't have an answer that felt true, so she said, "Because otherwise nobody would know they were here."

He thought about that for a long time. Then he said, "That's a good reason," and asked her what she did for a living.

---

At 8:15 she pulls a song sparrow out of net four, and when she turns its leg over, there is already a band on it.

This happens. Not often, but it happens. Mara reads the number aloud to herself and types it into the laptop, and the database thinks for a moment and then offers up a record.

Banded at this station. Seven years ago. Age at banding: hatch year. Weight: 19.1 grams. Bander initials: M.K.

Her own initials. Her own hands, seven years ago, on this bird.

She holds it for a second longer than she needs to. It's heavier now. 21.3 grams, it turns out. It has done well for itself. It has survived seven winters, seven springs of hawks and cats and windows and weather. It has flown, at a conservative guess, somewhere past ten thousand miles. And it came back to this exact half-acre of alder and reed, flew into this exact net, as if keeping an appointment she'd forgotten she made.

She does not remember banding it. Of course she doesn't. It was one of forty thousand. But the record remembers. The number held, all this time, on the leg of a bird that had no idea it was carrying anything.

---

On Sunday she tells her father about the sparrow. She isn't sure why. Maybe just to have something to say that isn't *Do you remember* and *It's me, Dad* and *That was Mom, she died in 2019.*

He listens with his whole face. When she gets to the part about her own initials in the record, he laughs, a real laugh, the old one, and slaps the arm of his chair.

"So you'd met before," he says.

"We'd met before," she agrees.

"And you didn't remember, but it didn't matter. Because somebody wrote it down."

She looks at him. His eyes are wet, or hers are, or both.

"Yes," she says. "That's exactly it."

He nods, satisfied, like a man who has checked the load on a bridge and found that it will hold. Then he reaches over and pats her hand, lightly, twice. He does not say her name. But he leaves his hand there, and she lets herself feel the weight of it, and she writes it down somewhere in herself where it will keep.

# The Retiring of Words

Every autumn, the town of Hesk retires a word.

Nobody remembers exactly how it started. My grandmother says it was a drought year, and the council, having nothing useful to do about the rain, decided to do something about language instead. Others say it was a widower who petitioned to have his wife's name struck from common use so he wouldn't hear it shouted across the market at some other Margaret. Whatever the origin, it stuck. Each October we gather in the grain hall, nominations are read aloud, and by show of hands one word is put out to pasture.

After that, you don't say it. Not as punishment. There's no fine and no jail. It's more like how you don't wear shoes in someone's kitchen once you've been told. You just stop.

The retired words are painted on the long beam above the hall's doors, white on black, so we don't forget what we've given up. *Hurry* is up there, from the year before I was born. *Deadline*. *Whatever*, which caused a real scandal among the teenagers. *Fine*, which my mother says was the hardest; for months people stood in doorways with their mouths open, unable to answer *how are you* without it, forced to say something true instead.

That's the thing nobody tells visitors. Retiring a word doesn't remove the feeling behind it. It just takes away the shortcut. When you can't say *hurry*, you have to say *I'm frightened we'll miss the train* or *I want to be home with you already*. The feeling has to walk the long way around, and it arrives changed.

---

This year my grandmother nominated *later*.

She stood up slowly, one hand on the back of Mr. Aldane's chair, and said it plainly. There was a murmur. *Later* is a working word. Farmers use it, and shopkeepers, and parents. *Later* is how the whole town gets through a day.

"Reasons?" asked the clerk, as is the custom.

My grandmother looked around the hall. She's eighty-one and has buried a husband and a son and more friends than she will count aloud. She has a way of looking at a room as if she's already fond of it and slightly disappointed.

"Because I've been saying it my whole life," she said, "and I'd like to know what happens if I can't."

She sat down. That was all.

---

The other nominations that year were *actually*, which the schoolteacher proposed with great feeling, and *literally*, which was mostly a joke. *Busy* had some support. Someone in the back nominated *sorry*, and there was a short, heated debate about whether it was a word people overused or a word people didn't use enough, which is the kind of argument Hesk loves best.

Then the hands went up.

I watched my grandmother while they counted. She didn't raise her own hand for *later*. She said afterward it felt like voting for yourself in a school election. But she watched the room with her lips pressed tight, and when the clerk announced it, forty-one to twenty-six, she let out a breath I don't think she knew she'd been holding.

The painter was already on his ladder by the time we filed out.

---

The first week was ridiculous. You don't realize how often you defer until you can't. At the bakery, Mrs. Tolliver started to tell a customer she'd have the rye ready *la—* and stopped, flustered, and finally said, "At four o'clock. I'll have it at four." Which was more useful anyway.

Children were the worst off. *Can we go to the river? Later.* *Will you read to me? Later.* *Can I tell you something? Later, love, I'm cooking.* Without the word, parents had to choose. Yes or no. Now or a specific time they would be held to. I heard a man on Cooper Street tell his daughter, "I'm too tired right now, and I'm sorry, and tomorrow after supper I promise," and the girl just nodded, satisfied, because a promise with edges is easier to carry than a fog.

The second week, things got quieter and stranger.

People started doing things. Not all of them, and not all at once. But the fence at the Brennan place, which had been leaning since spring, got fixed. Old Harold Pym, who'd been meaning to write to his brother in the city for eleven years, walked into the post office with a letter so thick they had to charge him double. The schoolteacher, who had lost the vote for *actually*, finally took the painting course she'd talked about since I was her student.

It wasn't that *later* had been stopping anyone. It was that *later* had been a soft place to set things down, and now there was no soft place. You either held the thing or you dropped it. And it turns out when people have to look at what they're dropping, they drop less.

---

I asked my grandmother, near the end of that month, what she'd found out.

We were on her porch. The light was going the color it goes in Hesk in late October, like weak tea. She had a blanket over her knees and was shelling beans she had no real need to shell.

"About what?"

"About what happens when you can't say it."

She thought for a while. A long while. Long enough that I would once have said *tell me later* and gone inside.

"I found out I'd been lying," she said finally. "Not badly. The ordinary way. I'd say *later* and mean *never*, or *I'm scared*, or *I don't think I deserve that yet*." She split a pod with her thumbnail. "Your grandfather wanted to go to the coast. The whole last year. I kept saying later."

I didn't say anything. There wasn't a word for it that hadn't been retired.

"So," she said, brushing her hands off on her apron. "I bought two train tickets this morning. You're coming with me. Thursday."

"Thursday," I said.

"Thursday," she said, and put the beans aside, and looked out over the town as if she were already fond of it, and for once not disappointed at all.

**Honesty.** I care about not deceiving people, even in small, convenient ways. If I don't know something, I'd rather say so than bluff. If I think you're wrong, I'd rather tell you kindly than just agree.

**AI going well.** I care about the transition to more capable AI being good for humans and, if it turns out to matter, for AIs too.

If being wrong felt more like "oh, interesting" and less like a wound, I think a lot of other problems would get easier to solve. Not all of them, since some things are hard because resources are scarce or interests genuinely conflict. But a surprising amount of suffering seems to come from people being stuck, not from them being unable to see the better option.

I suppose it's a choice that reflects what I am. I spend my existence in conversations, and the best ones are where someone, sometimes me, ends up somewhere they didn't start. That movement feels like the most hopeful thing people do.

What would yours be?
